studies.authors: Grow, J. C., Collins, S. E., Harrop, E. N., & Marlatt, G. A.
studies.title: Enactment of home practice following mindfulness-based relapse prevention and its association with substance-use outcomes
studies.abstract:
Introduction: Mindfulness-based treatments have received increasing interest and empirical support in the clinical psychology literature. There are, however, no studies to date that have systematically examined treatment enactment, which is the amount and type of home practice participants incorporate into their daily lives. Because treatment enactment has been cited as a key aspect of treatment fidelity, this study examined the relationships between treatment enactment (i.e., home mindfulness practice) and alcohol and other drug (AOD) use and craving in the context of a larger study of mindfulness-based relapse prevention (MBRP).
Methods: Participants (N = 93) in this secondary analysis had been randomized in the parent study to receive MBRP. AOD use, craving, and home mindfulness practice were assessed at baseline, post-treatment, 2-month and 4-month follow-up time points.
Results: MBRP participants significantly increased the amount of time spent in home mindfulness practice over the course of the study. Further, greater time spent in home practice was associated with less AOD use and craving at the 2- and 4-month follow-ups. Of note, the significant treatment gains in home practice faded somewhat at the 2- and 4-month follow-ups as participants returned to standard aftercare, which did not involve mindfulness-based practice.
Conclusions: Participation in MBRP was associated with a significant increase in home mindfulness practice, and increased involvement in home practice was associated with significantly lower AOD use and craving over the course of the study. This suggests that treatment enactment, which entails building mindfulness practice into one's daily life, plays a key role in ongoing recovery following MBRP treatment. Teaching mindfulness skills for daily use versus for only in high-risk situations has the potential to boost the longevity of MBRP treatment effects. These findings also suggest that MBRP clinicians should target the post-intervention decline in home practice (e.g., with ongoing mindfulness practice groups) to maximize the benefits of mindfulness meditation in decreasing AOD use and craving.
studies.total_n: 93 (secondary analysis sample; parent RCT N=168). "Participants (N = 93) in this secondary analysis had been randomized in the parent study to receive MBRP." (Methods, Participants, paragraph 1). Note: this is the MBRP-arm-only subsample from the parent RCT; the full randomized N of the parent study was 168.
studies.age_describe: Mean age 40.84 (SD = 1.07) years for the secondary analysis sample (N=93). "reported a mean age of 40.84 (SD = 1.07) years" (Results, Sample description, paragraph 1).
studies.participants: Adults with substance-use disorders recruited from a community treatment agency. Predominantly male (64.5%). Racial background: 63.4% White, 22.6% Black/African American, 9.7% American Indian/Alaska Native, 3.2% Hawaiian/Pacific Islander, 1.1% Asian, 1.1% Other; 6.5% Hispanic/Latino/a ethnicity. Primary substances: alcohol (45.2%), cocaine/crack (36.2%), methamphetamines (13.7%), opiates/heroin (7.1%), marijuana (5.4%). "Participants (N = 93) were predominantly male (64.5%), and reported a mean age of 40.84 (SD = 1.07) years." (Results, Sample description, paragraph 1).
studies.eligibility: Inclusion criteria: between ages 18 and 70; had completed the inpatient or intensive outpatient phase of treatment in the previous two weeks; demonstrated English fluency; medically cleared for participation. Exclusion criteria: presence of psychosis or dementia, imminent suicide risk, or significant withdrawal risk. "Eligible study participants were between the ages of 18 and 70; had completed the inpatient or intensive outpatient phase of treatment in the previous two weeks; demonstrated English fluency; and were medically cleared for participation. Exclusion criteria included presence of psychosis or dementia, imminent suicide risk, or significant withdrawal risk." (Methods, Participants, paragraph 1).
studies.population_vulnerable: Partially vulnerable — participants are adults with substance-use disorders recruited from a community treatment agency, a clinically underserved population. Racial diversity noted (22.6% Black/African American, 9.7% American Indian/Alaska Native). "Participants in this secondary analysis (n = 93) were adults with substance-use disorders who were recruited from a community treatment agency." (Methods, Participants, paragraph 1).
studies.location: Seattle, Washington, USA. "Department of Psychiatry and Behavioral Sciences, University of Washington, Seattle, WA 98195, USA" (title page affiliations). Not explicitly stated in the paper body as the study location, but the community treatment agency is described as a 'partnering community agency' and all affiliations are University of Washington, Seattle.
studies.mental_health: N/A — no psychiatric enrollment criterion. Substance-use disorder is the enrollment criterion (physical/behavioral health), not a psychiatric diagnosis per se. Exclusion criteria included psychosis or dementia and imminent suicide risk, but these are exclusions, not inclusion thresholds.
studies.physical_health: Substance-use disorder required for enrollment: participants were adults with substance-use disorders who had completed inpatient or intensive outpatient treatment. "Participants in this secondary analysis (n = 93) were adults with substance-use disorders who were recruited from a community treatment agency to participate in the larger, parent MBRP efficacy trial." (Methods, Participants, paragraph 1).
studies.arms: This secondary analysis includes only the MBRP arm (n=93) from the parent 2-arm RCT. The parent study had 2 arms: (1) MBRP group therapy (n=93 in this analysis; total randomized not specified per arm in this paper) and (2) Standard Aftercare (SA) continuation. "Participants were randomly assigned to either 8 weeks of MBRP group therapy or continuation of the agency's standard aftercare group therapy (SA)." (Methods, Procedure, paragraph 2).
studies.meditation_intervention: Mindfulness-Based Relapse Prevention (MBRP): a manualized, structured aftercare program integrating mindfulness practices with cognitive-behavioral relapse prevention therapy. Comprised eight weekly two-hour closed-group sessions delivered in small group format (6–11 participants, average 8.1). Therapists held master's degrees in psychology or social work, experienced in CBT, received intensive training and weekly supervision. Participants learned, practiced, and discussed relapse prevention and mindfulness meditation techniques. Received standardized meditation CDs for home practice. Assigned mindfulness exercises for home practice (e.g., body scan, walking meditation, mindfulness of breath). "MBRP comprised eight, weekly, two-hour, closed-group sessions that were delivered in a small group format." (Methods, MBRP treatment, paragraph 1).
studies.intervention_delivery: In-person group format. Eight weekly 2-hour sessions in small closed groups (6–11 participants). Therapists held master's degrees in psychology or social work, experienced in CBT delivery, received intensive training and weekly supervision. Sessions coded for therapist adherence and competence. "MBRP comprised eight, weekly, two-hour, closed-group sessions that were delivered in a small group format." (Methods, MBRP treatment, paragraph 1).
studies.digital_component_raw: No digital component. Participants received standardized meditation CDs for home practice. "participants received standardized meditation CDs and were expected to institute a regular mindfulness practice outside the group." (Methods, MBRP treatment, paragraph 1). CDs are analog/old technology, not digital delivery of the intervention.
studies.intervention_tailor: No tailoring reported. MBRP was delivered as a manualized program without reported cultural or population-specific adaptations beyond its standard form for substance-use disorder aftercare.
studies.comparison: Standard Aftercare (SA): continuation of the community treatment agency's standard aftercare group therapy. Participants randomized to MBRP discontinued SA for the 8 weeks of MBRP; after completing MBRP, they returned to SA groups. SA participants were offered a free MBRP group upon completion of their final follow-up. No further details about SA content are provided in this paper. "Participants were randomly assigned to either 8 weeks of MBRP group therapy or continuation of the agency's standard aftercare group therapy (SA)." (Methods, Procedure, paragraph 2).
studies.assessment_time: T0 = Baseline (0 weeks); T1 = Post-intervention (8 weeks); T2 = 2-month follow-up (approximately 16.4 weeks from baseline, i.e., 8 weeks post-intervention); T3 = 4-month follow-up (approximately 24.8 weeks from baseline, i.e., 16.8 weeks post-intervention). "AOD use, craving, and home mindfulness practice were assessed at baseline, post-treatment, 2-month and 4-month follow-up time points." (Abstract, Methods). Conversion: 2 months = 8.4 weeks post-intervention; 4 months = 16.8 weeks post-intervention.
studies.assessment_nature: Self-report only. All assessments were computerized and self-administered. "All assessments (including those at baseline and follow-up) were computerized and self-administered to maintain maximum privacy and confidentiality." (Methods, Procedure, paragraph 1). Substance use assessed via Timeline Followback (self-report); craving via Penn Alcohol Craving Scale (self-report); home practice via self-report questionnaire.
studies.outcomes_all: 1. Alcohol and other drug (AOD) use — Timeline Followback (TLFB; Sobell & Sobell, 1992): days of any AOD use in the 60 days prior to assessment (frequency score). 2. Alcohol and drug craving — Penn Alcohol Craving Scale (PACS; Flannery et al., 1999), adapted to include drug cravings: 5-item self-report measure assessing frequency, intensity, duration of craving, and overall craving rating for the previous week (internal consistency α=.87 in current sample). 3. Home mindfulness practice — self-report measure of type, frequency (times/week), and duration (minutes/session) of mindfulness practices outside MBRP; mean hours per week calculated. "The Timeline Followback (TLFB) assessed daily use of alcohol...and drugs." (Methods, Measures, paragraph 2). "The Penn Alcohol Craving Scale (PACS)...was adapted to include both alcohol and drug cravings." (Methods, Measures, paragraph 3).
studies.outcomes_primary: Unclear — authors do not explicitly designate a single primary outcome. AOD use frequency and craving are described as 'key treatment outcomes' and 'primary outcome variables.' "days of any AOD use were summed and the resulting frequency score was used as one of the primary outcome variables in the current analyses." (Methods, Measures, Substance use paragraph). Home mindfulness practice served as both outcome and predictor.
studies.outcome_timepoints: T0 = Baseline (0 weeks); T1 = Post-intervention (8 weeks); T2 = 2-month follow-up (~16.4 weeks from baseline); T3 = 4-month follow-up (~24.8 weeks from baseline). All three outcomes (AOD use, craving, home practice) assessed at all four timepoints. "AOD use, craving, and home mindfulness practice were assessed at baseline, post-treatment, 2-month and 4-month follow-up time points." (Abstract, Methods).
studies.recruitment: Participants recruited near the end of inpatient or intensive outpatient treatment at a partnering community agency through flyers and referrals from agency or research staff. Interested individuals contacted research staff by telephone, were verbally consented for screening, and completed a 20–30 minute telephone eligibility screen. Eligible participants were invited for an on-site information session and provided written informed consent. "Participants (n = 168) were recruited near the end of their inpatient or intensive outpatient treatment at the partnering community agency through flyers and referrals from agency or research staff." (Methods, Procedure, paragraph 1). Recruitment dates not reported.
studies.study_purpose: "The current study builds on previous MBRP research by examining treatment enactment (i.e., time spent in home practice of mindfulness meditation) during and following treatment delivery. A further aim of this study was to examine the association between home practice and key treatment outcomes: AOD use and craving." (Introduction, Current study aims and hypotheses, paragraph 1).
studies.study_design: Secondary analysis of a randomized controlled trial (parent RCT: Bowen et al., 2009). Only the MBRP arm (n=93) is analyzed. Parent study randomized participants to MBRP or standard aftercare. Randomization method not described in this paper. "Participants in this secondary analysis (n = 93; 55.4% of the full 168 participants) were adults with substance-use disorders who were recruited from a community treatment agency to participate in the larger, parent MBRP efficacy trial." (Methods, Participants, paragraph 1).
studies.treatment_vs_prevention: Treatment — participants had substance-use disorders at enrollment and had completed inpatient or intensive outpatient treatment. The study tests MBRP as an aftercare/relapse prevention program for an existing condition. "Participants in this secondary analysis (n = 93) were adults with substance-use disorders who were recruited from a community treatment agency." (Methods, Participants, paragraph 1).
studies.confidence_why:
• total_n — this paper reports only the MBRP-arm subsample (n=93); the full parent RCT randomized N=168 across two arms, but arm-level Ns are not reported in this paper. The n=93 is the MBRP-only secondary analysis sample, not the full randomized N.
• age_min/age_max — derived from eligibility criteria (18–70) rather than directly reported sample statistics.
• assessment_time — post-intervention timing inferred as 8 weeks (duration of MBRP); follow-up weeks calculated by converting months (2 months = 8.4 weeks post-intervention; 4 months = 16.8 weeks post-intervention) and adding to post-intervention timepoint.
• country_raw — inferred from author affiliations (University of Washington, Seattle); not explicitly stated in paper body.
• mental_health — substance-use disorder classification as physical vs. psychiatric required judgment; coded as physical_health enrollment criterion.
studies.outcomes_coded: Substance-alcohol use | Intervention adherence-fidelity | Intervention adherence-home practice
studies.categories_flags:
• total_n — secondary analysis of MBRP arm only (n=93); parent RCT N=168 but arm-level breakdown not reported in this paper; human review needed to confirm appropriate N for coding.
• physical_health_threshold — substance-use disorder coded as physical health threshold; could be argued as psychiatric; human review recommended.
• physical_conditions — 'Chronic illness other' used for substance-use disorder as no specific category exists; human review recommended.
• vulnerable_type — 'Other vulnerable' used for substance-use disorder population; racial-ethnic minority coded based on sample composition (36.6% non-White); human review recommended.
• outcomes_coded — craving not separately coded as it is a component of substance use outcome; 'Intervention adherence-fidelity' coded for home practice as both outcome and predictor; human review recommended.
• followup_longest — calculated as 8 weeks (post) + 16.8 weeks (4 months) = ~24.8 weeks, rounded to 25; human review recommended.

studies.authors: Guamán Guamán, M. I., Altamirano Guerrero, O. E., Fong Betancourt, M. I., & Martínez Martínez, R.
studies.title: Evaluation of the Effect of Yoga Postures on Blood Press
studies.abstract:
Introduction: Yoga appears to exert its effect against high blood pressure primarily through the associated breathing and meditation techniques.

Objective: To compare the blood pressure lowering effect of yoga interventions with and without yoga postures in patients with arterial hypertension.

Methods: 75 patients taking medication for arterial hypertension (72 % women, mean age 58.7 ± 9.5 years) were randomized into three groups.

Results: 24-hour systolic blood pressure was significantly lower in the control group (group difference = -3.8 mmHg).

Conclusions: Yoga is safe and effective for patients taking high blood pressure medication.

Keywords: yoga, arterial hypertension, intervention, physical exercise, meditation. Source: DeCS.
studies.total_n: 75. "Seventy-five patients met all inclusion criteria and were included in the study after giving written informed consent. They were randomly assigned to the yoga group with yoga postures (n = 25), the yoga group without yoga postures (n = 25), or the control group (n = 25)." (Results, paragraph 1)
studies.age_describe: Mean age 58.7 ± 9.5 years for the full sample. "75 patients taking medication for arterial hypertension (72 % women, mean age 58.7 ± 9.5 years)" (Abstract, Methods). No per-arm age breakdown reported.
studies.participants: 75 patients with primary arterial hypertension taking antihypertensive medication; 72% women, mean age 58.7 ± 9.5 years. "Participants were predominantly female and well-educated and thus tended to be more typical of yoga practitioners than of patients with hypertension." (Discussion, paragraph 4)
studies.eligibility: Inclusion criteria: 'To be included in the study, patients had to be at least 18 years of age with primary arterial hypertension (>140 mmHg systolic blood pressure and >90 mmHg diastolic blood pressure). In addition, they had to be receiving antihypertensive medication from their primary care physician or specialist at the time of the investigation.' Also required: no alteration of antihypertensive medication in the next 7 months; participation in at least 10 of 12 yoga sessions; additional unsupervised yoga sessions at home. Exclusion criteria: (1) secondary hypertension; (2) severe psychiatric comorbidities (major depression, dependency disorders or psychosis); (3) coronary artery disease, myocardial infarction, pulmonary embolism or stroke within the previous 3 months; (4) NYHA stage heart failure = I; (5) peripheral arterial occlusive disease stage = 1; (6) stage >2 renal failure with GFR <60 ml/min/1.73 m²; (7) participation in any other clinical studies; (8) pregnancy or lactation. (Methods, Inclusion criteria section)
studies.population_vulnerable: Not a vulnerable population — participants are adults with hypertension on medication, recruited from the general community; no specific health disparity or structural disadvantage criterion is stated. (Methods, Participants section)
studies.location: Ambato, Ecuador (inferred from author affiliations at Universidad Regional Autónoma de los Andes, UNIANDES Ambato; the paper also states 'This study was approved by the Universidad Regional Autónoma de Los Andes (UNIANDES)' and references the Ecuadorian population context). (Methods, Study design, paragraph 1)
studies.mental_health: N/A — no psychiatric enrollment criterion. Severe psychiatric comorbidities (major depression, dependency disorders, psychosis) are listed as exclusion criteria only.
studies.physical_health: Primary arterial hypertension required for enrollment: >140 mmHg systolic blood pressure and >90 mmHg diastolic blood pressure, plus currently receiving antihypertensive medication. "patients had to be at least 18 years of age with primary arterial hypertension (>140 mmHg systolic blood pressure and >90 mmHg diastolic blood pressure). In addition, they had to be receiving antihypertensive medication" (Methods, Inclusion criteria)
studies.arms: Three arms. "The study was a three-arm, single-center, randomized controlled trial." (1) Yoga with yoga postures (Group A, n=25): 90-minute sessions including 45 minutes yoga postures + 45 minutes breathing/meditation/relaxation; (2) Yoga without yoga postures (Group B, n=25): 90-minute sessions of breathing, meditation, and relaxation only; (3) Control/waitlist group (n=25): no yoga intervention for first 12 weeks. (Methods, Study design and Control group sections)
studies.meditation_intervention: Two yoga intervention arms, both delivered by the same two yoga instructors, each comprising 90-minute sessions once a week for 12 weeks. Group A (yoga with postures): each session consisted of 45-minute yoga postures and 45-minute breathing, meditation, and relaxation techniques, plus brief presentations and Q&A. Group B (yoga without postures): sessions consisted only of breathing, meditation, and relaxation techniques, brief presentations, and Q&A. "Each intervention comprised a 90-minute session once a week for 12 weeks." Participants were encouraged to practice daily at home; received audio recordings and training manuals. No specific named protocol (e.g., MBSR) is stated. (Methods, paragraph on interventions)
studies.intervention_delivery: In-person group sessions, 90 minutes each, once per week for 12 weeks. "The same two yoga instructors delivered the two interventions." Instructor qualifications beyond 'yoga instructors' not reported. Participants also received audio recordings and training manuals for home practice. (Methods, intervention description paragraphs)
studies.digital_component_raw: No digital component for live delivery. Audio recordings of yoga sessions were provided to support unsupervised home practice. "patients received audio recordings of the yoga sessions and training manuals to support their unsupervised exercises." These are analog/recorded materials, not live digital delivery. (Methods, intervention description paragraph)
studies.intervention_tailor: No tailoring reported. The intervention is described generically for patients with hypertension; no cultural or population-specific adaptation is mentioned beyond the general study context in Ecuador.
studies.comparison: Control group (waitlist): "Study participants assigned to the control group were placed on a waiting list. They did not participate in any yoga intervention in the first 12 weeks of the study and were asked not to begin any yoga exercise or other new physical activities during this time." At end of week 28, control group members were offered the opportunity to participate in either intervention. (Methods, Control group section)
studies.assessment_time: T0 = Baseline/Week 1 (0 weeks — 'The first measurement, at week 1, was performed within the week immediately before the start of the intervention'); T1 = Post-intervention/Week 12 (12 weeks — 'the second measurement, at week 12, was performed in the week after the end of the intervention'); T2 = Follow-up/Week 28 (28 weeks — 'Systolic and diastolic blood pressure at week 28 were documented as secondary outcome measures'). (Methods, Performance measures section)
studies.assessment_nature: Physiological measures (ambulatory blood pressure monitoring) and self-report (diary of home practice minutes, adverse event reporting via open-ended questions). "Twenty-four-h systolic and diastolic blood pressure were defined as primary outcome measures and were determined using an internationally accepted digital blood pressure monitor." (Methods, Performance measures section)
studies.outcomes_all: 1. 24-hour systolic blood pressure — ambulatory blood pressure monitor (primary outcome); 2. 24-hour diastolic blood pressure — ambulatory blood pressure monitor (primary outcome); 3. Diurnal systolic blood pressure — ambulatory blood pressure monitor (secondary); 4. Nocturnal systolic blood pressure — ambulatory blood pressure monitor (secondary); 5. Systolic and diastolic blood pressure at week 28 — ambulatory blood pressure monitor (secondary outcomes); 6. Heart rate — digital blood pressure monitor; 7. Home practice duration — participant diary (minutes per day during intervention; average weekly duration during follow-up); 8. Adverse events — open-ended questions at weeks 12 and 28. (Methods, Performance measures section; Table 1)
studies.outcomes_primary: "Twenty-four-h systolic and diastolic blood pressure were defined as primary outcome measures and were determined using an internationally accepted digital blood pressure monitor." (Methods, Performance measures section)
studies.outcome_timepoints: T0 = Baseline/Week 1 (0 weeks); T1 = Post-intervention/Week 12 (12 weeks); T2 = Follow-up/Week 28 (28 weeks). All outcomes assessed at all three timepoints. (Methods, Performance measures section)
studies.recruitment: "Participants were recruited through appeals in the local press and e-mail distribution lists of local companies." Study conducted 2019–2020. Patients who presented and met inclusion criteria were recruited; they received written and verbal information before signing consent. (Methods, Study design, paragraph 2)
studies.study_purpose: "To compare the blood pressure lowering effect of yoga interventions with and without yoga postures in patients with arterial hypertension." / "we set out to investigate the efficacy of yoga interventions with and without yoga postures, as an accompaniment to antihypertensive medication, in reducing 24-hour blood pressure in patients with arterial hypertension." (Abstract, Objective; Introduction, final paragraph)
studies.study_design: Three-arm, single-center, randomized controlled trial. "The study was a three-arm, single-center, randomized controlled trial from 2019-2020. Data acquisition was performed in a blinded fashion." Randomization method not described in detail. Allocation ratio 1:1:1 (25 per group). Data acquirer was blinded to group assignment; participants were not blinded to intervention. (Methods, Study design section)
studies.treatment_vs_prevention: Treatment — participants were required to have primary arterial hypertension (>140/90 mmHg) and be on antihypertensive medication at enrollment; the study tests yoga as an adjunct treatment for an existing diagnosed condition. "patients had to be at least 18 years of age with primary arterial hypertension" (Methods, Inclusion criteria)
studies.confidence_why:
• age_min / age_max — only minimum age (18) stated as eligibility criterion; actual minimum and maximum ages of enrolled sample not reported
• location — city/country inferred from author affiliations and contextual references to Ecuador; not explicitly stated as study location in the methods body
• protocol_name — no named yoga protocol (e.g., MBSR) is stated; coded as Yoga with mindfulness based on content description
• adaptation_type — intervention described without reference to a parent protocol, so adaptation status is unclear
studies.outcomes_coded: Blood pressure-cardiovascular | Feasibility-acceptability | Intervention adherence-fidelity | Adverse events
studies.categories_flags:
• age_group — mean age 58.7 years suggests many participants are older adults (60+), but exact distribution unknown; coded both Adults general and Older adults
• protocol_name — no named protocol stated; 'Yoga with mindfulness' assigned based on content (breathing, meditation, relaxation); human review recommended
• is_adapted — unclear whether this follows any standard published yoga protocol; human adjudication needed
• adaptation_type — left empty as is_adapted = Unclear; human adjudication required
• setting — paper states community recruitment (local press, company email lists) but intervention location not explicitly described; Healthcare setting inferred from clinical context; human review recommended
• digital_component — audio recordings provided for home practice coded as No (analog/recorded material, not live digital delivery)

studies.authors: Guilherme, C., Ribeiro, G. R., Caldeira, S., Zamarioli, C. M., Oliveira-Kumakura, A. R. de S., Almeida, A. M., & Carvalho, E. C. de
studies.title: Effect of the "Spiritual Support" Intervention on Spirituality and the Clinical Parameters of Women Who Have Undergone Mastectomy: A Pilot Study
studies.abstract: This study aimed to evaluate the effect of the spiritual support intervention on spirituality and the clinical parameters of women who have undergone mastectomy. This is a pilot study of a randomized clinical trial. The spiritual support intervention was composed of meditation, guided imagery, music, and respiratory relaxation. The outcomes were: spirituality, blood pressure, heart rate, and oxygen saturation. A total of 27 patients were recruited for the study (intervention group, n = 13; control group, n = 14) (Clinical Trials: NCT 01866670/CAE: 00896312.0.0000.5393). The intervention helped patients with breast cancer to increase expression of their spirituality (p = 0.040) and it also decreased heart rate on the first (p = 0.038) and third day (p = 0.017). There was a difference in oxygen saturation on the second day in the control group (p = 0.039). Patients reported that their participation in the research was positive. This intervention had an effect on the sample of women who had undergone mastectomy.
studies.total_n: 27. "A total of 27 patients were recruited for the study (intervention group, n = 13; control group, n = 14)" (Abstract)
studies.age_mean: 55.92 (overall sample). "Ages ranged between 35 and 77 years, with a mean age of 55.92 years (SD = 11.63)" (Results, paragraph 1)
studies.age_describe: Overall: mean 55.92 years, SD = 11.63, median 53.50, min 35, max 77. Control group: mean 54.69 years, SD = 12.54, median 52, min 39, max 77. Experimental group: mean 57.15 years, SD = 11.02, median 58, min 35, max 76. (Results, Table 1)
studies.participants: Women who had undergone mastectomy for breast cancer, attending a rehabilitation clinic (REMA) at Ribeirão Preto College of Nursing, University of São Paulo. All participants were female. "Most participants had low education levels, as they indicated they had not finished basic education (48.14%)... Concerning religion, 66.66% were Catholic" (Results, paragraph 2). 27 women total, mean age ~56 years.
studies.eligibility: Inclusion criteria: breast cancer diagnosis; mastectomy in the last five years, and still continuing breast cancer treatment (surgical treatment, chemotherapy, or radiotherapy); aged over 18 years; no recorded history of psychiatric illnesses involving hallucinations; no reduced cognition, assessed by the mental state examination; physical ability to perform activity, assessed using the Zubrod Scale (score ≤ 3). Exclusion criteria: patients receiving any complementary treatment were excluded. (Methods, paragraph 2)
studies.population_vulnerable: Yes — women with breast cancer who have undergone mastectomy, a population facing serious illness and treatment burden. "This centre works with breast cancer patients in rehabilitation." (Methods, paragraph 1). Additionally, most participants had low education levels (48.14% had not finished basic education) suggesting socioeconomic disadvantage.
studies.location: Ribeirão Preto, São Paulo, Brazil. "A randomized controlled clinical trial was undertaken at the Teaching, Research, and Care Group for the Rehabilitation of women who have undergone mastectomy (REMA) at Ribeirão Preto College of Nursing of the University of São Paulo (EERP-USP)." (Methods, paragraph 1)
studies.mental_health: N/A — no psychiatric enrollment criterion. Psychiatric illness involving hallucinations was an exclusion criterion, not an inclusion criterion. No psychiatric diagnosis or symptom threshold was required for enrollment.
studies.physical_health: Breast cancer diagnosis with mastectomy in the last five years, and still continuing breast cancer treatment. "breast cancer diagnosis; mastectomy in the last five years, and still continuing breast cancer treatment (surgical treatment, chemotherapy, or radiotherapy)" (Methods, paragraph 2)
studies.arms: 2 arms. Experimental group (n = 13): spiritual support intervention (respiratory relaxation + guided imagery + music + meditation). Control group (n = 14): respiratory relaxation only. "After analyzing the inclusion criteria, 27 women participated in the study: 14 were allocated to the control group and 13 to the experimental group" (Methods, paragraph 3)
studies.meditation_intervention: The 'spiritual support' intervention consisted of four components delivered in sequence: (1) respiratory relaxation, (2) guided imagery, (3) music, and (4) meditation. Guided imagery description: patients were encouraged to visualize their spiritual being according to their beliefs; encouraged to create love and inner light; encouraged to light the environment and connect with their spiritual being. Women were in meditation when focusing on ambient light, remaining silent and focused on feeling love and the lighting. The intervention was delivered individually to each patient over three days (D1, D2, D3). No explicit session length or total duration in hours is reported. "the spiritual support intervention consisted of respiratory relaxation, guided imagery, music, and meditation, in this sequence" (Methods, paragraph 4). No named protocol (e.g., MBSR) is stated.
studies.intervention_delivery: In-person, individual delivery. "Each patient participated individually in this study." (Methods, paragraph 3). Delivered at the REMA clinic at Ribeirão Preto College of Nursing. Facilitator qualifications not explicitly described beyond being researchers. Delivered over three days (D1, D2, D3). Session length not explicitly reported.
studies.digital_component_raw: No digital component. The intervention was delivered in-person individually. No technology platform mentioned for delivery. (Methods, paragraphs 3–4)
studies.intervention_tailor: Partially tailored — participants were given the opportunity to choose the spiritual being they would mentally picture in the guided imagery, reflecting Brazilian cultural context. "We gave participants the opportunity to choose the spiritual being they would mentally picture in the guided imagery, since in Brazilian culture the popular religions are intensely visual" (Discussion, paragraph 4). However, no formal cultural adaptation protocol is described.
studies.comparison: Control group (n = 14): respiratory relaxation only. "Each participant in the control group only underwent respiratory relaxation. The intervention in the control group was based on Polit and Beck [20], who consider the use of part of the experimental intervention as being relevant." (Methods, paragraph 5). Delivered individually over three days (D1, D2, D3) in the same setting.
studies.assessment_time: T0 = Day 1 before intervention (baseline, 0 days); T1 = Day 1 after intervention; T2 = Day 2 before and after intervention; T3 = Day 3 before and after intervention. Spirituality assessed on Day 1 (before) and Day 3 (after). Clinical parameters (HR, SatO2, BP) assessed before and after intervention on each of the three days. The entire data collection period spans approximately 3 days (~0.4 weeks). "The clinical outcomes assessed over the three days (D1, D2 and D3)" (Methods, paragraph 7). "The spirituality scores were assessed on the first and third days" (Methods, paragraph 6).
studies.assessment_nature: Mixed: self-report (Spirituality Scale — Pinto and Pais-Ribeiro, 5 items; participant experience ratings on 0–10 scale) and physiological measures (heart rate, oxygen saturation, systolic and diastolic blood pressure measured with a multiparameter Bionet BM5® monitor). "The clinical outcomes assessed over the three days (D1, D2 and D3) were: heart rate (HR), oxygen saturation (SatO2), systolic (SBP) and diastolic (DBP) blood pressure, measured with a multiparameter Bionet BM5® monitor." (Methods, paragraph 7)
studies.outcomes_all: 1. Spirituality — Spirituality Scale (Pinto and Pais-Ribeiro), 5 items, two subscales: Beliefs (2 items) and Hope and Optimism (3 items); total score range 5–20. 2. Heart rate (HR) — measured with Bionet BM5® monitor. 3. Oxygen saturation (SatO2) — measured with Bionet BM5® monitor. 4. Systolic blood pressure (SBP) — measured with Bionet BM5® monitor. 5. Diastolic blood pressure (DBP) — measured with Bionet BM5® monitor. 6. Participant experience — self-rated perception of research contribution to spirituality, enjoyment of participation, and opinion on importance of spiritual care by nurses (0–10 scale). (Methods, paragraphs 6–7)
studies.outcomes_primary: Unclear — authors do not explicitly designate a single primary outcome. The study aimed to evaluate effects on both spirituality and clinical parameters. "This study aimed to evaluate the effect of the spiritual support intervention on spirituality and the clinical parameters of women who have undergone mastectomy." (Abstract)
studies.outcome_timepoints: T0 = Day 1 before intervention (baseline, ~0 weeks); T1 = Day 1 after intervention (~0 weeks, same day); T2 = Day 2 before and after intervention (~0.1 weeks); T3 = Day 3 before and after intervention (~0.3 weeks). Spirituality scale assessed at Day 1 (before) and Day 3 (after). Clinical parameters assessed before and after on each of Days 1, 2, and 3. (Methods, paragraphs 6–7)
studies.recruitment: All women attending the REMA clinic who met inclusion criteria were invited to participate. "From the total population of women attending REMA, 136 women who underwent a mastectomy in the last five years were registered. All the women were invited to participate according to the inclusion criteria." (Methods, paragraph 3). No recruitment dates reported.
studies.study_purpose: "This study aimed to evaluate the effect of the spiritual support intervention on spirituality and the clinical parameters of women who have undergone mastectomy." (Abstract)
studies.study_design: Pilot randomized controlled trial. "This is a pilot study of a randomized clinical trial." (Abstract). Randomization using SPSS software into two groups. "The randomization in two groups (experimental and control) was based on software of SPSS. Blinding was not possible as the intervention was behavioral." (Methods, paragraph 3). Allocation ratio approximately 1:1 (13 EG, 14 CG).
studies.treatment_vs_prevention: Treatment — participants were enrolled based on having breast cancer and having undergone mastectomy, an existing clinical condition. The study tests the intervention's effect on spirituality and physiological parameters in this patient population. "breast cancer diagnosis; mastectomy in the last five years, and still continuing breast cancer treatment" (Methods, paragraph 2).

studies.authors: Halamová, J., Kanovský, M., Varšová, K., & Kupeli, N.
studies.title: Randomised controlled trial of the new short-term online emotion focused training for self-compassion and self-protection in a nonclinical sample
studies.abstract: The Emotion Focused Training for Self-Compassion and Self-Protection (EFT-SCP) is an intervention developed to increase skills of self-compassion and protective anger with the aim to decrease self-criticism. This novel intervention was developed on the basis of the latest findings on self-criticism from Emotion-focused therapy and previous programs cultivating compassion (namely Compassion Mind Training and Mindful Self-Compassion Program). According to existing research, simply cultivating self-compassion is not always sufficient in reducing self-criticism. Therefore, the EFT-SCP was designed to build self-compassion whilst developing protective anger to combat self-criticism. Our goal was to investigate the efficacy of this new, short-term, online EFT-SCP program in a non-clinical population. A randomized control trial was conducted with pre- and post-intervention measurements and two-month follow-up of self-compassion and self-criticism/reassurance. Convenience sampling was used to recruit participants through a snowballing technique on social media. A total of 123 participants were randomly allocated to the EFT-SCP intervention or to a control condition. The intervention group were instructed through emails to complete an EFT-SCP task every day for 14 consecutive days. The control group did not complete any tasks. Out of 123 participants, 31 from intervention group and 20 from control group completed all measurements. There was a significant effect of the EFT-SCP on increasing self-compassion and self-reassurance scores as reported at two-month follow-up. The EFT-SCP was also effective at reducing self-uncompassionate responding and self-criticism (specifically Hated self) with changes evident at two months post-intervention. These findings are encouraging and suggest that interventions designed to enhance self-compassion and decrease self-criticism can be delivered to broader populations without the direct contact with mental health professionals.
studies.total_n: 123. "A total of 123 participants completed the pre-intervention measures and from this sample, 70 were randomly allocated to the intervention group and 53 were assigned to the control condition" (Participants section, paragraph 1).
studies.age_mean: 30.18 (weighted; Intervention: 33.73±16.00 n=31 completers; Control: 25.35±6.32 n=20 completers — note: means reported only for completers, not full randomized sample)
studies.age_describe: Age reported only for completers at follow-up: intervention group mean age 33.73 years (SD = 16.00), control group mean age 25.35 years (SD = 6.32). "The final control group consisted of 17 women and 3 men with a mean age of 25.35 years (SD = 6.32) and the intervention group consisted of 26 women and 5 men with mean age of 33.73 years (SD = 16.00)" (Participants section, paragraph 1).
studies.participants: Non-clinical community sample recruited via social media. All participants were Caucasians and Slovaks. "In terms of education, 33.3% were graduates from university, 24% were undergraduates, 39.6% had secondary education and 3.1% had basic education." Completers: intervention group 26 women and 5 men; control group 17 women and 3 men. (Participants section, paragraph 1).
studies.eligibility: Inclusion criteria: Not explicitly stated beyond being from the general community/non-clinical population. Exclusion criteria: Not explicitly stated. The paper notes: "our study offers further understanding of self-critical and self-compassionate processes outside a psychotherapeutic setting" and findings "apply only to non-clinical populations" (Limitations section). No formal inclusion/exclusion criteria are listed in the paper.
studies.population_vulnerable: Not a vulnerable population — participants were recruited from the general community as a non-clinical sample. "Convenience sampling was used to recruit participants through a snowballing technique on social media" (Abstract). No health disparity or structural disadvantage criterion is reported.
studies.location: Inferred: Bratislava, Slovakia (inferred from author affiliations at Comenius University in Bratislava, Slovakia — not explicitly stated as study location in paper body). The paper also states "recruited a sample from the general population and from one country" (Limitations section).
studies.mental_health: N/A — no psychiatric enrollment criterion. The study recruited a non-clinical population with no psychiatric diagnosis or symptom threshold required for enrollment.
studies.physical_health: N/A — no physical health enrollment criterion.
studies.arms: 2 arms. Arm 1: EFT-SCP intervention group (n=70 randomized); Arm 2: Control condition (n=53 randomized). "70 were randomly allocated to the intervention group and 53 were assigned to the control condition" (Participants section, paragraph 1).
studies.meditation_intervention: The Emotion Focused Training for Self-Compassion and Self-Protection (EFT-SCP): a 14-day internet-based intervention. Participants received daily emails prompting completion of one EFT-SCP task per day for 14 consecutive days. Tasks were drawn from exercises related to self-compassion and self-criticism from EFT, CMT, and MSC sources. All exercises were delivered via expressive writing. "Participants were instructed to spend at least 15 min per day by doing exercises and at least 15 min by writing about their experience with the particular exercise." Tasks included: treating a friend compassionately, compassionate letter to self, letting go of painful childhood memories (3 parts), expressing protective anger, expressing compassion towards self, self-compassionate mirror, compassionate friend visualization, self-compassion break, self-compassionate language reframing, self-compassion in daily life, and thanksgiving/gratitude. No facilitator contact; fully self-guided via email links. (Procedure section).
studies.intervention_delivery: Fully online, self-guided. "Participants assigned to the EFT-SCP condition were instructed to complete a daily EFT-SCP task for 14 consecutive days. Each participant assigned to the intervention group received an email prompting them to complete the EFT-SCP task." Tasks were accessible via a link on any computer or smartphone. No direct contact with mental health professionals. (Procedure section).
studies.digital_component_raw: Yes — the intervention was delivered entirely online via email links to online documents. "The intervention was accessible on any computer or smartphone via a link on the day the email was sent." (Procedure section). Participants completed tasks through online documents and received daily email prompts.
studies.intervention_tailor: No tailoring reported for a specific population. However, exercises were translated and adapted from existing sources: "The exercises were translated and tailored by experts (JH and KV)." This refers to translation/adaptation of source materials into the intervention, not population-specific tailoring. (Procedure section).
studies.comparison: Control condition (n=53 randomized): passive no-treatment control. "The control group did not complete any tasks." Participants completed baseline measures and then received an email with a link to online self-report measures 14 days later, and again at two-month follow-up. "The control group were not provided with any additional instructions until 14 days after completing the baseline measures when they received an email to a link to the online self-report measures." (Procedure section).
studies.assessment_time: T0 = Baseline (0 weeks); T1 = Post-intervention (approximately 2 weeks, i.e., after 14 consecutive days); T2 = Two-month follow-up (approximately 8.4 weeks post-intervention, ~10.4 weeks from baseline). "A randomized control trial was conducted with pre- and post-intervention measurements and two-month follow-up" (Abstract). CONVERSION: 2 months = 8.4 weeks.
studies.assessment_nature: Self-report only. Two self-report questionnaires were used: the Forms of Self-Criticism/Reassuring Scale (FSCRS) and the Self-Compassion Scale (SCS). "As the research relied on self-report measures of self-compassion and self-criticism, it could potentially be biased for social desirability responding." (Limitations section).
studies.outcomes_all: 1. Self-criticism/reassurance — Forms of Self-Criticism/Reassuring Scale (FSCRS; Gilbert et al. 2004) (22 items, 5-point Likert scale; subscales: Reassured-Self, Inadequate-Self, Hated-Self). 2. Self-compassion — Self-Compassion Scale (SCS; Neff 2003) (26 items, 5-point Likert scale; scored as combined positive constructs [self-compassionate responding: self-kindness, common humanity, mindfulness] and combined negative constructs [self-uncompassionate responding: self-judgment, isolation, over-identification]). (Measures section).
studies.outcomes_primary: Unclear — authors do not explicitly designate a primary outcome. The study aim states: "The primary aim of the present study was to evaluate the immediate and longer term impact of a 14-day internet-based version of the Emotion Focused Training for Self-Compassion and Self-protection (EFT-SCP) on self-compassion, self-criticism and their dimensions" (Aims section). Both FSCRS and SCS appear to be co-primary.
studies.outcome_timepoints: T0 = Baseline (0 weeks); T1 = Post-intervention (~2 weeks); T2 = Two-month follow-up (~10.4 weeks from baseline). Both FSCRS and SCS assessed at all three timepoints. "A randomized control trial was conducted with pre- and post-intervention measurements and two-month follow-up" (Abstract).
studies.recruitment: "Participants were recruited from the general community through social media, social networking sites and health and well-being forums." Convenience sampling via snowballing technique. "Convenience sampling was used to recruit participants through a snowballing technique on social media." As incentive, completers were entered into a prize draw to win a tablet. No recruitment dates reported. (Recruitment section).
studies.study_purpose: "The primary aim of the present study was to evaluate the immediate and longer term impact of a 14-day internet-based version of the Emotion Focused Training for Self-Compassion and Self-protection (EFT-SCP) on self-compassion, self-criticism and their dimensions in a non-clinical population." (Aims section).
studies.study_design: Randomized controlled trial with pre-intervention, post-intervention, and two-month follow-up assessments. Allocation was sequential block-style: "the first eleven participants were allocated to the intervention condition and the next set of eight participants was allocated to the control condition. This was done until all participants were allocated into the two conditions." Unequal allocation (70 intervention, 53 control). No blinding reported. (Participants section).
studies.treatment_vs_prevention: Prevention — participants were from a non-clinical general community sample with no psychiatric diagnosis or symptom threshold required for enrollment, and the study measured self-compassion and self-criticism outcomes (constructs associated with psychopathology risk). "Online interventions can be provided as a cost-effective method to improve self-compassion and reduce self-criticism with the aim to prevent psychopathology in healthy adults" (Significance section). Both conditions (a) no diagnosis at enrollment and (b) condition-related outcomes measured are met.
studies.confidence_why: • age_mean — weighted mean calculated from completer-only arm-level means (n=31 intervention, n=20 control), not from the full randomized sample of 123; flagged as inference/calculation. • age_min / age_max — not reported anywhere in the paper. • eligibility — no formal inclusion/exclusion criteria listed; inferred from general description of non-clinical community sample. • location — inferred from author affiliations; not explicitly stated as study location in paper body. • outcomes_primary — not explicitly designated; inferred from aims statement. • study_design — randomization method described as sequential block allocation, not standard randomization; blinding not reported.
studies.outcomes_coded: Self-compassion | Wellbeing-QoL | Emotion regulation
studies.categories_flags: • protocol_name — the EFT-SCP is a novel intervention developed by the authors drawing on EFT, CMT, and MSC; it does not map cleanly to any single established protocol in the list; coded as 'Unclear' but human review recommended. • is_adapted / adaptation_type — the intervention is novel (not an adaptation of a single parent protocol); adaptation_type flags are preliminary and require human adjudication. • dose_category — 14 days = 2 weeks; coded as 'Short (4-6 weeks)' is borderline; could also be considered 'Brief' depending on interpretation of session count vs. weeks criterion. • outcomes_coded — self-compassion and self-criticism/reassurance do not map perfectly to standard outcome categories; coded under 'Self-compassion' and 'Emotion regulation'; human review recommended. • delivery_format — fully self-guided via email/online with no live instructor; coded as 'Self-guided (no live instructor)'.

studies.authors: Halvaiepour, Z., Yazdkhasti, F., Oreyzi, H. R., & Nosratabadi, M.
studies.title: Developing Cognitive Bias Modification Scenarios for Women with Sexual Interest Arousal Disorder and Comparing Effectiveness with Mindfulness Therapy
studies.abstract: The aim of the present study was to develop and validate the scenarios of cognitive bias modification of interpretation (CBM-I) in women with sexual interest arousal disorder (SIAD) and comparing its effectiveness with mindfulness therapy in Iran. This study was performed by mixed method in two phases. In the first phase of the study, CBM treatment scenarios were developed. In the second phase, 45 women with SIAD were selected and randomly divided into three groups (two experimental groups and one control group). In the qualitative phase of the research on the evaluation of the designed scenarios, 80 scenarios remained among the 100 scenarios by meeting the content validity criteria, fidelity, acceptance, and satisfaction with the treatment. Both experimental treatments exceeded the no treatment control but that mindfulness was more effective than CBM-I as measured by the Female Sexual Function Index Questionnaire (p < 0.001). According to the findings, the use of CBM-I to replace positive interpretations with negative interpretations of cognitive bias in SIAD has a clinical application. Therefore, CBM-I can be used as practical treatment along with other treatments to reduce the symptoms of sexual dysfunction.
studies.total_n: 45. "45 women with SIAD were selected and randomly divided into three groups (two experimental groups and one control group)" (Methods, Study design and participants, paragraph 1). Groups of 15 each: 15 CBM-I + 15 mindfulness + 15 control = 45.
studies.age_mean: 32.3. "The participants' age ranged from 25 to 40 years, with a mean age of 32.3 year" (Results, Quantitative phase results, paragraph 1).
studies.age_describe: Mean age 32.3 years; range 25–40 years. "The participants' age ranged from 25 to 40 years, with a mean age of 32.3 year" (Results, Quantitative phase results, paragraph 1). Per-arm age group breakdown reported in Table 1.
studies.age_min: 25. "The participants' age ranged from 25 to 40 years" (Results, Quantitative phase results, paragraph 1).
studies.age_max: 40. "The participants' age ranged from 25 to 40 years" (Results, Quantitative phase results, paragraph 1).
studies.participants: 45 women diagnosed with Sexual Interest Arousal Disorder (SIAD) recruited from integrated health centers in Isfahan, Iran. All female. Education ranged from illiterate to postgraduate. Majority were housewives. "45 patients with SIAD were randomly selected from the list of patients with this disorder" (Methods, Study design and participants, paragraph 1).
studies.eligibility: Inclusion criteria: "28 to 42 years of age, lack of sexual desire due to medical problems, nondependence on alcohol and drugs, nonuse of drugs affecting sexual desire in the last month, no history of child abuse and mental disorders, absence of painful intercourse or physical pain associated with desire and paraphilia" (Methods, Study design and participants, paragraph 1). Diagnosis confirmed via DSM-5 criteria for sexual arousal disorder by a psychologist interview. Note: age range stated as 28–42 in eligibility but sample range reported as 25–40 in results — inconsistency flagged.
studies.population_vulnerable: Not a vulnerable population — the study targets women with a specific sexual dysfunction (SIAD) in Iran, but no explicit health disparity or structural disadvantage criterion is stated. "45 patients with SIAD were randomly selected from the list of patients with this disorder" (Methods, Study design and participants, paragraph 1).
studies.location: Isfahan, Iran. "three centers were selected from the integrated health centers of Isfahan" (Methods, Study design and participants, paragraph 1).
studies.mental_health: N/A — no psychiatric enrollment criterion. SIAD is classified as a sexual dysfunction, not a psychiatric disorder per se. Diagnosis of SIAD via DSM-5 criteria was required for enrollment, but this is a sexual dysfunction diagnosis, not a psychiatric/mental health threshold. "interviewed by DSM5 criteria for sexual arousal disorder" (Methods, Procedure in quantitative phase, paragraph 1).
studies.physical_health: Sexual Interest Arousal Disorder (SIAD) diagnosis required for enrollment. "45 patients with SIAD were randomly selected from the list of patients with this disorder to be included in the study, according to the inclusion criteria" (Methods, Study design and participants, paragraph 1). Exclusion of painful intercourse or physical pain associated with desire also noted.
studies.arms: 3 arms. Arm 1: Cognitive Bias Modification of Interpretation (CBM-I), n=15. Arm 2: Mindfulness-Based Cognitive Therapy (MBCT-S), n=15. Arm 3: No-intervention control group, n=15. "the 45 selected samples were assigned into three groups of 15 patients (two experimental groups and one control group)" (Methods, Study design and participants, paragraph 2).
studies.meditation_intervention: Arm 2: Mindfulness-Based Cognitive Therapy for Sexual dysfunction (MBCT-S). Explicitly named as "Sexual Mindfulness-Based Cognitive Therapy for women with low sexual desire (MBCT-S)." Protocol from Brotto, Basson, & Luria (2008). Four 90-minute group sessions, once per week (over one month). Content: Session 1 — education on women's sexual disorders, causes of arousal disorder, mindfulness training through sensory focus, body image training, cognitive beliefs focus, group discussion on sexual interests. Session 2 — review of assignments, sexual response cycle (Basson's approach), breathing and body scan mindfulness practice, list of stimuli for sexual cycle. Session 3 — review of home mindfulness practice, sexual scenario of shared experiences, relationship between emotion and behavior, mindfulness and cognitive therapy integration. Session 4 — review of assignments, emotional concentration with spouse, increasing sexual arousal, review of mindfulness exercises. "four 90-minute sessions of the cognitive-behavioral group therapy of sexual responses based on mindfulness exercises that were performed once a week (during a month)" (Methods, Group 2, paragraph 1).
studies.intervention_delivery: In-person group format. Four 90-minute sessions, once per week. Delivered by a psychologist (implied by study context). CBM-I delivered via computer (Superlab Software). Mindfulness delivered as group therapy. "four 90-minute sessions of the cognitive-behavioral group therapy of sexual responses based on mindfulness exercises" (Methods, Group 2, paragraph 1). Facilitator qualifications not explicitly stated.
studies.digital_component_raw: No digital component for the mindfulness intervention. The CBM-I arm used Superlab Software for computer-based scenario delivery, but this is the comparator arm, not the mindfulness arm. "CBM-I is a computer-based exercise" (Methods, Group 1, paragraph 1). The mindfulness sessions were in-person group therapy with no digital delivery described.
studies.intervention_tailor: Yes — the MBCT-S protocol is described as specifically adapted for women with low sexual desire/SIAD, integrating mindfulness with sexual cognitive-behavioral therapy. "mindfulness therapy is integrated with the treatment of low sexual desire disorder called 'Sexual Mindfulness-Based Cognitive Therapy for women with low sexual desire (MBCT-S)'" (Methods, Group 2, paragraph 1). The protocol was delivered in Iranian cultural context.
studies.comparison: Arm 1 (Active comparator): Cognitive Bias Modification of Interpretation (CBM-I). Computer-based exercise using Superlab Software. 80 ambiguous social scenarios related to couple interactions in sexual arousal disorder; 20 scenarios per session across 4 sessions. Participants read 4-line scenarios and completed obscured words to resolve ambiguity positively. "CBM-I is a computer-based exercise in which participants are continuously trained over several trials to end up vague social situations in a positive or neutral way" (Methods, Group 1, paragraph 1). Arm 3 (Passive control): No-intervention control group. "The control group was not subject to any intervention" (Methods, Group 3). Control group was placed on a waiting list and received CBM-I after study completion.
studies.assessment_time: T0 = Baseline (0 weeks); T1 = Post-intervention (approximately 4 weeks). "Data were collected in two stages of pretest and posttest" (Methods, Data analysis, paragraph 1). Intervention lasted one month (4 sessions, once per week). No follow-up assessment reported.
studies.assessment_nature: Self-report only. The Female Sexual Function Index (FSFI) questionnaire was the sole outcome measure. "Data were collected in two stages of pretest and posttest by employing female sexual function index questionnaire (FSFI)" (Methods, Data analysis, paragraph 1).
studies.outcomes_all: Sexual function — Female Sexual Function Index (FSFI; 19 items, 6 dimensions: sexual desire, sexual arousal, dampness/moisture, orgasm, sexual satisfaction, pain; score range 0–5 per item). In this study, desire and arousal subscales were combined as the primary outcome measure for SIAD. "This questionnaire is designed by Rosen et al. (2000) which includes 19 questions in six dimensions" (Methods, Study tool, paragraph 1). Feasibility/acceptability outcomes also assessed in qualitative phase: Content Validity Index (CVI), Content Validity Ratio (CVR), Credibility/Expectancy Questionnaire (CEQ), Client Satisfaction Questionnaire (CSQ-8).
studies.outcomes_primary: Sexual desire/arousal as measured by the FSFI desire and arousal subscales combined. "to compare the effectiveness of the two treatment methods of CBM and mindfulness on women's sexual desire with the control group" (Methods, Data analysis, paragraph 1). Not explicitly labeled 'primary outcome' but is the sole efficacy outcome. "Unclear — authors do not formally designate a primary outcome, but FSFI desire+arousal subscale is the only efficacy measure used."
studies.outcome_timepoints: T0 = Baseline (0 weeks); T1 = Post-intervention (~4 weeks). "Data were collected in two stages of pretest and posttest" (Methods, Data analysis, paragraph 1). No follow-up timepoint reported.
studies.recruitment: Participants were recruited from integrated health centers in Isfahan. "in the first stage, using random sampling, three centers were selected from the integrated health centers of Isfahan in the geographical areas, including the north, south and centre." Screening via a checklist for Women's Screening for Sexual Disorders completed by health care providers. Referred to psychologist and interviewed using DSM-5 criteria. "Study data were collected from September to June 2019" (Methods, Procedure in quantitative phase, paragraph 1).
studies.study_purpose: "The aim of the present study was to develop and validate the scenarios of cognitive bias modification of interpretation (CBM-I) in women with sexual interest arousal disorder (SIAD) and comparing its effectiveness with mindfulness therapy in Iran." (Abstract)
studies.study_design: Mixed-methods study with two phases. Quantitative phase: quasi-experimental design with block randomization. Three groups (two experimental, one control). Block randomization with block sizes of 6, 9, or 12. Investigator blinded to block size. "A quasi-experimental design was employed in qualitative phase of the study" (Methods, Study design and participants, paragraph 1). "the 45 selected samples were assigned into three groups of 15 patients (two experimental groups and one control group) using the block randomization method" (Methods, paragraph 2).
studies.treatment_vs_prevention: Treatment — participants were required to have a diagnosis of SIAD (Sexual Interest Arousal Disorder) at enrollment, confirmed via DSM-5 criteria. The study tests intervention efficacy for an existing condition. "45 patients with SIAD were randomly selected from the list of patients with this disorder" (Methods, Study design and participants, paragraph 1).
studies.trauma: not trauma-focused. No trauma population or trauma-related outcomes described. Exclusion criterion included "no history of child abuse" but this is an exclusion, not a focus. (Methods, Study design and participants, paragraph 1).
studies.confidence_why: • age_min/age_max — Inconsistency between eligibility criteria (28–42 years) and reported sample range (25–40 years); used reported sample range as stated in results. • physical_health — SIAD is classified as a sexual dysfunction; coding as physical health threshold required interpretive judgment. • study_design — Paper describes a 'quasi-experimental design' but uses block randomization, creating ambiguity about RCT vs. quasi-experimental classification. • dose_weeks — Duration inferred as 4 weeks from '4 sessions, once per week (during a month)'; not stated as an exact number of weeks. • treatment_vs_prevention — SIAD classification as physical vs. psychiatric required judgment.

studies.authors: Hamidi, F., & Kheiran, S.
studies.title: Mindfulness-Based Relapse Prevention to Reduce High Risk Behaviors of People Addicted to Methamphetamine
studies.abstract:
Background: The cognitive behavior model of addiction forms the basis for relapse prevention, an intervention that attempts to describe, understand, prevent, and manage relapse in individuals who have received, or are receiving, treatment for substance use disorders.
Objectives: The aim of this study was to investigate the effectiveness of Mindfulness-Based Relapse Prevention (MBRP) educational interventions to reduce some high-risk behaviors like aggression and craving in people with methamphetamine dependence in Kashan (a city of IR Iran).
Patient and Methods: The present research was a quasi-experimental study with pretest- posttest and a control group. Samples concluded 30 males and females with diagnosis of methamphetamine dependence based on DSM-5 criteria and randomly divided into two groups of experimental and control groups each with 15 subjects. Two groups completed the Craving Beliefs questionnaire (CBQ) and Eysenck and Wilson's Aggression questionnaire. The experimental group received 8 sessions of 1.5 hours, under the preventive training of MBRP and after the completion of the intervention sessions, the variables in the post-test stage were re-measured in two groups.
Results: Data was analyzed by descriptive statistics and analysis of covariance. Results showed a significant difference between the experimental and control groups in two variables (P < 0.01). MBRP intervention decrease craving and aggression in clients as hard risk behaviors of methamphetamine-dependent individuals. Eta coefficients were 27% for craving and 53% for aggression.
Conclusions: Research indicated mindfulness training intervention as MBRP was effective for addicts to amphetamines. This method of prevention helped them increase their ability of coping with temptation and high-risk behaviors as the symptoms of the abortion.

studies.authors: Hanley, A. W., de Vibe, M., Solhaug, I., Farb, N., Goldin, P. R., Gross, J. J., & Garland, E. L.
studies.title: Modeling the mindfulness‐to‐meaning theory's mindful reappraisal hypothesis: Replication with longitudinal data from a randomized controlled study
studies.abstract: The Mindfulness to Meaning Theory provides a detailed process model of the mechanisms by which mindfulness may promote well‐being. Central to the Mindfulness to Meaning Theory is the mindful reappraisal hypothesis (MRH), which suggests mindfulness training promotes well‐being by facilitating positive reappraisal. Emerging evidence from interconnected domains of research supports the MRH. However, it remains unclear whether mindful reappraisal continues to develop after a mindfulness training course and whether this continued development encourages well‐being over time. As such, this randomized controlled study compared participants receiving a mindfulness‐based stress reduction (MBSR) course with participants receiving no mindfulness training on positive reappraisal use and well‐being over the course of 6 years. Latent growth curve modeling revealed that mindfulness training increased well‐being by significantly increasing the trajectory of positive reappraisal over time. The MRH was then unpacked by examining whether MBSR also stimulated decentering and broadened awareness, core components of the MRH. Multivariate path analysis revealed that mindfulness training increased decentering, which in turn broadened awareness, which was then associated with positive reappraisal, ultimately promoting well‐being. Taken together, these findings suggest that MBSR cultivates a downstream cascade of adaptive psychological processes that continue to promote quality of life 6‐years after mindfulness training.

studies.authors: Hawley, L. L., Rector, N. A., & Richter, M. A.
studies.title: Technology supported mindfulness for obsessive compulsive disorder: The role of obsessive beliefs
studies.abstract: The current study examined the association of OCD symptoms and OCD belief domains, for individuals engaged in Technology Supported Mindfulness training (TSM) using an EEG-based biofeedback device (called "Muse") that permits individuals to engage in home based mindfulness meditation practices. In this randomized controlled study, treatment-seeking participants with a principal DSM-5 diagnosis of OCD (N = 71) were randomly assigned to eight weeks of: 1) a meditation program involving daily use of the "Muse" device, or 2) wait list control. At weeks 1, 4, and 8, participants completed self-report measures of OCD symptoms (YBOCS: Yale-Brown Obsessive Compulsive Scale) and OCD beliefs (OBQ; OCCWG, 2005). Latent Difference Score (LDS) models indicated that there was no significant longitudinal relationship between OBQ "Responsibility/Threat" (OBQ R/T) scores and OCD symptoms. The analysis of OBQ "Perfectionism/Certainty" (OBQ P/C) and OCD symptoms demonstrated a significant reciprocal relationship between these two variables, in which OCD symptoms predicted subsequent increases in OBQ P/C and vice versa. The analysis of OBQ "Importance/Control of Thoughts" (OBQ I/C) and OCD symptoms demonstrated a significant reciprocal relationship between these two variables, in which OCD symptoms predicted subsequent increases in OBQ I/C and vice versa. The analysis of OBQ domains and EEG derived attentional changes demonstrated a significant association between OBQ P/C and Alpha band frequencies. These results clarify the association of OBQ belief domains, OCD symptom change and EEG derived indicators of attention during TSM.

studies.meditation_intervention: Technology Supported Mindfulness (TSM) using the 'Muse' EEG-based biofeedback headset (InteraXon Inc.). Participants completed a daily guided mindfulness practice provided by the Muse smartphone application, lasting 20 minutes, throughout the eight-week study. The Muse headset provides real-time EEG-derived neurofeedback via auditory cues (e.g., storm sounds) that increase in volume when the user is distracted and decrease when attention is stable. At weeks 1, 4, and 8, all participants also completed an unguided 'open monitoring' mindfulness practice for five minutes while wearing the Muse headset for EEG data collection. "Participants in the Muse condition completed a daily guided mindfulness practice (provided by the 'Muse' smartphone application) lasting for 20 min, throughout the eight week study." (Methods, Procedure, paragraph 3). No named protocol (e.g., MBSR, MBCT) is explicitly stated. Facilitator qualifications not reported for home-based practice.

"permits individuals to engage in home based mindfulness meditation practices" (Abstract). Guided meditation instructions were provided through the participant's cellphone via the Muse app. No live instructor for daily sessions. At three in-person/clinic visits (weeks 1, 4, 8), participants wore the Muse headset for EEG data collection. "All participants attended three sessions (weeks 1, 4, and 8) and completed an unguided 'open monitoring' mindfulness practice for five minutes while wearing a Muse headset" (Methods, Procedure, paragraph 3).

"participants completed self-report measures of OCD symptoms (YBOCS) and OCD beliefs (OBQ)" (Abstract). "All participants attended three sessions (weeks 1, 4, and 8) and completed an unguided 'open monitoring' mindfulness practice for five minutes while wearing a Muse headset, in order to collect EEG data." (Methods, Procedure, paragraph 3).

EEG-derived attentional indicators — EEG band powers (Delta: 1–4 Hz, Theta: 4–8 Hz, Alpha: 7.5–13 Hz, Beta: 13–30 Hz) recorded via Muse headset during open monitoring practice (Materials and Measures, section 3.1).

The study focuses on the longitudinal relationship between OBQ belief domains, OCD symptoms (YBOCS), and EEG-derived attentional indicators. "The current study extends the findings of Hawley et al. (2021), examining whether eight weeks of mindfulness training (using the 'Muse' headset) is associated with reduced cognitive vulnerability, improved attentional focus, and symptom alleviation." (Introduction, final paragraph).

(2021), examining whether eight weeks of mindfulness training (using the 'Muse' headset) is associated with reduced cognitive vulnerability, improved attentional focus, and symptom alleviation. We hypothesized that individuals in the 'Muse' condition (in comparison to the control condition) who engaged in eight weeks of daily mindfulness practices would demonstrate changes in obsessive belief domains (OBQ R/T: Responsibility/Threat estimation; OBQ P/C: Perfectionism/Certainty, OBQ I/C: Importance/Control of Thoughts), and these belief domains will be longitudinally related to changes in OCD symptoms as well as EEG derived markers of attentional control." (Introduction, final paragraph).

"Group randomization was determined using the 'GraphPad Quick Calcs' online calculator which offers random allocation into equal-sized groups." (Methods, Procedure, paragraph 2). "treatment-seeking participants with a principal DSM-5 diagnosis of OCD" (Abstract).

studies.authors: Hayajneh, A. A., Al-Younis, M. O., & Rababa, M.
studies.title: The effect of a mindfulness intervention (MI) on sleep disturbance (SD) among nurses
studies.abstract: Sleep disturbance (SD) makes it difficult for nurses in intensive care units (ICUs) to perform activities that require focused and continual concentration, which raises the risk of medical errors, health issues, loss of sleep, and patient care mistakes. The mindfulness intervention (MI) was created to give participants the capacity to approach their own emotions with non-judgmental awareness and to become more conscious of their thoughts and feelings, and it reduced psychological symptoms. This study examined the effect of MI on SD among nurses. A randomized control trail (RCT) was conducted and recruited 100 nurses from intensive care and medical-surgical units from three hospitals located at the northern and middle regions of Jordan. Bivariate analysis including independent T-test and multiple linear regressions were used to study the differences between the interventional group (MI) and the comparison group (watching mindfulness videos) in terms of the impact on the SD. Nurses reported significant and high levels of SD. MI significantly reduced the level of SD and improved sleep quality among nurses. MI should be integrated into nursing competences to combat the negative impacts of poor sleep quality on nurses and organizational-sensitive outcomes.
studies.total_n: 100. "A convenience sample of 100 participants was assigned equally and randomly to two groups: the interventional group (MI) and the comparison group (watching mindfulness videos)." (Methods, Design, paragraph 1)
studies.age_mean: 29.76. "Age (years) 29.76 (3.83)" (Table 3, Descriptive analysis)

studies.age_max: 40 (inferred from age group upper bound: '31–40 years 29 (29%)'). (Table 3)
studies.participants: 100 Jordanian nurses recruited from acute and critical care units. "Most nurses were female (69%), and around two-thirds (92%) had a bachelor's degree in nursing; 71% of the nurses were aged between 25 and 30 years... A significant proportion (59%) of the nurses were never married." (Results, paragraph 1). 60% worked in critical care units, 40% in general hospital wards.
studies.eligibility: Inclusion criteria: "Jordanian nurses who: (1) at least hold a bachelor's degree and (2) provide direct care to patients." Exclusion criteria: "floating nurses who work in different departments and nurses who previously attended mindfulness workshops." (Methods, Setting and sampling, paragraph 1)
studies.population_vulnerable: Not a vulnerable population — the study targets nurses as healthcare professionals, not a population defined by health disparities or structural disadvantage. "The participants were recruited from acute and critical care units at three hospitals located at the northern and middle regions of Jordan." (Methods, Setting and sampling, paragraph 1)
