studies.mental_health: N/A — no psychiatric enrollment criterion. Nurses were enrolled based on professional role and educational level, not psychiatric diagnosis or symptom threshold.
studies.physical_health: N/A — no physical health enrollment criterion. Enrollment was based on professional role (direct care nurses with bachelor's degree), not a physical health condition.
studies.arms: 2 arms. Arm 1: Interventional group (MI) — face-to-face mindfulness intervention sessions, n=50. Arm 2: Comparison group (watching mindfulness videos), n=50. "A convenience sample of 100 participants was assigned equally and randomly to two groups: the interventional group (MI) and the comparison group (watching mindfulness videos)." (Methods, Design, paragraph 1)
studies.meditation_intervention: A 4-week mindfulness intervention conducted face-to-face by a certified expert. Four weekly sessions of 1 hour each. Content: Week 1 — introduction to mindfulness and meditation, definitions, effects on body and mind, 15-min meditation exercise; Week 2 — breathing and body scan, 5-min mindful breathing technique, 15-min meditation exercise; Week 3 — mindfulness practices in daily life, relaxation, 15-min meditation including breathing and body scan; Week 4 — full mindfulness meditation session including intention, breathing, relaxation, centering, observing thoughts and feelings, sharing experience. "The MI sessions were conducted by an expert certified in psychotherapy, educational counseling, and MI. This expert and authors met the participants face-to-face in a hallway inside the hospital for one hour per session." (Methods, Data collection, paragraph 4; Table 1)
studies.intervention_delivery: In-person group delivery. "This expert and authors met the participants face-to-face in a hallway inside the hospital for one hour per session." Sessions were 1 hour each, once per week for 4 weeks. Facilitator was "an expert certified in psychotherapy, educational counseling, and MI." (Methods, Data collection, paragraph 4)
studies.digital_component_raw: No digital component. Text messages were used to send reminders to participants: "all participants adhered to complete all MI sessions due to sending frequent regular reminders via text messages by the PI." However, the intervention itself was delivered in-person. (Discussion, paragraph 7)
studies.intervention_tailor: No tailoring reported. The intervention was described as a general mindfulness program for nurses; no cultural adaptation or population-specific modifications were explicitly described.
studies.comparison: Comparison group watched four mindfulness-related videos, one per week for 4 weeks, each 30 minutes. Week 1: Meditation for stress (guided meditation for stress release, short body relaxation); Week 2: Meditation for stress (guided meditation with concentration and releasing accumulated pressure); Week 3: Meditation for deep sleep (before sleeping, letting go of thoughts); Week 4: Meditation for Loving Kindness (compassion for self and others). "The comparison group simply watched MI videos." (Methods, Data collection, paragraph 4; Table 2)
studies.assessment_time: T0 = Baseline (0 weeks); T1 = Post-intervention (4 weeks). "The two groups completed the questionnaire before the 1st session and after the 2nd, 3rd, and 4th sessions." MAAS was assessed weekly (weeks 1–4); PSQI was assessed at baseline and one month later. "data about the PSQI represents sleep quality over the last month measured at baseline (pre-test) and at the end of the month (post-test) after completed four MI sessions." (Methods, Statistical analysis, paragraph 1; Data collection, paragraph 4)
studies.assessment_nature: Self-report questionnaires only. MAAS (Mindful Attention Awareness Scale) and PSQI (Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index) are both self-report instruments. "The two groups completed the questionnaire before the 1st session and after the 2nd, 3rd, and 4th sessions." (Methods, Data collection, paragraph 4)
studies.outcomes_all: 1. Sleep disturbance/sleep quality — Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI) (19 items, 7 components, score range 0–21; higher score = worse sleep quality). 2. Mindfulness — Mindful Attention Awareness Scale (MAAS) (15 items, single factor, scores 1–6; higher score = higher dispositional mindfulness). Sociodemographic and professional variables also collected (age, gender, education, marital status, income, shift type, experience, department). (Methods, Measures section)
studies.outcomes_primary: Unclear — authors do not explicitly designate a primary outcome. However, the study title and stated aim focus on sleep disturbance: "This study examined the effect of MI on SD among nurses." PSQI appears to be the main outcome. (Abstract; Methods, Design)
studies.outcome_timepoints: MAAS: T0 = Baseline (0 weeks); T1 = Week 1 (1 week); T2 = Week 2 (2 weeks); T3 = Week 3 (3 weeks); T4 = Week 4 (4 weeks). PSQI: T0 = Baseline (0 weeks); T1 = Post-intervention/one month later (4 weeks). "This study used the MAAS questionnaire every week for one month... data about the PSQI represents sleep quality over the last month measured at baseline (pre-test) and at the end of the month (post-test)." (Methods, Data collection and Statistical analysis)
studies.recruitment: Convenience sampling from acute and critical care units at three hospitals in northern and middle Jordan. "Prior to the study, the investigator met with the manager of the intensive care unit and the medical-surgical units in each hospital that was chosen to coordinate the workflow of the study procedure... After discussing the inclusion and exclusion criteria, the researcher obtained a list of nurses who would participate." No recruitment dates reported. (Methods, Data collection, paragraph 1)
studies.study_purpose: "This study examined the differences in SD among nurses assigned to an interventional group (MI) or a comparison group (watching mindfulness videos). This study also aims to identify the factors associated with SD." (Introduction, final paragraph)
studies.study_design: Randomized controlled trial (RCT). "A randomized control trial (RCT) design was used in this study. A convenience sample of 100 participants was assigned equally and randomly to two groups." Allocation ratio 1:1 (50 per group). Blinding not reported. (Methods, Design, paragraph 1)
studies.treatment_vs_prevention: Enhancement — The participants are nurses (healthy working professionals) with no psychiatric diagnosis or clinical threshold required for enrollment. Sleep disturbance is measured as an outcome but no clinical sleep disorder diagnosis was required for enrollment. The study aims to reduce occupational sleep disturbance and improve wellbeing among nurses. "MI should be integrated into nursing competences to combat the negative impacts of poor sleep quality on nurses." (Abstract; Methods, Eligibility). Note: could also be classified as Treatment given that nurses reported high SD levels at baseline (mean PSQI = 8.50, above clinical threshold of 5), but no sleep disorder diagnosis was required for enrollment.

studies.title: The Effectiveness of Mindfulness on the Reduction of Anxiety and Depression of Divorced Women
studies.abstract: This aim of this study is to evaluate the effect of mindfulness on the reduction of anxiety and depression in the divorced women of Ahvaz city. The study sample has included 30 divorced women that have been randomly selected. The subjects have been randomly divided into the control and study groups. The measurement tools in this study were: Beck Depression Inventory (BDI-II), and Beck Anxiety Inventory (BAI). This study is experimental with pretest, posttest and control group. The study group has been exposed to 8 sessions of mindfulness training that every session has lasted for 2 hours, after that the posttest has been conducted on both the control and study groups. The analysis of data by the using multivariate analysis of variance (MANOVA) with (?=0.05) level of significance has showed that mindfulness can reduce anxiety and depression in divorced women.

studies.authors: Horenstein, A., Morrison, A. S., Goldin, P., ten Brink, M., Gross, J. J., & Heimberg, R. G.
studies.title: Sleep quality and treatment of social anxiety disorder
studies.abstract:
Background and Objectives: Poor sleep is prevalent among individuals with social anxiety disorder (SAD) and may affect treatment outcome. We examined whether: (1) individuals with SAD differed from healthy controls (HCs) in sleep quality, (2) baseline sleep quality moderated the effects of treatment (Cognitive–behavioral group therapy [CBGT] vs. mindfulness-based stress reduction [MBSR] vs. waitlist [WL]) on social anxiety, (3) sleep quality changed over treatment, and (4) changes in sleep quality predicted anxiety 12-months post-treatment.
Design: Participants were 108 adults with SAD from a randomized controlled trial of CBGT vs. MBSR vs. WL and 38 HCs.
Methods: SAD and sleep quality were assessed pre-treatment and post-treatment; SAD was assessed again 12-months post-treatment.
Results: Participants with SAD reported poorer sleep quality than HCs. The effect of treatment condition on post-treatment social anxiety did not differ as a function of baseline sleep quality. Sleep quality improved in MBSR, significantly more than WL, but not CBGT. Sleep quality change from pre- to post-treatment in CBGT or MBSR did not predict later social anxiety.
Conclusions: MBSR, and not CBGT, improved sleep quality among participants. Other results were inconsistent with prior research; possible explanations, limitations, and implications for future research are discussed. ClinicalTrials.gov identifier: NCT02036658.
studies.total_n: 108 (SAD participants from RCT) plus 38 healthy controls = 146 total. SAD participants: 'Participants (N = 146) comprised 108 treatment-seeking adults with a primary diagnosis of generalized SAD...who were enrolled in a RCT...as well as 38 healthy control participants (HCs).' (Methods, Participants, paragraph 1). Note: the RCT itself had 108 SAD participants randomized; the 38 HCs were not randomized.
studies.age_mean: 32.70 for SAD sample; 32.02 for HC sample. Full sample weighted mean: ((108×32.70)+(38×32.02))/146 = (3531.6+1216.76)/146 = 32.52 (weighted calculation)
studies.age_describe: SAD group: M = 32.70 (SD = 7.99); HC group: M = 32.02 (SD = 8.43). 'Age (M[SD]) 32.70 (7.99) [SAD]; 32.02 (8.43) [HC]' (Table 1, Sample demographic characteristics). No range or min/max reported.
studies.participants: 108 treatment-seeking adults with a primary diagnosis of generalized SAD (55.6% female; race/ethnicity: 43.5% White, 38.9% Asian, 9.3% Hispanic, 6.5% Mixed, 0.9% Black, 0.9% American Indian/Alaskan Native) and 38 healthy controls (60% female). 'Participants (N = 146) comprised 108 treatment-seeking adults with a primary diagnosis of generalized SAD according to DSM-IV...as well as 38 healthy control participants (HCs).' (Methods, Participants, paragraph 1). Less than half (42.6%) had comorbid conditions.
studies.eligibility: Inclusion criteria: '18 years of age or older, have a primary diagnosis of generalized SAD as evidenced by greater than moderate fear in five or more distinct social situations listed in the social phobia module of the Anxiety Disorders Interview Schedule for the DSM-IV-Lifetime Version (ADIS-IV-L), and score 60 or higher on the Liebowitz Social Anxiety Scale–Self-Report (LSAS-SR).' Exclusion criteria: 'Participants were excluded if they had a lifetime history of neurological disorders, cardiovascular disorders, thought disorders, eating disorders, or bipolar disorder; significant symptoms of post-traumatic stress disorder or obsessive compulsive disorder; major depressive episode in the past month; current substance or alcohol abuse/dependence; pharmacotherapy, CBT for anxiety, or any other psychotherapy in the past year; or previous MBSR or long-term meditation experience.' (Methods, Participants, paragraph 1)
studies.population_vulnerable: Not a vulnerable population — the sample consists of treatment-seeking adults with SAD recruited for a clinical trial; no specific health disparity or structural disadvantage criterion is described. 'Participants (N = 146) comprised 108 treatment-seeking adults with a primary diagnosis of generalized SAD.' (Methods, Participants, paragraph 1)
studies.location: Inferred: Stanford, California, USA (inferred from 'This study was approved by the Stanford University Institutional Review Board' and author affiliations at Stanford University — not explicitly stated as study location in paper body)
studies.mental_health: Primary diagnosis of generalized SAD required for enrollment, as evidenced by ADIS-IV-L criteria (greater than moderate fear in five or more distinct social situations) and LSAS-SR score ≥ 60. 'have a primary diagnosis of generalized SAD as evidenced by greater than moderate fear in five or more distinct social situations listed in the social phobia module of the ADIS-IV-L...and score 60 or higher on the Liebowitz Social Anxiety Scale–Self-Report (LSAS-SR).' (Methods, Participants, paragraph 1)
studies.physical_health: N/A — no physical health enrollment criterion
studies.arms: 3 arms: (1) Cognitive-Behavioral Group Therapy (CBGT), n=36; (2) Mindfulness-Based Stress Reduction (MBSR), n=36; (3) Waitlist (WL), n=36. 'Participants with SAD completed these measures prior to randomization to CBGT (n = 36), MBSR (n = 36), or WL (n = 36)' (Methods, Procedure, paragraph 1). Note: one MBSR group was excluded due to non-adherence, so actual analyzed n may differ.
studies.meditation_intervention: MBSR: 'The MBSR protocol followed the standard outline designed by Kabat-Zinn (1993), with some modifications to the protocol to match the duration of the CBGT group. The intervention included training in body scan meditation, sitting meditation, and mindful stretching, as well as a focus on the application of mindfulness as a method for noticing reactions and responding in new ways in social situations. The intervention also included additional readings and mindfulness exercises to supplement ongoing practice (Stahl & Goldstein, 2010).' 12 weekly 2.5-hour sessions in group format with 6 participants per group. (Methods, Procedure, paragraph 2)
studies.intervention_delivery: In-person group format. 'CBGT and MBSR were each comprised of 12 weekly, 2.5-hour sessions conducted in a group format with six participants per group.' (Methods, Procedure, paragraph 2). Facilitator qualifications not explicitly described in this paper; referred to parent RCT (Goldin et al., 2016) for full methodology details.
studies.digital_component_raw: No digital component. Sessions were in-person group format. Additional readings and a mindfulness workbook (Stahl & Goldstein, 2010) were provided as supplementary materials. 'The intervention also included additional readings and mindfulness exercises to supplement ongoing practice.' (Methods, Procedure, paragraph 2)
studies.intervention_tailor: Yes — the MBSR protocol was modified to match the duration of the CBGT group. 'The MBSR protocol followed the standard outline designed by Kabat-Zinn (1993), with some modifications to the protocol to match the duration of the CBGT group.' (Methods, Procedure, paragraph 2). Additionally, a focus on applying mindfulness in social situations was incorporated.
studies.comparison: Two comparison conditions: (1) Cognitive-Behavioral Group Therapy (CBGT): 'The CBGT protocol incorporated psychoeducation, cognitive restructuring skills, graduated exposure to feared social situations (both within session and at home), and an emphasis on relapse prevention and termination (Heimberg & Becker, 2002). Portions of the protocol developed by Hope, Heimberg, and Turk (2010) were also incorporated.' 12 weekly 2.5-hour sessions, group format, 6 participants per group. (2) Waitlist (WL): participants waited 12 weeks and were then randomized to CBGT or MBSR; their post-waitlist outcomes are not further considered in this paper. (Methods, Procedure, paragraphs 1-2)
studies.assessment_time: T0 = Baseline/pre-treatment (0 weeks); T1 = Post-treatment (12 weeks); T2 = 12-month follow-up (52 weeks, approximately). 'Participants with SAD completed these measures prior to randomization...and after completion of treatment or waitlist...All participants receiving CBGT or MBSR completed SAD symptom measures again 12 months post-treatment.' (Methods, Procedure, paragraph 1). CONVERSION: 12 months post-treatment ≈ 12 × 4.2 = 50.4 weeks after post-treatment, i.e., ~62 weeks from baseline.
studies.assessment_nature: Self-report measures only. Sleep quality assessed via Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI); social anxiety assessed via Liebowitz Social Anxiety Scale-Self Report (LSAS-SR); diagnostic assessment via ADIS-IV-L clinician-administered interview at baseline. 'Participants completed measures of social anxiety and perceived sleep quality, among other measures not considered here.' (Methods, Procedure, paragraph 1). Diagnostic interviews were clinician-administered: 'Diagnostic interviews were conducted at baseline using the ADIS-IV-L...interviews were conducted by doctoral-level or masters-level clinicians and trained doctoral students.' (Methods, Diagnostic assessment, paragraph 1)
studies.outcomes_all: 1. Sleep quality — Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI; 7 component items, global score 0–21, higher = poorer sleep quality; clinical cutoff = 5). 2. Social anxiety — Liebowitz Social Anxiety Scale-Self Report (LSAS-SR; 24 items, score range 0–144, assesses fear and avoidance of social and performance situations). 3. Diagnostic assessment — ADIS-IV-L (clinician-administered, baseline only). 'Sleep quality was assessed using the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI)...The primary outcome measure for this study was the Liebowitz Social Anxiety Scale-Self Report (LSAS-SR).' (Methods, Measures section)
studies.outcomes_primary: Social anxiety symptoms as measured by the LSAS-SR. 'The primary outcome measure for this study was the Liebowitz Social Anxiety Scale-Self Report (LSAS-SR).' (Methods, Treatment outcome, paragraph 1)
studies.outcome_timepoints: T0 = Baseline (0 weeks): PSQI and LSAS-SR assessed; T1 = Post-treatment (12 weeks): PSQI and LSAS-SR assessed; T2 = 12-month follow-up (~50.4 weeks post-treatment, ~62 weeks from baseline): LSAS-SR only (CBGT and MBSR participants only). 'SAD and sleep quality were assessed pre-treatment and post-treatment; SAD was assessed again 12-months post-treatment.' (Abstract, Methods)

'Participants (N = 146) comprised 108 treatment-seeking adults with a primary diagnosis of generalized SAD...who were enrolled in a RCT investigating the effects of CBGT vs. MBSR vs. WL for SAD (Goldin et al., 2016).' (Methods, Participants, paragraph 1). Recruitment channels not reported in this paper.
studies.study_purpose: To examine: '(1) whether self-reported sleep quality differed in individuals with SAD compared to healthy controls, (2) whether sleep quality moderated treatment outcome in CBGT vs. MBSR vs. WL for SAD (3) whether sleep quality improved over the course of CBGT or MBSR relative to WL and to each other, and (4) whether changes in sleep quality during treatment predicted social anxiety 12 months post-treatment.' (Introduction, final paragraph)
studies.study_design: Secondary analysis of a randomized controlled trial (RCT). 'Participants (N = 146) comprised 108 treatment-seeking adults with a primary diagnosis of generalized SAD...who were enrolled in a RCT investigating the effects of CBGT vs. MBSR vs. WL for SAD (Goldin et al., 2016).' (Methods, Participants, paragraph 1). Randomization method and allocation details not described in this paper; referred to parent RCT. Allocation ratio 1:1:1 (36 per arm).
studies.treatment_vs_prevention: Treatment — participants were required to have a primary diagnosis of generalized SAD at enrollment, with validated symptom thresholds (ADIS-IV-L criteria and LSAS-SR ≥ 60). The study tests intervention effects on an existing clinical condition. 'participants had to be 18 years of age or older, have a primary diagnosis of generalized SAD...and score 60 or higher on the Liebowitz Social Anxiety Scale–Self-Report.' studies.authors: Howarth, A., Riaz, M., Perkins-Porras, L., Smith, J. G., Subramaniam, J., Copland, C., Hurley, M., Beith, I., & Ussher, M.
studies.title: Pilot randomised controlled trial of a brief mindfulness-based intervention for those with persistent pain
studies.abstract: A pilot-randomised controlled trial (RCT) examined the effects of a brief mindfulness-based intervention (MBI) on persistent pain patients and assessed the feasibility of conducting a definitive RCT. A brief (15 min) mindfulness body-scan audio was compared with an active control administered in a clinic and then used independently over 1 month. Immediate effects of the intervention were assessed with brief measures of pain severity, distraction and distress. Assessments at baseline, 1 week and 1 month included pain severity and interference, mood, pain-catastrophizing, mindfulness, self-efficacy, quality of life and intervention acceptability. Of 220 referred patients, 147 were randomised and 71 completed all assessments. There were no significant immediate intervention effects. There were significant positive effects for ratings of intervention 'usefulness' at 1 week (p = 0.044), and pain self-efficacy at 1 month (p = 0.039) for the MBI group compared with control. Evidently, it is feasible to recruit persistent pain patients to a brief MBI study. Strategies are needed to maximise retention of participants.
studies.total_n: 147. 'A total of 147 were randomised' (Results, Recruitment and exclusions, paragraph 1). MBI n=37, Control n=34 per Table 2 (completers only); 147 total randomized confirmed in CONSORT flow diagram description.
studies.age_mean: 54 (weighted not required; full sample mean reported). 'The sample as a whole had a mean age of 54 years' (Results, Baseline demographics, paragraph 1). Arm-level: MBI mean 54.7 (SD 12.5), Control mean 52.8 (SD 12.2) per Table 2.
studies.age_describe: Full sample mean age 54 years. MBI group: mean 54.7 (SD 12.5); Control group: mean 52.8 (SD 12.2). 'The sample as a whole had a mean age of 54 years' (Results, Baseline demographics, paragraph 1); arm-level data from Table 2.
studies.participants: Persistent pain patients recruited from NHS physiotherapy and pain clinics in south London. 'The sample as a whole had a mean age of 54 years, over two-thirds were female, close to half were Caucasian, just over half were employed, nearly half were married or living with a partner, and over half had a diagnosis that included back pain.' (Results, Baseline demographics, paragraph 1). Recruitment predominantly from hospital physiotherapy department (n=113), with some from pain clinics (n=34).
studies.eligibility: Inclusion criteria: 'Patients were eligible if they were over 18 years of age, living with persistent pain [i.e., with a diagnosis of persistent pain or having had pain for more than 3 months past the time healing should have occurred], and able to hear audio recordings or have equipment to enable them to do so.' Exclusion criteria: 'Patients were excluded if they were considered too unwell to participate by the clinician or were unable to speak or read English sufficiently to understand and complete the self-administered questionnaires.' (Methods, Participants, paragraphs 2-3)
studies.population_vulnerable: Not a vulnerable population — participants are persistent pain patients from NHS clinics, defined by a clinical condition (chronic pain) rather than structural disadvantage or health disparity. The paper notes pain management disparities exist but does not recruit specifically on that basis. (Methods, Participants)
studies.location: South London, United Kingdom. 'Patients were recruited from three outpatient NHS physiotherapy and pain clinics at in south London.' (Methods, Participants, paragraph 1)
studies.mental_health: N/A — no psychiatric enrollment criterion. Persistent pain is the enrollment criterion; no psychiatric diagnosis or symptom threshold required for enrollment.
studies.physical_health: 'living with persistent pain [i.e., with a diagnosis of persistent pain or having had pain for more than 3 months past the time healing should have occurred]' (Methods, Participants, paragraph 2). Persistent pain diagnosis or pain duration >3 months required for enrollment.
studies.arms: Two arms. 1) MBI group: brief mindfulness body-scan audio (n=37 completers; randomized N not separately reported per arm but implied ~73-74 each from 147 total). 2) Control group: distraction audio (sequential readings from a non-fiction book) (n=34 completers). 'Patients were allocated their number in ascending order based on order of enrolment... to either the control or MBI group on a 1:1 basis.' (Methods, Randomisation, paragraph 1)
studies.meditation_intervention: Brief mindfulness body-scan audio (15 minutes). Based on a transcript from Breathworks, an established mindfulness organization specialising in supporting those with persistent pain. 'The audio recording directed the listener to scan their body with their attention systematically, starting with the toes and finishing with the crown of the head. Throughout this process, the listener was also encouraged to be aware of their breathing and to accept all thoughts and feelings, whether positive or negative, without trying to alter them in any way.' Administered once in clinic with researcher present, then used independently at home. Use requested at least 3 further times during first week; encouraged but not prescribed for subsequent 3 weeks. Additional audios (mindfulness breathing meditation and mindfulness moving meditation, also 15 min, also from Breathworks) provided but not recommended until after 1 week. Total duration: 1 month. No trained specialist required for delivery. (Methods, Interventions, MBI group section)
studies.intervention_delivery: Initial session delivered in-person in a clinical setting (physiotherapy or pain clinic medical side room or cubicle) with a researcher present. Subsequent sessions self-administered at home using MP3 player or personal device. 'The audio was administered in the presence of a researcher in the first instance, in a clinical setting... and a telephone follow up at 1 week and 1 month was conducted (in nearly all cases) by the same researcher.' No specialist training required. (Methods, Interventions, MBI group section)
studies.digital_component_raw: No digital component. Audio delivered via MP3 player (with earphones) or downloaded to personal device (smartphone/iPad). 'Patients in the MBI group were given an audio recording of a 15 min mindfulness body scan on an MP3 player (with earphones) or were offered the option of having the audio downloaded directly to a personal device of their choice, such as a smart phone or iPad.' The MP3 player and device download are analog/portable media delivery for home practice, not a digital intervention platform. Telephone follow-ups were used for behaviour change support but not for intervention delivery. (Methods, Interventions, MBI group section)
studies.intervention_tailor: Yes — the intervention was specifically developed and adapted for persistent pain patients. 'Based on prior qualitative research (Howarth et al., 2016a, b), the MBI was specifically developed to target those with persistent pain.' The body scan was extended from 10 to 15 minutes based on patient feedback, and the nature of the intervention was modified to be more self-management focused. Based on Breathworks transcripts specialising in persistent pain. (Methods, Interventions; Discussion)
studies.comparison: Active control: distraction audio. 'Patients in the control group were given eight, 15 min audio recordings of sequential readings from The English Village: History and Traditions (Wainwright, 2011), which is a non-fiction book considered not to include any strong emotive content.' Delivered via MP3 player or personal device. First session administered in clinic; subsequent sessions self-administered at home. Use requested at least 3 further times during first week; encouraged for subsequent 3 weeks. Matched to MBI for time, pacing, and narrator voice. (Methods, Interventions, Control group section)
studies.assessment_time: T0 = Baseline (0 weeks); T1 = Immediate post-intervention in clinic (same day, 0 weeks); T2 = During first week / end of first week (approximately 1 week); T3 = 1 month follow-up (approximately 4.2 weeks). 'Assessments at baseline, 1 week and 1 month included pain severity and interference, mood, pain-catastrophizing, mindfulness, self-efficacy, quality of life and intervention acceptability.' (Abstract). Brief measures also assessed immediately before and after audio in clinic and at last session during first week at home.
studies.assessment_nature: Self-report questionnaires only. Measures include: HADS, CAMS-R, BPI, PCS, EQ-5D-5L, single-item pain self-efficacy, single-item ADL limitation, brief single-item measures of distraction/pain severity/pain distress, usefulness ratings, recommendation ratings, previous experience item. Brief qualitative telephone interviews also conducted. 'Patients were asked to complete baseline measures' and 'complete brief psychological measures' (Methods, Procedure in clinic). No physiological or clinician-administered measures reported.
studies.outcomes_all: 1. Pain severity — Brief Pain Inventory (BPI) severity subscale (0–10); 2. Pain interference — Brief Pain Inventory (BPI) interference subscale (0–10); 3. Mood/Anxiety — Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale (HADS) anxiety subscale (0–21, 7 items); 4. Mood/Depression — Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale (HADS) depression subscale (0–21, 7 items); 5. Mindfulness — Cognitive and Affective Mindfulness Scale-Revised (CAMS-R) (10 items, 0–40); 6. Pain catastrophizing — Pain Catastrophizing Scale (PCS) (13 items, 0–52); 7. Health-related quality of life — EQ-5D-5L (5 domains: mobility, self-care, usual activities, pain/discomfort, anxiety/depression, each 1–5; plus VAS 0–100); 8. Pain self-efficacy — single item ('How confident have you been in managing your pain', 1–7); 9. Physical function/ADL limitation — single item ('how much has your work or other regular daily activities been limited', 1–5 at baseline, 1–7 at follow-up); 10. Distraction — single item ('Right now, I could be easily distracted', 1–7); 11. Pain distress — single item ('How distressing are your pain related symptoms right now?', 1–7); 12. Intervention usefulness — single item ('How useful did you find the audio guide for helping you to relax?', 1–5); 13. Recommendation — single item ('Would you recommend this audio guide to others', 1–5); 14. Previous experience with yoga/tai-chi/meditation — single item (1–7); 15. Adherence/audio use — self-monitoring diary (number of times listened). (Methods, Measures and schedule of assessment; Table 1)
studies.outcomes_primary: The immediate effects of the intervention (distraction, pain severity, pain distress immediately before and after audio). 'For the analysis of the primary outcomes, which were the immediate effects of the intervention, we assessed the effect of the body scan intervention versus the control intervention on ratings for the brief psychological measures administered immediately before and after the interventions.' (Methods, Statistical analysis, paragraph 1)
studies.outcome_timepoints: T0 = Baseline (0 weeks): BPI, CAMS-R, HADS, PCS, EQ-5D-5L, pain self-efficacy, ADL limitation, brief measures (pre-audio); T0 immediate post-audio (0 weeks, same session): brief measures (distraction, pain severity, pain distress); T1 = During/end of first week (~1 week): brief measures (pre/post last audio session), CAMS-R, usefulness, recommendation, previous experience items; T2 = 1 month (~4.2 weeks): HADS, CAMS-R, PCS, EQ-5D-5L, pain self-efficacy, ADL limitation. (Table 1, Schedule of data and measurement collection)
studies.recruitment: Patients recruited from three outpatient NHS physiotherapy and pain clinics in south London. 'All patients were initially screened by a clinician (i.e., physiotherapist or pain consultant). Those who met the inclusion criteria were given a patient information sheet (PIS) by the clinician and were asked if they consent to have their contact details passed to a researcher.' Recruitment took place over 2 years from January 2015 to January 2017. Predominantly from hospital physiotherapy department (n=113), with some from pain clinics (n=34). (Methods, Participants; Results, Recruitment and exclusions)
studies.study_purpose: 'The aim of the current study was to evaluate the effects of a brief MBI, which is a refinement of the intervention used in the latter study and assess the feasibility of conducting a definitive randomised controlled trial (RCT).' (Introduction, final paragraph)
studies.study_design: Pilot randomised controlled trial (RCT). 'This was a single centre, parallel group, RCT pilot study, designed to assess the immediate effects of a MBI, as well as the feasibility of conducting a definitive RCT.' Randomisation 1:1 using online Research Randomizer. Allocation concealed until baseline assessments completed. Not blinded to treatment allocation during delivery or outcome assessment; independent researcher blinded to allocation conducted initial analysis. (Methods, Design; Methods, Randomisation)
studies.treatment_vs_prevention: Treatment — participants have a diagnosis of persistent pain (chronic pain) required for enrollment, and the study tests intervention effects on pain-related outcomes in this existing condition. 'Patients were eligible if they were... living with persistent pain [i.e., with a diagnosis of persistent pain or having had pain for more than 3 months]' (Methods, Participants, paragraph 2).
studies.confidence_why: • total_n — 147 total randomized confirmed, but per-arm randomized N not explicitly stated (only completer N of 37 MBI and 34 control given in Table 2); arm-level randomized N inferred as approximately equal given 1:1 allocation. • age_min / age_max — not reported in paper; only mean ages provided. • digital_component_raw — MP3 player and device download are borderline; classified as non-digital (analog portable media) based on field definition, but could be interpreted as digital delivery.
studies.active_comparator_name: Distraction audio — sequential readings from 'The English Village: History and Traditions' (non-fiction book), 15-minute audio recordings, matched for time, pacing, and narrator voice to MBI audios. Human review needed.
studies.outcomes_coded: Pain | Anxiety | Depression | Wellbeing-QoL | Mindfulness trait-state | Self-efficacy-confidence | Feasibility-acceptability | Intervention adherence-fidelity

studies.authors: Hölzel, B. K., Hoge, E. A., Greve, D. N., Gard, T., Creswell, J. D., Brown, K. W., Barrett, L. F., Schwartz, C., Vaitl, D., & Lazar, S. W.
studies.title: Neural mechanisms of symptom improvements in generalized anxiety disorder following mindfulness training
studies.abstract: Mindfulness training aims to impact emotion regulation. Generalized anxiety disorder (GAD) symptoms can be successfully addressed through mindfulness-based interventions. This preliminary study is the first to investigate neural mechanisms of symptom improvements in GAD following mindfulness training. Furthermore, we compared brain activation between GAD patients and healthy participants at baseline. 26 patients with a current DSM-IV GAD diagnosis were randomized to an 8-week Mindfulness Based Stress Reduction (MBSR, N = 15) or a stress management education (SME, N = 11) active control program. 26 healthy participants were included for baseline comparisons. BOLD response was assessed with fMRI during affect labeling of angry and neutral facial expressions. At baseline, GAD patients showed higher amygdala activation than healthy participants in response to neutral, but not angry faces, suggesting that ambiguous stimuli reveal stronger reactivity in GAD patients. In patients, amygdala activation in response to neutral faces decreased following both interventions. BOLD response in ventrolateral prefrontal regions (VLPFC) showed greater increase in MBSR than SME participants. Functional connectivity between amygdala and PFC regions increased significantly pre- to post-intervention within the MBSR, but not SME group. Both, change in VLPFC activation and amygdala–prefrontal connectivity were correlated with change in Beck Anxiety Inventory (BAI) scores, suggesting clinical relevance of these changes. Amygdala–prefrontal connectivity turned from negative coupling (typically seen in down-regulation of emotions), to positive coupling; potentially suggesting a unique mechanism of mindfulness. Findings suggest that in GAD, mindfulness training leads to changes in fronto-limbic areas crucial for the regulation of emotion; these changes correspond with reported symptom improvements.
studies.total_n: 26 GAD patients (MBSR N=15, SME N=11) plus 26 healthy controls for baseline comparisons. Note: 29 GAD patients were originally recruited; 3 dropped out. The randomized N for the intervention trial is 26 GAD patients. "29 GAD patients were recruited to participate in the MRI study... Complete data sets were thus available from 26 GAD patients." (Methods, Participants, paragraph 1). The healthy controls were not randomized to intervention.
studies.age_mean: 37.9 (GAD patients); 35.7 (healthy participants). Weighted mean for GAD intervention arms: 38.5 (MBSR, n=15) and 35.6 (SME, n=11). Weighted mean for full GAD sample = (15×38.5 + 11×35.6)/26 = 37.27 (calculated; flagged in confidence_why).
studies.age_describe: GAD patients: mean 37.9 years (SD 12.2); Healthy participants: mean 35.7 years (SD 9.3). GAD MBSR subgroup: mean 38.5 years (SD 13.3); GAD SME subgroup: mean 35.6 years (SD 10.8). "Age mean years (SD): GAD 37.9 (12.2), Healthy 35.7 (9.3)" (Table 1).
studies.participants: 26 GAD patients (14 females, 12 males) with a current DSM-IV GAD diagnosis, and 26 healthy demographically matched individuals (16 females, 10 males). "All participants were right-handed, had no significant previous meditation experience (≤10 sessions) and complied with scanner safety requirements. The groups did not significantly differ in age, gender, and education level." (Methods, Participants, paragraph 2). Mean education: GAD 17.5 years (SD 2.5), Healthy 16.9 years (SD 1.9).
studies.eligibility: Inclusion criteria (GAD patients): current DSM-IV GAD diagnosis confirmed by SCID; right-handed; no significant previous meditation experience (≤10 sessions); compliance with scanner safety requirements; if medicated, stable dose for at least two months prior to enrollment and agreement to remain on stable dose. Inclusion criteria (healthy participants): no DSM-IV Axis I disorder; no medications that alter cerebral blood flow or metabolism; right-handed; no significant previous meditation experience. "Patients were included if they met a current DSM-IV GAD diagnosis." "Healthy participants were included if they did not meet any DSM-IV Axis I disorder, and did not take medications that alter cerebral blood flow or metabolism." (Methods, Participants, paragraphs 2–3). Exclusion criteria: not explicitly listed as a separate section, but implied by the above (e.g., left-handedness, prior meditation experience >10 sessions, scanner safety non-compliance).
studies.population_vulnerable: Not a vulnerable population — participants are adults with a clinical GAD diagnosis recruited for a treatment trial; no specific health disparity or structural disadvantage criterion is described. "GAD patients were recruited from among participants of a larger RCT" (Methods, Participants, paragraph 2).
studies.location: Inferred: Boston/Charlestown, Massachusetts, USA (inferred from author affiliations: Massachusetts General Hospital, 120 2nd Ave., Charlestown, MA; and acknowledgment: "This research was carried out at the Athinoula A. Martinos Center for Biomedical Imaging at the Massachusetts General Hospital" — not explicitly stated as study location in the paper body).
studies.mental_health: Current DSM-IV Generalized Anxiety Disorder (GAD) diagnosis required for enrollment in the patient group, confirmed by Structured Clinical Interview for DSM-IV (SCID). "Patients were included if they met a current DSM-IV GAD diagnosis." (Methods, Participants, paragraph 3).
studies.physical_health: N/A — no physical health enrollment criterion
studies.arms: 2 arms (intervention trial for GAD patients): (1) MBSR — Mindfulness Based Stress Reduction, N=15; (2) SME — Stress Management Education (active control), N=11. Additionally, 26 healthy participants included for baseline comparisons only (not randomized to intervention). "26 patients with a current DSM-IV GAD diagnosis were randomized to an 8-week Mindfulness Based Stress Reduction (MBSR, N = 15) or a stress management education (SME, N = 11) active control program." (Abstract).
studies.meditation_intervention: Mindfulness Based Stress Reduction (MBSR): explicitly named. 8-week manualized program. "consists of once-weekly, teacher-led group meetings (with duration of two hours in the current study) plus one 'day of mindfulness' in the sixth week of the course." Practices include sitting and walking meditation, yoga exercises, and the body scan. Participants also receive stress education. Home practice required: "participants are instructed to practice mindfulness exercises at home (with the help of an audio recording)." Average home practice: 1116 min (SD=499 min). Average classes attended: 7.27 (SD=0.59). (Methods, Interventions, paragraphs 1–2).
studies.intervention_delivery: In-person group format. Weekly 2-hour group sessions led by a teacher (Zayda Vallejo conducted MBSR courses, per Acknowledgments). 8 weeks plus one full-day retreat in week 6. Home practice supported by audio recordings. "once-weekly, teacher-led group meetings (with duration of two hours in the current study)" (Methods, Interventions, paragraph 1).
studies.digital_component_raw: No digital component. Audio recordings provided for home practice support. "participants are instructed to practice mindfulness exercises at home (with the help of an audio recording)" (Methods, Interventions, paragraph 1). Audio recordings are analog/CD-type materials, not digital delivery of the intervention.
studies.intervention_tailor: No tailoring reported. The paper describes standard MBSR as developed by Kabat-Zinn (1990) applied to GAD patients without reporting cultural or population-specific modifications.
studies.comparison: Stress Management Education (SME): active control program designed to match MBSR structurally. "The stress management education (SME) program was designed as an active control stress reduction intervention for MBSR to disentangle the effects of the mindfulness practice from other, potentially effective elements of the group program, such as a supportive social environment, instructor attention, participants' expectations, and physical exercise." Same in-class and home exercise time as MBSR, including a 'day of stress reduction' in week 6. Components: gentle physical exercises (matching yoga), nutrition and healthy lifestyle education (matching stress education). Jennifer Johnston conducted SME courses. Average home practice: 868 min (SD=413 min). Average classes attended: 7.00 (SD=0.76). (Methods, Interventions, paragraphs 3–4).
studies.assessment_time: T0 = Baseline/pre-intervention (0 weeks); T1 = Post-intervention (~8–9 weeks). "The scans took place within three weeks before and after the intervention period." MBSR mean inter-scan interval = 60.3 days (SD=4.4); SME mean = 63.5 days (SD=6.8). Converting: ~8.6 weeks (MBSR) and ~9.1 weeks (SME) from baseline to post. (Methods, Experimental Paradigm, paragraph 1).
studies.assessment_nature: Self-report questionnaires (BAI, PSS) and neuroimaging/physiological measures (fMRI BOLD response, functional connectivity). "BOLD response was assessed with fMRI during affect labeling of angry and neutral facial expressions." "The Beck Anxiety Inventory (BAI)... GAD patients completed the BAI before and after the intervention." "The 10-item version of the Perceived Stress Scale (PSS)" (Methods, Self-report data and fMRI sections).
studies.outcomes_all:
1. Anxiety severity — Beck Anxiety Inventory (BAI; 21-item multiple choice questionnaire) 
2. Perceived stress — Perceived Stress Scale (PSS; 10-item validated measure) 
3. Amygdala BOLD response — fMRI during affect labeling of angry, neutral, and happy facial expressions 
4. Frontal/insular cortex BOLD response — fMRI, including VLPFC (pars opercularis, pars triangularis, rostral middle frontal cortex) 
5. Amygdala–prefrontal functional connectivity — fMRI connectivity analysis using right amygdala seed 
6. Mindfulness trait-state — not explicitly mentioned
studies.outcomes_primary: Unclear — authors do not explicitly designate a single primary outcome. The study investigates neural mechanisms (fMRI BOLD response and functional connectivity) as the main focus, with BAI as the clinical correlate. "This preliminary study is the first to investigate neural mechanisms of symptom improvements in GAD following mindfulness training." (Abstract). No formal primary outcome designation is stated.
studies.outcome_timepoints: T0 = Baseline/pre-intervention (0 weeks); T1 = Post-intervention (~8.6–9.1 weeks, approximately 8–9 weeks). BAI and PSS assessed pre and post intervention. fMRI assessed pre and post intervention for GAD patients; healthy controls assessed at baseline only. "GAD patients completed the BAI before and after the intervention." (Methods, Self-report data, paragraph 1).
studies.recruitment: GAD patients recruited from participants of a larger RCT (Hoge et al., in press). Healthy participants recruited through local newspapers and email lists. "GAD patients were recruited from among participants of a larger RCT (Hoge et al., in press). Healthy participants were recruited through local newspapers and email lists advertising a stress-reduction intervention." (Methods, Participants, paragraph 2). Recruitment dates not reported.
studies.study_purpose: "The present randomized trial is an initial investigation of neural mechanisms underlying GAD symptom improvements following an eight-week mindfulness-based stress reduction (MBSR) program relative to a structurally equivalent, active control intervention." (Introduction, final paragraph).
studies.study_design: Randomized controlled trial (RCT) with active control; preliminary/pilot study. Block randomization based on time of enrollment. "Participants were assigned to either the MBSR program or the active control intervention, the stress management education (SME) program, based on the time of enrolment into the study (block randomization)" (Methods, Participants, paragraph 1). Blinding not reported. Healthy control group included for baseline comparisons only (not randomized).
studies.treatment_vs_prevention: Treatment — participants required to have a current DSM-IV GAD diagnosis at enrollment; the study tests MBSR efficacy for an existing anxiety disorder. "Patients were included if they met a current DSM-IV GAD diagnosis." (Methods, Participants, paragraph 3).
studies.confidence_why:
• age_mean — weighted mean for full GAD sample calculated from arm-level means (15×38.5 + 11×35.6)/26 = 37.27; not directly reported for full GAD sample as a single figure (Table 1 reports 37.9 for all GAD combined, which is used as primary value). 
• age_min / age_max — not reported anywhere in the paper. 
• total_n — 29 were randomized but 3 dropped out; 26 completed. The paper states 26 patients had complete data sets; the randomized N is technically 29 but the paper treats 26 as the analytic sample. Flagged. 
• location — inferred from author affiliations and acknowledgment; not explicitly stated as study location in paper body. 
• time_baseline_to_post — calculated from reported mean inter-scan intervals (~60–63 days ≈ 8.6–9 weeks); not stated as a fixed number of weeks.
studies.active_comparator_name: Stress Management Education (SME) — active control program matching MBSR in structure, including gentle physical exercises and nutrition/healthy lifestyle education, but without mindfulness practice
studies.outcomes_coded: Anxiety | Stress-distress | Brain imaging-neural | Emotion regulation
studies.categories_flags:
• active_comparator_name — human review recommended to confirm SME classification as 'Active-Non-mindfulness psychological' vs. other active category. 
• n_assessment_timepoints — coded as 2 (baseline + post) for GAD patients; healthy controls only assessed at baseline (1 timepoint). Coded based on GAD intervention sample. 
• time_baseline_to_post — calculated as ~9 weeks from reported mean inter-scan intervals (~60–63 days); not explicitly stated as a fixed week count. 
• total_n — 29 randomized, 26 completed; paper uses 26 as primary sample throughout.

studies.authors: Hsiao, Y.-Y., Tofighi, D., Kruger, E. S., Van Horn, M. L., MacKinnon, D. P., & Witkiewitz, K.
studies.title: The (Lack of) Replication of Self-Reported Mindfulness as a Mechanism of Change in Mindfulness-Based Relapse Prevention for Substance Use Disorders
studies.abstract: The development and evaluation of mindfulness-based interventions for a variety of psychological and medical disorders have grown exponentially over the past 20 years. Yet, calls for increasing the rigor of mindfulness research and recognition of the difficulties of conducting research on the topic of mindfulness have also increased. One of the major difficulties is the measurement of mindfulness, with varying definitions across studies and ambiguity with respect to the meaning of mindfulness. There is also concern about the reproducibility of findings given few attempts at replication. The current secondary analysis addressed the issue of reproducibility and robustness of the construct of self-reported mindfulness across two separate randomized clinical trials of mindfulness-based relapse prevention (MBRP), as an aftercare treatment for substance use disorder. Specifically, we tested the robustness of our previously published findings, which identified a latent construct of mindfulness as a significant mediator of the effect of MBRP on reducing craving following treatment. First, we attempted to replicate the findings in a separate randomized clinical trial of MBRP. Second, we conducted sensitivity analyses to test the assumption of the no-omitted confounder bias in a mediation model. The effect of MBRP on self-reported mindfulness and overall mediation effect failed to replicate in a new sample. The effect of self-reported mindfulness in predicting craving following treatment did replicate and was robust to the no-omitted confounder bias. The results of this work shine a light on the difficulties in the measurement of mindfulness and the importance of examining the robustness of findings.
studies.total_n: 366 (Study 1: n=168; Study 2: n=198). "we focused on the MBRP and TAU conditions in both study 1 (n = 168) and study 2 (n = 198)" (Method, Participants, paragraph 1). Note: these are the subsets used in secondary analyses, not the full original trial Ns.
studies.age_mean: Not reported (weighted mean not calculable; only study-level means provided without arm-level breakdown)
studies.age_describe: Study 1: mean age 40.5 (SD = 10.3); Study 2: mean age 38.2 (SD = 10.9). "with an average age of 40.5 (SD = 10.3)" and "with an average age of 38.2 (SD = 10.9)" (Method, Participants, paragraphs 2–3).
studies.participants: Adults with substance use disorders recruited from a private, nonprofit agency providing comprehensive care for alcohol and drug use disorders. Study 1: 63.7% male, 53.6% non-Hispanic white, 29.8% African American, average age 40.5. Study 2: 75.1% male, 52.8% non-Hispanic white, 24.6% African American, average age 38.2. "Participants were recruited from a private, nonprofit agency that provided comprehensive care for alcohol and drug use disorders." (Method, Participants, paragraph 1).
studies.eligibility: Inclusion criteria: ages 18 to 70, fluent in English, completed intensive outpatient or inpatient treatment in the previous 2 weeks. Exclusion criteria: psychosis, dementia, imminent suicide risk, significant withdrawal risk, or a need for more intensive treatment. "Participants were included if they were between the ages of 18 to 70, fluent in English, and had completed intensive outpatient or inpatient treatment in the previous 2 weeks. Exclusion criteria included the following: psychosis, dementia, imminent suicide risk, significant withdrawal risk, or a need for more intensive treatment." (Method, Participants, paragraph 1).
studies.population_vulnerable: Not a vulnerable population — participants have substance use disorders and are in aftercare treatment, but no specific health disparity or structural disadvantage criterion (e.g., racial-ethnic minority, low-income) was used as an enrollment criterion. The sample is racially diverse but not recruited on that basis. "Participants were recruited from a private, nonprofit agency that provided comprehensive care for alcohol and drug use disorders." (Method, Participants, paragraph 1).
studies.location: Inferred: Seattle, Washington area, USA (inferred from author affiliations at University of New Mexico and University of Washington IRB approval, and original studies conducted at a private nonprofit agency; not explicitly stated in paper body). "All procedures performed in our study were approved by the institutional review board at the University of Washington." (Compliance with Ethical Standards).
studies.mental_health: N/A — no psychiatric enrollment criterion. Substance use disorder is the clinical context (participants had completed inpatient/outpatient treatment), but no formal psychiatric diagnosis or validated symptom threshold was required for enrollment beyond completion of substance use treatment.
studies.physical_health: N/A — no physical health enrollment criterion explicitly stated beyond completion of intensive outpatient or inpatient treatment for substance use disorders.
studies.arms: Two arms per study (secondary analysis of two separate RCTs). Each study compared: (1) MBRP (mindfulness-based relapse prevention) vs. (2) TAU (treatment as usual). Study 1: MBRP + TAU (n=168 total); Study 2: MBRP + TAU (n=198 total; original study 2 had three arms but only MBRP and TAU were used here). "we focused on the MBRP and TAU conditions in both study 1 (n = 168) and study 2 (n = 198)" (Method, paragraph 3).
studies.meditation_intervention: Mindfulness-Based Relapse Prevention (MBRP): 8-week program following the MBRP treatment manual (Bowen et al. 2011a). Weekly 2-hour group sessions with groups of 6–10 persons facilitated by two therapists. Each session included meditation practices and exercises related to five central themes: automatic-pilot and its relationship to relapse, recognizing thoughts and emotions in relation to triggers, integrating mindfulness practices into daily life, practicing skills in high-risk situations, and the role of thoughts in relapse. Sessions began with a 20–30 minute guided meditation, followed by experiential exercises, discussions, and review of assignments. Participants assigned daily exercises and given meditation recordings for individual practice between sessions. Therapists held professional positions (master's degrees, doctoral training, or doctoral degrees in clinical psychology), participated in intensive training, engaged in daily meditation, received weekly supervision, and had personal mindfulness practice and experience attending intensive mindfulness meditation retreats. "The MBRP group received weekly, 2-hour group sessions that followed the MBRP treatment manual (Bowen et al. 2011a)." (Method, Procedure, MBRP section).
studies.intervention_delivery: In-person group format. Weekly 2-hour sessions, groups of 6–10 persons, two therapists per group. Therapists held master's or doctoral degrees in clinical psychology. Meditation recordings provided for home practice between sessions. "Two therapists facilitated groups of six to ten persons." (Method, Procedure, MBRP section).
studies.digital_component_raw: No digital component. Meditation recordings were provided for individual home practice between sessions, but the intervention itself was delivered in-person. "Participants were assigned daily exercises and were given meditation recordings for individual practice between group sessions." (Method, Procedure, MBRP section).
studies.intervention_tailor: No tailoring reported. The intervention followed the standard MBRP treatment manual without reported modifications. "The MBRP group received weekly, 2-hour group sessions that followed the MBRP treatment manual (Bowen et al. 2011a)." (Method, Procedure, MBRP section).
studies.comparison: Treatment as Usual (TAU): Standard outpatient aftercare designed to maintain abstinence through a twelve-step, process-oriented format. Primary treatment component was group sessions on specific topics (rational thinking skills, grief and loss, assertiveness, self-esteem, goal setting, effects of alcohol and other drugs on interpersonal relations and experience). TAU groups lasted 1.5 hours and met one to two times per week based on client need. No regular homework assigned. TAU therapists were licensed chemical dependency counselors with varying professional degrees. "The TAU condition received standard outpatient aftercare that was designed to maintain abstinence through a twelve-step, process-oriented format." (Method, Procedure, TAU section).
studies.assessment_time: Study 1: T0 = Baseline (0 weeks); T1 = Mid-treatment (approximately 4 weeks, not used in current analyses); T2 = Posttreatment (8 weeks); T3 = 2-month follow-up (16.8 weeks); T4 = 4-month follow-up (33.6 weeks). Study 2: T0 = Baseline (0 weeks); T1 = Posttreatment (8 weeks); T2 = 2-month follow-up (16.8 weeks); T3 = 4-month follow-up (33.6 weeks); T4 = 6-month follow-up (25.2 weeks); T5 = 12-month follow-up (50.4 weeks). Current analyses used baseline through 4-month follow-up. "Study 1 administered the PACS at baseline, mid-treatment, posttreatment, and 2- and 4-month follow-ups. Study 2 administered the PACS at baseline, posttreatment, and 2-, 4-, 6-, and 12-month follow-ups. For the current study, we examined craving from baseline through the 4-month follow-up." (Measures, Alcohol and Drug Craving section).
studies.assessment_nature: Self-report only. All measures (AAQ, FFMQ subscales, PACS) were self-report questionnaires. "both studies relied exclusively on self-report measures of mindfulness, acceptance, and craving" (Limitations and Future Directions, paragraph 1).
studies.outcomes_all: 1. Acceptance — modified Acceptance and Action Questionnaire (AAQ; 12 items: 9 original + 3 additional items assessing acceptance of uncomfortable present moment experiences; 7-point Likert scale). 2. Mindfulness — Five Facet Mindfulness Questionnaire (FFMQ) acting with awareness subscale (8 items, 5-point Likert scale) and nonjudgment subscale (8 items, 5-point Likert scale). 3. Alcohol and Drug Craving — adapted Penn Alcohol Craving Scale (PACS; 5 items assessing frequency, intensity, duration of craving and overall rating for prior week).
studies.outcomes_primary: Unclear — authors do not explicitly designate a primary outcome. The study is a secondary analysis focused on mediation: self-reported mindfulness as mediator and craving as the outcome. "we tested the robustness of our previously published findings, which identified a latent construct of mindfulness as a significant mediator of the effect of MBRP on reducing craving following treatment" (Abstract).
studies.outcome_timepoints: T0 = Baseline (0 weeks); T1 = Posttreatment (8 weeks); T2 = 2-month follow-up (16.8 weeks); T3 = 4-month follow-up (33.6 weeks). [Study 1 also had mid-treatment assessment excluded from current analyses; Study 2 had 6- and 12-month assessments not used in current analyses.] "For the current study, we examined craving from baseline through the 4-month follow-up." (Measures, Alcohol and Drug Craving section).
studies.recruitment: Participants were recruited from a private, nonprofit agency providing comprehensive care for alcohol and drug use disorders. Study 1 recruited from 1 site within the agency (2007–2008); Study 2 recruited from 2 sites within the same agency (2009–2012). "study 1 participants were recruited from 2007 to 2008 and study 2 participants were recruited from 2009 to 2012" (Discussion, paragraph 5).
studies.study_purpose: "The goal of the current study was to extend the findings of Witkiewitz et al. by examining whether the findings replicated in a new sample of individuals who received MBRP and completed all of the same assessments and to test whether the mediation model was robust to the no-omitted-confounder assumption." (Introduction, final paragraph).
studies.study_design: Secondary analysis of two separate randomized clinical trials (RCTs). Both original studies used randomization to MBRP vs. TAU (and a third arm in Study 2). Current paper is a secondary analysis examining mediation replication and sensitivity analyses across the two datasets. "The current secondary analysis addressed the issue of reproducibility and robustness of the construct of self-reported mindfulness across two separate randomized clinical trials of mindfulness-based relapse prevention (MBRP)" (Abstract).
studies.treatment_vs_prevention: Treatment — participants had substance use disorders and had completed intensive outpatient or inpatient treatment; MBRP was delivered as aftercare treatment for an existing condition. "as an aftercare treatment for substance use disorder" (Abstract).
studies.confidence_why: • total_n — the Ns reported (168 and 198) are the subsets used in secondary analyses (MBRP + TAU arms only), not the full original trial randomized Ns; flagged as secondary analysis limitation. • age_mean — weighted mean across studies not calculable because arm-level Ns within each study are not reported separately; only study-level means provided. • location — study location not explicitly stated in paper body; inferred from IRB (University of Washington) and original study context. • age_min/age_max — derived from eligibility criteria (18–70) rather than directly reported sample statistics. • assessment_time — months converted to weeks using 1 month = 4.2 weeks convention.
studies.outcomes_coded: Mindfulness trait-state | Substance-alcohol use
studies.categories_flags: • outcomes_coded — craving is the primary outcome; coded under 'Substance-alcohol use' as it measures craving for alcohol/drugs in a substance use disorder sample; could also be considered a psychological wellbeing measure. • n_assessment_timepoints — set to 4 (baseline, post, 2-month, 4-month) reflecting the timepoints used in current analyses; original studies had more timepoints. • followup_longest — set to 34 weeks (4-month follow-up × 4.2 = 16.8 weeks from post, ~33.6 weeks from baseline), rounded; Study 2 had 12-month follow-up but not used in current analyses. • setting — coded as Healthcare based on recruitment from a nonprofit substance use treatment agency; could also be Community. • physical_health_threshold — completion of inpatient/outpatient substance use treatment required, but this is a treatment-seeking criterion rather than a physical health threshold per se.

studies.authors: Hülsheger, U. R., Feinholdt, A., & Nübold, A.
studies.title: A low-dose mindfulness intervention and recovery from work: Effects on psychological detachment, sleep quality, and sleep duration
studies.abstract: Although playing a crucial role for the prevention of long-term health impairment, interventions aiming at the improvement of employees' recovery processes are still scarce. In this study, we therefore investigated the effectiveness of a low-dose mindfulness intervention for recovery from work. In addition, differential responding to the treatment in terms of treatment-by-baseline interactions was studied. A sample of 140 employees participated in a randomized field experiment with a self-training and a wait-list control group. Three central recovery processes (psychological detachment, sleep quality, and sleep duration) were assessed with event-sampling methodology involving daily measurements over 10 workdays. Growth curve analyses revealed intervention effects on sleep quality and sleep duration. No effects were found for psychological detachment after work and for the proposed treatment-by-baseline interactions. Our findings are discussed in the context of occupational health promotion in general and mindfulness-based interventions in specific.
studies.journal: Journal of Occupational and Organizational Psychology
studies.total_n: 140. 'The final sample therefore consisted of 140 participants (67, intervention group; 73, control group)' (Methods, Participants, paragraph 3)
studies.age_mean: 37.0. 'On average, they were 37 years of age (SD = 13.3)' (Methods, Participants, paragraph 3)
studies.age_describe: Overall mean age = 37 years (SD = 13.3). Intervention group M = 34.27; Control group M = 39.96 (p = .01; Cohen's d = −.45). 'On average, they were 37 years of age (SD = 13.3)' (Methods, Participants, paragraph 3)
studies.participants: Employees recruited from a broad range of organizations in Germany. 97 were female (69.3%), one participant failed to indicate gender. Held a variety of jobs including clerks, hairdressers, merchants, consultants, kindergarten teachers, health care professionals, civil servants, nurses, managers, etc. Mean organizational tenure 11.2 years (SD = 11.5). 'The sample was a convenience sample recruited from a broad range of organizations in Germany.' (Methods, Participants, paragraph 1)
studies.eligibility: Inclusion: Employees from organizations in Germany willing to participate in a diary study. No formal inclusion/exclusion criteria are explicitly stated beyond being employed. 'The sample was a convenience sample recruited from a broad range of organizations in Germany. The majority of participants was approached directly and mostly in person.' (Methods, Participants, paragraph 1). No explicit exclusion criteria reported.
studies.population_vulnerable: Not a vulnerable population — participants are general working adults recruited from a broad range of organizations; no health disparity or structural disadvantage criterion reported. 'The sample was a convenience sample recruited from a broad range of organizations in Germany.' (Methods, Participants, paragraph 1)
studies.location: Germany. 'The sample was a convenience sample recruited from a broad range of organizations in Germany.' (Methods, Participants, paragraph 1)
studies.mental_health: N/A — no psychiatric enrollment criterion
studies.physical_health: N/A — no physical health enrollment criterion
studies.arms: 2 arms. (1) Self-training mindfulness intervention group (n = 67); (2) Wait-list control group (n = 73). 'participants were randomly assigned to the intervention group or a wait-list control group' (Methods, Procedure, paragraph 1)
studies.meditation_intervention: A low-dose self-training mindfulness intervention developed by Hülsheger et al. (2013), building upon key elements of MBCT (Segal, Williams, & Teasdale, 2002) and MBSR (Kabat-Zinn, 1982, 1990). Integrated into a paper-and-pencil diary booklet spanning 10 workdays (2 workweeks). Included daily guided mindfulness meditations and informal mindfulness exercises: (1) Three-minute Breathing Space, (2) Body Scan, (3) Mindful Routine Activity, and (4) Loving Kindness Meditation (progressing from self to friend, neutral person, and disliked person). Audio files with guided meditations were provided for each exercise. Participants spent on average 10.5 min (SD = 7.0) per day on practices. No formal group meetings, retreats, or contact with a mindfulness trainer. 'The condensed intervention used in this study spans two workweeks and involves brief mindfulness practices (about 10 min) that can readily be integrated into participants' (work) life' (Introduction, paragraph 7)
studies.intervention_delivery: Self-administered, self-guided format via paper-and-pencil diary booklet with audio files for guided meditations. No live instructor, no group meetings. 'a pure self-training intervention and does not involve formal group meetings, retreats or contacts with a mindfulness trainer or coach' (Introduction, paragraph 7). Audio files provided for each exercise. Delivered over 10 workdays.
studies.digital_component_raw: No digital component. Audio files were provided for guided meditations as a complement to the paper-and-pencil self-training booklet. 'participants first received some brief written information as well as audio files with guided meditations' (Methods, The self-training intervention, paragraph 1). The primary delivery mode was paper-and-pencil diary booklet; audio files are analog/CD-type supplementary materials, not a digital platform delivering the intervention.
studies.intervention_tailor: No tailoring reported beyond the general adaptation to working adults (brief practices, self-administered format). 'daily mindfulness practices that were initially designed for clinical applications and targeted pain and other psychological symptoms were adapted to better fit work-related issues, such as work stress, work–life balance, and self-care' (Introduction, paragraph 6). This adaptation was part of the original intervention design by Hülsheger et al. (2013), not a new tailoring for this study.
studies.comparison: Wait-list control group (n = 73). Participants in the control group received the same paper-and-pencil diary booklet for 10 workdays but did not receive the self-training intervention during the study period. 'participants in the control group received a booklet with the self-training intervention after completion of the study' (Methods, Procedure, paragraph 2). No active intervention content was provided during the study period.
studies.assessment_time: T0 = Baseline general survey (0 weeks, before diary start); T1 = Daily diary assessments over 10 workdays (~2 weeks). No separate post-intervention or follow-up assessment beyond the 10-day diary period. 'Both groups participated in a diary study spanning 10 workdays and involving three daily measurement occasions (in the morning, at the end of work, and at bedtime).' (Methods, Procedure, paragraph 1). Approximately T1 = 2 weeks (10 workdays).
studies.assessment_nature: Self-report questionnaires only. General survey (trait mindfulness, psychological detachment, sleep quality, sleep duration, demographics) and daily diary surveys (sleep quality, sleep duration, work hours, mindfulness, psychological detachment). 'Data collection consisted of two parts: A general survey and the diary part including brief daily surveys that had to be answered three times a day' (Methods, Measures, paragraph 1). All items were self-report on 5-point Likert scales.
studies.outcomes_all:
1. Trait mindfulness — Mindfulness Attention and Awareness Scale (MAAS; Brown & Ryan, 2003), German version (Michalak et al., 2008), 15 items, 5-point Likert scale (general survey baseline)
2. State/daily mindfulness during work — 5-item state version of MAAS (Brown & Ryan, 2003), German translation, 5-point Likert scale (daily diary, end of work)
3. Psychological detachment from work — Recovery Experience Questionnaire (Sonnentag & Fritz, 2007), 4-item scale, 5-point Likert scale (general survey baseline and daily diary bedtime)
4. Sleep quality — Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index item (Buysse et al., 1989), single item, 5-point Likert scale (general survey baseline and daily diary morning)
5. Sleep duration — Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index item (Buysse et al., 1989), single item in hours (general survey baseline and daily diary morning)
6. Work hours — single item ('How many hours did you work today?') (daily diary, end of work, control variable)
(Methods, Measures, paragraphs 2–8)
studies.outcomes_primary: Unclear — authors do not explicitly designate a single primary outcome. The study focuses on three recovery outcomes: psychological detachment, sleep quality, and sleep duration. 'we focus on three key aspects, namely psychological detachment from work, sleep quality, and sleep duration' (Recovery from work section, paragraph 2)
studies.outcome_timepoints: T0 = Baseline general survey (0 weeks); T1 = Daily diary assessments over 10 workdays (days 1–10, approximately 0–2 weeks). No separate post-intervention or follow-up timepoint beyond the 10-day diary period. 'Both groups participated in a diary study spanning 10 workdays' (Methods, Procedure, paragraph 1)
studies.recruitment: Convenience sample from a broad range of organizations in Germany. 'The majority of participants was approached directly and mostly in person. Some participants were contacted via mail first. Others received a flyer with an invitation to the study from colleagues or supervisors.' 220 diary booklets distributed, 148 returned (67.3% response rate). No recruitment dates reported. (Methods, Participants, paragraph 1)
studies.study_purpose: 'we aim to contribute to this line of research by testing the effects of a low-dose self-training mindfulness intervention on recovery processes' — specifically psychological detachment, sleep quality, and sleep duration, and differential treatment-by-baseline interactions. (Introduction, paragraph 2)
studies.study_design: Randomized field experiment (randomized controlled trial) with two arms: self-training intervention group and wait-list control group. Combined with experience sampling methodology (ESM) involving daily measurements over 10 workdays. 'we used a randomized field experiment in combination with experience sampling methodology (ESM)' (The present study, paragraph 1). Randomization method not specified. No blinding reported.
studies.treatment_vs_prevention: Enhancement — participants are general working adults with no clinical diagnosis or symptom threshold required for enrollment. The study targets improvement of recovery processes (psychological detachment, sleep quality, sleep duration) in a non-clinical employee sample. 'The present sample was a non-clinical sample of employees.' (Discussion, paragraph 4). No prevention endpoint for a specific disorder is measured.
