studies.authors: Barghi Irani, Z., & Dehghan Saber, L.
studies.title: The Comparison of the Effectiveness of Mindfulness Based Therapy and Spiritual Therapy on Irrational Beliefs and Anxiety in the Older Women
studies.abstract: People in the old age are increasingly exposed to mental disorders such as anxiety and depression, due to the prevalence of numerous losses such as spouse, relatives, friends, occupation, social and economic status, beliefs, and suchlike. Therefore, the aim of the current study was to compare the effectiveness of mindfulness-based therapy (MBT) and spiritual therapy (ST) on irrational beliefs and anxiety in the older women. This was a semi-experimental study with pretest-posttest and follow-up with a control group design. The statistical population included all the elderly women who were the member of Jahandidegan center, Tehran among whom 45 (three groups containing 15 people) with the mean age of 60-70 (SD=4.58) were selected using convenience sampling method along with inclusion and exclusion criteria and assigned randomly into two experimental and one control group. Participants underwent Kabat's MBT and Gallanter and Siegel's ST in 90-minute sessions twice a week, and a follow-up test was performed one month after the posttest. Used to collect data were Jones's Irrational Belief and Spielberger's Overt and Covert Anxiety scales. The obtained data were analyzed by univariate analysis of covariance altogether with Bonferroni post-hoc. The results showed that both treatments were effective in reducing irrational beliefs and overt and covert anxiety, and this effect was persistent during the follow-up period (P<0.001). The comparison of MBT and ST showed that although there is no difference between the effectiveness of the two kinds of therapy on irrational beliefs, MBT is more effective than ST in reducing overt and covert anxiety (P<.001). According to the results, mindfulness-based and spiritual therapy can be used as effective interventions for reducing irrational beliefs and anxiety when it comes to designing programs regarding the promotion of mental health in the elderly.
studies.total_n: 45. 'Among whom 45 (three groups containing 15 people)... were selected using convenience sampling method along with inclusion and exclusion criteria and assigned randomly into two experimental and one control group.' (Abstract, paragraph 1). Note: The Methods section states 60 were initially screened, then 45 were selected and randomized.
studies.age_mean: Not reported. Only an age range with SD is provided: 'mean age of 60-70 (SD=4.58)'
studies.age_describe: Age range 60-70 years with SD=4.58. 'with the mean age of 60-70 (SD=4.58)' (Abstract, paragraph 1). No single mean value is reported.
studies.age_min: 60. 'mean age of 60-70' and inclusion criterion 'age range 60-70 years' (Methods, Participants section)
studies.participants: Elderly women members of the Jahandidegan (Jahandidegan) center in Tehran, Iran. All participants were female, aged 60-70 years. 'The statistical population included all the elderly women who were the member of Jahandidegan center, Tehran' (Abstract, paragraph 1). Three groups of 15 participants each: mindfulness group, spiritual therapy group, and control group.
studies.eligibility: Inclusion criteria: (1) age range 60-70 years; (2) high score on the overt and covert anxiety scale. Exclusion criteria: (1) disability or specific physical or mental illness; (2) neurological-cognitive disorder and Alzheimer's disease; (3) simultaneous participation in a treatment program or social work interventions. 'ملاکهای ورود عبارت از (1) دامنه سنی 70-60 سال، 2) نمره بالا در مقیاس اضطراب آشکار و پنهان بودند و ملاکهای خروج عبارت از (1) معلولیت یا بیماری جسمانی و روانی خاص دیگر، 2) ابتلا به اختلال عصبی-شناختی و بیماری آلزایمر، (3) شرکت همزمان در برنامه درمانی یا مداخلات مددکاری اجتماعی' (Methods, Participants section)
studies.population_vulnerable: Not a vulnerable population — the study targets elderly women in Tehran, Iran, but does not explicitly frame them as experiencing health disparities or structural disadvantage. They are recruited from a community center for the elderly.
studies.location: Tehran, Iran. 'The statistical population included all the elderly women who were the member of Jahandidegan center, Tehran' (Abstract, paragraph 1)
studies.mental_health: High score on the overt and covert anxiety scale required for enrollment. 'نمره بالا در مقیاس اضطراب آشکار و پنهان' [high score on the overt and covert anxiety scale] (Methods, inclusion criteria). Participants were screened with the Spielberger State-Trait Anxiety Inventory and selected based on their anxiety scores.
studies.physical_health: N/A — no physical health enrollment criterion. Physical illness was an exclusion criterion, not an inclusion criterion.
studies.arms: 3 arms. (1) Mindfulness-Based Therapy (MBT) group, n=15; (2) Spiritual Therapy (ST) group, n=15; (3) Control group (waitlist), n=15. 'assigned randomly into two experimental and one control group' (Abstract, paragraph 1)
studies.meditation_intervention: Mindfulness-Based Therapy (MBT) based on Kabat-Zinn (2013). 8 sessions of 90 minutes each, delivered twice per week, in group format at the Jahandidegan center. Content included: Session 1 - introduction, raisin exercise, body scan meditation (30 min), homework; Session 2 - body scan, discussion of homework, thoughts vs. feelings, sitting meditation; Session 3 - seeing/hearing exercise, sitting meditation with breathing, 3-minute breathing space, mindful body movements; Session 4 - breathing/sounds/thoughts attention, stress responses, mindful walking; Session 5 - sitting meditation, second series of mindful body movements; Session 6 - 3-minute breathing space, four meditation practices (1 hour); Session 7 - four-dimensional meditation, pleasant/unpleasant events exercise; Session 8 - review, meditation, coping with obstacles. Home practice assigned each session. 'ذهنآگاهی 8 جلسه 90 دقیقهای بر طبق راهنمای آموزشی کابات زین (2013)' (Methods, Procedure section)
studies.intervention_delivery: In-person group format, 90-minute sessions, twice per week, at the Jahandidegan center in Tehran. 'در کانون جهان دیدگان به صورت گروهی اجرا شد' [delivered in group format at the Jahandidegan center] (Methods, Procedure section). Facilitator qualifications not explicitly reported.
studies.digital_component_raw: No digital component. Sessions were delivered in-person at the Jahandidegan center. No mention of any digital or technology-based delivery. (Methods, Procedure section)
studies.intervention_tailor: No tailoring explicitly reported. The study uses Kabat-Zinn's (2013) mindfulness guide without describing cultural or population-specific adaptations, though the population is elderly Iranian women.
studies.comparison: Two comparison conditions: (1) Spiritual Therapy (ST) group: 10 sessions of 90 minutes each, twice per week, based on the protocol by Lotfi Kashani et al. (2013) / Vaziri and Lotfi Kashani (2013). Content included: Session 1 - introductions, group rules; Session 2 - meaning of spirituality, belief in higher power; Session 3 - self-observation, meditation technique introduction; Session 4 - meditation experiences; Session 5 - concept of infinity and connection to eternal force, loss; Session 6 - forgiveness; Session 7 - forgiveness and anger control; Session 8 - experiences from forgiveness; Session 9 - gratitude and meaning-making; Session 10 (implied). Delivered in group format at the Jahandidegan center. (2) Control group (waitlist): placed on a waiting list during the intervention period; received 5 sessions of 90 minutes after data collection was complete for ethical reasons. 'گروه کنترل در لیست انتظار برای آموزش قرار گرفت' (Methods, Procedure section)
studies.assessment_time: T0 = Baseline (0 weeks); T1 = Post-intervention (approximately 4-5 weeks, based on twice-weekly sessions — MBT: 8 sessions = ~4 weeks; ST: 10 sessions = ~5 weeks); T2 = Follow-up (approximately 8-9 weeks from baseline, one month after post-test). 'a follow-up test was performed one month after the posttest' (Abstract). Note: Exact post-intervention week not explicitly stated; estimated from session frequency.
studies.assessment_nature: Self-report questionnaires only. 'Used to collect data were Jones's Irrational Belief and Spielberger's Overt and Covert Anxiety scales' (Abstract). Both instruments are self-report measures.
studies.outcomes_all: 1. Irrational Beliefs — Jones's Irrational Belief Test (IBT; 100 items, 10 subscales: need for approval, high self-expectations, blame tendency, reaction to frustration, emotional irresponsibility, excessive worry/anxiety, problem avoidance, dependency, helplessness toward change, perfectionism; scored 1-5, lower = more rational). 2. State Anxiety (Overt Anxiety) — Spielberger State-Trait Anxiety Inventory (STAI), State subscale (20 items, range 20-80). 3. Trait Anxiety (Covert Anxiety) — Spielberger State-Trait Anxiety Inventory (STAI), Trait subscale (20 items, range 20-80). (Methods, Instruments section)
studies.outcomes_primary: Unclear — authors do not explicitly designate a primary outcome. Both irrational beliefs and anxiety (state and trait) are described as main outcome variables throughout the paper. 'the aim of the current study was to compare the effectiveness of mindfulness-based therapy (MBT) and spiritual therapy (ST) on irrational beliefs and anxiety' (Abstract)
studies.outcome_timepoints: T0 = Baseline (0 weeks); T1 = Post-intervention (~4-5 weeks); T2 = Follow-up (~8-9 weeks, one month after post-test). All three outcomes (irrational beliefs, state anxiety, trait anxiety) assessed at all three timepoints. 'هر سه گروه در مراحل پیش آزمون، پس آزمون و پیگیری از نظر اضطراب آشکار و پنهان و باورهای غیرمنطقی مورد ارزیابی قرار گرفتند' (Methods, Procedure section)
studies.recruitment: Participants were recruited from the Jahandidegan center for the elderly in Tehran. Center staff were asked to refer elderly women with anxiety symptoms to the researcher. 60 elderly women were initially selected using purposive sampling based on inclusion criteria, then screened with the anxiety scale, and 45 were randomly assigned to three groups of 15. 'پس از هماهنگی با مسئولان کانون جهان دیدگان شهر تهران از آنان خواسته شد تا سالمندان زن با نشانگان اضطراب را به پژوهشگر معرفی کنند' (Methods, Procedure section). Recruitment year: 1398 (Iranian calendar, approximately 2019-2020).
studies.study_purpose: 'the aim of the current study was to compare the effectiveness of mindfulness-based therapy (MBT) and spiritual therapy (ST) on irrational beliefs and anxiety in the older women' (Abstract, paragraph 1)
studies.study_design: Semi-experimental (quasi-experimental) study with pretest-posttest and one-month follow-up with a control group design. Random assignment to groups. 'This was a semi-experimental study with pretest-posttest and follow-up with a control group design' (Abstract). 'به روش تصادفی در سه گروه... گمارش شدند' [randomly assigned to three groups] (Methods, Participants section). No mention of blinding.
studies.treatment_vs_prevention: Treatment — participants were required to have high scores on the anxiety scale at enrollment ('نمره بالا در مقیاس اضطراب آشکار و پنهان' as inclusion criterion), indicating an existing anxiety condition. The study tests intervention efficacy for reducing existing anxiety and irrational beliefs in elderly women.

studies.authors: Jazaieri, H., Goldin, P. R., Werner, K., Ziv, M., & Gross, J. J.
studies.title: A Randomized Trial of MBSR Versus Aerobic Exercise for Social Anxiety Disorder
studies.abstract: Objective: Effective treatments for social anxiety disorder (SAD) exist, but additional treatment options are needed for nonresponders as well as those who are either unable or unwilling to engage in traditional treatments. Mindfulness-based stress reduction (MBSR) is one nontraditional treatment that has demonstrated efficacy in treating other mood and anxiety disorders, and preliminary data suggest its efficacy in SAD as well. Method: Fifty-six adults (52% female; 41% Caucasian; age mean [M] ± standard deviation [SD]: 32.8 ± 8.4) with SAD were randomized to MBSR or an active comparison condition, aerobic exercise (AE). At baseline and post-intervention, participants completed measures of clinical symptoms (Liebowitz Social Anxiety Scale, Social Interaction Anxiety Scale, Beck Depression Inventory-II, and Perceived Stress Scale) and subjective well-being (Rosenberg Self-Esteem Scale, Satisfaction with Life Scale, Self-Compassion Scale, and UCLA-8 Loneliness Scale). At 3 months post-intervention, a subset of these measures was readministered. For clinical significance analyses, 48 healthy adults (52.1% female; 56.3% Caucasian; age [M ± SD]: 33.9 ± 9.8) were recruited. MBSR and AE participants were also compared with a separate untreated group of 29 adults (44.8% female; 48.3% Caucasian; age [M ± SD]: 32.3 ± 9.4) with generalized SAD who completed assessments over a comparable time period with no intervening treatment. Results: A 2 (Group) x 2 (Time) repeated measures analyses of variance (ANOVAs) on measures of clinical symptoms and well-being were conducted to examine pre-intervention to post-intervention and pre-intervention to 3-month follow-up. Both MBSR and AE were associated with reductions in social anxiety and depression and increases in subjective well-being, both immediately post-intervention and at 3 months post-intervention. When participants in the randomized controlled trial were compared with the untreated SAD group, participants in both interventions exhibited improvements on measures of clinical symptoms and well-being. Conclusion: Nontraditional interventions such as MBSR and AE merit further exploration as alternative or complementary treatments for SAD. © 2012 Wiley Periodicals, Inc. J. Clin. Psychol. 68:715–731, 2012.
studies.total_n: 56. 'The remaining 56 participants were randomly assigned to either MBSR (n = 31) or AE (n = 25).' (Methods, RCT Participants, paragraph 2)
studies.age_describe: Full RCT sample: age mean [M] ± standard deviation [SD]: 32.8 ± 8.4. MBSR arm: M = 32.87 ± 8.83; AE arm: M = 32.88 ± 7.97. 'Fifty-six adults (52% female; 41% Caucasian; age mean [M] ± standard deviation [SD]: 32.8 ± 8.4) with SAD were randomized.' (Abstract, Method paragraph). Per-arm data from Table 1.
studies.participants: 56 adults with a principal diagnosis of generalized social anxiety disorder (SAD). '52% female; 41% Caucasian.' MBSR arm: n=31 (61.3% female, 41.9% Caucasian, 45.2% Asian); AE arm: n=25 (40% female, 40% Caucasian, 44% Asian). Mean education ~16.4-16.8 years. Many had current Axis-I comorbidities including generalized anxiety disorder, major depressive disorder, and specific phobia. (Methods, RCT Participants; Table 1)
studies.eligibility: Inclusion criteria: Adults meeting DSM-IV criteria for a principal diagnosis of generalized SAD (operationalized as a score of ≥50 on the LSAS-SR, a score of 4 or more on the ADIS-IV-L Clinician's Severity Rating for SAD, and ratings of 4 or higher for 5 or more specifically queried social/performance situations). Comorbid diagnoses of generalized anxiety disorder, major depressive disorder, obsessive compulsive disorder, agoraphobia without a history of panic attacks, or specific phobia were permitted. Exclusion criteria: Current pharmacotherapy or psychotherapy; history of medical disorders or head trauma; current psychiatric disorders other than those listed above; previously completed an MBSR course; regular meditation practice or exercise regime (defined as three or more times per week, for more than 2 months). 'Participants were excluded for current pharmacotherapy or psychotherapy, history of medical disorders or head trauma.' (Methods, Procedure, paragraph 1)
studies.population_vulnerable: Not a vulnerable population — participants are adults with generalized SAD recruited from the community; no specific health disparity or structural disadvantage criterion is described. (Methods, RCT Participants)
studies.location: San Francisco Bay Area, California, USA. 'Participants attended MBSR courses offered by seven different teachers in eight healthcare settings throughout the San Francisco Bay Area.' (Methods, Interventions, MBSR paragraph). Study conducted at Stanford University.
studies.mental_health: Principal diagnosis of generalized social anxiety disorder (SAD) required for enrollment, operationalized as: score ≥50 on the LSAS-SR, score of 4 or more on the ADIS-IV-L Clinician's Severity Rating for SAD, and ratings of 4 or higher for 5 or more specifically queried social/performance situations. 'Participants in this RCT were adults who met the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, 4th Edition (DSM-IV) criteria for a principal diagnosis of generalized SAD.' (Methods, RCT Participants, paragraph 1)
studies.physical_health: N/A — no physical health enrollment criterion
studies.arms: 2 arms. Arm 1: MBSR (mindfulness-based stress reduction), intervention arm, n=31. Arm 2: AE (aerobic exercise), active comparison condition, n=25. 'The remaining 56 participants were randomly assigned to either MBSR (n = 31) or AE (n = 25).' (Methods, RCT Participants, paragraph 2)
studies.meditation_intervention: Standard MBSR program (Kabat-Zinn, 1990). 'We administered the standard MBSR program (Kabat-Zinn, 1990), which comprises eight, weekly 2.5 hour group classes, a 1-day meditation retreat, and daily home practice.' Participants were trained in formal meditation practice (breath focus, body scan, open monitoring), brief informal practice, and Hatha yoga. Forms to monitor daily meditation and yoga practice were collected each week. MBSR instructors had 15.7 years (SD=4.1 years, range=10-20 years) of MBSR teaching experience. Courses offered by seven different teachers in eight healthcare settings throughout the San Francisco Bay Area. (Methods, Interventions, MBSR paragraph)
studies.intervention_delivery: In-person group format. Eight weekly 2.5-hour group classes plus a 1-day meditation retreat. Delivered in eight healthcare settings throughout the San Francisco Bay Area. MBSR instructors had 15.7 years (SD=4.1, range=10-20 years) of MBSR teaching experience. 'Participants attended MBSR courses offered by seven different teachers in eight healthcare settings throughout the San Francisco Bay Area, which were unaware of participant's clinical status.' (Methods, Interventions, MBSR paragraph)
studies.digital_component_raw: No digital component. Daily home practice was monitored via paper forms collected weekly. 'Forms to monitor daily meditation and yoga practice were collected each week.' (Methods, Interventions, MBSR paragraph)
studies.intervention_tailor: No tailoring reported. The paper states 'We administered the standard MBSR program (Kabat-Zinn, 1990)' with no mention of cultural or population-specific adaptations. (Methods, Interventions, MBSR paragraph)
studies.comparison: Aerobic exercise (AE) active comparison condition. 'We provided 2-month gym memberships to participants randomized to AE. Participants were asked to select a public health club or gym that they would be willing to attend for the duration of the study. To match the individual and group components of MBSR, participants in the AE intervention were required to complete at least two individual AE sessions (at moderate intensity) and one group AE session (other than meditation or yoga) each week during the 8-week intervention. Intensity of exercise and heart rate were not monitored. Guidance using gym equipment was not directly provided (though available through health club/gym personnel).' Duration: 8 weeks. (Methods, Interventions, AE paragraph)
studies.assessment_time: T0 = Baseline (0 weeks); T1 = Post-intervention (8 weeks); T2 = 3-month follow-up (approximately 20.6 weeks post-baseline, i.e., 8 weeks intervention + 12 weeks follow-up = ~20.6 weeks). Note: PSS-4 and ULS-8 were not administered at 3-month follow-up. 'Participants completed measures of clinical symptoms and well-being (described below) pre-interventions and post-interventions, and at 3 months post-intervention a subset of these measures were readministered.' (Methods, Procedure, paragraph 2). CONVERSION: 3 months = 3 × 4.2 = 12.6 weeks post-intervention; total from baseline = 8 + 12.6 = 20.6 weeks.
studies.assessment_nature: Self-report questionnaires only for outcome measures. Structured clinical interview (ADIS-IV-L) used for diagnosis at screening. 'At baseline and post-intervention, participants completed measures of clinical symptoms... and subjective well-being.' (Abstract, Method paragraph). All outcome instruments (LSAS-SR, SIAS-S, BDI-II, PSS-4, RSES, SWLS, SCS, ULS-8, KIMS) are self-report.
studies.outcomes_all:
1. Social anxiety symptoms — Liebowitz Social Anxiety Scale-Self-Report (LSAS-SR; 24 items, social interaction and performance situations)
2. Social anxiety — Social Interaction Anxiety Scale Straightforward Scale (SIAS-S; 17 items)
3. Depression — Beck Depression Inventory-II (BDI-II; 21 items)
4. Perceived stress — Perceived Stress Scale (PSS-4; 4 items; not administered at 3-month follow-up)
5. Self-esteem — Rosenberg Self-Esteem Scale (RSES; 10 items)
6. Life satisfaction — Satisfaction with Life Scale (SWLS; 5 items)
7. Self-compassion — Self-Compassion Scale (SCS; 26 items)
8. Loneliness/social integration — UCLA-8 Loneliness Scale (ULS-8; not administered at 3-month follow-up)
9. Mindfulness — Kentucky Inventory of Mindfulness Scale (KIMS; 39 items, 4 subscales: observing, describing, acting with awareness, accepting without judgment; administered pre- and post-intervention only)
(Methods, Assessment Measures section)
studies.outcomes_primary: Unclear — authors do not explicitly designate a primary outcome. The study examines 'measures of clinical symptoms and well-being' broadly. 'Separate 2 (Group) x 2 (Time) repeated-measures analyses of variance (ANOVAs) on measures of clinical symptoms and well-being were conducted.' (Methods, Statistical Analysis paragraph 1)
studies.outcome_timepoints: T0 = Baseline (0 weeks); T1 = Post-intervention (8 weeks) — all measures administered; T2 = 3-month follow-up (~20.6 weeks from baseline) — subset of measures (LSAS-SR, SIAS-S, BDI-II, RSES, SWLS, SCS administered; PSS-4 and ULS-8 NOT administered). 'The following measures of clinical and well-being symptoms were administered at pre-intervention, post-intervention, and at 3 months following the intervention, except where noted.' (Methods, Assessment Measures, paragraph 1)
studies.recruitment: Participants recruited through web-based community listings and referrals from mental health clinics and providers. 'All participants were recruited through web-based community listings and referrals from mental health clinics and providers.' An initial telephone screen and ADIS-IV-L were used to assess inclusion criteria. 77 potential participants met study inclusion criteria and were invited to participate; 21 discontinued prior to randomization. (Methods, Procedure, paragraphs 1-2)
studies.study_purpose: To examine the effects of a RCT of MBSR versus AE on clinical symptoms and well-being in adults with generalized SAD. 'To address this gap in the literature, we conducted a randomized controlled trial (RCT) of MBSR versus an active comparison condition, namely, AE in adults with SAD.' (Introduction, The Present Study paragraph)
studies.study_design: Randomized controlled trial (RCT). Two-arm parallel design. Randomization using Efron's biased coin randomization procedure. 'Participants were randomized to 8 weeks of either MBSR or AE using the Efron's biased coin randomization procedure. This method removes potential confounds related to unequal assignment at different time points over a multiyear study.' No blinding reported. (Methods, Procedure, paragraph 1)
studies.treatment_vs_prevention: Treatment — participants were required to have a principal diagnosis of generalized SAD (DSM-IV criteria, confirmed by structured clinical interview) at enrollment. The study tests intervention efficacy for an existing condition. 'Participants in this RCT were adults who met the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, 4th Edition (DSM-IV) criteria for a principal diagnosis of generalized SAD.' (Methods, RCT Participants, paragraph 1)

studies.authors: Jung, H. Y., Lee, H., & Park, J.
studies.title: Comparison of the effects of Korean mindfulness-based stress reduction, walking, and patient education in diabetes mellitus
studies.abstract: The purpose of this study was to compare the effects of Korean mindfulness-based stress reduction (K-MBSR), walking, and patient education regarding diabetes mellitus (DM) on stress response, glycemic control, and vascular inflammation in patients with diabetes mellitus. A cluster randomized trial including 56 adults with diabetes mellitus (K-MBSR group = 21, walking group = 18, patient education group = 17) was conducted between 13 July and 14 September 2012. The questionnaire included the Diabetes Distress Scale and Perceived Stress Response Inventory. Fasting blood samples were used to measure levels of cortisol, blood glucose, plasminogen activator inhibitor-1 (PAI-1), and tissue plasminogen activator (t-PA). There were no statistically significant differences between the effects of K-MBSR, walking, and patient education on stress, glycemic control, or vascular inflammation. However, in the K-MBSR and walking groups, significant reductions in the levels of serum cortisol and PAI-1 were observed. A significant reduction in psychological responses to stress was observed in the walking and patient education groups. Longitudinal studies could provide better insight into the impact of K-MBSR, walking, and patient education on health outcomes in adults with diabetes mellitus.
studies.total_n: 56. "A cluster randomized trial including 56 adults with diabetes mellitus (K-MBSR group = 21, walking group = 18, patient education group = 17) was conducted" (Abstract). Note: sum of arms = 21+18+17 = 56, consistent with reported total.
studies.age_mean: 66.27 (weighted; overall M=66.27, SD=8.36 reported directly in Table 2)
studies.age_describe: Overall mean age 66.27 (SD=8.36). K-MBSR group: M=67.00 (SD=9.13); Walking group: M=63.33 (SD=8.83); Patient education group: M=68.47 (SD=6.17). Age categories: <70 years = 62.5%; ≥70 years = 37.5%. (Table 2, Participant characteristics)
studies.participants: 56 adults with type 2 diabetes mellitus living in rural areas of South Korea. Gender: 48.2% male (n=27), 51.8% female (n=29). Mean age 66.27 years. Most had low educational levels: 57.1% elementary school graduates, 16.1% no formal education. Recruited from internal medicine outpatient department. "This study examined the effects of eight weeks of K-MBSR, walking, and patient education on stress, glycemic control, and vascular inflammation in 56 adults diagnosed with type 2 DM living in rural areas" (Conclusion, paragraph 1; Table 2)
studies.eligibility: Inclusion criteria: 'Patients who were diagnosed with type 2 diabetes more than six months prior to the initiation of the study and had a stable DM medication dosage, were included in the study.' Exclusion criteria: 'Patients who: (i) experienced complications, such as severe retinopathy or diabetic nephropathy; (ii) were prescribed psychiatric medication; (iii) had exercised regularly during the preceding month; or (iv) participated in any other interventional research were excluded from the study.' (Methods, Participants, paragraph 1)
studies.population_vulnerable: Yes — rural-dwelling older adults with diabetes mellitus in South Korea, a population with documented health disparities. 'In view of the higher prevalence of DM in rural (13.8%) compared with urban areas (9.6%) in South Korea, DM patients in rural areas require greater attention.' Also, 57.1% had only elementary school education and 16.1% had no formal education. (Introduction, Literature review, paragraph 2; Table 2)
studies.location: M city, Gyengsang province, South Korea. 'Participants were recruited from the internal medicine outpatient department of M hospital in M city, Gyengsang province, South Korea.' (Methods, Participants, paragraph 1)
studies.mental_health: N/A — no psychiatric enrollment criterion. Diabetes-related stress was measured as an outcome but was not a formal enrollment threshold. Exclusion of patients prescribed psychiatric medication is an exclusion criterion, not an enrollment threshold.
studies.physical_health: Type 2 diabetes mellitus diagnosis required for enrollment. 'Patients who were diagnosed with type 2 diabetes more than six months prior to the initiation of the study and had a stable DM medication dosage, were included in the study.' (Methods, Participants, paragraph 1)
studies.arms: 3 arms. (1) K-MBSR group (n=21): Korean mindfulness-based stress reduction plus patient education; (2) Walking group (n=18): walking exercise program plus patient education; (3) Patient education group (n=17): patient education only (control). 'A cluster randomized trial including 56 adults with diabetes mellitus (K-MBSR group = 21, walking group = 18, patient education group = 17)' (Abstract)
studies.meditation_intervention: The K-MBSR (Korean mindfulness-based stress reduction) program developed by Chang et al. (2007) was used. The PI conducted the program based on an audio-CD for eight weeks. Content included mindful walking, eating, and breathing, silent sitting meditation, body scan, mindful breathing, Hatha yoga, and breathing expansion. Eight themed weekly sessions were delivered twice per week (16 sessions total). Each session lasted 60–120 minutes. Patient education was also provided during the first meeting each week. Participants were encouraged to practice K-MBSR at home. 'The K-MBSR program developed by Chang et al. (2007) was used in the current study. The PI conducted the program, based on an audio-CD, for eight weeks, which facilitated mindful walking, eating, and breathing and silent sitting meditation.' (Methods, Interventions, K-MBSR section; Table 1)
studies.intervention_delivery: In-person group delivery at community health centers and hospitals near participants' homes. Sessions conducted twice per week for 8 weeks, each lasting 60–120 minutes. The PI (a nurse trained in K-MBSR who had completed the MBSR specialists course from the Korea Mindfulness-Based Stress Reduction Academy) conducted the program. Audio-CD used to facilitate practice. Up to 15 participants practiced on individual yoga mattresses. 'Community health centers and hospitals near the participants' homes were selected as the locations at which interventions were implemented. These locations were sufficiently large to allow 15 participants to practice meditation on individual yoga mattresses.' (Methods, Interventions, K-MBSR section)
studies.digital_component_raw: No digital component. An audio-CD was used to facilitate home practice and guide sessions, but this is an analog medium. 'The PI conducted the program, based on an audio-CD, for eight weeks.' (Methods, Interventions, K-MBSR section)
studies.intervention_tailor: Yes — the intervention is the Korean adaptation of MBSR (K-MBSR), developed by Chang et al. (2007) specifically for Korean populations. 'Chang et al. (2007) modified MBSR slightly and applied it to Koreans as K-MBSR. The intervention included a body scan, breathing awareness, and mindful walking, eating, and communication.' (Introduction, Literature review, paragraph 3)
studies.comparison: Two comparison conditions: (1) Walking exercise group (n=18): Participants received lectures on proper walking techniques, effects of exercise, precautions, and hypoglycemia avoidance. They walked briskly for 30–60 minutes, 3–4 times per week, wearing a pedometer. Walking intensity monitored via RPE scale (target RPE=12). Monitored via weekly telephone interviews and exercise diaries. Also received weekly patient education. (2) Patient education group (n=17): Received patient education only, once per week for 8 weeks. Content included DM definition, symptoms, self-management strategies (diet, exercise, stress management, foot care, medications, hypoglycemia, complications). Lectures were the main instructional method. 'Patient education was provided to all intervention groups once per week for eight weeks.' (Methods, Interventions sections)
studies.assessment_time: T0 = Baseline (0 weeks); T1 = Post-intervention (8 weeks). 'We used a cluster randomized trial design with eight week interventions...the study was conducted between 13 July and 14 September 2012.' (Methods, Design, paragraph 1). No follow-up assessment reported.
studies.assessment_nature: Both self-report and biological/physiological measures used. Self-report: Diabetes Distress Scale (questionnaire), Perceived Stress Response Inventory (questionnaire). Biological: plasma cortisol (radioimmunoassay), fasting blood glucose (Accu-Chek Active), serum PAI-1 (ELISA), serum t-PA (ELISA). 'Laboratory professionals collected brachial venous blood samples to measure plasma cortisol and vascular inflammatory response markers.' (Methods, Data collection, paragraph 4)
studies.outcomes_all: 1. Diabetes-related stress — Diabetes Distress Scale (17 items, 5-point scale, range 17–85; higher = more stress). 2. Psychological response to stress — Perceived Stress Response Inventory (39 items, 5-point scale, range 0–156; higher = more stress). 3. Cortisol — plasma cortisol measured via radioimmunoassay (reference: 5–25 μg/dL). 4. Blood glucose — fasting blood glucose measured via Accu-Chek Active (range 1–600 mg/dL; reference: 70–110 mg/dL). 5. Vascular inflammation — PAI-1 (serum, ELISA; reference: 2.4–43.8 ng/mL). 6. Vascular inflammation — t-PA (serum, ELISA; reference: 1–20 ng/mL).
studies.outcomes_primary: Stress response and blood glucose level designated as primary outcomes. 'The primary outcomes of the study were stress response and blood glucose level; the secondary outcome was vascular inflammation.' (Methods, Design, paragraph 1)
studies.outcome_timepoints: T0 = Baseline (0 weeks); T1 = Post-intervention (8 weeks). All outcomes assessed at both timepoints. 'Pre-test Post-test' design depicted in Figure 1. No follow-up timepoint reported.
studies.recruitment: Participants were recruited from the internal medicine outpatient department of M hospital in M city, Gyengsang province, South Korea. 'The principle investigator (PI) contacted the participants to assess their eligibility and enrolled them in the study.' Study conducted between 13 July and 14 September 2012. (Methods, Participants, paragraph 1; Data collection, paragraph 1)
studies.study_purpose: "We examined the effects of K-MBSR, walking, and patient education on stress response, glycemic control, and vascular inflammation in people with DM." (Methods, Study aim)
studies.study_design: Cluster randomized trial with three arms. 'We used a cluster randomized trial design with eight week interventions.' Participants were categorized into regional clusters to minimize contamination. 'The PI allocated the regional clusters to the three research groups using a table of random numbers. Group allocation information was concealed in a password-protected file.' Data collectors were blinded to group allocation. (Methods, Design; Data collection sections)
studies.treatment_vs_prevention: Treatment — participants were required to have a type 2 diabetes mellitus diagnosis for enrollment, and the study tested interventions for managing an existing condition (stress, glycemic control, vascular inflammation in DM patients). 'Patients who were diagnosed with type 2 diabetes more than six months prior to the initiation of the study...were included.' (Methods, Participants, paragraph 1)

studies.active_comparator_name: Walking exercise program; Patient education (diabetes self-management education only)

studies.authors: Kahn, J. R., Collinge, W., & Soltysik, R.
studies.title: Post-9/11 Veterans and Their Partners Improve Mental Health Outcomes with a Self-directed Mobile and Web-based Wellness Training Program: A Randomized Controlled Trial
studies.abstract: Background: Veterans with history of deployment in the Global War on Terror face significant and ongoing challenges with high prevalences of adverse psychological, physical, spiritual, and family impacts. Together, these challenges contribute to an emerging public health crisis likely to extend well into the future. Innovative approaches are needed that reach veterans and their family members with strategies they can employ over time in their daily lives to promote improved adjustment and well-being. Objective: The objective of this study was to evaluate effects of use of a Web-based, self-directed program of instruction in mind- and body-based wellness skills to be employed by Global War on Terror veterans and their significant relationship partners on mental health and wellness outcomes associated with postdeployment readjustment. Methods: We recruited 160 veteran-partner dyads in 4 regions of the United States (San Diego, CA; Dallas, TX; Fayetteville, NC; and New York, NY) through publicity by the Iraq and Afghanistan Veterans of America to its membership. Dyads were randomly allocated to 1 of 4 study arms: Mission Reconnect (MR) program alone, MR plus the Prevention and Relationship Enhancement Program (PREP) for Strong Bonds weekend program for military couples, PREP alone, and waitlist control. We administered a battery of standardized and investigator-generated instruments assessing mental health outcomes at baseline, 8 weeks, and 16 weeks. Dyads in the MR arms were provided Web-based and mobile app video and audio instruction in a set of mindfulness-related stress reduction and contemplative practices, as well as partner massage for reciprocal use. All participants provided weekly reports on frequency and duration of self-care practices for the first 8 weeks, and at 16 weeks. Results: During the first 8-week reporting period, veterans and partners assigned to MR arms used some aspect of the program a mean of 20 times per week, totaling nearly 2.5 hours per week, with only modest declines in use at 16 weeks. Significant improvements were seen at 8 and 16 weeks in measures of posttraumatic stress disorder, depression, sleep quality, perceived stress, resilience, self-compassion, and pain for participants assigned to MR arms. In addition, significant reductions in self-reported levels of pain, tension, irritability, anxiety, and depression were associated with use of partner massage. Conclusions: Both veterans and partners were able to learn and make sustained use of a range of wellness practices taught in the MR program. Home-based, self-directed interventions may be of particular service to veterans who are distant from, averse to, or prohibited by schedule from using professional services. Leveraging the partner relationship may enhance sustained use of self-directed interventions for this population. Use of the MR program appears to be an accessible, low-cost approach that supports well-being and reduces multiple symptoms among post-9/11 veterans and their partners.
studies.total_n: 320 individuals (160 dyads). 'We planned a sample of 160 dyads, with 40 dyads allocated to each arm.' 'All 320 participants completed their baseline surveys.' (Methods, Study Design, paragraph 2; Results, Sample, paragraph 1)
studies.age_mean: Not reported
studies.age_describe: Age is not reported in the paper. No mean, median, SD, or range for participant age is provided. (Not reported)
studies.participants: Post-9/11 veteran-partner dyads. 'The vast majority of veterans were male (147/181, 81.2%) and the vast majority of partners (129/139, 92.8%) were female.' Sample included 181 veterans and 139 nonveteran partners, with 21 dual-veteran dyads. 'Over half of the participants identified as white, followed by Hispanic, African American, Asian, Native American, and Hawaiian/Pacific Islander.' (Results, Demographics, paragraph 1)
studies.eligibility: Inclusion criteria: 'Eligible applicants were veteran-partner dyads in which the veteran had a history of deployment in a post-9/11 combat operation. This includes what the US DoD has labeled Operation Iraqi Freedom, Operation Enduring Freedom, and Operation New Dawn. As proof of deployment, veterans typically provided their Form DD214.' The partner could be 'a spouse, life partner, fiancé or fiancée, girlfriend or boyfriend, or in other significant relationship identified by the veteran as fulfilling the role of partner.' Exclusion criteria: No specific exclusion criteria related to mental or physical health parameters are stated. The paper notes: 'This study evaluated MR in a community-based sample with no inclusion or exclusion criteria related to specific mental or physical health parameters.' (Methods, Participants, Eligibility; Discussion, Limitations)
studies.population_vulnerable: Yes — post-9/11 combat veterans experiencing high rates of PTSD, chronic pain, and postdeployment mental health challenges. 'Veterans with history of deployment in the Global War on Terror face significant and ongoing challenges with high prevalences of adverse psychological, physical, spiritual, and family impacts.' Veterans are a population with documented health disparities and structural disadvantage related to military service. (Abstract, Background)
studies.location: San Diego, CA; Dallas, TX; Fayetteville, NC; and New York, NY, United States. 'We recruited study cohorts for all 4 study arms in each of 4 metropolitan areas: San Diego, CA; Dallas, TX; Fayetteville, NC; and New York, NY, USA.' (Methods, Publicity and Recruitment, paragraph 1)
studies.mental_health: N/A — no psychiatric enrollment criterion. The paper explicitly states: 'This study evaluated MR in a community-based sample with no inclusion or exclusion criteria related to specific mental or physical health parameters.' (Discussion, Limitations)
studies.physical_health: N/A — no physical health enrollment criterion. 'This study evaluated MR in a community-based sample with no inclusion or exclusion criteria related to specific mental or physical health parameters.' (Discussion, Limitations)
studies.arms: 4 arms. Arm 1: Mission Reconnect (MR) alone (n=40 dyads); Arm 2: MR + PREP for Strong Bonds (n=40 dyads); Arm 3: PREP for Strong Bonds alone (n=40 dyads); Arm 4: Waitlist control (n=40 dyads). 'The 4 arms to be studied were (1) MR alone, (2) MR+PREP, (3) PREP alone, and (3) a waitlist control. Sample size was determined by power analysis applied to the phase I feasibility data. We planned a sample of 160 dyads, with 40 dyads allocated to each arm.' (Methods, Study Design, paragraph 2)
studies.meditation_intervention: The Mission Reconnect (MR) program is a self-directed, multimedia mind- and body-based wellness program. It delivers instruction via videos, guided audio exercises, and written materials accessible on a program website and mobile device apps (iOS, Android, Windows Phone). Content is organized into three categories: (1) Connecting with yourself (morning gratitude, mirror greeting, loosening and relaxing, waking up the body, reset and refresh); (2) Connecting with quiet (centering — basic mindfulness using breath as anchor, movement into stillness, deep relaxation combining progressive relaxation and yoga nidra meditation); (3) Connecting with your partner (seeing each other — contemplative exercise for appreciation/compassion/forgiveness, giving/receiving massage). Audio exercises range from 1 to 22 minutes. A Program Overview video (54 minutes) and Massage Instruction video (37 minutes) are included. 'Dyads in the MR arms were provided Web-based and mobile app video and audio instruction in a set of mindfulness-related stress reduction and contemplative practices, as well as partner massage for reciprocal use.' No fixed total session count; self-directed use over 8–16 weeks. (Methods, The MR Program)
studies.intervention_delivery: Self-directed, digital delivery via website and mobile app. 'The program delivers the instruction by techniques grouped into three categories... Instruction is provided via videos, guided audio exercises, and written materials, all accessible on the program website and mobile device apps (iOS, Android, and Windows Phone versions).' No live instructor involved in ongoing delivery. A 90-minute in-person launch meeting was held at baseline to orient participants but provided no actual instruction in practices. Weekly e-newsletter from investigators provided general encouragement. (Methods, The MR Program; Methods, Protocols, MR-Only)
studies.digital_component_raw: Yes — the intervention is delivered via a program website and mobile device apps (iOS, Android, Windows Phone). 'Instruction is provided via videos, guided audio exercises, and written materials, all accessible on the program website and mobile device apps (iOS, Android, and Windows Phone versions).' (Methods, The MR Program, paragraph 4)
studies.intervention_tailor: Yes — the program was specifically designed and tailored for post-9/11 veterans and their partners. 'MR is designed as a dyadic intervention for post-9/11 veterans and their partners to use individually and together, teaching selected self-care strategies aimed at addressing short- and long-term impacts of deployment and promoting well-being.' Instructional videos were filmed with Iraq and Afghanistan veterans and their partners. Content addresses deployment-specific issues (PTSD, reintegration, moral injury). (Methods, The MR Program, paragraph 1; Introduction, paragraph 7)
studies.comparison: Arm 3 — PREP for Strong Bonds alone: 'A standardized program administered by military chaplains... a standardized, evidence-based program conducted during weekend residential retreats with experiential exercises, facilitated by Army Chaplain Corps-trained chaplains. The multidimensional program uses methods from cognitive behavioral therapy and communication-oriented marital enhancement programs.' 12 hours of content over a Friday evening to Sunday noon weekend. Content: communication, relationship building, problem solving, stress and relaxation, intimacy, forgiveness, commitment. 3 chaplains used across 4 cities. Arm 4 — Waitlist control: Participants attended a 90-minute launch meeting, received instructions for data collection, and were 'instructed to continue their usual behavior regarding self-care or wellness-related activity.' Given access to MR at end of study. (Methods, Study Design; Methods, Protocols, PREP-Only and Waitlist)
studies.assessment_time: T0 = Baseline (0 weeks); T1 = Post-intervention (8 weeks); T2 = Follow-up (16 weeks). 'A survey package was administered 3 times: at baseline (T1, prior to the launch meeting), at 8 weeks (T2), and at 16 weeks (T3, end of study).' (Methods, Data Collection, Survey Data)
studies.assessment_nature: Primarily self-report questionnaires. 'We used the following standardized instruments: the Perceived Stress Scale-10 item (PSS), Beck Depression Inventory (BDI), PTSD Checklist-Civilian version (PCL-C), Self-Compassion Scale (SCStotal), Response to Stressful Experiences Scale (RSES), Multidimensional Scale of Perceived Social Support (MSPSStotal), Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQItotal), and Revised Dyadic Adjustment Scale (RDAS).' Also included investigator-generated Likert-scaled pain items and weekly self-report logs. (Methods, Data Collection, Survey Data)
studies.outcomes_all:
1. Perceived stress — Perceived Stress Scale-10 item (PSS)
2. Depression — Beck Depression Inventory (BDI)
3. PTSD symptoms — PTSD Checklist-Civilian version (PCL-C)
4. Self-compassion — Self-Compassion Scale (SCStotal)
5. Resilience/response to stress — Response to Stressful Experiences Scale (RSES)
6. Perceived social support — Multidimensional Scale of Perceived Social Support (MSPSStotal)
7. Sleep quality — Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQItotal)
8. Dyadic adjustment/relationship satisfaction — Revised Dyadic Adjustment Scale (RDAS)
9. Pain (usual) — investigator-generated Likert scale (0–10), 'rating of usual pain level over the past week' (PainUsual)
10. Pain (best) — investigator-generated Likert scale (0–10), 'rating of best pain level over the past week' (PainBest)
11. Massage session effects — investigator-generated Likert scale (0–10) for pain, tension, irritability, anxiety/worry, depression before and after massage
12. Program use/fidelity — weekly reports of frequency and duration of each MR activity
13. User satisfaction — single item 0–10 scale at T3
14. Moral injury — 5 investigator-generated items (exploratory; results not reported in this paper)
(Methods, Data Collection, Survey Data and Weekly Reports)
studies.outcomes_primary: Primary outcomes: mental health outcomes associated with postdeployment readjustment. 'Aim 1 was to evaluate the impact of MR on mental health outcomes associated with postdeployment readjustment (primary outcomes). Hypothesis 1 was that veterans and partners assigned to MR would report significantly greater improvements in stress, depression, PTSD symptoms, self-compassion, sleep quality, resilience, social support, and relationship satisfaction compared with those in the non-MR comparison groups.' (Methods, Aims and Hypotheses, paragraph 1)
studies.outcome_timepoints: T0 = Baseline (0 weeks); T1 = 8 weeks post-baseline; T2 = 16 weeks post-baseline. Weekly reports collected at weeks 1–8 and at week 16. 'A survey package was administered 3 times: at baseline (T1, prior to the launch meeting), at 8 weeks (T2), and at 16 weeks (T3, end of study).' (Methods, Data Collection, Survey Data)
studies.recruitment: Recruited through Iraq and Afghanistan Veterans of America (IAVA). 'Iraq and Afghanistan Veterans of America provided publicity for recruitment through their website, social media channels, and geographically targeted emails to their membership announcing the study.' Recruitment targeted 4 metropolitan areas: San Diego, CA; Dallas, TX; Fayetteville, NC; and New York, NY. Prospective participants completed a web-based application and were interviewed by phone to determine candidacy. (Methods, Publicity and Recruitment)
studies.study_purpose: 'The objective of this study was to evaluate effects of use of a Web-based, self-directed program of instruction in mind- and body-based wellness skills to be employed by Global War on Terror veterans and their significant relationship partners on mental health and wellness outcomes associated with postdeployment readjustment.' (Abstract, Objective)
studies.study_design: 4-arm randomized controlled trial. 'We planned a 4-arm randomized controlled trial using a standard-of-care comparator to evaluate both comparative and additive effects over a 16-week period.' Random allocation generated through Randomization.com. Allocation ratio 1:1:1:1 (40 dyads per arm). No blinding reported. Intent-to-treat analysis used. (Methods, Study Design)
studies.treatment_vs_prevention: Enhancement — The study recruited a community-based sample with no inclusion or exclusion criteria related to specific mental or physical health parameters. 'This study evaluated MR in a community-based sample with no inclusion or exclusion criteria related to specific mental or physical health parameters.' The program targets general well-being and postdeployment readjustment in veterans without requiring a clinical diagnosis or symptom threshold. While PTSD and depression are measured as outcomes, they are not enrollment criteria. The focus is on promoting well-being and reducing symptoms in a non-clinical community sample. (Discussion, Limitations)

'Veterans with history of deployment in the Global War on Terror face significant and ongoing challenges with high prevalences of adverse psychological, physical, spiritual, and family impacts.' PTSD is a primary outcome measure and 29.3% of veterans had baseline PCL-C scores ≥50. (Abstract, Background; Results, PTSD Subanalysis)

studies.authors: Keefer, L., & Blanchard, E. B.
studies.title: The effects of relaxation response meditation on the symptoms of irritable bowel syndrome: results of a controlled treatment study
studies.abstract: In this study, Herbert Benson's (1975) Relaxation Response Meditation program was tested as a possible treatment for Irritable Bowel Syndrome (IBS). Participants were 16 adults who were matched into pairs based on presence of Axis I disorder, primary IBS symptoms and demographic features and randomized to either a six week meditation condition or a six week wait list symptom monitoring condition. Thirteen participants completed treatment and follow-up. All subjects assigned to the Wait List were subsequently treated. Patients in the treatment condition were taught the meditation technique and asked to practice it twice a day for 15 minutes. Composite Primary IBS Symptom Reduction (CPSR) scores were calculated for each patient from end of baseline to two weeks post-treatment (or to post wait list). One tailed independent sample t-tests revealed that Meditation was superior to the control (P=0.04). Significant within-subject improvements were noted for flatulence (P=0.03) and belching (P=0.02) by post-treatment. By three month follow-up, significant improvements in flatulence (P<0.01), belching (P=0.02), bloating (P=0.05), and diarrhea (P=0.03) were shown by symptom diary. Constipation approached significance (P=0.07). Benson's Relaxation Response Meditation appears to be a viable treatment for IBS. 2001 Elsevier Science Ltd. All rights reserved.
studies.total_n: 16. 'Participants were 16 adults who were matched into pairs based on presence of Axis I disorder, primary IBS symptoms and demographic features and randomized to either a six week meditation condition or a six week wait list symptom monitoring condition.' (Abstract, paragraph 1). Note: 21 were initially interviewed; 16 were randomized; 13 completed treatment.

studies.participants: Adults diagnosed with IBS by their personal physician or gastroenterologist. 'Twenty-one men and women who had been diagnosed with IBS by their personal physician or gastroenterologist were initially interviewed for the study.' Of 13 completers: 9 female, 4 male. Average years with IBS was 15.8 (SD=11.6). (Methods, Participants, paragraph 1; Table 1)

Exclusion criteria: met DSM-IV criteria for Bipolar I or II, schizophrenia, or other psychoses; actively suicidal. 'Participants were required to be above the age of 17, to experience gastrointestinal distress at least three days per week, and have received a diagnosis of IBS from their physician. Participants were excluded if they met DSM-IV criteria for Bipolar I or II, schizophrenia, or other psychoses, or if they were actively suicidal.' (Methods, Participants, paragraph 1)

studies.location: Albany, New York, USA. 'The University at Albany, State University of New York, Center for Stress and Anxiety Disorders, 1535 Western Avenue, Albany, NY 12203, USA' (Title page, author affiliations)
studies.mental_health: N/A — no psychiatric enrollment criterion. Participants were required to have IBS diagnosis; psychiatric diagnoses were assessed but not required for enrollment. Exclusion criteria included Bipolar I or II, schizophrenia, other psychoses, and active suicidality. (Methods, Participants, paragraph 1)
studies.physical_health: IBS diagnosis required for enrollment. 'Participants were required to be above the age of 17, to experience gastrointestinal distress at least three days per week, and have received a diagnosis of IBS from their physician.' (Methods, Participants, paragraph 1)
studies.arms: 2 arms. Arm 1: Relaxation Response Meditation (RRM) treatment condition (n=8 randomized, 6 completers initially treated). Arm 2: Wait list symptom monitoring condition (n=8 randomized, 7 completers). 'Participants were...randomized to either a six week meditation condition or a six week wait list symptom monitoring condition.' (Abstract, paragraph 1). Note: this was a multiple baseline matched pairs design; wait list participants were subsequently crossed over to treatment.
studies.meditation_intervention: Relaxation Response Meditation (RRM) based on Herbert Benson's (1975) protocol. Six weekly 30-minute individual treatment sessions. Content: patients were provided a rationale for RRM and how it might help with IBS; taught four main elements: selecting a quiet environment, assuming a comfortable position, focusing on the word 'one', and maintaining a passive attitude. Patients practiced the technique with the therapist present. Weekly sessions included review of GI diaries, review of relaxation monitoring forms, discussion of problems achieving the Relaxation Response, and additional instruction. Home practice: asked to practice twice a day for 15 minutes (most could only practice once a day). 'Relaxation Response Meditation (Benson, 1975) served as the basis for the six, 30 minute, weekly treatment sessions.' (Methods, Treatment, paragraph 1)
studies.intervention_delivery: In-person individual sessions. Six 30-minute weekly sessions. Delivered by the first author, 'an advanced doctoral student in clinical psychology trained in Relaxation Response Meditation (RRM).' (Methods, Treatment, paragraph 1)
studies.digital_component_raw: No digital component. Home practice involved practicing the technique independently; paper-and-pencil symptom diaries and relaxation monitoring forms were used. No digital or technology-based delivery described. (Methods, Treatment; Methods, Symptom Monitoring)
studies.intervention_tailor: No tailoring reported. The standard Benson (1975) Relaxation Response Meditation protocol was used without reported cultural or population-specific modifications. (Methods, Treatment, paragraph 1)
studies.comparison: Wait list symptom monitoring condition: participants monitored their GI symptoms on paper-and-pencil diaries for six weeks without receiving any active treatment. 'Patients in the symptom monitoring-only group were crossed over into the treatment plus symptom monitoring group after six weeks of baseline monitoring.' After the wait list period, all wait list participants received the same RRM treatment. (Methods, Procedures, paragraph 1)
studies.assessment_time: T0 = Baseline (0 weeks; 2-week baseline monitoring period prior to treatment); T1 = Post-treatment (approximately 8 weeks from start, i.e., 2 weeks after 6-week treatment ended); T2 = 3-month follow-up (approximately 20.6 weeks from baseline, based on 3 months = 12.6 weeks after post-treatment). 'All patients monitored their symptoms for two weeks after treatment had terminated, and for two weeks at the three month follow-up point.' (Methods, Procedures, paragraph 1)
studies.assessment_nature: Self-report measures: paper-and-pencil daily symptom diaries (GI symptoms rated 0–4 scale), expectancy/credibility questionnaire, side effects questionnaire, relaxation practice monitoring forms. Clinician-administered: Structured Clinical Interview for DSM-IV (SCID) administered by treating therapist and trained doctoral-level students. 'After the structured GI history interview, the treating therapist and other trained doctoral-level students administered the Structured Clinical Interview for DSM-IV (SCID).' Individual GI symptoms — daily symptom diary (0–4 scale): abdominal pain, abdominal tenderness, diarrhea, constipation, bloating, belching, flatulence; also diarrhea frequency count. 3. Treatment expectancy and credibility — questionnaire (item count not reported). 4. Side effects — questionnaire assessing collateral changes (headache, backache, other chronic pain, hypertension, smoking, appetite/weight, energy level, concentration, anxiety, depression, sleep problems, worrying, jumpiness, enjoyment of life, sexual problems). 5. Relaxation practice frequency — self-monitoring forms (start/finish time, relaxation level before/after). (Methods, Measures, paragraphs 1–4)
studies.outcomes_primary: Composite Primary Symptom Reduction (CPSR) Score. 'Composite Primary IBS Symptom Reduction (CPSR) scores were calculated for each patient from end of baseline to two weeks post-treatment.' (Abstract, paragraph 1; Methods, Between Group Comparison, paragraph 1)

'All patients monitored their symptoms for two weeks after treatment had terminated, and for two weeks at the three month follow-up point.' (Methods, Procedures, paragraph 1)
studies.recruitment: Participants were recruited through local gastroenterologists and newspaper advertisements. 'Participants were recruited through local gastroenterologists and newspaper advertisements.' (Methods, Participants, paragraph 1). Recruitment dates not reported. Initial phone screen followed by in-person interview.
studies.study_purpose: 'The present study sought to examine the effects of Benson's Relaxation Response Meditation on the symptoms of Irritable Bowel Syndrome.' Three hypotheses: (1) active treatment superior to wait list for primary GI symptoms; (2) all patients would show significant decrease in individual GI symptoms after treatment; (3) treatment gains maintained at 3-month follow-up. studies.authors: Kelly, A. C., Zuroff, D. C., Foa, C. L., & Gilbert, P.
studies.title: Who Benefits from Training in Self-Compassionate Self-Regulation? A Study of Smoking Reduction
studies.abstract: Self-compassion has been found to promote well-being but research has yet to examine whether training in self-compassion improves self-regulation (Gilbert, 2005, 2009; Neff, 2003). the present study sought to examine the impact and moderators of a self-compassion intervention on the self-regulation of cigarette smoking. one hundred and twenty-six smokers seeking to quit were randomly assigned to one of four interventions, of which one involved engaging in self-compassionate imagery and self-talk at every urge to smoke. Multilevel modeling revealed that over three weeks, the self-compassion intervention reduced daily smoking more quickly than a baseline self-monitoring condition but at the same rate as two other imagery-based self-talk interventions. Moderators of self-compassion training emerged. the self-compassion intervention reduced smoking more rapidly if participants were low in readiness to change; were high in the trait of self-criticism; and had vivid imagery during the intervention exercises. findings suggest that training oneself to self-regulate from a self-compassionate stance might be especially effective for individuals who are able to visualize a compassionate image and whose personality and motivation would be expected to undermine the impact of traditional treatments.
studies.journal: Journal of Social and Clinical Psychology
studies.total_n: 126. "The initial recruited sample consisted of 126 individuals." (Methods, Participants, paragraph 2)
studies.age_mean: 24.42. "The final sample consisted of 64 females and 55 males with a mean age of 24.42 (SD = 6.54)." (Methods, Participants, paragraph 2)
studies.age_describe: Mean age = 24.42 (SD = 6.54) for the final analytic sample. No per-arm breakdown reported. "The final sample consisted of 64 females and 55 males with a mean age of 24.42 (SD = 6.54)." (Methods, Participants, paragraph 2)
studies.participants: Adult smokers seeking to quit or reduce smoking, recruited via online advertisements. Final analytic sample: 64 females and 55 males, mean age 24.42 (SD=6.54). Ethnic composition: 76 Caucasian (63.9%), 5 Hispanic/Latin (4.2%), 10 Middle-Eastern (8.4%), 19 Asian (16%), 9 mixed race (7.6%). "The final sample consisted of 64 females and 55 males with a mean age of 24.42 (SD = 6.54)." (Methods, Participants, paragraph 2)
studies.eligibility: Inclusion criteria: smoked for at least one year; identified as current smokers (average of one cigarette per day or more); indicated wanting to quit in the next six months (assessed by stage of change). Exclusion criteria: current psychotherapy; current use of psychotropic medications; current use of nicotine substitute products; participation in formal smoking cessation programs in the last six months; current alcohol or drug abuse; a friend, romantic partner, or relative in the study. "To be eligible, individuals had to have smoked for at least one year, identify themselves as current smokers (smoking an average of one cigarette per day or more), and indicate wanting to quit in the next six months." (Methods, Participants, paragraph 1)
studies.population_vulnerable: Not a vulnerable population — participants are general community adult smokers with no specific health disparity or structural disadvantage criterion. "Participants were recruited via advertisements for smoking cessation or reduction on McGill Classifieds, Craigslist, and Facebook." (Methods, Participants, paragraph 1)
studies.location: Montreal, Canada (McGill University). "Participants were recruited via advertisements for smoking cessation or reduction on McGill Classifieds, Craigslist, and Facebook." Author affiliation: McGill University, Montreal, Canada. (Title page)
studies.mental_health: N/A — no psychiatric enrollment criterion. Exclusion criteria included current psychotherapy and psychotropic medication use, but no psychiatric diagnosis or symptom threshold was required for enrollment.
studies.physical_health: Smoking status required for enrollment: "identify themselves as current smokers (smoking an average of one cigarette per day or more)" and "smoked for at least one year." (Methods, Participants, paragraph 1)
studies.arms: Four arms. "one hundred and twenty-six smokers seeking to quit were randomly assigned to one of four interventions." (1) Self-compassion intervention — imagery-based self-compassionate self-talk; (2) Self-energizing intervention — imagery-based energizing self-talk; (3) Self-controlling intervention — imagery-based directive self-talk; (4) Baseline self-monitoring condition — daily self-monitoring only. (Abstract; Methods, Procedure)
studies.meditation_intervention: The self-compassion intervention was based on Gilbert's (2005, 2009) Compassionate Mind Training (CMT) and compassion-focused therapy. It consisted of imagery-based self-talk exercises. In the first lab session (~45 minutes total slideshow), participants: (1) received a rationale for self-compassionate imagery; (2) created an ideal compassionate image; (3) completed CMT imagery exercises (visualizing age, appearance, facial expressions, postures, inner emotions of the image); (4) wrote a compassionate self-letter. For three weeks, at every urge to smoke, participants were instructed to: (1) visualize their compassionate image; (2) relate to themselves from the image's perspective (imagined dialogue, talking aloud, or writing); (3) feel themselves receiving compassion. All four conditions also included daily self-monitoring exercises (recording cigarettes smoked/resisted twice daily). "The self-compassion intervention...involved engaging in self-compassionate imagery and self-talk at every urge to smoke." (Abstract; Methods, Self-Compassion Intervention section)
studies.intervention_delivery: In-person lab session for initial training (~45 minutes: 20-minute self-monitoring component + additional 25-minute imagery/self-talk component), delivered individually via PowerPoint slideshow with audio via headphones. Home-based self-help exercises for three weeks. Research assistant administered. No specific facilitator credentials reported. "The slideshow for the baseline self-monitoring condition lasted approximately 20 minutes, whereas those for the enhanced imagery/self-talk conditions lasted an additional 25 minutes." (Methods, Procedure, paragraph 1)
studies.digital_component_raw: No digital component. Participants submitted daily cigarette records by e-mail after weeks 1 and 2, and completed short questionnaires from home by e-mail, but the intervention itself was delivered via in-person slideshow with audio. "participants were also e-mailed short questionnaires to complete from home after weeks 1 and 2 of the study." (Methods, Procedure, paragraph 2). The e-mail was used for data collection, not intervention delivery.
studies.intervention_tailor: No tailoring reported. The intervention was developed for smokers generally, with no cultural or population-specific adaptations described.
studies.comparison: Three comparison conditions: (1) Baseline self-monitoring condition: participants received a rationale for self-monitoring, completed smoking diary forms twice daily (recording situations, feelings, thoughts around last two cigarettes smoked or resisted), and re-read forms at end of each day. Slideshow ~20 minutes. (2) Self-energizing intervention: identical format to self-compassion but participants visualized an energizing image and used enthusiastic, cheerful self-talk at every urge to smoke. (3) Self-controlling intervention: identical format but participants visualized a firm, instructive image and used directive, controlling self-talk at every urge to smoke. All three enhanced conditions also included the self-monitoring component. "The slideshows for the self-energizing and self-controlling intervention conditions were identical in format to the self-compassion condition, but differed in content." (Methods, Self-Energizing and Self-Controlling Interventions section)
studies.assessment_time: T0 = Baseline/pre-study week (0 weeks); T1 = End of Week 1 (1 week); T2 = End of Week 2 (2 weeks); T3 = End of Week 3 / second lab session (3 weeks). "Participants came to the lab on two occasions three weeks apart." "they were also e-mailed short questionnaires to complete from home after weeks 1 and 2 of the study." (Methods, Procedure)
studies.assessment_nature: Primarily self-report: daily cigarette diary (self-report), questionnaires (DEQ, SCS, Smoking Stage of Change, imagery vividness ratings, compliance measures). No physiological or biological measures reported. "Although biochemical tests are typically considered the most valid measure of cigarette consumption, self-reports demonstrate high accuracy." (Methods, Measures, CPD section)
studies.outcomes_all:
1. Cigarettes Per Day (CPD) — self-reported daily cigarette count (primary behavioral outcome; pre-study week + 3 study weeks)
2. Readiness to Change — Smoking Stage of Change–Short Form (DiClemente et al., 1991; 3 items; 0–5 scale)
3. Trait Self-Criticism — Depressive Experiences Questionnaire McGill Revision self-criticism subscale (DEQ; 30 items; 7-point Likert) and Self-Compassion Scale (SCS; Neff, 2003; 26 items, 6 subscales)
4. Imagery Vividness — 4-item scale (Marks, 1973; 5-point scale) assessed at end of weeks 1, 2, and 3
5. Compliance with self-monitoring exercises — weekly checklist (0 to >4 times per day)
6. Compliance with imagery/self-talk exercises — 6-item scale (1–7) assessed weekly
"In each of our three primary analyses, participants' average CPD over the four time points...served as the dependent variable." (Results, Analytic Strategy)
studies.outcomes_primary: Cigarettes Per Day (CPD) — rate of smoking reduction over three weeks. "In each of our three primary analyses, participants' average CPD over the four time points (i.e., the week previous to the study and the first, second, and third weeks of the study) served as the dependent variable." (Results, Analytic Strategy)
studies.outcome_timepoints: T0 = Pre-study week baseline (0 weeks); T1 = Week 1 (1 week); T2 = Week 2 (2 weeks); T3 = Week 3 (3 weeks). Moderator variables (readiness to change, self-criticism) assessed at baseline. Imagery vividness assessed at end of weeks 1, 2, and 3. Compliance assessed weekly. "participants' average CPD over the four time points (i.e., the week previous to the study and the first, second, and third weeks of the study)" (Results, Analytic Strategy)
studies.recruitment: "Participants were recruited via advertisements for smoking cessation or reduction on McGill Classifieds, Craigslist, and Facebook. Interested individuals completed a short screening questionnaire online." Eligible participants were then invited to participate. No recruitment dates reported. (Methods, Participants, paragraph 1)
studies.study_purpose: "The current study sought to extend research by Adams and Leary (2007) by developing and testing a three-week self-compassion intervention designed to help individuals resist urges to smoke. We were interested in determining first, whether self-compassion would facilitate the self-regulation of cigarette consumption and second, whether there would be moderators of these effects." (Methods, The Current Study section)
studies.study_design: Randomized controlled trial (RCT) with four arms. "one hundred and twenty-six smokers seeking to quit were randomly assigned to one of four interventions." Randomization used SAS 9.1 output. No blinding reported. "the research assistant examined the randomization output from SAS 9.1 (SAS Institute, 2008) to determine the condition to which the participant had been assigned." (Methods, Procedure, paragraph 1)
studies.treatment_vs_prevention: Treatment — participants are current smokers (active behavior/substance use) enrolled specifically because they smoke and want to quit, and the study tests whether the intervention reduces smoking. "one hundred and twenty-six smokers seeking to quit were randomly assigned to one of four interventions." (Abstract)

studies.authors: Khine, W. W. T., Voong, M. L., Ng, T. K. S., Feng, L., Rane, G. A., Kumar, A. P., Kua, E. H., Mahendran, R., Mahendran, R., & Lee, Y.-K.
studies.title: Mental awareness improved mild cognitive impairment and modulated gut microbiome
studies.abstract: There is ample scientific and clinical evidence of the effects of gut microbiota on the brain but no definitive evidence that the brain can affect changes in gut microbiota under the bi-directional gut-brain axis concept. As there is no pharmacotherapeutic intervention for the early stages of cognitive decline, research has focused on cognitive stimulation in reversing or slowing the impairment. Elderly patients diagnosed with mild cognitive impairment underwent a randomized-control trial of mindful awareness practice. Neuropsychological assessments, inflammatory markers, and gut microbiota profiles were tested. Here, we report that their cognitive impairment was improved and associated with changes in gut bacterial profile. A cognition-score-dependent-abundance was observed in Ruminococcus vs Recognition Trials (RT), Digit Span Backward (DSB), Semantic Fluency Span (SFS) and Memory Domain (MD); Coprococcus vs DSB, Color Trails Test 2 (CTT2) and Block Design (BD); Parabacteroides vs DSB and SFS; Fusobacterium vs DSB and CTT2; Enterobacteriaceae vs BD and SFS; Ruminococcaceae vs DSB; Phascolarctobacterium vs MD. The study showed for the first-time, alteration in the cognitive capacity leading to the corresponding changes in microbiota profiles. This strongly suggests that signals from the different segments of brain could dictate directly or indirectly the abundances of specific gut microbes.
studies.total_n: 28 MCI patients were randomly assigned to the MAP intervention. Additionally, 40 Normal Aging subjects provided comparison data. The randomized MCI group n=28. 'After the neuropsychological diagnosis was made, 123 subjects (46 MCI and 77 Normal Aging subjects) participated in the study and 28 MCI patients (mean age 71.3 years, 71.4% female and 96.4% Chinese) were randomly assigned to undergo a Mindful Awareness Program (MAP) intervention for 9 months.' (Materials and Methods, Study design, paragraph 2). Total randomized to intervention: 28.

Note: Table 1 reports mean age as 65 for Normal Aging and 67 for MCI, while the Methods text states 71.3 for MAP group and 69 for Normal Aging. These are inconsistent; human review recommended.
