studies.participants: Community-living elderly Chinese individuals of both genders, aged 60–85 years, diagnosed with mild cognitive impairment (MCI). MAP group: 71.4% female, 96.4% Chinese. 'A cohort of community-living elderly Chinese individuals aged 60-85 years of both genders was recruited at the Training and Research Academy (TaRA), Singapore.' (Materials and Methods, Study design, paragraph 1).
studies.eligibility: Inclusion criteria: 'elderly individuals who fulfilled the operational criteria/definition of MCI with at least, one age-education adjusted neuropsychological test Z score less than (-)1.5, did not meet Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (DSM-5) criteria for dementia, had memory/cognitive complaints, preferably corroborated by a reliable informant, had intact activities of daily living, did function independently and could travel on their own to the site of the MAP program.' Exclusion criteria: 'those who had a neurological condition such as epilepsy, Parkinson's disease, a major psychiatric condition such as major depressive disorder, significant visual or hearing impairment, color blindness, upper and lower limb motor difficulties, suffered from a terminal illness and participated in another interventional study at the same time.' (Materials and Methods, Study design, paragraph 1).
studies.population_vulnerable: Not a vulnerable population in the sense of structural disadvantage — participants are elderly individuals with mild cognitive impairment, a clinical condition, but the study does not specifically target a population defined by health disparities or structural disadvantage. 'A cohort of community-living elderly Chinese individuals aged 60-85 years of both genders was recruited at the Training and Research Academy (TaRA), Singapore.' (Materials and Methods, Study design, paragraph 1).
studies.location: Training and Research Academy (TaRA), Singapore. 'A cohort of community-living elderly Chinese individuals aged 60-85 years of both genders was recruited at the Training and Research Academy (TaRA), Singapore.' (Materials and Methods, Study design, paragraph 1).
studies.mental_health: N/A — no psychiatric enrollment criterion. MCI is a neurocognitive condition, not a psychiatric diagnosis. Participants were required to fulfill MCI criteria (at least one age-education adjusted neuropsychological test Z score less than -1.5, not meeting DSM-5 criteria for dementia). Major psychiatric conditions (e.g., major depressive disorder) were exclusion criteria. (Materials and Methods, Study design, paragraph 1).
studies.physical_health: Mild Cognitive Impairment (MCI) diagnosis required for enrollment: 'elderly individuals who fulfilled the operational criteria/definition of MCI with at least, one age-education adjusted neuropsychological test Z score less than (-)1.5, did not meet Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (DSM-5) criteria for dementia.' (Materials and Methods, Study design, paragraph 1).
studies.arms: The study has 2 groups: (1) MAP intervention group — 28 MCI patients randomly assigned to the Mindful Awareness Program for 9 months; (2) Normal Aging comparison group — 40 Normal Aging subjects providing stool and blood samples (not randomized, observational comparison). 'After the neuropsychological diagnosis was made, 123 subjects (46 MCI and 77 Normal Aging subjects) participated in the study and 28 MCI patients...were randomly assigned to undergo a Mindful Awareness Program (MAP) intervention for 9 months. 40 Normal Aging subjects...provided stool and blood samples.' (Materials and Methods, Study design, paragraph 2).
studies.meditation_intervention: The intervention is called the Mindful Awareness Program (MAP). It involved 'group work mindfulness-based practices for older adults guided by in-house trained staff.' Practices included: mindfulness of the senses (focusing on five sensory perceptions: sounds, sight, scents, taste and touch), body scan practice (scanning different body parts for sensations), walking meditation (concentrating on the detail process of walking movement), movement nature (observing flexibility, strength and confidence while moving the body naturally), and visuomotor limb tasks (training mind-body coordination). 'In the initial three months, guided interventions were provided for 40 minutes weekly and the subjects practiced daily. Serving as self-control, the remaining six months of guided practices were conducted for 45 minutes monthly instead.' Total duration: 9 months. No medication, dietary or lifestyle changes were involved. (Materials and Methods, Study design, paragraphs 3–4).
studies.intervention_delivery: In-person group sessions. 'MAP was led weekly for 3 months and then monthly for 6 months, by an experienced instructor.' Sessions were 40 minutes weekly for the first 3 months, then 45 minutes monthly for the remaining 6 months. Delivered by 'in-house trained staff' and 'an experienced instructor.' Participants also practiced daily at home. (Introduction, paragraph 4; Materials and Methods, Study design, paragraphs 3–4).
studies.digital_component_raw: No digital component. The intervention was delivered in-person by an experienced instructor. No technology platform mentioned for delivery. (Materials and Methods, Study design, paragraphs 3–4).
studies.intervention_tailor: The MAP was described as 'group work mindfulness-based practices for older adults' (citing McBee 2008, 2014 — Mindfulness-Based Elder Care), suggesting it was adapted for older adults. 'Participants in the MAP group were taught mindful awareness practice techniques: group work mindfulness-based practices for older adults.' (Materials and Methods, Study design, paragraph 3). The program was specifically designed for elderly individuals with MCI.
studies.comparison: The comparison group was a Normal Aging group of 40 community-living elderly subjects (mean age 69 years, 72.5% female, 100% Chinese) who did not receive any intervention. They provided stool and blood samples at baseline only (Timepoint 1). This was not a randomized control arm but an observational comparison group. '40 Normal Aging subjects (mean age 69 years, 72.5% female and 100% Chinese) provided stool and blood samples.' (Materials and Methods, Study design, paragraph 2).
studies.assessment_time: T0 = Baseline (0 weeks); T1 = 3 months post-baseline (approximately 12.6 weeks); T2 = 9 months post-baseline (approximately 37.8 weeks). 'Stool and blood samples were collected at baseline, 3 months and 9 months and represented as Timepoint 1, Timepoint 2 and Timepoint 3 respectively.' (Introduction, paragraph 4). Conversion: 3 months = 3 × 4.2 = 12.6 weeks; 9 months = 9 × 4.2 = 37.8 weeks.
studies.assessment_nature: Both self-report and non-self-report measures were used. Non-self-report measures included: neuropsychological tests (clinician-administered: RAVLT, Digit Span, Block Design, Color Trails Test, Semantic Fluency Span, MMSE, CDR), biological samples (blood for telomere length, BDNF, DHEAS, hs-CRP; fecal samples for gut microbiota profiling and fecal water cytokines). Self-report included food frequency questionnaire. 'The neuropsychological assessments and the stool...and blood...samples collection were made at baseline...at 3-months...and 9-months.' (Materials and Methods, Study design, paragraph 2).
studies.outcomes_all: 1. Cognitive function — RAVLT (Delayed Recall, Recognition Trial, Memory Domain); Digit Span Backward; Block Design; Color Trails Test 2; Semantic Fluency Span (neuropsychological test battery, Z scores). 2. Global cognitive screening — Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE, range 0–30, modified version). 3. Clinical dementia staging — Clinical Dementia Rating (CDR). 4. Depression — Geriatric Depression Scale (GDS). 5. Anxiety — Geriatric Anxiety Index (GAI). 6. Telomere length — Telomere Restriction Fragment (TRF) length analysis (bp). 7. Plasma BDNF — ELISA (pg/ml). 8. Plasma DHEAS — ELISA (ng/ml). 9. Plasma hs-CRP — ELISA (µg/ml). 10. Gut microbiota profile — 16S rRNA gene sequencing (alpha diversity: Chao1, Shannon; beta diversity: weighted/unweighted UniFrac; relative abundance of bacterial genera). 11. Fecal water cytokines — IL-1β, IL-2, IL-4, IL-5, IL-6, IL-8, IL-10, IL-12, TNF-α, IFN-γ, GM-CSF (LUNARIS Human 11-Plex cytokine kit, pg/ml). 12. Nutritional intake — Food Frequency Questionnaire (FFQ). (Materials and Methods, Cognitive assessment; Blood samples collection; Gut microbiota profiling; Fecal water cytokines analysis).
studies.outcomes_primary: Unclear — authors do not explicitly designate a primary outcome. The study appears to focus on cognitive function improvement and gut microbiota changes. 'Neuropsychological assessments, inflammatory markers, and gut microbiota profiles were tested.' (Abstract). The main finding reported is: 'their cognitive impairment was improved and associated with changes in gut bacterial profile.' (Abstract).
studies.outcome_timepoints: T0 = Baseline (0 weeks); T1 = 3 months (12.6 weeks); T2 = 9 months (37.8 weeks). All outcomes (neuropsychological tests, blood biomarkers, gut microbiota, fecal cytokines) assessed at all three timepoints for the MAP group. Normal Aging group assessed at baseline only. 'The neuropsychological assessments and the stool...and blood...samples collection were made at baseline (both MCI/MAP-Timepoint 1 and Normal Aging groups), at 3-months (MAP-Timepoint 2) and 9-months (MAP-Timepoint 3).' (Materials and Methods, Study design, paragraph 2).
studies.recruitment: Participants were recruited at the Training and Research Academy (TaRA), Singapore. 'A cohort of community-living elderly Chinese individuals aged 60-85 years of both genders was recruited at the Training and Research Academy (TaRA), Singapore.' Screening involved MMSE with education-adjusted cut-offs, followed by full neuropsychological assessment battery and clinical review by a panel of consultants. Recruitment dates not reported. (Materials and Methods, Study design, paragraphs 1–2; Cognitive assessment section).
studies.study_purpose: To examine whether improvements in cognition from a mindful awareness practice intervention were associated with changes in gut microbiota profile in elderly MCI patients, thereby demonstrating the brain-to-gut direction of the gut-brain axis. 'We then introduced a psychosocial intervention: Mindful Awareness Program (MAP), involving elderly with MCI aged 60 to 85 years, to determine if improvements in cognition were associated with changes in the gut bacteria.' (Introduction, paragraph 4).
studies.study_design: Randomized controlled trial (RCT) with a non-randomized Normal Aging comparison group. '28 MCI patients...were randomly assigned to undergo a Mindful Awareness Program (MAP) intervention for 9 months.' Randomization method not described in detail. No control arm for the MCI group — the reduced-frequency phase (months 4–9) served as a self-control. 'Extension of the MAP intervention in the subsequent 6 months with frequency reduced to monthly guided sessions, which served as self-control in the study.' (Materials and Methods, Study design; Results, paragraph 3). Registered at ClinicalTrials.gov ID NCT02286791.
studies.treatment_vs_prevention: Treatment — participants were required to have a diagnosis of MCI at enrollment, and the study tested whether the intervention could improve or reverse cognitive impairment. 'Elderly patients diagnosed with mild cognitive impairment underwent a randomized-control trial of mindful awareness practice.' (Abstract). 'The inclusion criteria were: elderly individuals who fulfilled the operational criteria/definition of MCI.' (Materials and Methods, Study design, paragraph 1).

studies.authors: Kosari, F., Sabahi, P., & Makvand Hosseini, S.
studies.title: Comparative Effects of Parent Management Training Combined With ACT and Mindful Parenting on Parent-child Relationship
studies.abstract:
Background: Considering the profound influence of parent-child relationships on child vulnerability and mental health, prioritizing the improvement of this bond becomes crucial. While combined programs have garnered substantial recognition for their heightened effectiveness, regrettably, no research has yet explored a comparative analysis of their efficacy. This study aims to assess and compare the effectiveness of combining parent management training (PMT) with both acceptance commitment therapy (ACT) and mindful parenting in improving the parent-child relationship.
Methods: The study employed a quasi-experimental design, specifically a pre-test and post-test method, with a three-month follow-up period. A control group was included to enhance the validity of the results. The statistical population comprised all mothers of preschool children in Semnan City, Iran in 2022. Using convenience sampling, 36 mothers were selected and randomly assigned to three groups, two experimental groups and one control group. Random assignment was achieved using a lottery-based method without replacement. The sample in experimental groups participated in an integrated training program, which consisted of two-hour sessions conducted eight times per week. Conversely, the control group was placed on a waiting list. The data analysis phase involved utilizing SPSS software, version 23 and applying multivariate covariance analysis.
Results: The results of the study indicated that both combined programs exhibited a significant impact on reducing conflicts within the parent-child relationship and fostering closeness (P<0.001). However, no significant effect was observed on parent-child dependency (P>0.05). Additionally, no significant difference was observed between the two combined programs regarding their effectiveness in enhancing the parent-child relationship. These results remained consistent during the follow-up stage.
Conclusion: This study highlighted that these programs have exhibited a significant capacity to enhance the parent-child relationship by fostering a sense of closeness and effectively mitigating conflicts. These results indicated that the integration of ACT or mindful parenting principles with PMT can provide valuable interventions for enhancing parent-child.
Keywords: Parenting, Mindfulness, Acceptance and commitment therapy, Child
studies.total_n: 36. "Using convenience sampling, 36 mothers were selected and were then randomly assigned to three groups, two experimental groups and one control group." (Methods, paragraph 4)

Children: Mindful parenting group Mean±SD = 5.75±0.452; ACT-based parenting group Mean±SD = 6.50±0.52; Control group Mean±SD = 5.42±0.51. "The Mean±SD in the mindful parenting group was 36.58±3.02 for mothers and 5.75±0.452 for children." (Results, paragraph 1)
studies.participants: Mothers of preschool children (aged 5–7 years) in Semnan City, Iran. All participants were female (mothers). Education levels ranged from high school diploma to PhD. "The distribution of working mothers and housewives in the mindful parenting group was 8(66.5%) and 4(33.3%), respectively." (Results, paragraph 1)
studies.eligibility: Inclusion criteria: (1) having a child aged between 5 and 7 years; (2) residing with a spouse; (3) willingness to participate in the parenting sessions; (4) minimum educational qualification of at least a high school diploma. Exclusion criteria: (1) presence of psychological disorders or use of psychiatric medications by either the mother or the child (assessed via psychological interview); (2) chronic diseases affecting either the mother or the child; (3) absenteeism from over two training sessions; (4) marital separation or divorce; (5) diminishing tendency to actively engage in the research; (6) simultaneously receiving psychological services. "The inclusion criteria included several essential factors. First, participants were required to have a child aged between 5 and 7 years." (Methods, Eligibility, paragraph 1)
studies.population_vulnerable: Not a vulnerable population — the study recruited mothers of preschool children from the general community in Semnan City, Iran, with no specific health disparity or structural disadvantage criterion. "The statistical population comprised all mothers of preschool children in Semnan City, Iran in 2022." (Methods, paragraph 1)
studies.location: Semnan City, Iran. "The statistical population comprised all mothers of preschool children in Semnan City, Iran in 2022." (Methods, paragraph 1)
studies.mental_health: N/A — no psychiatric enrollment criterion. Mothers with psychological disorders were excluded, but no psychiatric diagnosis or symptom threshold was required for enrollment.
studies.physical_health: N/A — no physical health enrollment criterion. Chronic disease was an exclusion criterion, not an inclusion criterion.
studies.arms: 3 arms. Arm 1 (EX1): Combined program of mindful parenting and PMT (n=12); Arm 2 (EX2): Combined program of ACT-based parenting and PMT (n=12); Arm 3 (Control): Waitlist control (n=12). "36 mothers were selected and were then randomly assigned to three groups, two experimental groups and one control group." (Methods, paragraph 4)
studies.meditation_intervention: Two mindfulness-related intervention arms: (1) Combined mindful parenting and PMT (EX1): 8 weekly sessions, 2 hours each. Based on Bögels and Restifo's mindful parenting program (2014) combined with Sanders' PMT model. Sessions covered: automatic parenting and fight-flight-freeze reactions, beginner's mind perspective, self-kindness and yoga, responding vs. reacting, intergenerational models, rebuilding parent-child relationship, mindful rules and behavior charts, summarizing mindful parenting principles. (2) Combined ACT-based parenting and PMT (EX2): 8 weekly sessions, 2 hours each. Based on Coyne and Murrell's 'The Joy of Parenting' (2009) combined with Sanders' PMT model. Sessions covered: psychological processes and reactive parenting, parental values, functional analysis of challenging situations, mindfulness training for emotions, managing tantrums, recognizing parenting mistakes, self-care and ideal parent comparison, fostering commitment. "Twelve mothers in one experimental group underwent the combined program of mindful parenting and PMT, which consisted of eight weekly sessions, with each session lasting two hours." (Methods, Research implementation process, paragraph 2)
studies.intervention_delivery: In-person group format. Eight weekly sessions, each lasting two hours. Delivered by the researcher who "completed a comprehensive training program on PMT and parenting skills based on ACT, in addition to mindful parenting, at esteemed institutions under the guidance of highly qualified and experienced professional instructors." (Methods, Research implementation process, paragraph 5). Due to COVID-19, some components (e.g., mindful eating) were replaced with recorded materials for home practice.
studies.digital_component_raw: No digital component. Note: due to COVID-19 restrictions, recorded materials were provided for participants to engage in mindful eating exercises at home. "the researcher provided recorded materials for participants to engage in mindful eating exercises at home" (Study limitations, paragraph 1). This was an analog/recorded supplement, not a digital delivery platform.
studies.intervention_tailor: Yes — the intervention was adapted for Iranian mothers of preschool children. Additionally, due to COVID-19 restrictions, the 'mindful eating' component could not be performed during sessions and was replaced with recorded materials for home practice. "due to the necessity of adhering to health protocols, the practice of 'mindful eating' cannot be performed during the sessions. Instead, the researcher provided recorded materials for participants to engage in mindful eating exercises at home." (Study limitations, paragraph 1)
studies.comparison: Waitlist control group (n=12): Mothers placed on a waiting list and received no intervention during the study period. "The control group was placed on a waiting list." (Methods, paragraph 4). Post-study intervention was not described.
studies.assessment_time: T0 = Baseline/Pre-test (0 weeks); T1 = Post-intervention (8 weeks); T2 = Follow-up (approximately 20 weeks, i.e., 8 weeks intervention + 3-month follow-up = 8 + 12.6 = ~20.6 weeks). "The training program spanned two months, and upon completion, a post-test assessment was administered to all three groups. Furthermore, a three-month follow-up evaluation was conducted to assess the long-term effects." (Methods, Research implementation process, paragraph 1)
studies.assessment_nature: Self-report questionnaire only. The Pianta Parent-Child Relationship Scale (PCRS) is a parent-report instrument. "Pianta parent-child relationship scale (PCRS)... is a 33-item instrument utilized to assess various aspects of the parent-child relationship." (Methods, Measures, paragraph 1)
studies.outcomes_all: Parent-child relationship — Pianta Parent-Child Relationship Scale (PCRS; 33 items, 3 subscales: Conflict, Closeness, Dependency; 5-point Likert scale). "Pianta parent-child relationship scale (PCRS), developed by Pianta in 1992, is a 33-item instrument utilized to assess various aspects of the parent-child relationship. It encompasses dimensions, such as parent-child dependency, perceived conflicts, and the degree of closeness." (Methods, Measures, paragraph 1)
studies.outcomes_primary: Unclear — authors do not explicitly designate a primary outcome. The study aim is to assess the parent-child relationship broadly. "The primary focus was to assess the impact of these interventions on the enhancement of the parent-child relationship." (Introduction, final paragraph)
studies.outcome_timepoints: T0 = Baseline/Pre-test (0 weeks); T1 = Post-intervention (~8 weeks); T2 = Follow-up (~20.6 weeks). All outcomes (PCRS total and subscales) assessed at all three timepoints. "Table 1 presents the Mean±SD values of the control and experimental groups in three phases, pre-test, post-test, and follow-up." (Results, paragraph 1)
studies.recruitment: Convenience sampling from mothers of preschool children in Semnan City, Iran in 2022. Participants were invited to attend a briefing session. "Initially, the potential participants were invited to attend a briefing session where the research objectives and session procedures were thoroughly explained." (Methods, Research implementation process, paragraph 1). Recruitment dates not specified beyond 2022.

studies.title: Mindfulness in informal caregivers of palliative patients
studies.abstract:
Objectives: Mindfulness is a concept of growing impact on psychotherapy and has been shown to be effective for stress reduction and to improve psychological well-being. Existential Behavioural Therapy (EBT) was developed to support relatives of palliative care (PC) patients to cope with their situation during caregiving and bereavement. Mindfulness training was a core element of the intervention. We investigated the relationship between mindfulness, mental distress, and psychological well-being in informal caregivers, and evaluated if the effects of the intervention were mediated by mindfulness.
Methods: Relatives of PC inpatients took part in a randomized-controlled EBT trial and completed the Cognitive and Affective Mindfulness Scale-Revised, items from the Five Facets of Mindfulness as well as the Brief Symptom Inventory, the Satisfaction with Life Scale, the WHOQOL-BREF, a numerical rating scale on quality of life (range 0–10), and the Schedule for Meaning in Life Evaluation at pre- and post-intervention, and a 3- and 12-months follow-up.
Results: One-hundred-and-thirty carers were included, most of them (71.6%) recently being bereaved at the beginning of the intervention. High correlations between mindfulness and mental distress (r = −0.51, p < 0.001) as well as life satisfaction (r = 0.52, p < 0.001) were found. Mindfulness was a significant predictor of improvement in psychological distress, meaning in life and quality of life three months after the intervention. The EBT effects were partly mediated by mindfulness.
Significance of results: Mindfulness seems to be a promising concept in supporting informal caregivers of PC patients. Further research is needed to identify the required format and intensity of mindfulness practice necessary for improvement.
studies.total_n: 130. 'One-hundred-and-sixty informal caregivers took part in the trial; mindfulness data were available for 130 participants.' (Results, Sample, paragraph 1). Note: 160 were randomized; 130 had mindfulness data available.
studies.age_mean: 54.3 (weighted; Intervention: 54.5±13.6 n=73; Control: 54.0±13.2 n=57)
studies.age_describe: Total sample M=54.3, SD=13.4. Intervention group: M=54.5, SD=13.6; Control group: M=54.0, SD=13.2. 'Age (in years): M + SD 54.5 + 13.6 [intervention] 54.0 + 13.2 [control] 54.3 + 13.4 [total]' (Table 1, Sample characteristics).
studies.participants: Informal caregivers (relatives) of palliative care inpatients, including both active caregivers and bereaved relatives. 'most of them (71.6%) recently being bereaved at the beginning of the intervention.' 70.8% women. Partners predominant (61.5%). 80.8% caring for cancer patients. (Table 1, Sample characteristics).
studies.eligibility: Inclusion criteria: (1) relative of a PC patient (life expectancy ≤6 months), (2) at least 21 years old, (3) without severe psychiatric disease or significant cognitive impairment, and (4) sufficient knowledge of German. 'Inclusion criteria were: (1) relative of a PC patient (life expectancy ≤6 months), (2) at least 21 years old, (3) without severe psychiatric disease or significant cognitive impairment, and (4) sufficient knowledge of German.' (Methods, paragraph 2). Exclusion criteria: severe psychiatric disease or significant cognitive impairment (stated as exclusion within inclusion criteria).
studies.population_vulnerable: Yes — informal caregivers of palliative care patients, a population under significant caregiving burden and bereavement stress. 'Relatives of palliative care (PC) patients are highly burdened during caregiving and bereavement... Studies indicate that 30–50% suffer from depression, anxiety, or adjustment disorders.' (Introduction, paragraph 1).
studies.location: Munich, Germany. 'Interdisciplinary Center for Palliative Medicine, Ludwig-Maximilians-University, Munich, Germany' (author affiliations). 'The study was approved by the Research Ethics Committee of the Munich University Hospital.' (Methods, paragraph 2).
studies.mental_health: N/A — no psychiatric enrollment criterion. Exclusion of severe psychiatric disease or significant cognitive impairment is stated, but no psychiatric diagnosis or symptom threshold is required for enrollment. (Methods, paragraph 2).
studies.physical_health: N/A — no physical health enrollment criterion. Participants are relatives/caregivers of palliative patients, not patients themselves. (Methods, paragraph 2).
studies.arms: Two arms. (1) Intervention: Existential Behavioural Therapy (EBT) group (n=73); (2) Control: treatment-as-usual control group (n=57). 'a randomized controlled trial (with equal randomization 1:1) evaluating EBT in comparison to a treatment-as-usual control group' (Methods, paragraph 1). Note: n=73 and n=57 are from the 130 with mindfulness data; total randomized was 160.
studies.meditation_intervention: Existential Behavioural Therapy (EBT) — a group-based intervention with mindfulness training as a core element. Six sessions, maximum 10 participants per group, 22 hours in total. 'The EBT groups (six sessions, maximum of 10 participants/group, 22 hours in total) were led by trained psychotherapists.' Information on mindfulness given during first meetings. Every session included formal mindfulness practice (e.g., following one's breath while noticing and letting go of all thoughts, feelings and sensations) for at least 15 minutes. Participants received CD recordings with mindfulness exercises and were encouraged to practice at home at least twice a day for a minimum of 10 minutes. Informal mindfulness (performing daily activities mindfully) was also practiced. (Methods, paragraph 3).
studies.intervention_delivery: In-person group format. Six sessions, 22 hours total, maximum 10 participants per group. Led by trained psychotherapists. CD recordings provided for home practice. 'The EBT groups (six sessions, maximum of 10 participants/group, 22 hours in total) were led by trained psychotherapists.' (Methods, paragraph 3).
studies.digital_component_raw: No digital component. CD recordings were provided for home mindfulness practice. 'Participants received CD recordings with mindfulness exercises and were encouraged to practice at home at least twice a day for a minimum of 10 minutes.' (Methods, paragraph 3). CDs are analog/old technology, not digital delivery.
studies.intervention_tailor: Yes — the EBT intervention was specifically developed for informal caregivers of palliative care patients. 'Existential Behavioural Therapy (EBT) has been developed to support informal caregivers facing the imminent or recent loss of a family member in a PC setting.' (Introduction, paragraph 5). Population-specific content tailored to caregiving and bereavement context.
studies.comparison: Treatment-as-usual (TAU) control group. 'a randomized controlled trial (with equal randomization 1:1) evaluating EBT in comparison to a treatment-as-usual control group in informal caregivers of PC patients.' (Methods, paragraph 1). No further description of TAU content is provided in this paper.
studies.assessment_time: T1 = Baseline (0 weeks); T2 = Post-intervention (approx. 6 weeks after T1); T3 = 3-month follow-up (approx. 18.2 weeks after T2, i.e., ~24.2 weeks from baseline); T4 = 12-month follow-up (~52 weeks after end of intervention, i.e., ~58 weeks from baseline). 'Self-report questionnaires were completed before (T1) and after intervention (T2, approx. 6 weeks after T1), and at follow-ups three (T3) and 12 (T4) months after the end of the intervention.' (Measures, paragraph 1). Conversion: 3 months = 12.6 weeks post-T2 (~18.6 weeks from baseline); 12 months = 50.4 weeks post-T2 (~56.4 weeks from baseline).
studies.assessment_nature: Self-report questionnaires only. 'Self-report questionnaires were completed before (T1) and after intervention (T2, approx. 6 weeks after T1), and at follow-ups three (T3) and 12 (T4) months after the end of the intervention.' (Measures, paragraph 1).
studies.outcomes_all:
1. Mindfulness (trait/dispositional) — Cognitive and Affective Mindfulness Scale-Revised (CAMS-R; 12 items, categories: Attention, Present-focus, Awareness, Acceptance)
2. Mindfulness facets — Five Facets of Mindfulness (FFMQ; 3 highest-loading items per factor: Non-reactivity, Observing, Acting with awareness, Describing, Non-judging)
3. Psychological distress — Brief Symptom Inventory (BSI; subscales: depression, anxiety, somatization; Global Severity Index [GSI]; T-values gender-adjusted)
4. Quality of life — WHOQOL-BREF (26 items, total score range 0–100)
5. Quality of life — Numerical Rating Scale (QoL-NRS; range 0–10)
6. Life satisfaction — Satisfaction with Life Scale (SWLS; 5 items, range 1–7)
7. Meaning in life — Schedule for Meaning in Life Evaluation (SMiLE)
8. Mindfulness practice frequency — self-reported formal and informal practice (times/week) (Methods, Measures section).
studies.outcomes_primary: Unclear — authors do not designate a single primary outcome. The study investigates relationships between mindfulness, mental distress, and well-being, and tests mediation. 'The aims of this study were (1) to assess if dispositional mindfulness is related to mental distress and psychological well-being... (2) to evaluate whether the effect of the EBT intervention... was mediated by mindfulness, and (3) to explore the impact of formal and informal practice.' (Aims section).
studies.outcome_timepoints: T1 = Baseline (0 weeks); T2 = Post-intervention (~6 weeks); T3 = 3-month follow-up (~18.6 weeks from baseline, i.e., ~12.6 weeks post-T2); T4 = 12-month follow-up (~56.4 weeks from baseline, i.e., ~50.4 weeks post-T2). All outcomes assessed at all four timepoints. 'Self-report questionnaires were completed before (T1) and after intervention (T2, approx. 6 weeks after T1), and at follow-ups three (T3) and 12 (T4) months after the end of the intervention.' (Measures, paragraph 1).
studies.recruitment: Relatives of PC inpatients at the Interdisciplinary Center for Palliative Medicine, Ludwig-Maximilians-University, Munich. Recruitment period: June 2008 to June 2010. 'Ten EBT groups consisting of averagely 7.3±1.1 participants were successfully carried out between 06/2008–06/2010.' (Results, Sample, paragraph 1). Specific recruitment channels not described in this paper; referred to Fegg et al., 2013.
studies.study_purpose: To investigate the relationship between mindfulness, mental distress, and psychological well-being in informal caregivers of palliative care patients, and to evaluate whether the effects of the EBT intervention were mediated by mindfulness. 'We investigated the relationship between mindfulness, mental distress, and psychological well-being in informal caregivers, and evaluated if the effects of the intervention were mediated by mindfulness.' (Abstract, Objectives).
studies.study_design: Randomized controlled trial (RCT), equal randomization 1:1. 'a randomized controlled trial (with equal randomization 1:1) evaluating EBT in comparison to a treatment-as-usual control group.' (Methods, paragraph 1). Blinding not reported. This paper is a secondary analysis of the RCT focusing on mindfulness as mediator.
studies.treatment_vs_prevention: Treatment — participants are informal caregivers of palliative patients experiencing significant psychological burden and bereavement; the intervention targets existing distress. 'Relatives of palliative care (PC) patients are highly burdened during caregiving and bereavement... Studies indicate that 30–50% suffer from depression, anxiety, or adjustment disorders.' (Introduction, paragraph 1). The intervention aims to support coping with an existing stressful situation.
studies.confidence_why:
• total_n — 160 were randomized but only 130 had mindfulness data; the paper uses n=130 as the analytic sample. The randomized N is stated as 160 but arm-level Ns in Table 1 sum to 130. Flagged.
• age_mean — weighted mean calculated from arm-level means and Ns (73 and 57 from Table 1); calculation flagged.
• age_min / age_max — not reported; only minimum age eligibility criterion (21 years) stated.
• year — paper states 'Received February 17, 2013; Accepted March 22, 2013' and copyright 2013, but filename says 2015; year coded as 2013 per paper text.
• assessment_time — T3 and T4 converted from months to weeks (3 months = 12.6 weeks post-T2; 12 months = 50.4 weeks post-T2); calculation flagged.
• followup_longest — calculated as ~56.4 weeks from baseline (6 weeks to T2 + 50.4 weeks to T4); flagged as calculation.
studies.outcomes_coded: Stress-distress | Depression | Anxiety | Wellbeing-QoL | Mindfulness trait-state | Meaning-purpose-spirituality
studies.categories_flags:
• protocol_name — EBT (Existential Behavioural Therapy) is a named intervention but not a standard mindfulness protocol; coded as Unclear as it does not map to established mindfulness protocols in the list.
• is_adapted — EBT was developed specifically for this population; adaptation status relative to a parent protocol is unclear since EBT is the original protocol.
• adaptation_type — not applicable given is_adapted = Unclear; human adjudication needed.
• dose_weeks — intervention described as 6 sessions over approximately 6 weeks (T2 approx. 6 weeks after T1); exact weekly schedule not stated, inferred from T1-T2 interval.
• setting — participants are relatives of PC inpatients; intervention likely delivered at hospital/palliative care center but not explicitly stated.

studies.authors: Kral, T. R. A., Davis, K., Korponay, C., Hirshberg, M. J., Hoel, R., Tello, L. Y., Goldman, R. I., Rosenkranz, M. A., Lutz, A., & Davidson, R. J.
studies.title: Absence of structural brain changes from mindfulness-based stress reduction: Two combined randomized controlled trials
studies.abstract: Studies purporting to show changes in brain structure following the popular, 8-week mindfulness-based stress reduction (MBSR) course are widely referenced despite major methodological limitations. Here, we present findings from a large, combined dataset of two, three-arm randomized controlled trials with active and waitlist (WL) control groups. Meditation-naïve participants (n = 218) completed structural magnetic resonance imaging scans during two visits: baseline and postintervention period. After baseline, participants were randomly assigned to WL (n = 70), an 8-week MBSR program (n = 75), or a validated, matched active control (n = 73). We assessed changes in gray matter volume, gray matter density, and cortical thickness. In the largest and most rigorously controlled study to date, we failed to replicate prior findings and found no evidence that MBSR produced neuroplastic changes compared to either control group, either at the whole-brain level or in regions of interest drawn from prior MBSR studies.
studies.total_n: 264 randomized (MBSR n=90, WL n=84, HEP n=90); final analytic sample n=218 (MBSR n=75, HEP n=73, WL n=70). "Following baseline data collection, participants were randomized to one of three groups...MBSR (n = 90...WL (n = 84...or the HEP active control intervention (n = 90)" (Participants section, paragraph 2). Note: abstract states n=218 which is the analytic sample; randomized N=264 is from Methods.
studies.age_describe: Randomized sample: MBSR mean 46.6 ± 11.8 years (n=90, 53 female); WL mean 46.0 ± 11.7 years (n=84, 53 female); HEP mean 45.4 ± 12.5 years (n=90, 55 female). Analytic sample (T2 completers): MBSR mean 47.3 ± 11.9 years (n=75); HEP mean 46.0 ± 12.7 years (n=73); WL mean 46.8 ± 11.6 years (n=70). Dataset 1 age range: 26–66; Dataset 2 age range: 25–65. "average age, 45.7 ± 12.0 years" for 256 participants with baseline MRI data. (Participants section, paragraph 2–3; Table 1)
studies.age_min: 25 (Dataset 2 minimum across groups; Table 1 reports minimum of 25 for MBSR, HEP, WL in Dataset 2, and 26 for Dataset 1)
studies.participants: Meditation-naïve healthy adults from the Madison, WI community. "We recruited healthy human participants within the Madison, WI, community using flyers, online advertisements, and advertisements in local media for a study of 'health and well-being' or the 'benefits of health wellness classes.'" Predominantly White (majority), mixed sex (156 female out of 256 with baseline MRI). (Participants section, paragraph 1; Table 1)
studies.eligibility: Inclusion: adults between 18 and 65 years old; no prior training or formal practice in meditation or mind-body techniques (e.g., Tai chi); no expertise in physical activity, music, or nutrition. Exclusion: used psychotropic or nervous system altering medication; current diagnosis of sleep disorder; psychiatric diagnosis in the past year; any history of bipolar or schizophrenic disorders; history of brain damage or seizures; medical condition that would affect ability to safely participate in study procedures. "Participants were included if they were adults between 18 and 65 years old with no prior training or formal practice in meditation or mind-body techniques...Participants were excluded from enrollment if they had used psychotropic or nervous system altering medication, a current diagnosis of sleep disorder, a psychiatric diagnosis in the past year, any history of bipolar or schizophrenic disorders, history of brain damage or seizures, or a medical condition that would affect the participants ability to safely participate in study procedures." (Participants section, paragraph 1)
studies.population_vulnerable: Not a vulnerable population — participants were healthy community adults with no specific vulnerability criterion. "We recruited healthy human participants within the Madison, WI, community" with no health disparity or structural disadvantage criterion. (Participants section, paragraph 1)
studies.location: Madison, Wisconsin, USA. "Classes for both interventions (MBSR and HEP) were taught through the Integrative Health program at the University of Wisconsin School of Medicine and Public Health in Madison, WI." (Participants section, paragraph 3)
studies.mental_health: N/A — no psychiatric enrollment criterion. Participants were excluded if they had a psychiatric diagnosis in the past year, but no psychiatric condition was required for enrollment.
studies.physical_health: N/A — no physical health enrollment criterion. Exclusion for sleep disorder diagnosis and medical conditions affecting participation are exclusion criteria, not enrollment thresholds.
studies.arms: Three arms. "three-arm randomized controlled trials with active and waitlist (WL) control groups": (1) MBSR intervention (n=90 randomized, n=75 analytic); (2) Health Enhancement Program (HEP) active control (n=90 randomized, n=73 analytic); (3) Waitlist (WL) control (n=84 randomized, n=70 analytic). (Abstract; Participants section, paragraph 2)
studies.meditation_intervention: Explicitly named MBSR (Mindfulness-Based Stress Reduction). "The MBSR courses were delivered by experienced and certified MBSR instructors and consisted of practices and teachings aimed at increasing mindfulness, including yoga, meditation, and body awareness." 8-week program, 9 possible classes (participants attended average 8.14 classes). Home practice required; participants recorded daily practice logs; average home practice 32 hours (SD 20 hours; range 2–85 hours). (Participants section, paragraph 3; MBSR practice time section)
studies.intervention_delivery: In-person group format. "Classes for both interventions (MBSR and HEP) were taught through the Integrative Health program at the University of Wisconsin School of Medicine and Public Health in Madison, WI." Delivered by "experienced and certified MBSR instructors." Session count: 9 possible classes over 8 weeks. (Participants section, paragraph 3)
studies.digital_component_raw: No digital component. No technology-based delivery described. Home practice supported by participant-maintained logs. (Participants section, paragraph 3)
studies.intervention_tailor: No tailoring reported. The study used the standard MBSR protocol as described. "The intervention and randomization procedures were identical to those detailed by MacCoon et al." (Participants section, paragraph 3)
studies.comparison: Two control conditions: (1) Health Enhancement Program (HEP) active control: "The HEP course served as an active control, which was matched to MBSR and consisted of exercise, music therapy, and nutrition education and practices." 9 possible classes over 8 weeks; delivered by instructors at the same facility; validated in a separate study (MacCoon et al.). HEP participants practiced average 56 hours at home (SD 33 hours; range 7–255 hours), attended average 8.44 of 9 classes. (2) Waitlist (WL) control: passive waitlist, no intervention during the study period. (Participants section, paragraph 3; MBSR practice time section)
studies.assessment_time: T1 = Baseline (0 weeks); T2 = Post-intervention (~17.2 weeks, average time between scans). "Participants completed a baseline data collection visit before randomization and a second visit following the 8-week intervention period." Average time between scans was 120.6 days (~17.2 weeks), but most of this gap was due to lag between T1 scan and intervention start; T2 scan was prioritized close to intervention end (average 19.4 days after last MBSR class). A third long-term follow-up (~6 months after T2) was collected for sample 2 but not included in current analysis. (Data collection section, paragraph 1; Experimental design section)
studies.assessment_nature: Self-report questionnaire (FFMQ) and biological/physiological measures (structural MRI: gray matter volume, gray matter density, cortical thickness). "At each visit, participants attended a 24-hour laboratory session that included an MRI scan and the FFMQ, among other measures as part of a larger multisession, multiproject study." (Data collection section, paragraph 1)
studies.outcomes_all: 1. Gray matter volume (GMV) — structural MRI, surface-based analysis (FreeSurfer), multiple ROIs (left/right amygdala, left/right hippocampus, left/right caudate, left/right insula, posterior cingulate, left TPJ, cerebellum, cerebellum/brainstem) and whole-brain analysis. 2. Gray matter density (GMD) — VBM (SPM12), sensitivity analysis. 3. Cortical thickness (CT) — structural MRI, surface-based analysis (FreeSurfer), whole-brain and ROI. 4. Mindfulness — Five Facet Mindfulness Questionnaire (FFMQ). "We assessed changes in gray matter volume, gray matter density, and cortical thickness." "We examined self-reported mindfulness based on the Five Facet Mindfulness Questionnaire (FFMQ)." (Abstract; Mindfulness section; Data collection section)
studies.outcomes_primary: Unclear — authors do not explicitly designate a single primary outcome. The study assessed GMV, GMD, and CT as the main neuroimaging outcomes, with FFMQ as a manipulation check. "We assessed changes in gray matter volume, gray matter density, and cortical thickness." (Abstract; Introduction)
studies.outcome_timepoints: T0 = Baseline (0 weeks); T1 = Post-intervention (~8 weeks, following the 8-week intervention period). All outcomes (GMV, GMD, CT, FFMQ) assessed at both timepoints. A third follow-up (~34 weeks post-baseline, ~6 months after T2) was collected for sample 2 but not analyzed in this paper. (Data collection section; Experimental design section)
studies.recruitment: "We recruited healthy human participants within the Madison, WI, community using flyers, online advertisements, and advertisements in local media for a study of 'health and well-being' or the 'benefits of health wellness classes.'" Two trials: Sample 1 baseline collection February 2010–May 2011; Sample 2 baseline collection November 2014–March 2017. (Participants section, paragraph 1; Experimental design section)
studies.study_purpose: "The current study aimed to address these limitations by integrating a waitlist (WL) and a well-matched active control group with larger sample sizes...in a set of two rigorous, randomized controlled trials (RCTs) with pre-post designs...to test for structural changes that were specific to mindfulness meditation training, rather than nonspecific effects associated with well-being interventions more generally." Specifically to conceptually replicate prior findings of MBSR-related changes in brain structure (GMD, GMV, CT). (Introduction, paragraph 5)
studies.study_design: Combined dataset from two three-arm RCTs (NCT01057368 and NCT02157766). "The present study was registered with ClinicalTrials.gov and combined data across two clinical trials...Both datasets were collected with the same rigorous methods and three-arm RCT design." Randomization used "a stratified block assignment procedure to ensure age- and gender-balanced groups." All study staff except participant coordinator and project manager were blind to group assignment. Pre-post design. (Experimental design section; Participants section, paragraph 2)
studies.treatment_vs_prevention: Enhancement — participants were healthy community adults with no psychiatric or physical health enrollment criterion. The study tested whether MBSR produces structural brain changes and improvements in mindfulness in a non-clinical sample. "the current set of RCTs used a relatively long list of inclusion/exclusion criteria, including exclusion for use of psychotropic medication or psychiatric diagnosis in the past year, resulting in unusually healthy samples with, e.g., very low levels (or absence) of baseline anxiety and negative affect." (Discussion, paragraph 4)
studies.confidence_why: • total_n — The abstract reports n=218 (analytic sample) while the randomized N=264 is derived from summing arm-level randomized counts (90+84+90) reported in the Participants section. Calculation required. • age_mean — Weighted mean calculated from arm-level means and sample sizes; not directly reported as a single overall mean for the randomized sample. • outcome_timepoints — The post-intervention timing is described as 'following the 8-week intervention period' but the average time between scans was 120.6 days (~17 weeks) due to scheduling lag; the actual post-intervention scan was ~19 days after last class, making exact week-from-baseline timing ambiguous. • outcomes_primary — No primary outcome explicitly designated; inference required.
studies.active_comparator_name: Health Enhancement Program (HEP) — matched active control consisting of exercise, music therapy, and nutrition education and practices (MacCoon et al., 2012)
studies.outcomes_coded: Mindfulness trait-state | Brain imaging-neural
studies.categories_flags: • active_comparator_name — Human review recommended to confirm HEP classification and description. • age_group — Age range 18–66 spans into older adults (60+); both categories selected. • time_baseline_to_post — Set to 8 weeks (intervention duration) but actual scan timing was variable (average ~17 weeks from baseline due to scheduling lag); human review recommended. • followup_exists — A 6-month follow-up was collected for sample 2 but explicitly excluded from this analysis; coded No for this paper's analysis but human review may be warranted.

studies.authors: Kuyken, W., Byford, S., Taylor, R. S., Watkins, E., Holden, E., White, K., Barrett, B., Byng, R., Evans, A., Mullan, E., & Teasdale, J. D.
studies.title: Mindfulness-Based Cognitive Therapy to Prevent Relapse in Recurrent Depression
studies.abstract: For people at risk of depressive relapse, mindfulness-based cognitive therapy (MBCT) has an additive benefit to usual care (H. F. Coelho, P. H. Canter, & E. Ernst, 2007). This study asked if, among patients with recurrent depression who are treated with antidepressant medication (ADM), MBCT is comparable to treatment with maintenance ADM (m-ADM) in (a) depressive relapse prevention, (b) key secondary outcomes, and (c) cost effectiveness. The study design was a parallel 2-group randomized controlled trial comparing those on m-ADM (N = 62) with those receiving MBCT plus support to taper/discontinue antidepressants (N = 61). Relapse/recurrence rates over 15-month follow-ups in MBCT were 47%, compared with 60% in the m-ADM group (hazard ratio = 0.63; 95% confidence interval: 0.39 to 1.04). MBCT was more effective than m-ADM in reducing residual depressive symptoms and psychiatric comorbidity and in improving quality of life in the physical and psychological domains. There was no difference in average annual cost between the 2 groups. Rates of ADM usage in the MBCT group was significantly reduced, and 46 patients (75%) completely discontinued their ADM. For patients treated with ADM, MBCT may provide an alternative approach for relapse prevention.
studies.journal: Journal of Consulting and Clinical Psychology
studies.total_n: 123. 'One hundred twenty-three patients who could be located, agreed to participate, and met the inclusion criteria were randomized to either MBCT (N = 61) or m-ADM (N = 62) treatment.' (Results, Patient Flow, paragraph 2)
studies.age_describe: MBCT group: M = 48.95 (SD = 10.55), Range 26–66; m-ADM group: M = 49.37 (SD = 11.84), Range 21–72. 'Age (in years) M (SD) 48.95 (10.55) [MBCT] 49.37 (11.84) [m-ADM] Range 26–66 [MBCT] 21–72 [m-ADM]' (Table 1, Baseline Characteristics)
studies.participants: Adults with recurrent depression currently on antidepressant medication, recruited from primary care settings in Devon, England. Predominantly female (77% MBCT, 76% m-ADM) and White (98–100%). 'The study was conducted in primary care settings across a range of urban and rural locations in Devon, England.' (Participants, paragraph 1)
studies.eligibility: Inclusion criteria: 'three or more previous episodes of depression meeting criteria for depression according to the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (4th ed.; DSM–IV); 18 years of age or older; and on a therapeutic dose of m-ADM in line with the British National Formulary for at least the previous 6 months and is in either full or partial remission from the most recent episode of depression.' Exclusion criteria: 'comorbid diagnoses of current substance dependence; organic brain damage; current/past psychosis; bipolar disorder; persistent antisocial behavior; persistent self-injury requiring clinical management/therapy; unable to engage with MBCT for physical, practical, or other reasons (e.g., very disabling physical problem, unable to comprehend materials); and formal concurrent psychotherapy.' (Participants, paragraph 3)
studies.population_vulnerable: Not a vulnerable population — participants are adults with recurrent depression in primary care, predominantly White (98–100%), no specific structural disadvantage or health disparity criterion. 'White: n (%) 60 (98) [MBCT] 62 (100) [m-ADM]' (Table 1, Baseline Characteristics)
studies.location: Devon, England, United Kingdom. Primary care settings across urban and rural locations. 'The study was conducted in primary care settings across a range of urban and rural locations in Devon, England.' (Participants, paragraph 1)
studies.mental_health: Three or more previous episodes of major depression (DSM-IV criteria) required for enrollment, currently in full or partial remission. 'three or more previous episodes of depression meeting criteria for depression according to the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (4th ed.; DSM–IV)' and 'is in either full or partial remission from the most recent episode of depression.' (Participants, paragraph 3)
studies.physical_health: N/A — no physical health enrollment criterion. Being on antidepressant medication is a psychiatric treatment criterion, not a physical health threshold.
studies.arms: 2 arms. Arm 1: MBCT plus support to taper/discontinue antidepressants (N = 61). Arm 2: Maintenance antidepressant medication (m-ADM) (N = 62). 'a parallel 2-group randomized controlled trial comparing those on m-ADM (N = 62) with those receiving MBCT plus support to taper/discontinue antidepressants (N = 61).' (Abstract)
studies.meditation_intervention: MBCT (Mindfulness-Based Cognitive Therapy) as described in Segal, Williams, & Teasdale (2002). 'a manualized, group-based skills training program designed to enable patients to learn skills that prevent the recurrence of depression.' Delivered in groups of 9–15 patients. Sessions: 2-hr sessions over 8 consecutive weeks, followed by four follow-up sessions in the following year. Session content included 'guided mindfulness practices (i.e., body scan, sitting meditation, yoga); inquiry into patients' experience of these practices; review of weekly homework (i.e., 40 min of mindfulness practice per day and generalization of session learning); and teaching/discussion of cognitive–behavioral skills.' Adequate dose defined as attendance at ≥4 of 8 sessions. Participants also supported to taper/discontinue ADM. (Interventions, MBCT section, paragraphs 1–3)
studies.intervention_delivery: In-person group format, 9–15 patients per group, 2-hour sessions. 'The MBCT relapse prevention intervention was delivered in primary care settings with MBCT groups of 9–15 patients.' Therapists were 'either a clinical psychologist or an occupational therapist (three and two groups, respectively). Both therapists had undergone a training program taught and supervised by one of the developers of MBCT (John D. Teasdale), had experience of running at least two supervised pilot groups, and had an ongoing personal mindfulness practice.' (Interventions, MBCT section, paragraphs 2–3)
studies.digital_component_raw: No digital component. 'All trial groups were videotaped with digital cameras for therapist supervision, checks on therapist competence, and checks on treatment adherence.' — cameras used for supervision only, not for intervention delivery. Home practice used audio recordings (not explicitly stated as digital). (Interventions, MBCT section, paragraph 3)
studies.intervention_tailor: No tailoring reported. The intervention followed the standard MBCT treatment protocol (Segal, Williams, & Teasdale, 2002) without reported cultural or population-specific modifications.
studies.comparison: Maintenance antidepressant medication (m-ADM): 'The m-ADM relapse prevention intervention comprised maintenance of the ADM treatment that was an inclusion criterion for the study. Patients were monitored and treated by their physicians in primary care settings. During the maintenance phase, physicians were asked to manage m-ADM in line with standard clinical practice and the British National Formulary. Primary care physicians were asked to meet with patients regularly to review their medication treatment.' Medication adherence was actively monitored and supported by the research team. (Interventions, Maintenance antidepressant treatment section)
studies.assessment_time: T0 = Baseline (0 weeks); T1 = 1 month post-treatment (approximately 12–13 weeks from randomization, as MBCT ran 8 weeks plus follow-up sessions); T2 = 3 months (12.6 weeks); T3 = 6 months (25.2 weeks); T4 = 9 months (37.8 weeks); T5 = 12 months (50.4 weeks); T6 = 15 months (63 weeks). 'Patients were assessed by research staff blind to treatment allocation at intake and then again every 3 months up to 15 months postrandomization.' (Outcome Measures, paragraph 1). Note: Table 2 reports '1 month posttreatment' and '15 months follow-up' as labeled timepoints.
studies.assessment_nature: Both self-report and non-self-report measures used. Self-report: BDI-II, WHOQOL-BREF, subjective distress rating, MMAS, AD-SUS. Clinician/interviewer-administered: HRSD (observer-rated, interviewer-administered), SCID (structured clinical interview for relapse/recurrence and comorbidity). 'the observer-rated interviewer-administered, 17-item version of the HRSD' and 'the depression module of the Structured Clinical Interview for DSM–IV (SCID)' (Outcome Measures, paragraphs 1–3)
studies.outcomes_all:
1. Depressive relapse/recurrence — SCID depression module (DSM-IV criteria for major depressive disorder; time to relapse as primary outcome)
2. Severity of relapse/recurrence — DSM-IV specifiers (scale range 1–4: mild, moderate, severe without psychotic features, severe with psychotic features)
3. Duration of relapse/recurrence — months meeting SCID criteria
4. Subjective distress of relapse — patient-rated 1–100 scale
5. Residual depressive symptoms — Hamilton Rating Scale for Depression (HRSD), 17-item, observer-rated interviewer-administered
6. Residual depressive symptoms — Beck Depression Inventory-II (BDI-II), 21-item self-report
7. Psychiatric comorbidity — SCID relevant modules (number of comorbid DSM-IV Axis I diagnoses)
8. Quality of life — WHOQOL-BREF, 26-item self-report (physical, psychological, social, environment domains)
9. Service use — Adult Service Use Schedule (AD-SUS)
10. Medication adherence — Morisky Medication Adherence Scale (MMAS)
11. Antidepressant medication usage — days on ADM, self-report at follow-ups and practice databases
12. Cost effectiveness — incremental cost-effectiveness ratios (ICER) per relapse prevented and per depression-free day
(Outcome Measures section; Service Use, Productivity Losses, and Cost section)
studies.outcomes_primary: Time to relapse/recurrence of depression. 'Time from randomization to depressive relapse/recurrence was the primary outcome measure, with patients followed up at 3-month intervals for 15 months.' Assessed using the SCID depression module. (Design, paragraph 2; Outcome Measures, Primary outcome measure section)
studies.outcome_timepoints: T0 = Baseline (0 weeks); T1 = 3 months (12.6 weeks); T2 = 6 months (25.2 weeks); T3 = 9 months (37.8 weeks); T4 = 12 months (50.4 weeks); T5 = 15 months (63 weeks). 'Patients were assessed by research staff blind to treatment allocation at intake and then again every 3 months up to 15 months postrandomization.' Table 2 also reports a '1 month posttreatment' timepoint for secondary outcomes. (Outcome Measures, paragraph 1; Table 2)
studies.recruitment: Computerized practice database search to identify patients prescribed ADM for previous 6 months. Medical records consulted to check eligibility. Primary care physicians screened lists and wrote letters to potential participants. Research officer contacted potential participants by telephone for verbal consent and eligibility screening. Eligible and willing patients attended intake assessment. 'Recruitment was designed to screen as wide a population as possible in primary care.' (Participants, paragraphs 1–2)
studies.study_purpose: 'The primary aim of this trial was to examine whether MBCT provides an alternative approach to m-ADM in preventing depressive relapse/recurrence.' Secondary aims: 'to compare MBCT and m-ADM in terms of residual depressive symptoms, comorbid psychiatric diagnoses, quality of life, and cost effectiveness' and 'to establish if MBCT enabled patients to taper/discontinue their ADM.' (Method, Design, paragraph 3)
studies.study_design: Parallel 2-group randomized controlled trial. 'Block randomization (block size = 4) to the two groups was performed by an independent statistician using computer-generated quasi-random numbers. Randomization was stratified according to patients' symptomatic status at intake assessment by using the Hamilton Rating Scale for Depression.' Research staff conducting follow-ups were blind to treatment condition. (Design, paragraph 1)
studies.treatment_vs_prevention: Treatment — participants had a confirmed diagnosis of recurrent major depression (3+ previous episodes) and were currently on antidepressant medication, in full or partial remission. The study tests MBCT as a relapse prevention intervention for an existing, established condition. 'Study participants had a history of three or more previous episodes of depression, had been treated with a therapeutic dose of ADM over the last 6 months, and were currently either in full or partial remission from the most recent episode.' (Design, paragraph 1)

studies.authors: Laicher, H., Int-Veen, I., Woloszyn, L., Wiegand, A., Kroczek, A., Sippel, D., Leehr, E. J., Lawyer, G., Albasini, F., Frischholz, C., Mössner, R., Nieratschker, V., Rubel, J., Fallgatter, A., Ehlis, A.-C., & Rosenbaum, D.
studies.title: In situ fNIRS measurements during cognitive behavioral emotion regulation training in rumination-focused therapy: A randomized-controlled trial
studies.abstract: Repetitive negative thinking (RNT), including rumination, plays a key role in various psychopathologies. Although several psychotherapeutic treatments have been developed to reduce RNT, the neural correlates of those specific treatments and of psychotherapy in general are largely unknown. Functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) offers the potential to investigate the neural correlates of psychotherapeutic techniques in situ. Therefore, in this study we investigated the efficacy and neural correlates of a fNIRS adapted Mindfulness-based Emotion Regulation Training (MBERT) for the treatment of depressive rumination in 42 subjects with major depressive disorder (MDD) in a cross-over designed randomized controlled trial. Using psychometric measures, subjective ratings and fNIRS, we analyzed in situ changes in depressive symptom severity, ruminative thoughts and cortical activity in the Cognitive Control Network (CCN). Our results show that MBERT is effective in treating depressive symptoms and rumination. On a neural level, we found consistently higher cortical activation during emotion regulation training compared to control trials in the bilateral inferior frontal gyrus (IFG) and dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC). Furthermore, cortical oxygenation decreased from session to session in the bilateral DLPFC. The relevance of the results for the psychotherapeutic treatment of MDD as well as further necessary investigations are discussed.
studies.age_describe: Mean age of the analyzed sample was 32.33 (SD = 10.98) years. (Methods, Participants, paragraph 2)
studies.participants: 42 patients with major depressive disorder (MDD); 69% female; mean age 32.33 (SD=10.98) years; diagnoses included recurrent MDD (n=40) and first episode MDD (n=2); average BDI-II score at study start was 26.51 (SD=7.78). 'The mean age of this analyzed sample was 32.33 (SD = 10.98) years, and 69 % of the patients included in the analyses were female.' (Methods, Participants, paragraph 2)
studies.eligibility: Inclusion criteria: aged 18–60 years; ICD-10 diagnosis F32.x, F33.x or F34.1 (MDD group); no prior participation in a TSST study. Exclusion criteria: diabetes mellitus, kidney insufficiency, hypertension, dysrhythmia, Cushing syndrome, current substance abuse, adrenal insufficiency, cortisone medication, pacemaker, craniocerebral trauma, any current primary mental or personality disorder except MDD diagnoses; acute suicidality; BDI-II > 50; strong decompensation under social stress in the past. 'Participants could be included in the study if they were between 18 and 60 years old, had never participated in a study with a Trier Social Stress Test (TSST) procedure and did not meet any of the following exclusion criteria: diabetes mellitus, kidney insufficiency, hypertension, dysrhythmia, cushing syndrome, current substance abuse, adrenal insufficiency, cortisone medication, pacemaker, craniocerebral trauma as well as any current primary mental or personality disorder, except ICD-10 diagnosis F32.x, F33.x and F34.1 in the group of the depressive sample (MDD).' (Methods, Participants, paragraph 1)
studies.population_vulnerable: Not a vulnerable population — participants are adults with MDD recruited from a university hospital and outpatient settings; no specific health disparity or structural disadvantage criterion is described. (Methods, Participants)
studies.location: Tuebingen, Germany; 'All measurements were performed in the premises of the Clinic for Psychiatry and Psychotherapy Tuebingen.' (Methods, Procedures, paragraph 1)
studies.mental_health: ICD-10 diagnosis F32.x, F33.x or F34.1 (major depressive disorder) required for enrollment. 'Participants could be included...except ICD-10 diagnosis F32.x, F33.x and F34.1 in the group of the depressive sample (MDD).' (Methods, Participants, paragraph 1)
studies.physical_health: N/A — no physical health enrollment criterion
studies.arms: 2 arms: (1) MBERT (Mindfulness-based Emotion Regulation Training; n=21 initially), (2) TAU (Treatment as Usual; n=21 initially). Cross-over design: groups switched after the first phase. 'MDD patients were block-randomized...to either MBERT (n = 21) or TAU (n = 21).' (Methods, Procedures, paragraph 2)
studies.meditation_intervention: MBERT (Mindfulness-based Emotion Regulation Training): an eight-session psychotherapeutic training combining mindfulness-based and cognitive behavioral emotion regulation strategies. Preceded by one psychoeducative CBT session (50 min) on emotions, aberrant ER, and rumination. Each of the eight training sessions (~1–1.5 hours) consisted of 20 training trials (40 s each) alternating with 20 control (rest) trials (40 s each). Four ER strategies trained: (1) focus attention on affective state, (2) acceptance/tolerance of emotions mindfully, (3) cognitive reframing/reappraisal, (4) distancing. Sessions delivered twice per week with at least one rest day between sessions. Between sessions, patients encouraged to practice ER strategies and use a free-access meditation app ('Meditation Time'). Delivered by one male psychotherapist-in-training supervised by a senior CBT therapist. 'Following these first promising results, we developed an eight-session psychotherapeutic training, combining mindfulness-based as well as cognitive behavioral ER therapy: Mindfulness-based Emotion Regulation Training (MBERT).' (Introduction, paragraph 5; Methods, MBERT, paragraphs 1–4)
studies.intervention_delivery: In-person individual sessions (~1–1.5 hours each); delivered by one male psychotherapist-in-training (first author HL), supervised by a senior CBT therapist. Patients sat in front of a table with fNIRS cap; therapist sat at 90-degree angle. Plexiglass shield and face mask used due to COVID-19. 'The psychotherapeutic training sessions followed a predefined script...and were all executed by the same male psychotherapist in training (first author HL), who was supervised and in cases of illness represented by a senior CBT therapist (last author DR).' (Methods, MBERT, paragraph 1)
studies.digital_component_raw: Yes — participants were encouraged to use a free-access smartphone/app ('Meditation Time') for mindfulness training and meditation between sessions. 'Between sessions the patients were encouraged to practice the taught ER strategies in their daily lives and to also do mindfulness training and meditation using a free-access application ("Meditation Time").' (Methods, MBERT, paragraph 4). Note: the primary intervention delivery was in-person; the app was a between-session home practice supplement.
studies.intervention_tailor: No tailoring reported — the MBERT was developed specifically for depressive rumination in MDD but is not described as culturally adapted or linguistically translated. It was designed as a novel protocol for this population. (Methods, MBERT)
studies.comparison: TAU (Treatment as Usual): 'no additional interventions with unrestricted continuation of existing treatments.' Participants in the TAU arm continued any existing treatments (psychotherapy, medication) without restriction but received no additional MBERT sessions. 'we compared MBERT in a RCT with treatment as usual (TAU; no additional interventions with unrestricted continuation of existing treatments).' (Introduction, paragraph 5; Methods, Procedures, paragraph 2)
studies.assessment_time: T0 = Baseline/t1 (0 weeks); T1 = Mid-study/t2 (~4–5 weeks, after first treatment phase); T2 = End of study/t3 (~9–10 weeks, after second treatment phase). 'For approximately four to five weeks, the treatment group received the MBERT...After this first phase of the study, all patients completed a TSST (t2)...After completion of this phase a final TSST (t3) was assessed.' (Methods, Procedures, paragraph 2). Note: exact week counts for t2 and t3 are approximated from the described ~4–5 week phases; total study participation was approximately ten weeks.
studies.assessment_nature: Self-report questionnaires (BDI-II, SWE, SCS-D, SRQ, CTQ, EMA); physiological/biological measure (fNIRS cortical oxygenation); subjective ratings during sessions (burden, self-compassion, equanimity, effort). 'Using psychometric measures, subjective ratings and fNIRS, we analyzed in situ changes in depressive symptom severity, ruminative thoughts and cortical activity.' (Abstract)
studies.outcomes_all: 1. Depressive symptom severity — Beck Depression Inventory II (BDI-II; Hautzinger et al., 2009); 2. Self-efficacy — Skala zur Allgemeinen Selbstwirksamkeitserwartung (SWE; Jerusalem & Schwarzer, 2003); 3. Self-compassion — Self-Compassion Scale German Version (SCS-D; Hupfeld & Ruffieux, 2011); 4. State rumination — State Rumination Questionnaire (SRQ; study-specific); 5. Childhood trauma — Childhood Trauma Questionnaire German version (CTQ; Klinitzke et al., 2012); 6. Cortical oxygenation (O2Hb) — fNIRS in bilateral IFG, bilateral DLPFC, somatosensory association cortex (SAC); 7. Subjective burden — in-session rating; 8. Subjective self-compassion — in-session rating; 9. Equanimity — in-session rating; 10. Effort — in-session rating; 11. Therapeutic techniques/interventions — session protocol (qualitative/frequency data); 12. Ecological momentary assessments (EMA) — stress, stressful events, rumination, equanimity, self-compassion, mindfulness, sleep quality (results reported elsewhere).
studies.outcomes_primary: Primary outcomes: depressive symptom severity (BDI-II), self-compassion (SCS-D), and self-efficacy (SWE). 'we hypothesized a reduction in depressive symptoms as well as increases in self-compassion and self-efficacy due to the MBERT compared to TAU (primary outcomes).' (Introduction, paragraph 5)
studies.outcome_timepoints: T0 = Baseline/t1 (0 weeks): BDI-II, SWE, SCS-D, SRQ, CTQ assessed; T1 = Mid-study/t2 (~4–5 weeks): BDI-II, SWE, SCS-D, SRQ assessed; T2 = End of study/t3 (~9–10 weeks): BDI-II, SWE, SCS-D, SRQ assessed. fNIRS and subjective ratings assessed during each of the 8 training sessions (within-session and across-session). EMA collected throughout study participation (results reported elsewhere). (Methods, Procedures, paragraph 2)
studies.recruitment: Participants recruited via emails and flyers at the University Hospital of Tuebingen, the University of Tuebingen, and via outpatient psychotherapists. 'We recruited participants via emails and flyers at the University Hospital of Tuebingen, the University of Tuebingen and via outpatient psychotherapists.' (Methods, Participants, paragraph 1). Recruitment dates not reported.
studies.study_purpose: To investigate the efficacy and neural correlates of a fNIRS-adapted Mindfulness-based Emotion Regulation Training (MBERT) for the treatment of depressive rumination in MDD. 'in this study we investigated the efficacy and neural correlates of a fNIRS adapted Mindfulness-based Emotion Regulation Training (MBERT) for the treatment of depressive rumination in 42 subjects with major depressive disorder (MDD) in a cross-over designed randomized controlled trial.' (Abstract)

Staff performing TSSTs were blinded to group assignment. 'MDD patients were block-randomized after completion of t1 (counterbalanced for sex and severity of depressive symptoms using Excel...depending on the corresponding values determined at t1) to either MBERT (n = 21) or TAU (n = 21).' studies.treatment_vs_prevention: Treatment — participants were required to have an ICD-10 diagnosis of MDD (F32.x, F33.x, or F34.1) at enrollment, and the study tests the efficacy of MBERT for reducing depressive symptoms and rumination in this existing condition. 'we investigated the efficacy and neural correlates of a fNIRS adapted Mindfulness-based Emotion Regulation Training (MBERT) for the treatment of depressive rumination in 42 subjects with major depressive disorder (MDD).' (Abstract)
