studies.authors: Landry, J. M.
studies.title: Physiological and Psychological Effects of a Himalayan Singing Bowl in Meditation Practice: A Quantitative Analysis
studies.abstract:
Purpose. To determine the physiological and psychological effects of adding a Himalayan singing bowl (HSB) to a directed relaxation (DR) session.
Design. Randomized crossover study.
Setting. Community-based counseling practice.
Subjects. Fifty-one participants completed two randomly assigned sessions beginning with either 12 minutes of HSB or silence, followed by a 20-minute DR session.
Intervention. Random order of HSB intervention/silence prior to DR.
Measures. Blood pressure (BP), heart rate (HR), Positive and Negative Affect Schedule (PANAS) scores measured before and after both sessions.
Analysis. Analysis of variance (ANOVA) compared differences between variables over time between both study days, and analysis of covariance (ANCOVA) analyzed changes from baseline, controlling for baseline, age, and sex.
Results. Fifty-one participants completed both sessions. There was a greater decline in systolic BP (p = .044) and HR (p = .003) with HSB compared to silence prior to DR. Changes in diastolic BP were greater with HSB, with a nonsignificant trend (p = .073). Hypertensive subjects (n = 20) had similar and significant BP changes with HSB and silence when compared to normotensive subjects (n = 31). PANAS scores fell significantly with both interventions.
Conclusions. BP and HR responses were enhanced by HSB exposure. HSB may be used as an adjunct to DR to produce physiological and psychological responses prior to DR.
studies.total_n: 51. 'Fifty-one participants completing both sessions were included in the analyses.' Note: 56 consented and completed the first session; 5 did not return for the second session. The crossover design means all 51 completed both conditions. (Methods, paragraph 4)
studies.age_describe: Mean age 50.5 ± 10 years, range 26–69 years. 'Participants had a mean age of 50.5 ± 10 (range = 26–69 years).' (Results, paragraph 1)
studies.participants: 51 adult participants (16 male, 35 female), mean age 50.5 ± 10 years. 20 (39%) were hypertensive and 31 were normotensive. 'Fifty-one adult participants (16 male, 35 female) completed both study sessions.' (Results, paragraph 1)
studies.eligibility: Inclusion: Healthy adult participants recruited via convenience sampling. 'Fifty-six healthy adult participants consented to participate.' (Methods, paragraph 4). Exclusion criteria not explicitly stated. Participants were not queried for prior experience with meditation or stress management training.
studies.population_vulnerable: Not a vulnerable population — participants described as 'healthy adult participants' recruited from the general community with no indication of health disparities or structural disadvantage. (Methods, paragraph 4)
studies.location: Andover, Massachusetts, USA. Community-based counseling practice. Author affiliation: 'JourneyZend, L.L.C., 68 Main Street, Andover, MA 01810.' (Title page)
studies.mental_health: N/A — no psychiatric enrollment criterion. Participants described as 'healthy adult participants'; no psychiatric diagnosis or symptom threshold required for enrollment. (Methods, paragraph 4)
studies.physical_health: N/A — no physical health enrollment criterion explicitly required. Note: 20 participants (39%) were identified as hypertensive post-enrollment based on published guidelines, but hypertension was not a stated inclusion criterion. (Methods, paragraph 4)
studies.arms: 2 conditions in a crossover design. Condition 1: Himalayan Singing Bowl (HSB) — 12 minutes of HSB exposure followed by 20-minute directed relaxation (DR). Condition 2: Silence — 12 minutes of silence followed by 20-minute directed relaxation (DR). All 51 participants completed both conditions in random order. 'The study used a crossover design with random order assignment of each participant to two study conditions, 12 minutes of HSB exposure or silence, prior to a DR session.' (Methods, paragraph 1)
studies.meditation_intervention: The intervention consisted of 12 minutes of Himalayan Singing Bowl (HSB) exposure followed by a 20-minute directed relaxation (DR) session. The HSB protocol ('The Landry Method') involved the investigator alternately striking and rubbing a bowl with a leather puja: 'The bowl was rubbed along the rim for 15 seconds allowing for the sound to trail off to silence. It was then struck softly every 15 seconds for a series of four times each time allowing the sound to trail off to silence. This sequence was repeated for 12 minutes.' The bowl vibrated at a B flat pitch. Participants sat upright on an office couch with approximately 12-inch distance between the bowl and the participant's ear. The DR session used a 20-minute recording of the researcher's voice. Total session duration: 32 minutes. (Methods, paragraphs 1–2)
studies.intervention_delivery: In-person, individual format. The investigator sat next to the participant and administered the HSB. DR was delivered via audio recording of the researcher's voice. 'Participants sat upright on an office couch, and the investigator sat next to the participant creating approximately a 12-inch distance between the bowl and the participant's ear.' Facilitator qualifications: Jayan Marie Landry, PhD, MSN, ARNP-BC. (Methods, paragraph 2)
studies.digital_component_raw: No digital component. The DR session used an audio recording (medium not specified — likely CD or tape). 'After either the HSB or silence, subjects then listened to a 20-minute DR recording using the researcher's voice.' No digital delivery platform described. (Methods, paragraph 1)
studies.intervention_tailor: No tailoring reported. The intervention was administered uniformly to all participants with no reported cultural or population-specific modifications.

studies.authors: Maddock, A., Hevey, D., D'Alton, P., & Kirby, B.
studies.title: A Randomized Trial of Mindfulness-Based Cognitive Therapy with Psoriasis Patients
studies.abstract:
Objectives The objective of the present study was to investigate the effect of mindfulness-based cognitive therapy (MBCT) on psoriasis patients' symptoms, anxiety, depression, and psychological well-being. The study also examined if MBCT significantly impacted the domain and mediating variables of a clinically modified Buddhist psychological model (CBPM), which are acceptance, mindfulness, self-compassion, aversion, non-attachment, attention, rumination, and worry.
Methods One hundred and one participants were randomly allocated to MBCT (n = 51) or TAU (n = 50). Participants were measured pre-treatment, post-treatment, and after a 3-month follow-up period.
Results Analyses revealed that when baseline variables were controlled, there was a significant reduction or increase in the hypothesized direction for each variable over time in the MBCT group, but not in the treatment as usual group.
Conclusions The results suggest that MBCT may be a useful adjunct therapy for those suffering from psoriasis and the associated psychological symptoms relating to the condition.

studies.authors: Malinowski, P., Moore, A. W., Mead, B. R., & Gruber, T.
studies.title: Mindful Aging: The Effects of Regular Brief Mindfulness Practice on Electrophysiological Markers of Cognitive and Affective Processing in Older Adults
studies.abstract: There is growing interest in the potential benefits of mindfulness meditation practices in terms of counteracting some of the cognitive effects associated with aging. Pursuing this question, the aim of the present study was to investigate the influence of mindfulness training on executive control and emotion regulation in older adults, by means of studying behavioral and electrophysiological changes. Participants, 55 to 75 years of age, were randomly allocated to an 8-week mindful breath awareness training group or an active control group engaging in brain training exercises. Before and after the training period, participants completed an emotional-counting Stroop task, designed to measure attentional control and emotion regulation processes. Concurrently, their brain activity was measured by means of 64-channel electroencephalography. The results show that engaging in just over 10 min of mindfulness practice five times per week resulted in significant improvements in behavioral (response latency) and electrophysiological (N2 event-related potential) measures related to general task performance. Analyses of the underlying cortical sources (Variable Resolution Electromagnetic Tomography, VARETA) indicate that this N2-related effect is primarily associated with changes in the right angular gyrus and other areas of the dorsal attention network. However, the study did not find the expected specific improvements in executive control and emotion regulation, which may be due to the training instructions or the relative brevity of the intervention. Overall, the results indicate that engaging in mindfulness meditation training improves the maintenance of goal-directed visuospatial attention and may be a useful strategy for counteracting cognitive decline associated with aging.
studies.total_n: 56. "Fifty-six older adults (range: 55–75 years; mean: 64.5 years; 15 males) were recruited from the general population" (Methods, Participants, paragraph 1). Note: final analytic samples were 22 per group for behavioral and 18 per group for ERP analyses.
studies.age_describe: Mean age 64.5 years, range 55–75 years. "Fifty-six older adults (range: 55–75 years; mean: 64.5 years; 15 males) were recruited" (Methods, Participants, paragraph 1). No SD reported for the full sample.
studies.participants: Older adults aged 55–75 years recruited from the general population. "Fifty-six older adults (range: 55–75 years; mean: 64.5 years; 15 males) were recruited from the general population (retired: N=38; working: N=18). The sample had a varied educational background (ranging from no formal qualification to postgraduate degrees), with a mean of 13.0 years spent in education." (Methods, Participants, paragraph 1). 15 males, 41 females (inferred from total N=56 and 15 males reported).
studies.eligibility: Inclusion criteria: Older adults aged 55–75 years. No formal psychiatric or physical health threshold stated. Participants were randomly allocated after recruitment from the general population. Exclusion criteria: Participants were excluded from analyses if they had more than 30% loss of EEG data or a hit rate below 85% in the neutral condition. "Based on our a priori criterion participants were excluded from both electrophysiological and behavioral analyses if they had a hit rate below 85% in the neutral condition, as this would suggest either poor task understanding or/and difficulties with response-key mapping." (Methods, Data Analyses, paragraph 3). No other explicit eligibility criteria stated in the paper.
studies.population_vulnerable: Not a vulnerable population — participants were older adults (55–75 years) from the general population with no reported health disparities or structural disadvantage. "Fifty-six older adults (range: 55–75 years; mean: 64.5 years; 15 males) were recruited from the general population" (Methods, Participants, paragraph 1).
studies.location: Inferred: Liverpool, UK (inferred from author affiliations — Liverpool John Moores University and University of Liverpool — not explicitly stated as study location in paper body)
studies.mental_health: N/A — no psychiatric enrollment criterion
studies.physical_health: N/A — no physical health enrollment criterion
studies.arms: 2 arms. (1) Mindfulness Training Group (MTG): 8-week mindful breath awareness meditation; (2) Brain Training Group (BTG): active control engaging in mental arithmetic exercises. "Participants were randomly allocated to the mindfulness training group or to the active control group." (Methods, Participants, paragraph 2). Final analytic sample: 22 per group for behavioral analyses, 18 per group for ERP analyses.
studies.meditation_intervention: Mindful breath awareness meditation. Participants were introduced to a simple mindful breath awareness practice taught by a meditation teacher of a Tibetan Buddhist tradition with close to 20 years of teaching experience. "Participants were required to focus their attention on the sensations accompanying their breathing, either attending to the experience at the nostrils, around the diaphragm or the movement of the abdomen when inhaling and exhaling, without manipulating the breath in any form." Whenever attention wandered, participants were to redirect focus back to breathing sensations. Instructions included a non-judgmental, non-evaluative, curious attitude toward arising thoughts, feelings, or sensations. Duration: 8 weeks. Home practice: minimum 10 min per day, at least 5 days per week. Group sessions: four 90-min group sessions over 8 weeks, consisting of psycho-educative components, inquiry-based discussions, and group meditation practice. Actual average practice: approximately 13 min per day, 5 days per week. (Methods, Procedure, paragraphs 1–3)
studies.intervention_delivery: Hybrid: in-person group sessions (four 90-min sessions over 8 weeks) plus daily home practice. "Over the course of the 8 weeks, they attended four 90-min group sessions that consisted of psycho-educative components, inquiry-based discussions, and group meditation practice." Home practice was self-guided (minimum 10 min/day, 5 days/week). Teacher: "a meditation teacher of a Tibetan Buddhist tradition with close to 20 years of teaching experience." (Methods, Procedure, paragraphs 1–2)
studies.digital_component_raw: No digital component. No technology-based delivery described. Home practice was self-guided without mention of apps, recordings, or digital platforms. (Methods, Procedure)
studies.intervention_tailor: No tailoring reported. The intervention is described as a standard mindful breath awareness practice with no explicit cultural or population-specific adaptations mentioned, though it was delivered to older adults.
studies.comparison: Brain Training Group (BTG): active control condition involving mental arithmetic calculations. "Participants allocated to the active control condition took part in a brain training group (BTG). The training involved active, effortful cognitive processes... Participants in the BTG were asked to engage in mental arithmetic calculations." Group sessions matched MTG for frequency (four sessions) and duration (6 hours total), including psycho-educative components (healthy aging lectures), group discussions, and in-group exercises. Home practice: exercise booklets containing 100 arithmetic calculations (~10–15 min) to be completed 5 days per week for 8 weeks. (Methods, Procedure, paragraphs 4–6)
studies.assessment_time: T0 = Baseline (0 weeks); T1 = Post-intervention (8 weeks). "Before being allocated to the specific training group and attending the first group session (i.e., at baseline/T1) and after completion of the training program (at T2) all participants completed several questionnaires and engaged in a set of computer-based tasks while their EEG was recorded." Note: the paper uses T1 for baseline and T2 for post-intervention. (Methods, Procedure, paragraph 7)
studies.assessment_nature: Both self-report and non-self-report measures used. Self-report: FFMQ (mindfulness), GSE (self-efficacy), WEMWBS (mental well-being), cognitive/physical activity scale. Non-self-report/behavioral: response times and accuracy on ecStroop task, simple reaction time task, Spatial Short Term Memory task (SSTM). Physiological/neuroimaging: 64-channel EEG recording during task performance, ERP components (N2, P3b), VARETA source localization. "their brain activity was measured by means of 64-channel electroencephalography" (Abstract).
studies.outcomes_all:
1. Executive control and attentional performance — Emotional-Counting Stroop Task (ecStroop): response times (RT) and hit rates (HR) across four conditions (incongruent, negative, positive, neutral) (Methods, Procedure)
2. Electrophysiological markers of attentional control — N2 ERP component (fronto-central, 270–340 ms at FCz) (Methods, Data Analyses)
3. Electrophysiological markers of emotional processing — P3b ERP component (520–650 ms at Pz) (Methods, Data Analyses)
4. Cortical source localization — VARETA analysis of N2 changes (Methods, Data Analyses)
5. Trait mindfulness — Five Facet Mindfulness Questionnaire (FFMQ; Baer et al. 2006, 2008; 39 items, 5 subscales: Non-reactivity, Observing, Acting with Awareness, Describing, Non-judging; total score range 39–195) (Methods, Measures)
6. Self-efficacy — Generalized Self-Efficacy Scale (GSE; Schwarzer & Jerusalem 1995; 10 items; score range 10–40) (Methods, Measures)
7. Mental well-being — Warwick-Edinburgh Mental Well-Being Scale (WEMWBS; Tennant et al. 2007; 14 items; score range 14–70) (Methods, Measures)
8. Working memory — Spatial Short Term Memory task (SSTM; Lewandowsky et al. 2010) (Methods, Measures)
9. Processing speed — Simple reaction time task (20 trials, mean of final 15) (Methods, Measures)
10. Cognitive and physical activity — Adapted leisure activity scale (29 items: 14 cognitive, 15 physical; cognitive score 0–98, physical score 0–105) (Methods, Measures)
11. Training adherence — Weekly training logs recording days and time of practice (Methods, Measures)
12. Self-reported mindfulness changes — Five Facet Mindfulness Questionnaire subscales (FFMQ-O, FFMQ-A) (Results, Control Variables)
studies.outcomes_primary: Unclear — authors do not explicitly designate a single primary outcome. The study aim focuses on executive control and emotion regulation: "the aim of the present study was to investigate the influence of mindfulness training on executive control and emotion regulation in older adults, by means of studying behavioral and electrophysiological changes" (Abstract). The ecStroop behavioral and ERP measures appear to be the main outcomes, but no formal primary outcome designation is made.

(i.e., at baseline/T1) and after completion of the training program (at T2) all participants completed several questionnaires and engaged in a set of computer-based tasks" (Methods, Procedure, paragraph 7). No follow-up beyond post-intervention.
studies.recruitment: "Fifty-six older adults (range: 55–75 years; mean: 64.5 years; 15 males) were recruited from the general population" (Methods, Participants, paragraph 1). Specific recruitment channels (e.g., flyers, advertisements) are not reported. Recruitment dates/period not reported.
studies.study_purpose: "The aim of the present study was to investigate the influence of mindfulness training on executive control and emotion regulation in older adults, by means of studying behavioral and electrophysiological changes." (Abstract). Additionally: "A central question of this study was whether older participants (55–75 years of age) would benefit from MT and display improvements in their cognitive functions." (Discussion)
studies.study_design: Randomized active-controlled study. "Participants were randomly allocated to the mindfulness training group or to the active control group." (Methods, Participants, paragraph 2). Randomization method not specified. No blinding reported. Two-arm parallel design with pre-post assessment. Described as "Randomized active controlled study" in the keywords.
studies.treatment_vs_prevention: Enhancement — participants were healthy older adults from the general population with no psychiatric or physical health diagnosis required for enrollment. The study tests whether mindfulness practice can improve cognitive performance and potentially counteract age-related cognitive decline. "Demonstrating that cognitive performance can be improved by a rather modest amount of mindfulness meditation practice encourages further explorations of MT as a potentially useful strategy for counteracting cognitive decline associated with aging." (Conclusion). No clinical diagnosis or symptom threshold required at enrollment.

studies.authors: Jastrowski Mano, K. E., Salamon, K. S., Hainsworth, K. R., Anderson Khan, K. J., Ladwig, R. J., Davies, W. H., & Weisman, S. J.
studies.title: A Randomized, Controlled Pilot Study of Mindfulness-based Stress Reduction for Pediatric Chronic Pain
studies.abstract: Context • It is estimated that 1 in 5 children in the United States is affected by chronic pain. Increasing adaptive coping strategies and decreasing stress may be important in treatment. Research has suggested that mindfulness can help alleviate symptoms associated with medical illnesses and increase quality of life. Little is known about the effectiveness of mindfulness-based stress reduction (MBSR) in youth, partly due to insufficient methodological rigor in related studies. Objective • The primary purpose of the present study was to examine the feasibility, acceptability, and effectiveness of MBSR for a treatment-seeking sample of youth with chronic pain. Design • The current study was the first randomized, controlled pilot study of MBSR for pediatric chronic pain. The research team had intended to use block randomization involving a total of five recruitment waves, with each wave consisting of one MBSR group and one psychoeducation group. Due to difficulties with recruitment and attrition before the start of either group, however, only MBSR was conducted at each wave after the first wave. Setting • Participants were recruited from a multidisciplinary pain clinic in a large, Midwestern children's hospital. Participants • The final sample included six adolescents between the ages of 12 and 17 y, four in the MBSR group and two in the psychoeducation group. Intervention • Weekly sessions for the MBSR group were 90 min in length and followed a structured protocol. Sessions included a review of homework, an introduction to and practice of meditation, discussion of the session, and a review of the home practice assignment. The psychoeducation group participated in six group sessions, which were based on a cognitive-behavioral model of pain, and discussion topics included the nature of chronic pain and stress management. Primary Outcome Measures • Health-related quality of life, pain catastrophizing, anxiety, functional disability, mindfulness, and treatment acceptability were all assessed pre- and postintervention as well as at follow-up. Results • Recruitment and retention difficulties were experienced. Qualitative examination of participants' scores suggested increased mindfulness but inconsistent patterns on other outcome measures. Conclusions • The research team highlighted critical challenges faced by potential researchers aiming to investigate MBSR for pediatric chronic pain, and the study provides recommendations for research and implications for clinical practice. (Altern Ther Health Med. 2013;19(6):8-14.)

(Methods, Participants, paragraph 1)

'Participants were recruited from a multidisciplinary pain clinic in a large, Midwestern children's hospital.' (Abstract, Setting)

studies.mental_health: N/A — no psychiatric enrollment criterion. Suicidality and serious mental illness were exclusion criteria, not inclusion criteria. 'The study excluded youth who... were presenting with current suicidality or a serious mental illness.' (Methods, Participants, paragraph 1)

studies.arms: 2 arms. Arm 1: MBSR group (n=4 received intervention; n=26 allocated). Arm 2: Psychoeducation group (n=2 received intervention; n=6 allocated). 'Allocated to MBSR Group (n = 26)... Allocated to Psychoeducation (n = 6)' (Figure 1)
studies.meditation_intervention: MBSR explicitly named. 'The MBSR intervention was modeled on the work of Jon Kabat-Zinn et al and used the same adolescent-specific adaptations as described by Beigel et al.' 6 weekly sessions, 90 minutes each. Content included: body awareness and basic yoga, relaxation techniques (diaphragmatic breathing), body-scan meditation, walking meditation, appreciation of self and respect for uniqueness, nonjudgmental observation of thoughts, and gratitude meditation. Sessions included homework review, introduction to and practice of meditation, discussion, and home practice assignment review. Participants received a journal and a compact disc with sitting and body-scan meditations. Homework: 30 minutes per day, 6 days per week. Primary MBSR practitioner had studied with Kabat-Zinn and had 11 years of facilitator experience. A second mindfulness practitioner with 10 years of MBSR experience ran a concurrent parent session. (Methods, MBSR Group section)
studies.intervention_delivery: In-person group format. Weekly 90-minute group sessions over 6 weeks. 'Weekly MBSR group sessions were 90 minutes in length and followed a structured protocol.' Primary facilitator had 'studied with Kabat-Zinn and had 11 years of experience as a facilitator.' A second practitioner with '10 years of MBSR experience' ran a concurrent parent session. (Methods, MBSR Group section)

'The MBSR intervention was modeled on the work of Jon Kabat-Zinn et al and used the same adolescent-specific adaptations as described by Beigel et al.' studies.comparison: Psychoeducation group: 'The psychoeducation group designed for this study consisted of six weekly group sessions. Based on a cognitive-behavioral model of pain, the psychoeducation sessions covered various topics, including the nature of chronic pain—anatomy/physiology and misconceptions about pain—and stress management. The psychoeducation group also covered general topics such as ways to improve communication skills with peers and parents.' Facilitator was 'an experienced pediatric psychotherapist and clinical nurse specialist with expertise in pediatric chronic pain.' (Methods, Psychoeducation Group section)

studies.authors: Mantzios, M., & Giannou, K.
studies.title: Group vs. Single Mindfulness Meditation: Exploring Avoidance, Impulsivity, and Weight Management in Two Separate Mindfulness Meditation Settings
studies.abstract: Recent research has identified that mindfulness meditation in group settings supports people who are trying to lose weight. The present research investigated mindfulness meditation in group and individual settings, and explored the potential impact on weight loss and other factors (i.e. mindfulness, impulsivity, and avoidance) that may assist or hinder weight loss. Specifically, the hypotheses tested were that the group setting assisted dieters more than the individual setting by reducing weight, cognitive-behavioral avoidance, and impulsivity and by increasing mindfulness. Participants (n = 170) who were trying to lose weight were randomly assigned to practice meditation for 6 weeks within a group or independently. Measurements in mindfulness, cognitive-behavioral avoidance, impulsivity, and weight occurred twice (pre- and post-intervention). Results indicated that participants in the group setting lost weight and lowered their levels of cognitive-behavioral avoidance, while impulsivity and mindfulness remained stable. On the other hand, participants in the individual condition lost less weight, while there was an increase in cognitive-behavioral avoidance and mindfulness scores, but a decrease in impulsivity. Seeing that benefits and limitations observed in group settings are not replicated when people meditate alone, this study concluded that mindfulness meditation in individual settings needs to be used with caution, although there are some potential benefits that could aid future weight loss research.
studies.total_n: 170. "One hundred and seventy students attending a Greek university initially signed up to participate in this study. From those, 83 were randomly assigned to the group meditation setting and 87 to the individual meditation setting." (Methods, Participants, paragraph 1)

studies.participants: University students at a Greek university who were trying to lose weight. Completers: n = 152 (65 females and 87 males), BMI M = 28.74, range = 25.2–33.6, SD = 1.57. "One hundred and fifty-two participants (n = 152) completed the interventions and follow-up measurements (i.e. 65 females and 87 males with a BMI M = 28.74, range = 25.2–33.6, SD = 1.57 and Age M = 22.9, SD = 4.45)" (Methods, Participants, paragraph 1)
studies.eligibility: Inclusion: Participants who wanted to lose weight and were about to start their diet; BMI between 18.5 and 40 (overweight range implied by BMI M = 28.74). Exclusion: EAT-26 scores exceeding 20 (indicating probable eating disorder) — referred to clinician; underweight (BMI ≤ 18.5) — referred to clinician; clinically obese (BMI ≥ 40) — referred to clinician; any drug use and abuse, medical conditions, or eating disorders. "Eight participants from the individual meditation setting were excluded at the very beginning, because preliminary results indicated a high probability of suffering from eating disorders (that was based on the eating attitudes test scores which exceeded the score of 20)... underweight (i.e. BMI ≤ 18.5) and clinically obese (i.e. BMI ≥ 40) participants were set to be excluded" (Methods, Participants, paragraph 1)
studies.population_vulnerable: Not a vulnerable population — participants are university students trying to lose weight; no explicit health disparity or structural disadvantage criterion reported. "One hundred and seventy students attending a Greek university initially signed up to participate in this study." (Methods, Participants, paragraph 1)
studies.location: Inferred: Greece (inferred from 'students attending a Greek university' and scales translated into Greek — not explicitly stated as a specific city or institution in the paper body)
studies.mental_health: N/A — no psychiatric enrollment criterion
studies.physical_health: Participants were required to be trying to lose weight and have a BMI between 18.5 and 40 (overweight). "general BMI cut-off scores were set at the beginning of this study, where underweight (i.e. BMI ≤ 18.5) and clinically obese (i.e. BMI ≥ 40) participants were set to be excluded" (Methods, Participants, paragraph 1)
studies.arms: Two arms. Arm 1: Group meditation setting (n = 83 randomized; n = 76 completers). Arm 2: Individual meditation setting (n = 87 randomized; n = 76 completers). "83 were randomly assigned to the group meditation setting and 87 to the individual meditation setting" (Methods, Participants, paragraph 1)
studies.meditation_intervention: Both arms received the same mindfulness meditation protocol — breath-focused sitting meditation. A one-day introductory session was conducted by a qualified mental health practitioner with experience in Buddhist Mahayana and Theravada traditions and mindfulness meditation. Participants practiced for 6 weeks. Sessions lasted approximately 20 minutes. The practice focused attention on the breathing experience; when attention shifted, meditators were encouraged to notice and accept thoughts non-judgmentally and return attention to the breath. Psycho-educational material (online resources by Jon Kabat-Zinn, T.N. Hanh, etc.) was provided but not forced. Group setting: participants attended live group sessions at an open recreational area on site, with three daily session options per day for 6 weeks. Individual setting: participants received a 20-minute audio file on a compact disk and practiced independently. Participation logs were provided. No specific named protocol (e.g., MBSR) was used. "A protocol was created for the meditation instructor (i.e. a qualified mental health practitioner, with several years of practical experience in Buddhist Mahayana and Theravada traditions and mindfulness meditation) to introduce mindfulness meditation to all participants in a one-day session" (Methods, Materials, paragraph 5)
studies.intervention_delivery: Group setting: in-person group sessions, approximately 20 minutes each, at an open recreational area on site, led by a qualified mental health practitioner with experience in Buddhist Mahayana and Theravada traditions. Three daily session options offered for scheduling flexibility. Individual setting: self-guided using a 20-minute audio file on compact disk, no live instructor present during practice. "The sessions lasted about 20 minutes for the group setting and the audio file used was also 20 minutes." (Methods, Materials, paragraph 5)
studies.digital_component_raw: No digital component. The individual setting used a compact disk (audio file) for home practice. "participants in the individual setting were given the mindfulness meditation audio file recorded on a compact disk" (Methods, Procedure and Design, paragraph 1)
studies.intervention_tailor: Yes — scales and protocol were translated into Greek for this Greek university student population. "all scales were translated into Greek" and the Greek version of the protocol is available from the first author. (Methods, Materials, paragraph 3)
studies.comparison: This study compares two active mindfulness meditation conditions against each other; there is no passive control or waitlist group. Arm 1 (Group setting): in-person guided group meditation, 20-minute sessions, 6 weeks, led by a qualified practitioner. Arm 2 (Individual setting): self-guided meditation using a 20-minute audio CD, 6 weeks, no live instructor. "the aim was to explore the differences between individual and group settings" (Discussion, paragraph 8). Authors acknowledge the absence of a no-treatment control: "ideally this study should have benefited from a control group" (Discussion, paragraph 8).
studies.assessment_time: T0 = Baseline (0 weeks); T1 = Post-intervention (6 weeks). "Measurements in mindfulness, cognitive-behavioral avoidance, impulsivity, and weight occurred twice (pre- and post-intervention)." (Abstract); "After 6 weeks, participants again received a questionnaire pack and their weight was also measured." (Methods, Procedure and Design, paragraph 2)
studies.assessment_nature: Self-report questionnaires (MAAS, BIS-11, CBAS, Participant Information Form) and physical measurement (weight and height measured by two general practitioners). "their weight and height were measured by two general practitioners" (Methods, Procedure and Design, paragraph 1)
studies.outcomes_all: 1. Weight/BMI — measured by two general practitioners (Body Mass Index, range 25.2–33.6 in sample); 2. Mindfulness — Mindful Attention and Awareness Scale (MAAS; Brown & Ryan, 2003; 15 items, range 15–90); 3. Impulsivity — Barratt Impulsivity Scale (BIS-11; Patton et al., 1995; 30 items, range 30–120); 4. Cognitive-Behavioral Avoidance — Cognitive-Behavioral Avoidance Scale (CBAS; Ottenbreit & Dobson, 2004; 31 items, range 31–155); 5. Eating attitudes (screening only) — Eating Attitudes Test (EAT-26; Garner et al., 1982; cut-off score of 20 used for exclusion); 6. Meditation adherence — Participation Logs (daily practice logs); 7. Perceived adherence to meditation schedule and diet — two additional questions at follow-up (1–5 scale). "Analyses follow a format of primary and secondary outcomes. studies.title: Brief Meditation and the Interaction between Emotional Interference and Anxiety
studies.abstract: This pilot study assessed the effects of a five day focused meditation training on the interplay between emotional interference and anxiety in a non clinical sample randomized into two groups (experimental=13; control=18). Emotional interference was indexed comparing the reaction times in an attention span task with negative or neutral distracting images. Anxiety experienced during the task was also assessed through self-report. Only in the control group higher anxiety levels interacted with greater emotional interference and a worse evaluation of valence and arousal of emotional images. These preliminary findings suggest that meditation may help modulating anxiety effects on bias to negative stimuli, and that even a short training may facilitate self-regulatory processes.

Note: 46 were initially randomized; 31 completed. The abstract states experimental=13 and control=18, matching the final sample. The randomized N was 46 but the final/analyzed sample was 31. studies.authors: Minami, H., Brinkman, H. R., Nahvi, S., Arnsten, J. H., Rivera-Mindt, M., Wetter, D. W., Litvin Bloom, E., Price, L. H., Vieira, C., Donnelly, R., McClain, L. M., Kennedy, K. A., D'Aquila, E., Fine, M., McCarthy, D. E., Thomas, J. G., Hecht, J., & Brown, R. A.
studies.title: Rationale, design and pilot feasibility results of a smartphone-assisted, mindfulness-based intervention for smokers with mood disorders: Project mSMART MIND
studies.abstract: Background: Although individuals with psychiatric disorders are disproportionately affected by cigarette smoking, few outpatient mental health treatment facilities offer smoking cessation services. In this paper, we describe the development of a smartphone-assisted mindfulness smoking cessation intervention with contingency management (SMI-CM), as well as the design and methods of an ongoing pilot randomized controlled trial (RCT) targeting smokers receiving outpatient psychiatric treatment. We also report the results of an open-label pilot feasibility study. Methods: In phase 1, we developed and pilot-tested SMI-CM, which includes a smartphone intervention app that prompts participants to practice mindfulness, complete ecological momentary assessment (EMA) reports 5 times per day, and submit carbon monoxide (CO) videos twice per day. Participants earned incentives if submitted videos showed CO ≤ 6 ppm. In phase 2, smokers receiving outpatient treatment for mood disorders are randomized to receive SMI-CM or enhanced standard treatment plus non-contingent CM (EST). Results: The results from the pilot feasibility study (N = 8) showed that participants practiced mindfulness an average of 3.4 times/day (≥ 3 min), completed 72.3% of prompted EMA reports, and submitted 68.0% of requested CO videos. Participants reported that the program was helpful overall (M = 4.85/5) and that daily mindfulness practice was helpful for both managing mood and quitting smoking (Ms = 4.50/5). Conclusions: The results from the feasibility study indicated high levels of acceptability and satisfaction with SMI-CM. The ongoing RCT will allow evaluation of the efficacy and mechanisms of action underlying SMI-CM for improving cessation rates among smokers with mood disorders.
studies.total_n: 8 (open-label pilot feasibility study only; RCT target N=60 not yet completed). "The results from the pilot feasibility study (N = 8)" (Abstract, Results). For the RCT: "We intend to enroll a total of 60 participants with 30 randomized to SMI-CM and 30 to EST" (Methods, Phase II, Sample size considerations).
studies.age_mean: 55.25 (pilot feasibility study, N=8; RCT baseline not yet reported)
studies.age_describe: Mean age = 55.25 (SD = 4.59) for the pilot feasibility study (N=8). "Age 55.25 (4.59)" (Table 4, Participant demographics and baseline characteristics).
studies.participants: Pilot study: N=8, all female, 50% Hispanic, 50% Black or African American, 37.5% White, 12.5% Asian; 87.5% had high school diploma/GED or less; all had household incomes < $25,000; 75% on disability. "All participants (N = 8) were female, 4 (38.5%) were white, 4 (50.0%) were Hispanic, 7 (87.5%) had a high school diploma/GED or less, all reported household incomes of less than $25,000, and 75% were on disability." (Results, Participant characteristics, paragraph 1). RCT target: smokers with mood disorders receiving outpatient psychiatric treatment.
studies.eligibility: Inclusion criteria (RCT): 1) 18 years of age or older; 2) smoking at least 5 cigarettes daily for the past 6 months; 3) English-speaking; 4) intent to quit smoking in the next 3 months; 5) attended a minimum of 3 treatment visits in the past 3 months at the clinic; 6) have a depressive disorder or bipolar disorder; 7) currently receiving treatment for depression or bipolar disorder. Exclusion criteria (RCT): 1) acute psychiatric symptomatology including current active suicidal ideation; 2) current diagnosis of dementia, cognitive impairment, intellectual disability and/or autistic disorder sufficient to impair provision of informed consent or study participation; 3) diagnosis of a psychotic disorder; 4) current (non-nicotine) substance use disorder with the exception of individuals with at least 6 months of abstinence or currently receiving treatment; 5) regular use (4 or more days per week) of other tobacco products or marijuana; 6) use of pharmacotherapy for smoking cessation (excluding NRT) in the past month or current use of NRT; 7) intention to quit smoking using pharmacotherapy other than transdermal nicotine patches; 8) pregnant, breastfeeding, or planning to become pregnant within 6 months; 9) significant history of cardiovascular disease; 10) lack of a stable home address. (Methods, Phase II, Participants and setting, paragraph 1)
studies.population_vulnerable: Yes — low-income individuals with psychiatric disorders (mood disorders) receiving outpatient psychiatric treatment. "all reported household incomes of less than $25,000" and "smokers receiving outpatient treatment for mood disorders" (Abstract; Results, Participant characteristics). Also noted: "The generalization of these findings to other populations may be limited as all participants in this feasibility study were low socioeconomic status (household incomes of less than $25,000)" (Discussion, paragraph 3).
studies.location: Bronx, NY, United States. "Participants are recruited from an outpatient psychiatric clinic in the Bronx, NY" (Methods, Phase II, Participants and setting, paragraph 1). Acknowledgements reference Montefiore Behavioral Health Center.
studies.mental_health: Depressive disorder or bipolar disorder required for enrollment. "have a depressive disorder or bipolar disorder" and "currently receiving treatment for depression or bipolar disorder" (Methods, Phase II, Participants and setting, paragraph 1).
studies.physical_health: Smoking at least 5 cigarettes daily for the past 6 months required for enrollment. "smoking at least 5 cigarettes daily for the past 6 months" (Methods, Phase II, Participants and setting, paragraph 1). Note: significant history of cardiovascular disease is an exclusion criterion, not an inclusion criterion.
studies.arms: Two arms in the RCT: 1) SMI-CM (smartphone-assisted mindfulness-based intervention with contingency management), intervention arm, target N=30; 2) EST (enhanced standard treatment plus non-contingent CM), comparison arm, target N=30. "The primary aim of the RCT is to test the efficacy of SMI-CM against a comparison intervention, enhanced standard treatment plus non-contingent CM (EST)... We intend to enroll a total of 60 participants with 30 randomized to SMI-CM and 30 to EST." (Methods, Phase II, Study design). Pilot feasibility study had only 1 arm (SMI-CM, N=8).
studies.meditation_intervention: SMI-CM (smartphone-assisted mindfulness-based intervention with contingency management). Adapted from Mindfulness-Based Addiction Treatment (MBAT). Components: (1) Individual counseling sessions — 2 in-person sessions (50–60 min each) at 10 days and 3 days prior to target quit date, and 2 brief phone sessions (15–20 min each) at 3 and 10 days after target quit date. Sessions include psychoeducation, smoking cessation counseling, and introduction to mindfulness theory and practice. (2) Smartphone app — prompts mindfulness practice 5 times/day, EMA reports 5 times/day, CO video submission twice/day. (3) Mindfulness practice — 38 days total (10 days pre-quit, 28 days post-quit); 14 guided recordings (5–7 min each) covering breath awareness, body scan, loving-kindness, urge surfing, walking meditation, etc. (4) Contingency management — monetary incentives for biochemically verified abstinence (CO ≤ 6 ppm) for 2 weeks post-quit. Nicotine patches provided up to 8 weeks. "Individual sessions were adapted from a previous Mindfulness-Based Addiction Treatment [25]" (Methods, Phase 1, Individual counseling sessions).
studies.intervention_delivery: Hybrid delivery: in-person individual counseling sessions (2 sessions, 50–60 min each) plus phone counseling sessions (2 sessions, 15–20 min each), supplemented by a smartphone app for daily mindfulness practice, EMA, and CO video submission. "It consists of individual counseling sessions (delivered in-person and via phone) and a smartphone intervention" (Methods, Phase 1, SMI-CM intervention development). Mindfulness recordings developed by MF, described as "a mindfulness expert who has been involved in previous research studies of mindfulness interventions for smoking cessation" (Methods, Phase 1, Mindfulness practice).
studies.digital_component_raw: Yes — smartphone app (Samsung Galaxy Grand Prime/J3) provided to participants, used to deliver mindfulness practice prompts and recordings, EMA reports, and CO video submission. "The smartphone app was developed in collaboration with TelASK Technology Inc.... The application randomly prompts participants 5 times per day... to complete EMA reports, as well as to engage in mindfulness practice" (Methods, Phase 1, Smartphone application).
studies.intervention_tailor: Yes — adapted for smokers with mood disorders (depressive disorder or bipolar disorder) receiving outpatient psychiatric treatment. Sessions include psychoeducation on depression and smoking cessation. "Provide psychoeducation on depression and smoking cessation, nicotine dependence, and health benefits of quitting" (Table 1). Also adapted from MBAT for this population. Cultural/linguistic note: Spanish-speaking participants were included (37.5% spoke Spanish as first language) but no explicit language adaptation is described.
studies.comparison: Enhanced Standard Treatment plus Non-Contingent CM (EST): same number of individual smoking cessation counseling sessions as SMI-CM (2 in-person sessions [35 min] and 2 brief phone sessions [15–20 min]), up to 8 weeks of nicotine patches, CO video submission with non-contingent incentives (yoked to SMI-CM participant), and EMA reports — but WITHOUT mindfulness components. "EST individual session content is identical to SMI-CM except it lacks the mindfulness components." (Methods, Phase II, Individual counseling sessions). Non-contingent incentives: EST participants earn incentives regardless of CO levels, yoked to a matched SMI-CM participant.
studies.assessment_time: Pilot feasibility study: T0 = Baseline (~14 days prior to quit date, 0 weeks); T1 = Pre-quit (3 days prior to quit date, ~-0.4 weeks); T2 = 2-week post-quit follow-up (~2 weeks post-quit); T3 = 4-week post-quit follow-up (~4 weeks post-quit); T4 = 3-month post-quit follow-up (~12.6 weeks post-quit). "Self-report measures and interview questions are administered at baseline (approximately 14 days prior to target quit date), pre-quit (3 days prior to target quit date), and post-quit follow-up assessments (2 weeks, 4 weeks, and 3 months after target quit date)." (Methods, Phase II, Assessment visits). Note: baseline is ~2 weeks before quit date; weeks from baseline to post-quit assessments: T1 pre-quit ≈ 1.6 weeks; T2 ≈ 3.6 weeks; T3 ≈ 5.6 weeks; T4 ≈ 14.2 weeks from baseline.
studies.assessment_nature: Both self-report and non-self-report measures used. Self-report questionnaires (FFMQ, AAQ, PROMIS depression/anxiety, PANAS, ASRM, DTS, PSRS, FTCD, MNWS, TAA, MRSS), EMA via smartphone, biochemical verification of smoking abstinence (expired CO analysis, saliva cotinine), clinician-administered diagnostic interview (M.I.N.I. International Neuropsychiatric Interview 7.0), and qualitative semi-structured interview. "Self-report measures and interview questions are administered at baseline" and "biochemically verified by expired carbon monoxide (CO) analysis" (Methods, Phase II, Assessment visits and Smoking outcomes).

12. Perceived stress reactivity — Perceived Stress Reactivity Scale (PSRS, 23 items)
13. Depression — PROMIS Depression Short Form 8a (8 items)
14. Anxiety — PROMIS Anxiety Short Form 8a (8 items)
15. Positive and negative affect — Positive and Negative Affect Scale (PANAS, 20 items)
16. Manic symptoms — Altman Self-Rating Mania Scale (ASRM, 5 items)
17. Alcohol and drug use — Timeline Follow-Back (TLFB)
18. Treatment history — Treatment history interview
19. Program evaluation — 5-point helpfulness ratings (overall program, counseling, mindfulness, CM)
20. Qualitative interview — semi-structured interview on intervention experience
21. EMA measures — smoking behavior, mindfulness, experiential avoidance, affect, withdrawal, craving, motivation, confidence, temptations, alcohol/drug use
22. Adherence — completion rates of mindfulness practice, CO video submission, EMA reports
(Methods, Phase II, Measures; Table 3)

"The primary aim of the RCT is to test the efficacy of SMI-CM against a comparison intervention... Effect size estimates will include odds ratios for 7-day point-prevalence abstinence" (Methods, Phase II, Study design and Sample size considerations).

"Self-report measures and interview questions are administered at baseline (approximately 14 days prior to target quit date), pre-quit (3 days prior to target quit date), and post-quit follow-up assessments (2 weeks, 4 weeks, and 3 months after target quit date)." (Methods, Phase II, Assessment visits).

"Participants are recruited from an outpatient psychiatric clinic in the Bronx, NY via an in-person approach by research assistants in the waiting rooms, paper flyers displayed in the outpatient clinic, and medical staff referral." studies.authors: Mirmoeini, P., Bayazi, M. H., & Khalatbari, J.
studies.title: Comparing the Effectiveness of Acceptance and Commitment Therapy and Compassion Focused Therapy on Worry Severity and Loneliness Among the Patients With Multiple Sclerosis
studies.abstract:
Aims Because of the increasing number of patients with multiple sclerosis (MS) and the psychological complications that affect this group, the current study has compared the effectiveness of Acceptance and Commitment Therapy (ACT) and Compassion Focused Therapy (CFT) on these patients.
Methods & Materials This research is a quasi-experimental study with a pretest-post-test design and a control group. A total of 45 patients with MS were selected from the patients of an MS Clinic in Tehran City, Iran, in 2019. Then, they were randomly divided into two experimental groups of ACT and CFT and one control group. The participants completed the social and emotional loneliness scale for adults and the Penn State worry questionnaire before and after the intervention. The experimental groups participated in eight sessions of ACT and ten sessions of CFT. The control group did not receive any intervention, and in the end, a post-test was taken. The obtained data were examined by analysis of covariance
Findings Findings obtained from univariate analysis of covariance at the statistical level of P<0.05 were F=42.60 for loneliness and F=5.90 for worry, which indicates the more effectiveness of ACT.
Conclusion It is suggested that ACT treatment be given more attention in controlling patients' psychological symptoms.

studies.title: Yoga Effects on Physical Activity and Sexual Satisfaction among Iranian Women with Multiple Sclerosis: A Randomized Controlled Trial
studies.abstract: Background: Multiple Sclerosis (MS) is a chronic and disabling disease resulting in disabilities in young and middle-aged persons. In this study, researchers explored the effect of yoga techniques on physical activities and sexual function among some Iranian women with MS. Materials and Methods: In this study, 60 Iranian women with multiple sclerosis (MS) were placed in two equally divided control and case groups through random selection to assess pre- and post- effects of yoga exercises on their physical activities and sexual satisfaction levels. Women in case group were offered a series of yoga training and exercises for 3 months, which consisted of 8 sessions per month for 60 to 90 minutes at each session. Yoga training program included the 3 principles of slow motions (Hatayoga), respiratory exercises (Pranayama) and centralization to control mind via meditation, expansion and stasis (Rajayoga). After 3 months both groups were surveyed using the initial questionnaire to evaluate and compare findings with the base-line data. Results: Researchers found significant statistical difference in physical activity and sexual satisfaction levels among the women in case group (P=0.001). Women in case group showed improvement in physical ability while women in control group manifested exacerbated symptoms. Conclusion: Yoga techniques may improve physical activities and sexual satisfaction function of women with MS. Key Words: Yoga; Multiple sclerosis; Quality of life; Sexual satisfaction

studies.title: Brief Mindfulness Intervention vs. Health Enhancement Program for Patients Undergoing Dialysis: A Randomized Controlled Trial
studies.abstract: Background: Between 20–50% of patients undergoing maintenance dialysis for end-stage kidney disease experience symptoms of depression and/or anxiety, associated with increased mortality, greater health care utilization, and decreased quality of life. It is unknown whether mindfulness-based interventions can improve depression and anxiety symptoms in patients receiving this treatment. Methods: We conducted an 8-week multicenter randomized controlled trial comparing a brief mindfulness intervention (BMI) vs. an active control (Health Enhancement Program [HEP]) in 55 patients receiving dialysis with symptoms of depression and/or anxiety. The primary outcome was change in Patient Health Questionnaire-9 (PHQ-9) depression scores, with a primary analysis in participants with baseline PHQ-9≥ 10, and a secondary analysis including all participants. The secondary outcome was change in Generalized Anxiety Disorder-7 (GAD-7) anxiety scores with corresponding primary and secondary analyses. Results: Both BMI and HEP reduced depressive symptoms, with no difference between trial arms (PHQ-9 change =−7.0 vs.−6.1, p = 0.62). BMI was more effective than HEP in reducing anxiety (GAD-7 change =−8.7 vs.−1.4, p = 0.01). Secondary analyses revealed no differences between arms. Conclusions: For patients undergoing dialysis, both BMI and HEP may be helpful interventions for depression symptoms, and BMI may be superior to HEP for anxiety symptoms. Mindfulness-based and other psychosocial interventions may be further evaluated in those undergoing dialysis as treatment options for symptoms of depression and anxiety.
studies.total_n: 55. 'Of these, 9 were refused and 55 were randomized.' (Results, Participant Flow, paragraph 1). Treatment group n=25, Active Control group n=30 (Table 1).
studies.age_mean: 62.2 (total sample). 'Age, yr 62.2 ± 12.0' (Table 1, Baseline Demographic and Clinical Characteristics).
studies.age_describe: Total sample mean age: 62.2 ± 12.0 years. Treatment group: 58.7 ± 12.2 years. Active control group: 64.9 ± 11.2 years. 'Age, yr 62.2 ± 12.0 [total], 58.7 ± 12.2 [treatment], 64.9 ± 11.2 [control]' (Table 1, Baseline Demographic and Clinical Characteristics). No range or median reported.
studies.participants: Adult patients receiving in-center thrice weekly dialysis for end-stage kidney disease with symptoms of depression and/or anxiety. 'Participants had a similar number of medical conditions (7.0 (IQR 5.0–8.0)) and were taking an average of 10.0 (IQR 8.0–13.0) medications. Twenty-nine percent of participants had a history of a psychiatric diagnosis.' 58.2% female, mean age 62.2 years. (Results, Baseline Characteristics, paragraph 1 and Table 1).
studies.eligibility: Inclusion criteria: 'Adult participants aged ≥18 years were included if they were receiving in-center thrice weekly dialysis for any duration and had symptoms of depression and/or anxiety, as indicated by a score ≥ 6 on the Patient Health Questionnaire (PHQ-9) and/or the General Anxiety Disorder-7 (GAD-7).' Exclusion criteria: 'Patients were excluded if they had significant cognitive impairment suggestive of dementia (score < 3 on the Mini-Cog), showed signs of acute psychosis, were experiencing suicidal ideation or intent as assessed by item 9 of PHQ-9, were currently receiving psychotherapy, were an incident patient, had hearing difficulties, or did not speak English or French.' (Methods, Participants, paragraph 1).
studies.population_vulnerable: Yes — patients with end-stage kidney disease (ESKD) receiving maintenance dialysis, a population with high rates of depression and anxiety, increased mortality, and limited treatment access. 'Up to 50% of patients undergoing dialysis experience symptoms of depression and anxiety... levels of depression and anxiety are rarely assessed in patients receiving dialysis, and the majority of affected patients are not receiving effective treatment.' (Introduction, paragraph 1).
studies.location: Montreal, Canada. 'Participants were recruited and enrolled... from in-center dialysis units at four tertiary-care hospitals in Montreal, Canada: the Jewish General Hospital, Centre hospitalier de l'Université de Montréal (CHUM), and the McGill University Health Centre (Montreal General Hospital and Lachine Hospital).' (Methods, Participants, paragraph 1).
studies.mental_health: Symptoms of depression and/or anxiety required for enrollment, as indicated by a score ≥ 6 on the PHQ-9 and/or GAD-7. 'had symptoms of depression and/or anxiety, as indicated by a score ≥ 6 on the Patient Health Questionnaire (PHQ-9) and/or the General Anxiety Disorder-7 (GAD-7)' (Methods, Participants, paragraph 1).
studies.physical_health: End-stage kidney disease requiring in-center thrice weekly dialysis. 'Adult participants aged ≥18 years were included if they were receiving in-center thrice weekly dialysis for any duration' (Methods, Participants, paragraph 1).
studies.arms: Two arms. 1) Brief Mindfulness Intervention (BMI) — treatment arm, n=25. 2) Health Enhancement Program (HEP) — active control arm, n=30. 'We conducted an 8-week multicenter randomized controlled trial comparing a brief mindfulness intervention (BMI) vs. an active control (Health Enhancement Program [HEP]) in 55 patients' (Abstract, Methods).
studies.meditation_intervention: Brief Mindfulness Intervention (BMI): 'While undergoing dialysis, participants received two chair-side 20 min sessions of BMI per week for 8 weeks. Most sessions included around 15 min of guided mindfulness meditation techniques drawn from mindfulness-based cognitive therapy (MBCT). These mindfulness meditation techniques included a body scan, mindful eating, guided breath meditation, mindful movement, and loving-kindness meditation. Techniques emphasized paying attention to specific elements of one's moment-to-moment sensory experience with a non-judgmental attitude. In addition, participants learned material about mindfulness and how to apply it to daily life. Participants could individually check-in with the interventionist and ask any questions for 3–5 min after each session. Interventions were delivered in English or French via audio headsets, allowing up to 4–6 participants to receive instruction simultaneously while an interventionist delivered instructions in patients' sightline. A 10-minute daily home mindfulness practice was encouraged.' Total: 16 sessions over 8 weeks, 20 min each (320 min in-session). (Methods, Treatment: Brief Mindfulness Intervention, paragraph 1).
studies.intervention_delivery: In-person group delivery at dialysis chair-side. 'Interventions were delivered in English or French via audio headsets, allowing up to 4–6 participants to receive instruction simultaneously while an interventionist delivered instructions in patients' sightline.' Two interventionists: 'One interventionist was a registered social worker with facilitator certification in MBCT and a personal mindfulness practice of over 7 years. The other was a psychologist and certified MBSR teacher and a MBCT facilitator with over 40 years of clinical mental health experience.' (Methods, Treatment and Interventionists sections).
studies.digital_component_raw: No digital component. Audio headsets were used to deliver audio instructions in-person at the dialysis chair-side. 'Interventions were delivered in English or French via audio headsets, allowing up to 4–6 participants to receive instruction simultaneously while an interventionist delivered instructions in patients' sightline.' (Methods, Treatment, paragraph 1). This is an analog audio delivery tool, not a digital platform.
studies.intervention_tailor: Yes — the intervention was adapted for delivery during dialysis (chair-side format) and condensed to a brief format. 'While undergoing dialysis, participants received two chair-side 20 min sessions of BMI per week for 8 weeks.' The brief format (400 total minutes) was specifically designed for the dialysis setting. 'Our study also suggests that brief program formatting (400 total minutes), while about 40–70% shorter than most psychosocial interventions, may lead to similar benefits.' (Discussion, paragraph 1). Delivered in English or French for the Montreal population.
studies.comparison: Health Enhancement Program (HEP): active control. 'HEP was previously designed and used as an active control in mindfulness-based intervention trials to control for several non-program-specific intervention factors including facilitator attention, expectation for positive change, treatment duration, format (e.g., individual vs. group), and time spent on at-home practice. It was structurally equivalent to the mindfulness meditation program (two 20-minute sessions per week for 8-weeks, delivered via audio-headsets in groups of 4–6 participants, with 3–5 min for questions or discussion), and encouraged the same amount of home practice (implementing health-enhancing habits for 10 min daily). Each session involved educational and activity-based sessions on light exercise, sleep, stress and anxiety, nutrition, journaling, and music enjoyment with drawing.' (Methods, Active Control: Health Enhancement Program, paragraph 1).
studies.assessment_time: T0 = Baseline (0 weeks); T1 = Post-intervention (8 weeks). 'The primary outcome was the between-group difference in the 8-week change in depressive symptoms as measured by the PHQ-9' (Methods, Efficacy Outcome Measures, paragraph 1). No follow-up beyond 8 weeks reported.
studies.assessment_nature: Self-report questionnaires only. PHQ-9 and GAD-7 are self-report instruments. 'The PHQ-9 is a widely-used 9-item self-report questionnaire used to assess depressive symptom severity.' (Methods, Efficacy Outcome Measures, paragraph 1). Qualitative open-ended survey also used for participant feedback.
studies.outcomes_all: 1. Depression — Patient Health Questionnaire-9 (PHQ-9) (9 items, score range 0–27). 2. Anxiety — Generalized Anxiety Disorder-7 (GAD-7) (7 items, score range 0–21). 3. Feasibility outcomes — recruitment rate, dropout rate, non-attendance rate. 4. Qualitative participant experience — 10-item open-ended survey on perceived benefit, skills learned, and satisfaction. 'The primary outcome was the between-group difference in the 8-week change in depressive symptoms as measured by the PHQ-9... The secondary outcome was the between group difference in 8-week change in anxiety symptoms as measured by the GAD-7.' (Methods, Efficacy Outcome Measures).
studies.outcomes_primary: Depression symptoms as measured by the PHQ-9. 'The primary outcome was the between-group difference in the 8-week change in depressive symptoms as measured by the PHQ-9, with a prespecified primary analysis in the subgroup of patients with baseline PHQ-9 scores ≥ 10, and a secondary analysis with all randomized participants.' (Methods, Efficacy Outcome Measures, paragraph 1).
studies.outcome_timepoints: T0 = Baseline (0 weeks); T1 = Post-intervention (8 weeks). 'The primary outcome was the between-group difference in the 8-week change in depressive symptoms' (Methods, Efficacy Outcome Measures, paragraph 1). No additional follow-up timepoints reported.
studies.recruitment: Recruited by three research assistants between May 2018 and March 2019 from in-center dialysis units at four tertiary-care hospitals in Montreal, Canada. 'Participants were recruited and enrolled by three research assistants between May 2018 and March 2019 from in-center dialysis units at four tertiary-care hospitals in Montreal, Canada.' Of 400 potential participants, 112 were screened with PHQ-9 and GAD-7, 64 met eligibility criteria, 9 refused, and 55 were randomized. (Methods, Participants, paragraph 1; Results, Participant Flow, paragraph 1).
studies.study_purpose: 'We aimed to conduct a randomized controlled trial (RCT) to evaluate the efficacy of a brief mindfulness intervention (BMI) against an active control health enhancement program (HEP) in reducing symptoms of depression and anxiety in patients undergoing dialysis.' (Introduction, final paragraph).
studies.study_design: 8-week multicenter assessor-blinded parallel RCT. 'We conducted an 8-week assessor-blinded parallel RCT comparing BMI vs. HEP.' Randomization 1:1 ratio using computerized random number generator, stratified by site and baseline PHQ-9 score (≥10 vs. <10). 'Assessors were blinded to participant group assignment.' (Methods, Study Design and Randomization sections).
studies.treatment_vs_prevention: Treatment — participants were required to have symptoms of depression and/or anxiety (PHQ-9 and/or GAD-7 score ≥ 6) at enrollment, and the study tests intervention efficacy for these existing symptoms. 'had symptoms of depression and/or anxiety, as indicated by a score ≥ 6 on the Patient Health Questionnaire (PHQ-9) and/or the General Anxiety Disorder-7 (GAD-7)' (Methods, Participants, paragraph 1).
studies.confidence_why: None
studies.active_comparator_name: Health Enhancement Program (HEP) — structured psychoeducation/activity program covering light exercise, sleep, stress and anxiety, nutrition, journaling, and music enjoyment with drawing. Human review needed.
studies.outcomes_coded: Depression | Anxiety | Feasibility-acceptability

studies.authors: Neff, K. D., & Germer, C. K.
studies.title: A Pilot Study and Randomized Controlled Trial of the Mindful Self-Compassion Program
studies.abstract: Objectives: The aim of these two studies was to evaluate the effectiveness of the Mindful Self-Compassion (MSC) program, an 8-week workshop designed to train people to be more self-compassionate. Methods: Study 1 was a pilot study that examined change scores in self-compassion, mindfulness, and various wellbeing outcomes among community adults (N = 21; mean [M] age = 51.26, 95% female). Study 2 was a randomized controlled trial that compared a treatment group (N = 25; M age = 51.21; 78% female) with a waitlist control group (N = 27; M age = 49.11; 82% female). Results: Study 1 found significant pre/post gains in self-compassion, mindfulness, and various wellbeing outcomes. Study 2 found that compared with the control group, intervention participants reported significantly larger increases in self-compassion, mindfulness, and wellbeing. Gains were maintained at 6-month and 1-year follow-ups. Conclusions: The MSC program appears to be effective at enhancing self-compassion, mindfulness, and wellbeing.
studies.total_n: 54 (Study 2 RCT). 'Fifty-four people signed up for the study and were randomly assigned to the intervention or to a waitlist control group.' (Study 2, Method, Participants, paragraph 1). Note: abstract states N=25 treatment and N=27 control (total=52), but Methods states 54 were randomized; 2 were dropped from analyses. Randomized N = 54 used here.
studies.age_mean: 50.09 (weighted; Intervention: 51.21±12.02 n=25; Control: 49.11±11.59 n=27, using abstract arm Ns for weighting). Note: weighted mean calculated as (25×51.21 + 27×49.11)/52 = 50.09.
studies.age_describe: Study 2 (RCT): Intervention group M age = 51.21 (SD = 12.02); Control group M age = 49.11 (SD = 11.59). Study 1 (pilot): M age = 51.26 (SD = 11.28). 'Intervention participants (M age = 51.21, SD = 12.02) were 78% female and 84% Caucasian; Control participants (M age = 49.11, SD = 11.59) were 82% female and 85% Caucasian.' (Study 2, Method, Participants, paragraph 1)
studies.participants: Community adults recruited from the greater Boston area. Study 2 (RCT): intervention group 78% female, 84% Caucasian, 80% had a graduate degree, 74% had prior meditation experience; control group 82% female, 85% Caucasian, 74% had a graduate degree, 78% had prior meditation experience. 'Participants were mostly highly educated, middle-aged females who had prior meditation experience.' (General Discussion, Limitations, paragraph 1)
studies.eligibility: No formal inclusion or exclusion criteria are explicitly stated in the paper. Participants were recruited from the community via internet announcements, therapist/meditation teacher referrals, and yoga studio email notifications. 'Participants were recruited in the same way as Study 1' (Study 2, Method, Participants, paragraph 1). No diagnostic thresholds or health criteria are reported as enrollment requirements.
studies.population_vulnerable: Not a vulnerable population — participants were community adults, predominantly highly educated, middle-aged, Caucasian females with prior meditation experience. 'Participants were mostly highly educated, middle-aged females who had prior meditation experience. This was by no means a diverse sample.' (General Discussion, Limitations, paragraph 1)
studies.location: Inferred: Greater Boston area, Massachusetts, USA (inferred from 'Participants were recruited from the greater Boston area' — Study 1, Method, Participants, paragraph 1; and author affiliations at University of Texas at Austin and Harvard Medical School)
studies.mental_health: N/A — no psychiatric enrollment criterion
studies.physical_health: N/A — no physical health enrollment criterion
studies.arms: Study 2 (RCT) has 2 arms: (1) MSC intervention group (N=25 per abstract, 24 analyzed); (2) Waitlist control group (N=27). 'This study implemented a 2 (experimental vs. waitlist control group) X 2 (baseline, post-treatment) randomized study design.' (Study 2, paragraph 1)
studies.meditation_intervention: The Mindful Self-Compassion (MSC) program: explicitly named. 8-week program, weekly 2-hour sessions (2 or 2.5 hours), plus a half-day retreat between sessions 4 and 5 (4 hours in silence). Session topics: Week 1 introduction/review of self-compassion; Week 2 mindfulness foundations; Week 3 applying self-compassion; Week 4 compassionate inner voice; Week 5 core values; Week 6 difficult emotions; Week 7 challenging relationships; Week 8 appreciation of positive aspects. Formal practices: loving-kindness meditation (LKM), affectionate breathing, compassion-focused LKM variant. Informal practices: hand on heart, self-compassion phrases. Homework: 40 minutes of self-compassion practice per day (formal and informal combined), including writing letters to oneself from a compassionate friend perspective. Co-led by two clinical psychologists with long-term mindfulness meditation practice and extensive professional experience with mindfulness-based and acceptance-based psychotherapy. 'The MSC program consisted of 8 weekly meetings, with participants meeting in the evening for 2 hours once a week over the course of 8 weeks.' (Study 1, Intervention, paragraph 1)
studies.intervention_delivery: In-person group format. 'Participants meeting in the evening for 2 hours once a week over the course of 8 weeks.' Co-led by 'two clinical psychologists with long-term personal practices of mindfulness meditation and extensive professional experience with mindfulness-based and acceptance-based psychotherapy.' (Study 1, Intervention, paragraphs 1–2). Measures completed online.
studies.digital_component_raw: No digital component. Intervention delivered in-person. Measures were completed online ('Baseline and postintervention measures were completed online 2 weeks before and after the program' — Study 1, Measures, paragraph 1), but this is data collection only, not intervention delivery.
studies.intervention_tailor: No tailoring reported. The program was delivered as developed, with no reported cultural or population-specific adaptations.
studies.comparison: Waitlist control group (N=27): participants were randomly assigned to a waitlist and did not receive the MSC program during the study period. 'Those on the waitlist took the course after the intervention group, but were not surveyed again.' (Study 2, Measures, paragraph 3). No active treatment was provided to the control group during the study period.
studies.assessment_time: Study 2 (RCT): T0 = Baseline (0 weeks; 2 weeks before program start); T1 = Post-intervention (approximately 10 weeks from baseline, i.e., 2 weeks after 8-week program); T2 = 6-month follow-up (approximately 35.2 weeks from post, i.e., ~45 weeks from baseline); T3 = 1-year follow-up (approximately 52 weeks from post, i.e., ~62 weeks from baseline). Also interim assessments at Weeks 3 and 6 of the program for self-compassion only. 'All participants filled out self-report measures online 2 weeks before and 2 weeks after the intervention.' (Study 2, Measures, paragraph 1). 'Participants in the intervention group were given all the study measures 6 months and 1 year after completion of the program.' (Study 2, Measures, paragraph 2). Note: exact week counts from baseline are approximate due to the 2-week pre/post buffer.
studies.assessment_nature: Self-report questionnaires only. 'All participants filled out self-report measures online 2 weeks before and 2 weeks after the intervention.' (Study 2, Measures, paragraph 1). All outcome instruments are self-report scales.
studies.outcomes_all:
1. Self-compassion — Self-Compassion Scale (SCS; 26-item long form in Study 1; 12-item SCS-short form in Study 2; 5-point scale; subscales: Self-Kindness, Self-Judgment, Common Humanity, Isolation, Mindfulness, Over-Identification)
2. Mindfulness — Freiburg Mindfulness Inventory (FMI; 14-item short version; 4-point scale) in Study 1; Cognitive and Affective Mindfulness Scale – Revised (CAMS-R) in Study 2
3. Social connectedness — Social Connectedness Scale (Lee & Robbins, 1995; 5-point scale)
4. Happiness — Subjective Happiness Scale (4-item; 7-point scale)
5. Life satisfaction — Satisfaction with Life Scale (Diener et al., 1985; 5-item)
6. Depression — Beck Depression Inventory (BDI; 20-item; 4-point scale)
7. Anxiety — Spielberger State-Trait Anxiety Inventory – Trait form (STAI; 20-item; 5-point scale)
8. Stress — Perceived Stress Scale (PSS; 10-item; 5-point scale)
9. Compassion for others — Compassion Scale (Pommier, 2011; 6 subscales: Kindness, Indifference, Common Humanity, Separation, Mindfulness, Disengagement; 5-point scale) [Study 2 only]
10. Avoidance — Avoidance subscale of the Impact of Event Scale – Revised (IES-R; Weiss & Marmar, 1997) [Study 2 only]
11. Program evaluation — single item overall rating (5-point scale, poor to excellent)
studies.outcomes_primary: Unclear — authors do not explicitly designate a single primary outcome. Self-compassion appears to be the primary focus: 'we hypothesized that participants would report higher levels of self-compassion, mindfulness, social connectedness, happiness, and life satisfaction, as well as lower levels of depression, anxiety, and stress.' (Study 1, paragraph 1). Self-compassion is consistently listed first and receives the most detailed analysis.
studies.outcome_timepoints:
Study 1 (pilot): T0 = Baseline (0 weeks); T1 = Post-intervention (~10 weeks); T2 = 6-month follow-up (~35 weeks from post, self-compassion and mindfulness only).
Study 2 (RCT): T0 = Baseline (0 weeks); interim T = Week 3 and Week 6 of program (self-compassion only); T1 = Post-intervention (~10 weeks); T2 = 6-month follow-up (~35 weeks from post, intervention group only); T3 = 1-year follow-up (~62 weeks from baseline, intervention group only). 'Participants in the intervention group were given all the study measures 6 months and 1 year after completion of the program.' (Study 2, Measures, paragraph 2)
studies.recruitment: Participants recruited from the greater Boston area via internet announcements, referrals by local therapists and meditation teachers, and email notifications from the yoga studio where training was held. 'Individuals who signed up for the research study received a substantially reduced fee for the training program.' (Study 1, Method, Participants, paragraph 1). No recruitment dates reported.
studies.study_purpose: To evaluate the effectiveness of the Mindful Self-Compassion (MSC) program. 'The aim of these two studies was to evaluate the effectiveness of the Mindful Self-Compassion (MSC) program, an 8-week workshop designed to train people to be more self-compassionate.' (Abstract)
studies.study_design: Study 1: Uncontrolled pilot study (pre/post design). Study 2: Randomized controlled trial (RCT). '2 (experimental vs. waitlist control group) X 2 (baseline, post-treatment) randomized study design, yielding a between-groups comparison condition.' (Study 2, paragraph 1). Randomization method not described. No blinding reported.
studies.treatment_vs_prevention: Enhancement — participants were community adults with no required diagnosis or symptom threshold at enrollment. The study targets general wellbeing, self-compassion, and psychological flourishing in a non-clinical sample. 'Participants were mostly highly educated, middle-aged females who had prior meditation experience. This was by no means a diverse sample.' (General Discussion, Limitations). No clinical condition was required for enrollment.
