studies.authors: Nübold, A., & Hülsheger, U. R.
studies.title: Personality states mediate the effect of a mindfulness intervention on employees' work outcomes: A randomized controlled trial
studies.abstract: In the last decade, organizational researchers have increasingly recognized the value of studying personality states at work. This line of research has to date mainly focused on outcomes of and situational antecedents of personality state change at work. In this study, we draw on social cognitive theory of self-regulation and the social investment principle to test if a structured intervention can bring about changes in employees' personality states at work. Specifically, we investigate the effect of a four-week low-dose mindfulness intervention delivered via a mobile application on employees' personality state change in a multi-group experiment with a passive and an active control group. Employees (N = 162), either practicing mindfulness, doing brain training exercises, or not receiving any treatment were tracked in a diary study across a period of four weeks. Results of growth curve analyses showed that compared to the control groups, the mindfulness intervention led to significantly more increases in employees' daily mindfulness, emotional stability and agreeableness across the four-week period. Furthermore, daily agreeableness and emotional stability mediated the effect of the intervention on daily job satisfaction and performance. No intervention effects were found for daily openness, conscientiousness, and extraversion. Implications are discussed for research and practice.
studies.age_describe: Mean age of 34 years (SD = 10.87). 'Employees had a mean age of 34 years (SD = 10.87)' (Methods, Sample, paragraph 3). No per-arm age breakdown reported.
studies.participants: Employees recruited from a variety of organizations in Europe. 'The final sample consisted of 162 employees... The sample consisted of 98 women (60.5%) and 58 men (35.8%). Six individuals (3.7%) did not indicate their gender. Employees had a mean age of 34 years (SD = 10.87) and worked 39.38 hours a week on average (SD = 10.24). Employees were stemming from a number of different nations, such as Germany (81.4%), Greece (9.3%), the Netherlands (2.5%), or Austria (1.2%).' (Methods, Sample, paragraph 3)
studies.eligibility: Inclusion criteria: 'every participant was required to work at least part-time, i.e., a minimum of 20 hours per week, and have profound knowledge in English as the mindfulness intervention was provided in English.' (Methods, Sample, paragraph 2). No formal exclusion criteria reported.
studies.population_vulnerable: Not a vulnerable population — participants are working adults from various organizations in Europe with no reported health disparities or structural disadvantage. 'Participants of our study were recruited from a variety of different organizations in Europe.' (Methods, Sample, paragraph 2)

studies.arms: Three arms. 'Participants were randomly assigned to one of three groups. The intervention group included 55 participants, the active control group included 49 participants, and the waitlist control group included 58 participants.' (Methods, Design and procedure, paragraph 1). Arm 1: Mindfulness intervention (Headspace app, n=55); Arm 2: Active control (brain training app Memorado, n=49); Arm 3: Passive/waitlist control (no treatment, n=58).
studies.meditation_intervention: The mindfulness intervention was delivered via the Headspace app. 'The mindfulness intervention was provided via an app offered by Headspace Inc. (www.headspace.com). It consisted of guided mindfulness exercises that lasted around 10 minutes and should be practiced on a daily basis for the period of 30 days.' (Methods, Design and procedure, paragraph 1). Content included body scan and mindful breathing exercises reflecting typical MBSR practices. 'The Headspace app consists of brief instructive videos and daily guided mindfulness exercises reflecting typical mindfulness meditation practices as they are also known from MBSR (Kabat-Zinn, 1990), such as the body scan or mindful breathing exercises.' After an introductory phase of 10 days with basic exercises, participants could engage in more advanced exercises. Duration: 4 weeks (30 days), ~10 minutes per day, self-administered. No facilitator qualifications reported (app-based, self-guided).
studies.intervention_delivery: Self-guided via smartphone app (Headspace). 'The mindfulness intervention was provided via an app offered by Headspace Inc.' Daily sessions of approximately 10 minutes. No live instructor. Participants could practice wherever and whenever they chose. (Methods, Design and procedure and The mindfulness intervention sections)
studies.digital_component_raw: Yes — the intervention was delivered entirely via a smartphone/mobile application (Headspace app). 'The mindfulness intervention was provided via an app offered by Headspace Inc. (www.headspace.com).' (Methods, Design and procedure, paragraph 1)
studies.intervention_tailor: No tailoring reported. The Headspace app was used as commercially available. No cultural or population-specific adaptations described.
studies.comparison: Active control: Brain training app (Memorado). 'The active control group received 30-day access to the brain-training app offered by Memorado (www.memorado.com). Participants got a personalized training plan including five different games each day... The games focused for instance on the improvement of memory and concentration and also lasted around 10 minutes each day.' (Methods, Design and procedure, paragraph 1). Duration: 30 days, ~10 minutes/day, app-based. Passive/waitlist control: 'The passive control group was informed that they would receive a voucher for either app at the end of the four-week period after study completion.' No treatment during the study period. (Methods, Design and procedure, paragraph 1)
studies.assessment_time: T0 = Baseline (0 weeks); T1–T8 = Eight daily assessments (two per week on Tuesdays and Thursdays) across 4 weeks (weeks 1–4). 'daily surveys were sent out to all three groups every Tuesday and Thursday afternoon (3 p.m.) during the four-week period, resulting in a maximum of eight assessments per person.' (Methods, Design and procedure, paragraph 2). No follow-up assessment beyond the 4-week period.
studies.assessment_nature: Self-report only. 'The use of self-report data is very common in diary studies on mindfulness and personality states.' (Discussion, Limitations, paragraph 2). All measures (mindfulness, Big Five personality states, job satisfaction, task performance) were self-reported via daily questionnaires.
studies.outcomes_all: 1. Daily mindfulness — 9-item composite scale: 5-item state version of Mindful Attention and Awareness Scale (MAAS; Brown & Ryan, 2003; Michalak et al., 2008) + adapted 4-item Accept Without Judgment subscale of KIMS (Baer et al., 2004); 7-point Likert scale; average α = .90. 2. Big Five personality states — 6 pairs of bipolar adjectives each for: Neuroticism, Agreeableness, Openness, Conscientiousness, Extraversion (Bleidorn, 2009); 5-point scale (-2 to +2); average α: extraversion .67, agreeableness .77, openness .80, neuroticism .85, conscientiousness .85. 3. Daily job satisfaction — 3 items from Brayfield & Rothe (1951) job satisfaction index adapted to current day; 5-point Likert scale; average α = .75. 4. Daily task performance — 3 items from Williams & Anderson (1991) adapted to current day; 5-point Likert scale; average α = .83. (Methods, Measures section)
studies.outcomes_primary: Unclear — authors do not explicitly designate a single primary outcome. The study tests effects on Big Five personality states as primary theoretical outcomes, with job satisfaction and performance as distal outcomes. 'we investigate the effect of a four-week low-dose mindfulness intervention delivered via a mobile application on employees' personality state change' (Abstract).
studies.outcome_timepoints: T0 = Baseline (0 weeks); T1–T8 = Eight daily assessments across 4 weeks (approximately weeks 1–4, assessed on Tuesdays and Thursdays). All outcomes (daily mindfulness, Big Five personality states, job satisfaction, task performance) assessed at all eight daily timepoints. No follow-up beyond 4 weeks. (Methods, Design and procedure, paragraph 2)
studies.recruitment: Participants recruited via research assistants' personal networks, information sessions within companies, and professional/social media sites. 'Participants of our study were recruited from a variety of different organizations in Europe via research assistants' personal network, through information sessions within companies, or via professional and social media sites such as LinkedIn.' Snowball procedure used; exact response rate not specifiable. 199 participants initially clicked the survey link; 162 active participants remained. (Methods, Sample, paragraphs 1–2)
studies.study_purpose: 'we investigate the effect of a four-week low-dose mindfulness intervention delivered via a mobile application on employees' personality state change in a multi-group experiment with a passive and an active control group' and 'test if a structured intervention can bring about changes in employees' personality states at work.' (Abstract and Introduction)
studies.study_design: Randomized controlled trial (RCT) with three groups (multi-group field experiment). 'Participants were randomly assigned to one of three groups.' (Methods, Design and procedure, paragraph 1). Combined with a diary design (8 daily assessments over 4 weeks). Randomization method not described in detail. No blinding of participants to condition reported (though study was broadly labeled as 'app use and daily perceptions and experiences at work' to reduce demand characteristics). Hypotheses not preregistered.
studies.treatment_vs_prevention: Enhancement — participants are healthy working adults with no clinical diagnosis or symptom threshold required for enrollment. The study tests effects on personality states, job satisfaction, and performance as general wellbeing and work outcomes. 'Participants of our study were recruited from a variety of different organizations in Europe' with no clinical or at-risk criterion. (Methods, Sample, paragraph 2)

studies.authors: Omidi, A., & Hamidian, S.
studies.title: Effectiveness of a Combined Mindfulness-Based Cognitive Therapy and Mindfulness-Based Stress Reduction Intervention on Depression Symptoms and Quality of Life in a Group of Iranian Veterans with Posttraumatic Stress Disorder
studies.abstract:
Background: Comorbidity of anxiety and mood disorders is rather common, making the treatment of each disorder more difficult. Posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD) is one of the anxiety disorders with a high degree of association with depression; PTSD-depression comorbidity can significantly affect the quality of life of the ones affected. Hence, using the best way to deal with each of these disorders is highly recommended.
Objectives: The current study aimed at evaluating the effectiveness of a combined treatment of mindfulness-based stress reduction (MBSR) and mindfulness-based cognitive therapy (MBCT) on PTSD and comorbid depression in combat veterans.
Methods: Among patients referring to Kashan Veterans Counseling Center, 62 patients diagnosed with comorbid PTSD and depression according to diagnostic and statistical manual of mental disorders-fourth edition-text revision (DSM-IV-TR) were selected, and randomly assigned into the two groups of case and control. The study was conducted in 2012.
Results: Statistical analysis showed that after the intervention, the depression scores of the case group significantly decreased, while the similar trend was not observed in the control group (P < 0.05). Furthermore, the total score and the scores of "mental health" and "social functioning" subscales of quality of life significantly increased in the case group.
Conclusions: According to the observed results, it seems that the combined treatment administered to the case group could aid the participants overcoming depression symptoms and subsequently raised their quality of life.
Keywords: Cognitive Therapy, Depression, Mindfulness, Posttraumatic Stress Disorder, Veterans
studies.total_n: 62. "62 patients meeting the inclusion criteria were selected and using simple randomization method by the table of random numbers, were assigned into the case and the control groups (each consisted of 31 individuals)." (Materials and Methods, Patients and Design, paragraph 1)
studies.age_mean: Not reported
studies.age_describe: Age range 35–49 years. Groups matched by age. Distribution: 35–39 years: case 8 (25.8%), control 7 (22.6%); 40–44 years: case 21 (67.7%), control 22 (71%); 45–49 years: case 2 (6.5%), control 2 (6.5%). "The patients aged 35 - 49 years and the two groups were matched by age, educational level, and occupational status." (Materials and Methods, Patients and Design, paragraph 1; Table 2)
studies.participants: Male Iranian combat veterans with comorbid PTSD and mild to moderate depression attending the Veterans Counseling Center of Kashan, Iran. All participants were employed and receiving psychiatric treatments at baseline. "The current case-control study was conducted on a group of male patients attending Veterans Counseling Center of Kashan, Iran." (Materials and Methods, Patients and Design, paragraph 1)
studies.eligibility: Inclusion criteria: diagnosis of comorbid PTSD and mild to moderate depression according to DSM-IV-TR diagnostic criteria; attending Veterans Counseling Center of Kashan. Exclusion criteria: psychosis, bipolar disorder, depression symptoms due to a disease, and substance dependency. "The inclusion criterion was a diagnosis of comorbid PTSD and mild to moderate depression according to the diagnostic and statistical manual of mental disorders-fourth edition-text revision's (DSM-IV-TR) diagnostic criteria. The exclusion criteria were psychosis, bipolar disorder, depression symptoms due to a disease, and substance dependency." (Materials and Methods, Patients and Design, paragraph 1)
studies.population_vulnerable: Yes — Iranian combat veterans (Iran–Iraq War) with PTSD and comorbid depression, a population experiencing war-related trauma and associated mental health burden. "Due to the large number of imposed war's veterans in Iran, as well as veterans affected by war all around the world with disorders similar to those of the participants of the present study..." (Discussion, paragraph 7)
studies.location: Kashan Veterans Counseling Center, Kashan, Iran. "The current case-control study was conducted on a group of male patients attending Veterans Counseling Center of Kashan, Iran." (Materials and Methods, Patients and Design, paragraph 1)
studies.mental_health: Comorbid PTSD and mild to moderate depression required for enrollment, diagnosed according to DSM-IV-TR criteria. "The inclusion criterion was a diagnosis of comorbid PTSD and mild to moderate depression according to the diagnostic and statistical manual of mental disorders-fourth edition-text revision's (DSM-IV-TR) diagnostic criteria." (Materials and Methods, Patients and Design, paragraph 1)
studies.physical_health: N/A — no physical health enrollment criterion
studies.arms: 2 arms. Arm 1 (case/intervention group): combined MBCT+MBSR protocol, n=31. Arm 2 (control group): treatment as usual (TAU), n=31. "were assigned into the case and the control groups (each consisted of 31 individuals)" (Materials and Methods, Patients and Design, paragraph 1)
studies.meditation_intervention: Combined MBCT and MBSR protocol. "The treatment protocol for the experimental group was designed using the MBCT for depression by Segal et al., and the MBSR curriculum developed by Jon Kabat-Zinn." Eight weekly sessions of approximately two hours each. Content included: psychoeducation about depression and mindfulness, body scan meditation, mindful self-efficacy, behavioral activation, sitting meditation, awareness of thoughts/feelings/body sensations, stress responding vs. reacting, dealing with difficult emotions, modifying dysfunctional beliefs, acceptance, interpersonal mindfulness, relapse prevention action plan. Delivered by an experienced clinical psychologist in the field of mindfulness-based methods. Dropout defined as participation in fewer than 6 of 8 sessions; no dropouts occurred. (Materials and Methods, Intervention, paragraph 1; Table 1)
studies.intervention_delivery: In-person group format. Eight weekly sessions of approximately two hours each. "The protocol consists of eight weekly sessions of approximately two hours each and the intervention was conducted by an experienced clinical psychologist in the field of mindfulness-based methods." (Materials and Methods, Intervention, paragraph 1)
studies.digital_component_raw: No digital component. No technology-based delivery described; intervention was in-person group sessions. (Materials and Methods, Intervention)
studies.intervention_tailor: Yes — the protocol was specifically combined and tailored for veterans with comorbid PTSD and depression. "since the study sample had comorbid depression and PTSD...the combination of two protocols- i.e. MBCT and MBSR, seems to have the greatest effect on the veterans' severity of depression and QOL." (Background, paragraph 6; Objectives)
studies.comparison: Treatment as usual (TAU): control group continued their existing psychiatric treatment, which included taking medication for depression and anxiety prescribed by their psychiatrists. "the control group continued their treatment as usual (TAU) which included taking medication for depression and anxiety prescribed by their psychiatrists." (Materials and Methods, Intervention, paragraph 2)
studies.assessment_time: T0 = Baseline (0 weeks); T1 = Post-intervention (8 weeks). "The protocol consists of eight weekly sessions" with pre and post assessments reported in Table 3. (Materials and Methods, Intervention; Results, Table 3)
studies.assessment_nature: Self-report questionnaires (BDI-II for depression; SF-12 for quality of life) and clinician-administered interview (SCID-I for diagnosis). "A clinical psychologist with Master's degree interviewed the participants using the structured clinical interview for DSM-IV (SCID) to ensure the accuracy of the diagnosis." (Materials and Methods, Patients and Design, paragraph 1; Measures sections)
studies.outcomes_all:
1. Depression severity — Beck Depression Inventory-II (BDI-II; 21 items, scored 0–3 per item, total range 0–63) (Materials and Methods, Measures, 3.5.2)
2. Quality of life — 12-Item Short Form Health Survey (SF-12; 12 items, 8 subscales: physical functioning, role limitation due to physical problems, role limitations due to emotional problems, vitality, mental health, social functioning, bodily pain, general health; scores 0–100) (Materials and Methods, Measures, 3.5.3)
studies.outcomes_primary: Unclear — authors do not explicitly designate a single primary outcome. Both depression (BDI-II) and quality of life (SF-12) are described as key outcomes in the objectives: "evaluating the effectiveness of a combined treatment of mindfulness-based stress reduction (MBSR) and mindfulness-based cognitive therapy (MBCT) on PTSD and comorbid depression in combat veterans." (Abstract, Objectives)
studies.outcome_timepoints: T0 = Baseline (0 weeks); T1 = Post-intervention (8 weeks). Both BDI-II and SF-12 assessed at both timepoints. "the mean BDI score of the intervention group decreased from 29.03...to 19.8" (Results, paragraph 1; Table 3)
studies.recruitment: Participants were recruited from patients attending the Veterans Counseling Center of Kashan, Iran. "Of the 160 cases in the medical center, 62 patients meeting the inclusion criteria were selected." The study was conducted in 2012. Diagnosis confirmed via SCID interview. (Materials and Methods, Patients and Design, paragraph 1)
studies.study_purpose: "The current study aimed at evaluating the effectiveness of a combined treatment of mindfulness-based stress reduction (MBSR) and mindfulness-based cognitive therapy (MBCT) on PTSD and comorbid depression in combat veterans." (Abstract, Objectives)

"The current case-control study...using simple randomization method by the table of random numbers, were assigned into the case and the control groups." No blinding reported. Allocation ratio 1:1. (Materials and Methods, Patients and Design, paragraph 1)

"The inclusion criterion was a diagnosis of comorbid PTSD and mild to moderate depression according to the diagnostic and statistical manual of mental disorders-fourth edition-text revision's (DSM-IV-TR) diagnostic criteria." studies.authors: Orchowski, L. M., Merrill, J. E., Oesterle, D. W., Barnett, N. P., Borsari, B., Zlotnick, C., Haikalis, M. P., & Bekowitz, A. D.
studies.title: Integrated Alcohol Use and Sexual Assault Prevention Program for College Men Who Engage in Heavy Drinking: Randomized Pilot Study
studies.abstract:
Background: Sexual assault is prevalent on college campuses and most commonly is perpetrated by men. Problematically, there is a dearth of evidence-based prevention programs targeting men as perpetrators of sexual aggression. The Sexual Assault and Alcohol Feedback and Education (SAFE) program is an integrated alcohol and sexual assault prevention intervention for college men who engage in heavy drinking that aims to address sexual aggression proclivity and alcohol use outcomes by incorporating social norms theory, bystander intervention, and motivational interviewing.
Objective: This study aims to examine the initial feasibility-, acceptability-, and efficacy-related outcomes of a randomized pilot trial of an integrated alcohol and sexual assault prevention program for college men who engage in heavy drinking.
Methods: This study included 115 college men who engaged in heavy drinking, who were randomly assigned to the SAFE program or a mindfulness-based control condition (MBCC). The feasibility of implementation, adequacy of participant retention, fidelity and competency of program administration, and satisfaction and utility of the intervention were evaluated. The primary outcomes of alcohol use and sexual aggression were evaluated at 2 and 6 months after baseline. The secondary outcomes of perceived peer norms, risks for sexual aggression, and bystander intervention were also assessed. The extent to which the motivational interviewing session with personalized normative feedback facilitated changes in the proximal outcomes of drinking intentions, motivation to change, and self-efficacy was also examined.
Results: The study procedures resulted in high program completion and retention (>80%), high fidelity to the program manual (>80% of the content included), high competency in program administration, and high ratings of satisfaction and program utility in addressing sexual relationships and alcohol use. Both groups reported declines in the number of drinks per week and number of heavy drinking days. Compared with the MBCC participants, the SAFE participants reported higher motivation to change alcohol use after the program, as well as greater use of alcohol protective behavioral strategies at 6 months. Compared with the MBCC participants, the SAFE participants also reported lower perceived peer engagement in sexual coercion, perceived peer comfort with sexism, and peer drinking norms at 2 and 6 months. However, no group differences were observed in sexual aggression severity, rape myth acceptance, or the labeling of sexual consent. Results regarding bystander intervention intentions were mixed, with the MBCC group showing decreased intentions at 2 months and the SAFE group reporting increased intentions at both 2 and 6 months.
Conclusions: The findings provide promising evidence for the feasibility, acceptability, utility, and preliminary efficacy of the SAFE program in reducing alcohol use and positively influencing perceived peer norms and intentions for bystander intervention among college men who drink.
Trial Registration: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT05773027; https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT05773027
studies.total_n: 115. "This study included 115 college men who engaged in heavy drinking, who were randomly assigned to the SAFE program or a mindfulness-based control condition (MBCC)." (Methods, Participants and Study Eligibility Criteria, paragraph 1)
studies.age_mean: 19.98 (Table 1, Participant characteristics)

studies.age_min: 18. "Participants included 115 men aged between 18 and 22 years" (Methods, Participants and Study Eligibility Criteria, paragraph 1)
studies.age_max: 22. "Participants included 115 men aged between 18 and 22 years" (Methods, Participants and Study Eligibility Criteria, paragraph 1)
studies.participants: 115 college men aged 18–22 enrolled at a large northeastern public university in the United States who engaged in heavy drinking. Predominantly White (87.8%), non-Hispanic (88.7%). 32.2% in a social fraternity. "Participants included 115 men aged between 18 and 22 years currently enrolled at a large northeastern public university in the United States." (Methods, Participants and Study Eligibility Criteria, paragraph 1)
studies.eligibility: Inclusion criteria: (1) engaging in 2 or more episodes of binge drinking in the past month (≥5 drinks per day for men on the same occasion); (2) engaging in oral, vaginal, or anal sexual intercourse with a female partner ≥1 times in the past 4 months; (3) men aged 18–22 currently enrolled at the university. Exclusion criteria: displaying symptoms consistent with alcohol use withdrawal (score ≥23 on Alcohol Use Withdrawal Symptom Checklist); reporting current suicidal or homicidal ideation; meeting criteria consistent with a diagnosis of antisocial personality disorder (ASPD) (≥3 domains of problem behavior with no remorse). "Inclusion criteria for the study included engaging in 2 or more episodes of binge drinking in the past month... Exclusion criteria included displaying symptoms consistent with alcohol use withdrawal, reporting current suicidal or homicidal ideation, or meeting criteria consistent with a diagnosis of antisocial personality disorder (ASPD)." (Methods, Participants and Study Eligibility Criteria, paragraphs 1–2)
studies.population_vulnerable: Not a vulnerable population — participants are college men at a northeastern US university, predominantly White and non-Hispanic. No structural disadvantage or health disparity criterion is specified. "Aligning with the demographics of the university, the racial and ethnic diversity in the sample was limited." (Discussion, paragraph 7)
studies.location: A large northeastern public university in the United States. Sessions completed at the psychology training clinic at the local university. "Participants included 115 men aged between 18 and 22 years currently enrolled at a large northeastern public university in the United States." (Methods, Participants and Study Eligibility Criteria, paragraph 1). Specific city/state not explicitly stated in paper body.
studies.mental_health: N/A — no psychiatric enrollment criterion. Heavy drinking (≥2 binge drinking episodes in past month) is the behavioral enrollment criterion, not a psychiatric diagnosis or validated symptom threshold for a mental health condition. Exclusion criteria included ASPD and suicidal/homicidal ideation, but these are exclusion criteria, not inclusion criteria.
studies.physical_health: N/A — no physical health enrollment criterion. Heavy drinking (≥2 episodes of binge drinking in past month, defined as ≥5 drinks per day) is a behavioral criterion. "Inclusion criteria for the study included engaging in 2 or more episodes of binge drinking in the past month, defined by the Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration as the consumption of ≥5 drinks per day for men on the same occasion." (Methods, Participants and Study Eligibility Criteria, paragraph 1)
studies.arms: 2 arms. Arm 1: SAFE (Sexual Assault and Alcohol Feedback and Education) intervention, n=58. Arm 2: Mindfulness-Based Control Condition (MBCC), n=57. "115 college men who engaged in heavy drinking, who were randomly assigned to the SAFE program or a mindfulness-based control condition (MBCC)." (Abstract, Methods)
studies.meditation_intervention: The MBCC (Mindfulness-Based Control Condition) is the mindfulness arm. It was developed for the purpose of this study as an active attention- and dose-matched control. It is described as 'a multisession mindfulness-based stress reduction program, based on prior research on mindfulness intervention.' Session 1 (90 min, individual): participants met one-on-one with a facilitator to explore life in college, identify lifestyle factors contributing to stress, discuss exercise and nutrition, and were introduced to mindfulness and meditation practice. Session 2 (2 hours, group-based): addressed common stressors on campus, engaged in mindfulness and meditation exercises, and learned to apply these skills in everyday life. Session 3 (90 min, group-based booster, 2 months after session 1): continued building mindfulness and meditation skills and discussed how mindfulness and meditation had impacted their lives since session 2. Total: 3 sessions. Facilitators were trained male program facilitators (postbaccalaureate research assistants or graduate students in clinical psychology doctoral programs). "participants in the comparison group received a multisession mindfulness-based stress reduction program, based on prior research on mindfulness intervention. The MBCC was developed for the purpose of this study." (Intervention, MBCC Group)
studies.intervention_delivery: In-person delivery. Session 1 was individual (one-on-one with facilitator, 90 min). Sessions 2 and 3 were group-based (2 hours and 90 min respectively). Facilitators were trained male program facilitators — postbaccalaureate research assistants or graduate students in clinical psychology doctoral programs. Sessions conducted at the psychology training clinic at a local university. "All the sessions were conducted by a trained male program facilitator. One facilitator administered session 1, and sessions 2 and 3 were administered by a 2-person team." (Intervention, Facilitators)
studies.digital_component_raw: No digital component. The intervention was delivered in-person. A web-based survey was used for follow-up data collection, and DatStat Illume software was used to generate personalized normative feedback printouts for the SAFE arm, but these are data collection/preparation tools, not digital delivery of the MBCC intervention itself. "Assessment and intervention sessions were completed in private individual or group interview rooms within the psychology training clinic at a local university." (Ethical Considerations)
studies.intervention_tailor: No tailoring reported for the MBCC. The MBCC was developed specifically for this study as a control condition matched to SAFE in dose and format, but no cultural or population-specific tailoring is described. "The MBCC was developed for the purpose of this study." (Intervention, MBCC Group)
studies.comparison: The SAFE (Sexual Assault and Alcohol Feedback and Education) program is the active comparator to the MBCC. SAFE is a 3-session integrated alcohol and sexual assault prevention program grounded in social norms theory, bystander intervention, and motivational interviewing. Session 1 (90 min, individual): brief motivational intervention with personalized normative feedback (PNF) addressing alcohol use, sexual behaviors, alcohol-related sexual consequences, consent, and bystander intervention, using MI techniques. Session 2 (2 hours, group-based workshop): discusses frequency of alcohol use, sexual activity, and sexual assault on campus; sexual consent; false accusations; bystander intervention; data to dispel misperceptions. Session 3 (90 min, group-based booster, 2 months after session 1): continues discussion of sexual assault on campus and small group bystander intervention practice. "The SAFE intervention is a multisession program that uses MI and the social norms approach." (Intervention, The SAFE Program)
studies.assessment_time: T0 = Baseline (0 weeks); T1 = Post-session 1 (same day as baseline, proximal outcomes only); T2 = 2-month follow-up (approximately 8.4 weeks); T3 = 6-month follow-up (approximately 25.2 weeks). "The primary outcomes of alcohol use and sexual aggression were evaluated at 2 and 6 months after baseline." (Abstract, Methods). Conversion: 2 months = 8.4 weeks; 6 months = 25.2 weeks.
studies.assessment_nature: Mixed: self-report questionnaires (majority of measures), interviewer-administered measures (Timeline Follow Back for alcohol use), and external rater assessments (fidelity checklists, MITI ratings of session recordings). "Some measures were administered by a trained male interviewer, and other measures were self-administered." (Study Procedures, paragraph 1). "An outside rater assessed the fidelity to the program protocol using adherence checklists." (Measures, Research Question 3)
studies.outcomes_all: PRIMARY OUTCOMES: (1) Alcohol use — Timeline Follow Back (number of standard drinks per day over past 4 weeks; derived: average drinks/week, number of heavy drinking days in past month); (2) Protective behavioral strategies — Self-Control Questionnaire (37 items, 1–5 scale); (3) Sexual aggression — Sexual Experiences Survey-Short Form Perpetration (frequency and severity score 0–63). SECONDARY OUTCOMES — Peer norms: (4) Peer drinking norms — Drinking Norms Rating Form (perceived weekly alcohol consumption of peers); (5) Perceived peer engagement in sexual coercion — Sexual Social Norms Inventory subscale; (6) Perceived peer comfort with sexism — Sexual Social Norms Inventory subscale; (7) Perceived peer engagement in bystander intervention — 20-item scale (1–5). Risk factors for sexual aggression: (8) Rape myth acceptance — Illinois Rape Myth Acceptance Scale short form (20 items, 1–7); (9) Hypergender ideology — Hypergender Ideology Scale short form (19 items, 1–6); (10) Labeling of sexual consent — scenario-based measure (1–10). Bystander intervention: (11) Bystander intervention intentions — Bystander Attitudes Scale (51 items, 1–5); (12) Confidence to help friends — Brief Intent to Help Friends scale (10 items, 0–100); (13) Confidence to help strangers — Intent to Help Strangers scale (8 items, 0–100). PROXIMAL SESSION 1 OUTCOMES: (14) Motivation to change drinking — Contemplation Ladder (single item, 0–10); (15) Self-efficacy for reducing drinking — Brief Situational Confidence Questionnaire (single item, 0–100%); (16) Drinking intentions — weekly calendar (total intended drinks/week). FEASIBILITY/PROCESS: (17) Program attendance/completion rates; (18) Retention rates; (19) Fidelity — adherence checklists; (20) Competency — MITI 4.2 global ratings; (21) Satisfaction — Client Satisfaction Questionnaire-8 (CSQ-8, 8 items, 1–4); (22) Perceived utility — 10-item adapted scale (1–3); (23) Facilitator competency — 9-item nonjudgmental style scale (1–4).
studies.outcomes_primary: Primary outcomes are alcohol use and sexual aggression. "The primary outcomes of alcohol use and sexual aggression were evaluated at 2 and 6 months after baseline." (Abstract, Methods). Also stated: "For exploratory analyses of group differences in primary and secondary outcomes... we examined whether SAFE varied from MBCC in the primary target outcomes of alcohol use and sexual aggression." (Secondary Research Questions, paragraph 2)
studies.outcome_timepoints: T0 = Baseline (0 weeks): all primary, secondary, and proximal outcomes assessed; T1 = Immediately post-session 1 (0 weeks, same day): proximal outcomes only (motivation to change, self-efficacy, drinking intentions); T2 = 2-month follow-up (8.4 weeks): primary and secondary outcomes; T3 = 6-month follow-up (25.2 weeks): primary and secondary outcomes, plus exit interview satisfaction for SAFE subsample. "The primary outcomes of alcohol use and sexual aggression were evaluated at 2 and 6 months after baseline." (Abstract, Methods)
studies.recruitment: Men were recruited via a list from the university registrar of all men aged 18–22 currently enrolled. A random sample of 10,500 students received an email with a link to a confidential web-based screening portal. The study was described as addressing alcohol consumption and dating among college men. 496 men completed web-based screening; 238 (48%) met inclusion criteria; 121 (50.8%) presented for in-person screening; 115 enrolled. Recruitment dates not reported. "Men were recruited for the study using a list from the university registrar of all men currently enrolled at the university aged between 18 and 22 years... A random sample of 10,500 students received an email with a link to a confidential web-based study screening portal." (Recruitment and Screening Procedures, paragraph 1)
studies.study_purpose: "The purpose of this study was to conduct a pilot randomized evaluation of the SAFE program to assess the preliminary feasibility and acceptance of the program among college men who engage in heavy drinking and to examine preliminary program outcomes in comparison with an active attention- and dose-matched control group." (Purpose of This Study, paragraph 1)
studies.study_design: Randomized pilot trial (2-arm). "115 college men who engaged in heavy drinking, who were randomly assigned to the SAFE program or a mindfulness-based control condition (MBCC)." Randomization method not described in detail. Allocation ratio approximately 1:1 (SAFE n=58, MBCC n=57). No blinding reported. "The aims and methodology of this study align with those of a stage 1B intervention development study." (Purpose of This Study, paragraph 2)
studies.treatment_vs_prevention: Prevention — participants are heavy-drinking college men without a formal psychiatric diagnosis at enrollment (behavioral criterion only: ≥2 binge drinking episodes/month), and the study measures sexual aggression perpetration and alcohol use as study endpoints. The program aims to prevent sexual aggression and reduce alcohol use in a high-risk but non-diagnosed sample. "The purpose of this study was to conduct a pilot randomized evaluation of the SAFE program to assess the preliminary feasibility and acceptance of the program among college men who engage in heavy drinking." (Purpose of This Study, paragraph 1)

studies.authors: Pan, W.-L., Gau, M.-L., Lee, T.-Y., Jou, H.-J., Liu, C.-Y., & Wen, T.-K.
studies.title: Mindfulness-based programme on the psychological health of pregnant women
studies.abstract:
Problem: Preparation of psychological well-being is an important component of antenatal education for childbirth, but few courses focus on this component.
Background: The psychosocial health of pregnant women is known to affect perinatal outcomes. Psychosocial stress in women has been associated with increased obstetric interventions and has been shown to affect the health of both mother and child.
Aim: To explore the efficacy of an eight-week Mindfulness-Based Childbirth and Parenting programme on reducing prenatal stress, depression, mindfulness, and childbirth self-efficacy.
Methods: In this prospective and randomized controlled trial study, 104 women between 13 and 28 weeks gestation were enrolled and assigned randomly into two groups. Participants in the experimental group received mindfulness-based programme and practice-at-home with audio recordings. The comparison group received traditional education classes. Psychological health was assessed at baseline, post-intervention, and 36-week gestation.
Findings: Significant differences were seen in both groups in terms of changes over time in stress, depression, childbirth self-efficacy, and mindfulness, as compared with baseline. In gestation week 36, stress scores were slightly higher and childbirth self-efficacy and mindfulness scores were lower for both groups, but all scores were relatively better in the experimental than in the comparison group.
Conclusions: Perinatal mental health problems affect mothers, their infants, and society. The eight-week mindfulness programme effectively reduced self-perceived stress and depression and increased childbirth self-efficacy and mindfulness. Future research is needed to explore the potential benefits, mechanisms, and effects on maternal and infant birth outcomes of mindfulness.
studies.total_n: 104. 'A total of 104 women were included in the present study' (Methods, Participants, paragraph 2). Note: Table 2 reports n=96 completers (intervention n=51, comparison n=45); 8 lost to follow-up.
studies.age_mean: 32.83 (full sample; Table 2: 'Age (M ± SD) 32.83 ± 3.83')
studies.age_describe: Full sample mean age: 32.83 ± 3.83 years. Intervention group: 32.65 ± 3.78; Comparison group: 33.04 ± 3.91. (Table 2, Characteristics of participants)
studies.age_min: 20. 'were at least 20 years old' (Methods, Participants, paragraph 1)
studies.participants: Pregnant women at 13–28 weeks gestation with singleton pregnancies, recruited from a regional hospital in northern Taiwan. 'A total of 104 women were included in the present study.' Predominantly married (95.8%), university-educated (87.5%), employed (19.8% employed, 79.2% unemployed). Mean gestational age 20.99 ± 4.96 weeks. (Table 2, Methods, Participants)
studies.eligibility: Inclusion criteria: 'visited an obstetrician at the target hospital during the recruitment period, could communicate sufficiently in Chinese, were at 13–28 weeks gestation with a singleton pregnancy, and were at least 20 years old.' Also required to 'express willingness to give vaginal birth and to attend childbirth education programmes.' Exclusion criteria: 'Pregnant women were excluded who had a diagnosed psychosis or if they or their foetuses had any medical complications.' (Methods, Participants, paragraph 1)
studies.population_vulnerable: Not a vulnerable population — participants are pregnant women from a regional hospital in Taiwan with no specific health disparity or structural disadvantage criterion. 'A total of 104 women were included in the present study' (Methods, Participants, paragraph 2). The sample is predominantly married, educated, and not identified as a disadvantaged group.
studies.location: Regional hospital in northern Taiwan. 'The research was performed from February 2016 to May 2017 at a regional hospital in northern Taiwan' (Methods, Design and data collection, paragraph 1). Acknowledgements identify Taiwan Adventist Hospital as the recruitment site.
studies.mental_health: N/A — no psychiatric enrollment criterion. Participants were not required to meet a psychiatric diagnosis or symptom threshold. Psychosis was an exclusion criterion. (Methods, Participants, paragraph 1)
studies.physical_health: Pregnancy required for enrollment. 'were at 13–28 weeks gestation with a singleton pregnancy' (Methods, Participants, paragraph 1). Willingness to give vaginal birth also required.
studies.arms: Two arms. 1) Experimental group: MBCP programme (n=51 completers); 2) Comparison group: conventional childbirth education (n=45 completers). 'The participants were assigned to the experimental and comparison groups using random allocation software' (Methods, Design and data collection, paragraph 2).
studies.meditation_intervention: The experimental group participated in an MBCP (Mindfulness-Based Childbirth and Parenting) programme. 'The experimental group participated in an MBCP programme that was designed by Nancy Bardack. This programme, based on MBSR, uses the transformative experience of pregnancy, childbirth, and postpartum-related adjustments in self-awareness training.' The curriculum was adapted from the original MBCP using the Veringa et al. time course: 8 weekly 3-hour classes (combining original weeks 1 and 2 into one week) plus one 7-hour silent retreat day. Content included eating meditation, breathing meditation, body scan, mindful movement/yoga, sitting meditation, pain meditations using ice, loving-kindness meditation, psychoeducation on newborn needs, and breastfeeding mindfulness. Participants also required to listen to audio recordings at home 6 times per week for 30 minutes each. Facilitator was the principal investigator, trained by the International Childbirth Education Association, trained in MBSR by Jon Kabat-Zinn, received professional MBCP training from Nancy Bardack, and taught yoga to pregnant women. (Methods, Intervention, paragraphs 1–3; Table 1)
studies.intervention_delivery: In-person group format. Eight weekly 3-hour classes plus one 7-hour silent retreat day. 'The course was conducted entirely by the principal investigator of the present study, who was trained in Taiwan by the International Childbirth Education Association and was trained on the MBSR programme designed by Jon Kabat-Zinn.' Home practice via audio recordings (6 times/week, 30 min each). (Methods, Intervention, paragraphs 2–3)
studies.digital_component_raw: No digital component. Participants were required to listen to programme-related audio recordings at home six times a week for 30 min each. 'the participants are required to listen to programme-related audio recordings at home six times a week for 30 min each' (Methods, Intervention, paragraph 2). Audio recordings are analog/CD-type home practice materials, not digital delivery of the intervention.
studies.intervention_tailor: Yes — the MBCP programme was adapted from the original 9-week format. 'this curriculum was designed using the MBCP time course outlined by Veringa et al., which combines the first- and second-week courses of the original MBCP into one week, sets the time for each class at three hours, and holds one seven-hour silent retreat.' This condensed the programme from 9 to 8 weeks to reduce attrition. (Methods, Intervention, paragraph 2)
studies.comparison: Conventional childbirth education. 'The participants in the comparison group were given conventional childbirth education at the research hospital. The comparison group course taught pregnancy-related physiological and psychological information and self-care skills during pregnancy and after childbirth. The course was provided for a total of two times over a two-month period.' Standard medical care was provided to both groups by physicians and nurses. (Methods, Intervention, paragraph 3)
studies.assessment_time: T0 = Baseline (0 weeks); T1 = Post-intervention (approximately 8 weeks after baseline); T2 = 36 weeks gestation (timing relative to baseline varies by participant gestational age at enrollment, approximately 8–23 weeks after baseline depending on enrollment gestational age). 'The following validated self-report measures were administered before (T0) and after (T1) the intervention, as well as during the follow-up at 36 weeks gestation (T2).' (Methods, Measures, paragraph 1). Note: exact weeks from baseline to T2 not explicitly stated; 36-week gestation is the fixed timepoint.
studies.assessment_nature: Self-report only. 'The following validated self-report measures were administered before (T0) and after (T1) the intervention, as well as during the follow-up at 36 weeks gestation (T2).' All four instruments (PSS, EPDS, CBSEI-C32, FFMQ) are self-report questionnaires. (Methods, Measures, paragraph 1)
studies.outcomes_all:
1. Perceived stress — Perceived Stress Scale (PSS; 10 items, 0–4 response scale, higher = more stress) (Methods, Measures, 2.4.1)
2. Depression — Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS; 10 items, 0–3 per item, cut-off >13 for depression) (Methods, Measures, 2.4.2)
3. Childbirth self-efficacy — Chinese Childbirth Self-Efficacy Inventory short form (CBSEI-C32; two subscales: Outcome Expectancy OE-16 and Efficacy Expectancy EE-16, 1–10 scale) (Methods, Measures, 2.4.3)
4. Mindfulness — Five Facet Mindfulness Questionnaire (FFMQ; 39 items, 5 facets: observing, describing, acting with awareness, non-judging, non-reactivity; 1–5 Likert scale) (Methods, Measures, 2.4.4)
studies.outcomes_primary: Unclear — authors do not explicitly designate a single primary outcome. The aim states: 'To explore the efficacy of an eight-week Mindfulness-Based Childbirth and Parenting programme on reducing prenatal stress, depression, mindfulness, and childbirth self-efficacy.' All four outcomes appear co-primary. (Abstract, Aim)
studies.outcome_timepoints: T0 = Baseline (0 weeks); T1 = Post-intervention (~8 weeks); T2 = 36 weeks gestation (variable weeks from baseline depending on enrollment gestational age). All four outcomes (PSS, EPDS, CBSEI-C32, FFMQ) assessed at all three timepoints. 'The following validated self-report measures were administered before (T0) and after (T1) the intervention, as well as during the follow-up at 36 weeks gestation (T2).' (Methods, Measures, paragraph 1)
studies.recruitment: Participants were recruited from a regional hospital in northern Taiwan. 'Eligibility for the present study included all pregnant women who: visited an obstetrician at the target hospital during the recruitment period.' Recruitment period: February 2016 to May 2017. 'A total of 134 participants were interviewed. The data of 30 of these were excluded from further analysis afterward due to unwillingness to participate.' (Methods, Design and data collection; Results, paragraph 1)
studies.study_purpose: 'To explore the efficacy of an eight-week Mindfulness-Based Childbirth and Parenting programme on reducing prenatal stress, depression, mindfulness, and childbirth self-efficacy.' (Abstract, Aim)
studies.study_design: Prospective randomized controlled trial with parallel design. 'This randomized controlled trial and parallel design study.' Random allocation using software with block sizes of 6, 8, and 12 in a 1:1 ratio. Single-blind (RAs blinded to group assignment). 'allocations were blinded to the researchers... the research administrators (RAs) who recruited the participants remained blinded to participant group assignments throughout the trial period.' (Methods, Design and data collection, paragraphs 1–2)
studies.treatment_vs_prevention: Prevention — participants are pregnant women without a required psychiatric diagnosis or symptom threshold at enrollment (psychosis was an exclusion criterion). The study measures stress, depression, mindfulness, and childbirth self-efficacy as endpoints. Both conditions are met: (a) no diagnosis/threshold required at enrollment, and (b) condition-related outcomes (stress, depression) are measured. 'Preventive MBCP interventions were provided to pregnant women with the objective of alleviating their psychological problems' (Introduction, final paragraph). Source quote + citation: (Introduction, paragraph 7)
studies.confidence_why:
• total_n — 104 randomized per abstract/methods, but Table 2 reports n=96 completers; the randomized N is used per extraction rules but the discrepancy is flagged.
• age_max — not explicitly reported; only minimum age (20 years) stated in eligibility.
• assessment_time — T2 is defined as '36 weeks gestation' rather than a fixed number of weeks post-baseline; exact weeks from baseline to T2 varies by participant enrollment gestational age (13–28 weeks), so cannot be precisely converted to weeks from baseline without individual-level data.
• time_baseline_to_post — inferred as approximately 8 weeks based on the 8-week programme duration, not explicitly stated as weeks from baseline.
• treatment_vs_prevention — classified as Prevention based on no psychiatric threshold at enrollment and condition-related outcomes measured; some interpretation required as the paper describes 'preventive' intent but participants are already pregnant and experiencing some stress.
studies.active_comparator_name: Conventional childbirth education — two sessions over two months covering pregnancy-related physiological and psychological information and self-care skills (Methods, Intervention, paragraph 3). Human review needed.
studies.outcomes_coded: Stress-distress | Depression | Mindfulness trait-state | Self-efficacy-confidence | Pregnancy-perinatal
studies.categories_flags:
• adaptation_type — human adjudication required; coded as Condensed-abbreviated (9→8 weeks by merging weeks 1–2) and Population-specific content (pregnancy/childbirth-specific content); cultural adaptation not explicitly described.
• active_comparator_name — human review needed; comparator is conventional childbirth education (2 sessions over 2 months), not a named psychological intervention.
• followup_longest — T2 is defined as 36 weeks gestation rather than a fixed number of weeks post-baseline; cannot be precisely converted without individual enrollment gestational age data.
• dose_sessions — coded as 9 (8 weekly classes + 1 retreat day); paper describes 8 weekly classes plus one 7-hour retreat, totaling 9 sessions.

studies.authors: Panjwani, U., Gupta, H. L., Singh, S. H., Selvamurthy, W., & Rai, U. C.
studies.title: EFFECT OF SAHAJA YOGA PRACTICE ON STRESS MANAGEMENT IN PATIENTS OF EPILEPSY
studies.abstract: An attempt was made to evaluate the effect of Sahaja yoga meditation in stress management in patients of epilepsy. The study was carried out on 32 patients of epilepsy who were randomly divided into 3 groups: group I subjects practised Sahaja yoga meditation for 6 months, group II subjects practised postural exercises mimicking Sahaja yoga and group III served as the epileptic control group. Galvanic skin resistance (GSR), blood lactate and urinary vinyl mandelic acid (U-VMA) were recorded at 0, 3 and 6 months. There were significant changes at 3 & 6 months as compared to 0 month values in GSR, blood lactate and U-VMA levels in group I subjects, but not in group II and group III subjects. The results indicate that reduction in stress following Sahaja yoga practice may be responsible for clinical improvement which had been earlier reported in patients who practised Sahaja yoga.
studies.journal: Indian Journal of Physiology and Pharmacology
studies.total_n: 32. 'The study was carried out on 32 patients of epilepsy who were randomly divided into 3 groups' (Abstract). Group I n=10, Group II n=10, Group III n=12 (Methods, Subjects).
studies.age_describe: Mean (SE) age 22.5 (1.18) years for the full sample. Group I: 24.6±2.1 years; Group II: 23.7±2.5 years; Group III: 19.7±1.4 years. 'Thirty female and 2 male epileptics in the age group of 15-35 years, mean (SE) age 22.5 (1.18) years were studied.' (Methods, Subjects, paragraph 1).
studies.age_min: 15. 'in the age group of 15-35 years' (Methods, Subjects, paragraph 1).
studies.age_max: 35. 'in the age group of 15-35 years' (Methods, Subjects, paragraph 1).
studies.participants: 32 epileptic patients (30 female, 2 male), age 15-35 years, with primary idiopathic epilepsy, attending the Neurology Clinic, Lady Hardinge Medical College and Smt. S.K. Hospital. 'Thirty female and 2 male epileptics in the age group of 15-35 years, mean (SE) age 22.5 (1.18) years were studied.' (Methods, Subjects, paragraph 1).
studies.eligibility: Inclusion criteria: '(i) patients clinically diagnosed as having primary idiopathic epilepsy (clinical seizure; CT scans or MRI did not reveal any abnormality), (ii) greater than four seizures in 3 months and (iii) awareness of every seizure episode by self or family member.' Exclusion criteria: Not explicitly reported. (Methods, Subjects, paragraph 1).
studies.population_vulnerable: Not a vulnerable population — participants are epilepsy patients but no specific health disparity or structural disadvantage criterion is described. 'The subjects were epileptics attending the Neurology Clinic, Lady Hardinge Medical College and Smt. S.K. Hospital.' (Methods, Subjects, paragraph 1).
studies.location: Delhi/New Delhi, India. 'Defence Institute of Physiology and Allied Sciences, Delhi - 110 054 and Lady Hardinge Medical College and Smt. S. K. Hospital, New Delhi - 110 001' (Title page, author affiliations).
studies.mental_health: N/A — no psychiatric enrollment criterion. Epilepsy is the enrollment condition; stress is measured as an outcome, not an enrollment criterion.
studies.physical_health: Primary idiopathic epilepsy with greater than four seizures in 3 months required for enrollment. 'patients clinically diagnosed as having primary idiopathic epilepsy (clinical seizure; CT scans or MRI did not reveal any abnormality), (ii) greater than four seizures in 3 months' (Methods, Subjects, paragraph 1).
studies.arms: 3 arms. Group I (n=10): Sahaja yoga meditation for 6 months; Group II (n=10): mimicking exercises (postural exercises mimicking Sahaja yoga) for 6 months; Group III (n=12): epileptic control group (no intervention). 'group I subjects practised Sahaja yoga meditation for 6 months, group II subjects practised postural exercises mimicking Sahaja yoga and group III served as the epileptic control group.' (Abstract).
studies.meditation_intervention: Sahaja yoga meditation. Participants practised twice daily for 20-30 minutes under the guidance of a trained 'Sahaja Yogi' or instructor for 6 months. Sessions involved sitting in silent meditation with feet dipped in warm saline water. A typical session consisted of 'questions and assertions by the subject. Thereafter the subject practised silent meditation. If a thought came to the mind, she/he was instructed to simply witness the thought but not to flow deeper into it.' Subjects gradually reported a state of 'thoughtless awareness'. Participants reported to the Department of Physiology on all working days for the first month and thereafter twice a week for the remaining period. 'The patients in group I practised Sahaja yoga twice daily for 20-30 minutes under the guidance of a trained Sahaja Yogi or instructor.' (Methods, Practice programmes).
studies.intervention_delivery: In-person group/supervised. Sessions conducted at the Department of Physiology and in a room in the Medical Out Patient Department. Delivered by a trained 'Sahaja Yogi' or instructor. 'They reported to the Department of Physiology on all working days for the first month and thereafter twice a week for the remaining period.' Session length: 20-30 minutes. (Methods, Practice programmes).
studies.digital_component_raw: No digital component. No technology used to deliver the intervention. Home practice involved sitting meditation with feet in warm saline water; no digital tools mentioned. (Methods, Practice programmes).
studies.intervention_tailor: No tailoring reported. The intervention is described as standard Sahaja yoga practice as described in a referenced source (Her Holiness Mataji Shri Nirmala Devi, 1979), with no population-specific adaptations noted.
studies.comparison: Group II (n=10): Mimicking exercises — subjects 'were provided with the same environment and attention as group I subjects. However, actual meditation was not practised by these subjects. The subjects were instructed to simply place their hand at different positions as during Sahaja yoga practice and thereafter sit quietly with their eyes closed.' Duration: 6 months. Group III (n=12): Epileptic control group — 'did not practise Sahaja yoga or mimicking but served as controls.' No specific activities described. (Methods, Practice programmes).
studies.assessment_time: T0 = Baseline (0 weeks); T1 = 3 months (approximately 12.6 weeks); T2 = 6 months (approximately 25.2 weeks). 'GSR, blood lactate and urinary vinyl mandelic acid (U-VMA) were recorded at 0, 3 and 6 months.' (Abstract).
studies.assessment_nature: Physiological and biological measures only. Galvanic skin resistance (GSR) — physiological measure; blood lactate — biological sample; urinary VMA — biological sample. No self-report questionnaires reported. 'Galvanic skin resistance (GSR), blood lactate and urinary vinyl mandelic acid (U-VMA) were recorded at 0, 3 and 6 months.' (Abstract).
studies.outcomes_all: 1. Galvanic Skin Resistance (GSR) — measured using Biotrainer model GBF-102R, units x100 Kohms (physiological measure of sympathetic activity/stress). 2. Blood lactate levels — measured using YSI model 23-L Lactate Analyser, units mmol/L (biochemical marker of stress/relaxation). 3. Urinary vinyl mandelic acid (U-VMA) — estimated by Pisano et al. method, units mg/day (catecholamine metabolite, marker of sympathoadrenal activity/stress). (Methods, GSR; Blood lactate; U-VMA sections).
studies.outcomes_primary: Unclear — authors do not explicitly designate a primary outcome. All three measures (GSR, blood lactate, U-VMA) appear to be co-equal outcomes. 'Galvanic skin resistance (GSR), blood lactate and urinary vinyl mandelic acid (U-VMA) were recorded at 0, 3 and 6 months.' (Abstract).
studies.outcome_timepoints: T0 = Baseline (0 weeks); T1 = 3 months (approximately 12.6 weeks); T2 = 6 months (approximately 25.2 weeks). All three outcomes (GSR, blood lactate, U-VMA) assessed at all three timepoints. 'GSR, blood lactate and urinary vinyl mandelic acid (U-VMA) were recorded at 0, 3 and 6 months.' (Abstract).
studies.recruitment: Participants were epileptics attending the Neurology Clinic, Lady Hardinge Medical College and Smt. S.K. Hospital. 'The subjects were epileptics attending the Neurology Clinic, Lady Hardinge Medical College and Smt. S.K. Hospital. An informed, written consent was obtained from each subject prior to enrolment in the study.' Recruitment dates not reported. (Methods, Subjects, paragraph 1).
studies.study_purpose: To evaluate the effect of Sahaja yoga meditation in stress management in patients of epilepsy. 'An attempt was made to evaluate the effect of Sahaja yoga meditation in stress management in patients of epilepsy.' (Abstract). More specifically, 'we investigated the effect of Sahaja yoga practice on Galvanic Skin Resistance (GSR), Blood lactate of levels, parameters of levels of tension or relaxation in order to study whether reduction in the level of stress is responsible for clinical improvement in epileptics following Sahaja yoga practice.' studies.authors: Parker, J. C., Gilbert, G. S., & Thoreson, R. W.
studies.title: Anxiety management in alcoholics: A study of generalized effects of relaxation techniques
studies.abstract: In order to investigate the effects of progressive relaxation training (Bernstein & Borkovec, 1973) and meditation training (Beary & Benson, 1974) on generalized arousal in alcoholics, 30 subjects were selected from an inpatient alcohol treatment unit of a Veterans Administration hospital. The subjects were appropriately screened and randomly assigned to one of the following groups: (a) progressive relaxation training (PRT); (b) meditation training (MT); or (c) quiet rest control group (QR). The groups met 3 times per week for a total of 3 weeks. The measures of arousal employed in this study were state anxiety (Speilberger, Gorsuch & Lushene, 1970). systolic and diastolic blood pressure, heart rate. and spontaneous GSR. These measures of generalized arousal were collected once each week at a specified time for all subjects. The results revealed generalized effects for blood pressure, but not for the other dependent measures. In addition, the PRT and MT groups did not exhibit increased blood pressure as observed in control subjects. The potential contribution of these techniques to the treatment of alcoholism is discussed.

studies.authors: Pots, W. T. M., Meulenbeek, P. A. M., Veehof, M. M., Klungers, J., & Bohlmeijer, E. T.
studies.title: The Efficacy of Mindfulness-Based Cognitive Therapy as a Public Mental Health Intervention for Adults with Mild to Moderate Depressive Symptomatology: A Randomized Controlled Trial
studies.abstract:
Objective: Although there has been growing evidence for the efficacy of mindfulness-based cognitive therapy (MBCT) for different clinical populations, its effectiveness as a public mental health intervention has not been studied. The present study evaluates a community-based MBCT intervention for adults with mild to moderate depressive symptomatology in a large multi-site, pragmatic randomized controlled trial.
Method: The participants with mild to moderate depressive symptomatology were recruited from the general population and randomized to the MBCT intervention (n = 76) or to a waiting list control group (n = 75). Participants completed measures before and after the intervention. Participants in the experimental condition also completed these measures at a 3-month follow-up.
Results: In the experimental condition significant reductions in depression, anxiety, and experiential avoidance, and improvements in mindfulness and emotional- and psychological mental health were found, compared to the waiting list (effect sizes Cohen's d = 0.31–0.56). These effects were sustained at the 3-month follow-up. The likelihood of a clinically significant change in depressive symptoms was significantly higher for the MBCT group [odds ratio (OR) 3.026, p ,0.01 at post-treatment; NNT = 5.10].
Discussion: MBCT as a public mental health intervention for adults with mild to moderate depressive symptoms seems effective and applicable in a natural setting.
Trial Registration: Nederlands Trial Register NTR2096
studies.total_n: 151. "the included 151 participants were randomly assigned to the MBCT intervention (n = 76) and the waiting list condition (n = 75)" (Results, Enrollment, paragraph 1)
studies.age_describe: Mean age 47.93 (SD = 11.29, range 20–81) for total sample; MBCT group: M = 47.99 (SD = 10.59), range 24–74; Waiting list: M = 47.88 (SD = 12.02), range 20–81. "Participants had a mean age of 48 years (SD = 11.29, range 20–81)" (Results, Baseline characteristics, paragraph 1; Table 1)
studies.participants: Adults with mild to moderate depressive symptomatology recruited from the general population via community mental health centers. Predominantly female (78.1%), majority Dutch origin (96%), majority living with partner (75.5%), majority with paid job (66.9%), high education level (65.5%). "Participants had a mean age of 48 years (SD = 11.29, range 20–81) and were predominantly female (78.1%). The majority was of Dutch origin (96%), had a paid job (66.9%), and were living with a partner (75.5%)." (Results, Baseline characteristics, paragraph 1; Table 1)
studies.eligibility: Inclusion criteria: 'adults of 18 years and over, presenting depressive symptoms.' Exclusion criteria: 'diagnosed with a current severe major depressive episode (MDE; eight or nine out of a total of nine symptoms) or when having a moderate to high suicide risk, according to the Dutch version of the Mini International Neuropsychiatric Interview (MINI)'; 'receiving psychological or pharmacological treatment for mental complaints within the last three months'; 'presence of other severe mental or social problems warranting treatment or likely to interfere with participation in the group course.' (Methods, Participants and procedure, paragraph 1)
studies.population_vulnerable: Not a vulnerable population — participants are general community-dwelling adults with mild to moderate depressive symptoms, recruited from the general population in the Netherlands. No specific health disparity or structural disadvantage criterion is reported. (Methods, Participants and procedure)
studies.location: Netherlands; four community mental health centers from both urban and rural areas. "Four Dutch community mental health centers, from both urban and rural areas, participated in the study." (Methods, Participants and procedure, paragraph 1)
studies.mental_health: Mild to moderate depressive symptomatology required for enrollment. "The inclusion criteria were: adults of 18 years and over, presenting depressive symptoms." Exclusion if severe MDE (8 or 9 of 9 symptoms on MINI). (Methods, Participants and procedure, paragraph 1)
studies.physical_health: N/A — no physical health enrollment criterion
studies.arms: 2 arms. Arm 1: MBCT intervention (n = 76); Arm 2: Waiting list control (n = 75). "participants were randomly assigned...either to MBCT or to the waiting list control" (Methods, Design, paragraph 1)
studies.meditation_intervention: MBCT (Mindfulness-Based Cognitive Therapy) adapted as a public mental health intervention, delivered according to guidelines of Segal et al. (2002). Adapted from original MBCT: sessions reduced from 2.5 hours to 1.5 hours; daily home practice reduced from 45 minutes to 15 minutes; sessions extended from 8 to 11 sessions to preserve all original elements. Key themes: awareness (sessions 1, 2, 3), acceptance (sessions 5, 7, 9, 10), disengaging from thoughts (sessions 4, 6, 8), evaluation/integration (session 11). Daily homework exercises including guided and unguided meditations, homework registration forms, and information booklet. Group sizes 8–15 participants. "the eight-session training was extended to 11 sessions...participants were asked to practice meditations for 15 minutes a day instead of the original 45 minutes a day, and the sessions were limited to 1,5 hours instead of the original 2,5 hours." (Methods, Intervention)
studies.intervention_delivery: In-person group format, 11 sessions of 1.5 hours each, over approximately 11 weeks. Delivered at community mental health centers. Facilitators were experienced psychologists and mental health nurses with extensive training in original MBCT protocol and group psychotherapy, and meditation experience ranging from 2 to 15 years. "The MBCT instructors were all experienced psychologists and mental health nurses, with extensive former training in the original MBCT protocol by Segal [9] and Group psychotherapy. The trainers were also experienced meditators, with meditation experience ranging from 2 to 15 years." (Methods, Therapists)
studies.digital_component_raw: No digital component. Participants received guided (taped) and unguided meditations, homework registration forms, and information booklets as analog materials. "participants received weekly homework registration forms, guided (taped) and unguided meditations, and information in a booklet." (Methods, Intervention)
studies.intervention_tailor: Yes — adapted from original MBCT for a public mental health/community population. Session length reduced from 2.5 to 1.5 hours; daily home practice reduced from 45 to 15 minutes; number of sessions extended from 8 to 11 to preserve all original content. "In order to lower the threshold for people without severe distress to participate in MBCT, the participants were asked to practice meditations for 15 minutes a day instead of the original 45 minutes a day, and the sessions were limited to 1,5 hours instead of the original 2,5 hours." (Methods, Intervention)
studies.comparison: Waiting list control condition (n = 75). Participants waited approximately 3 months before receiving the MBCT intervention. "The control condition consisted of a waiting list, where wait-listed people were free to use other kinds of care. The wait-listed participants knew that they could start the training after the experimental condition had completed the intervention, i.e. after 3 months." (Methods, Design, paragraph 1; Methods, Waiting list control)
studies.assessment_time: T0 = Baseline (0 weeks); T1 = Post-treatment (approximately 12.6 weeks [3 months]); T2 = Follow-up for MBCT group / post-treatment for waiting list (approximately 25.2 weeks [6 months after baseline]). "Measurements were taken at baseline (T0), and at post-treatment after 3 months (T1). In order to study the stability of the effect of MBCT, the patients in the experimental group received a follow-up measurement (T2) at 6 months after baseline." (Methods, Measures, paragraph 1). Note: 1 month = 4.2 weeks; 3 months = 12.6 weeks; 6 months = 25.2 weeks.
studies.assessment_nature: Self-report questionnaires only. "All measures were self-report: no psychiatric diagnoses were available because participants were recruited from the general public." (Discussion, Limitations, paragraph 1). Screening used the MINI structured interview administered by mental health nurses.

"Participants were recruited from November 2009 until October 2010, through advertisements in regional newspapers, information booklets and general practitioners." (Methods, Participants and procedure, paragraph 1)

"The aim of this study was to evaluate the effect of mindfulness-based cognitive therapy modified as a public mental health intervention for depressive symptomatology" and "MBCT implemented as a public mental health intervention for adults with mild to moderate depressive symptomatology may decrease the risk of developing a MDE."
