studies.authors: Puente, A. E.
studies.title: Psychophysiological Investigations on Transcendental Meditation
studies.abstract: Two experiments were conducted to evaluate the psychophysiological changes reported to occur during the practice of transcendental meditation. In Experiment I, 47 volunteers solicited from the community were randomly assigned to transcendental meditation (TM), Benson's relaxation response (BRR), or no treatment (NT) instruction. Respiration rate, heart rate, electromyogram, electroencephalogram, and skin conductance level were recorded during the practice of each technique, approximately 1 week after terminating instruction. The results indicate that while BRR, TM, and NT exhibited different physiological patterns, none of the techniques showed a clear superiority in reducing tonic physiological arousal. In Experiment II, 30 volunteers with previous experience were assigned to one of three groups based on their meditating experience (range 16-96 months). The same physiological signals as in Experiment I were also recorded in this experiment during TM practice. The results suggest that individuals with 1.5 years of meditation experience exhibited physiological arousal levels similar to those seen in persons with over 5 years' experience.
studies.total_n: 77 (47 in Experiment I + 30 in Experiment II). "Forty-seven subjects...were chosen from the local community" (Experiment I, Method, Subjects); "Thirty subjects...participated in this experiment" (Experiment II, Method, Subjects). Note: these are two separate experiments reported in one paper.
studies.age_mean: 26.81 (Experiment I full sample mean age reported); Experiment II age not reported as a single mean.
studies.age_describe: Experiment I: mean age = 26.81 years overall; TM subgroup mean age = 27.29 years; BRR subgroup mean age = 26.55 years; NT subgroup mean age = 26.5 years. Experiment II: age not reported as mean. "Forty-seven subjects (males = 24, females = 23, mean age = 26.81 years)" (Experiment I, Method, Subjects). Experiment II age range implied by meditation experience range of 16-96 months but no age statistics given.
studies.participants: Experiment I: 47 community volunteers (24 males, 23 females, mean age 26.81 years) randomly assigned to TM, BRR, or NT. Experiment II: 30 experienced TM meditators (14 males, 16 females) recruited through a local TM center, grouped by meditation experience (range 16-96 months). "Forty-seven subjects (males = 24, females = 23, mean age = 26.81 years) were chosen from the local community in response to a call for volunteers in meditation study." (Experiment I, Method, Subjects); "Thirty subjects (males = 14, females = 16), recruited through the local TM center, participated in this experiment." (Experiment II, Method, Subjects)
studies.eligibility: Experiment I Inclusion: community volunteers responding to a call for participation in a meditation study. Exclusion: "Individuals having medical conditions currently being treated by a physician, possessing an estimated below-average intelligence, and/or exhibiting psychotic symptomatology were excluded." (Experiment I, Method, Subjects). Experiment II Inclusion: volunteers with previous TM experience recruited through local TM center; grouped by meditation experience score derived from Meditation Experience Questionnaire. No explicit exclusion criteria stated for Experiment II.
studies.population_vulnerable: Not a vulnerable population — participants were community volunteers and experienced meditators with no reported health disparities or structural disadvantage. "Forty-seven subjects...were chosen from the local community in response to a call for volunteers" (Experiment I, Method, Subjects).
studies.location: Inferred: Athens, Georgia, USA (inferred from author affiliation 'University of Georgia' and reference to 'University of Georgia Research Pool' — not explicitly stated as study location in paper body)
studies.mental_health: N/A — no psychiatric enrollment criterion. Psychotic symptomatology was an exclusion criterion, not an inclusion criterion.
studies.physical_health: N/A — no physical health enrollment criterion. Medical conditions currently being treated by a physician were an exclusion criterion, not an inclusion criterion.
studies.arms: Experiment I: 3 arms. (1) Transcendental Meditation (TM) — n=17 completers (originally 20); (2) Benson's Relaxation Response (BRR) — n=20; (3) No Treatment (NT) — n=10. Experiment II: 3 groups based on meditation experience level — Group 1 (low experience, n=16), Group 2 (moderate experience, n=6), Group 3 (high experience, n=8). "subjects were randomly assigned to one of the treatment conditions" (Experiment I, Method, Subjects); "Each subject was assigned to one of three different groups according to the Meditation Experience Questionnaire" (Experiment II, Method, Subjects).
studies.meditation_intervention: Experiment I TM arm: Training administered according to the methods of Maharishi Mahesh Yogi (1973). Six 1.5-hour sessions over 1 week. First two sessions: introduction to TM (structure, nature, universal appeal, requirements; principles, mechanics, tradition). Third session: ritual conducted mostly in Sanskrit culminating in participant receiving an individual mantra. Final three sessions: lecture and discussion of practical considerations, mechanics of stress reduction, and development of human potential through TM. Administered by a qualified TM teacher. Participants practiced twice daily (morning and early evening) for 1 week after instruction. Physiological recording occurred approximately 5-7 days after last instruction session during a 20-minute practice period. "Training in transcendental meditation (TM) was administered according to the methods of Maharishi Mahesh Yogi (1973). There were six 1.5-hour sessions over a period of 1 week." (Experiment I, Method, Procedure). Experiment II: Experienced TM meditators (range 16-96 months) practiced TM during the same physiological recording protocol.
studies.intervention_delivery: In-person, individual/group format not specified. Six 1.5-hour sessions over 1 week delivered by a qualified TM teacher. "Training in the technique was done by a qualified TM teacher." (Experiment I, Method, Procedure). Physiological recording conducted in a "sound-attenuating, electrically shielded chamber" (Experiment I, Method, Apparatus).
studies.digital_component_raw: No digital component. Physiological signals recorded on chart paper with a Grass Model 7 polygraph. No technology used to deliver the intervention. "All physiological variables were recorded on chart paper with a Grass Model 7 polygraph." (Experiment I, Method, Apparatus).
studies.intervention_tailor: No tailoring reported. TM was administered according to the standard methods of Maharishi Mahesh Yogi (1973) without reported modification.
studies.comparison: Experiment I: (1) Benson's Relaxation Response (BRR): Six 1.5-hour sessions over 1 week, same format as TM. Third session included a modified, simplified TM ritual; instead of a mantra, participants used the word 'one'. Same topics covered in final three sessions as TM. Administered by the same instructor as TM. n=20. (2) No Treatment (NT): No instruction of any kind administered. n=10. Subjects had opportunity to learn either technique after study completion. "Training for the other experimental condition was administered according to the method described by Benson (1975). There were six 1.5-hour sessions over a period of 1 week." (Experiment I, Method, Procedure). Experiment II: No comparison condition — three groups of experienced TM meditators differing only in meditation experience level.
studies.assessment_time: Experiment I: T0 = Baseline (0 weeks, recorded during 5-minute adaptation period immediately before technique practice); T1 = Post-instruction (~1-2 weeks, approximately 5-7 days after last instruction session). "subjects were tested 5-7 days after the last day of instruction" (Introduction, Experiment I factors). Experiment II: Single assessment timepoint during TM practice session; no pre-post design. Exact timing relative to enrollment not specified beyond recruitment.
studies.assessment_nature: Physiological measures (non-self-report): respiration rate, heart rate, electromyogram (EMG), electroencephalogram (EEG), skin conductance level (SCL) recorded via polygraph. Self-report: Post-Physiological Questionnaire (1-7 scale, 15 items), General Information Questionnaire, Intraversion-Extraversion Questionnaire (Social Reaction Inventory, Experiment II only). "Respiration rate, heart rate, electromyogram, electroencephalogram, and skin conductance level were recorded during the practice of each technique" (Abstract).
studies.outcomes_all: 1. Respiration Rate (RR) — peaks per minute, physiological measure; 2. Heart Rate (HR) — peaks per minute, physiological measure; 3. Electromyogram (EMG) — frontalis muscle, μVolts, physiological measure; 4. Electroencephalogram (EEG) — % time in alpha (8-13 CPS, 20-100 μVolts), physiological measure; 5. Skin Conductance Level (SCL) — μMHOS, physiological measure; 6. Post-Physiological Questionnaire — 15-item self-report (1-7 scale) assessing awareness of physiological changes, sleepiness, restlessness, ease/pleasantness of practice, mental/physical relaxation, alertness, representativeness of practice; 7. General Information Questionnaire — mantra use, social contacts, treatment expectations, continuation intentions; 8. Intraversion-Extraversion Questionnaire (Social Reaction Inventory) — Experiment II only. "Respiration rate, heart rate, electromyogram, electroencephalogram, and skin conductance level were recorded" (Abstract); "subjects were administered two short questionnaires" (Experiment I, Method, Procedure).
studies.outcomes_primary: Unclear — authors do not designate a primary outcome. The study evaluates multiple psychophysiological variables simultaneously. "Two experiments were conducted to evaluate the psychophysiological changes reported to occur during the practice of transcendental meditation." (Abstract).
studies.outcome_timepoints: Experiment I: T0 = Baseline (0 weeks, 5-minute pre-technique recording); T1 = During technique (~1-2 weeks post-instruction, 20-minute practice session approximately 5-7 days after last instruction). Experiment II: Single timepoint — during TM practice session. "subjects were tested 5-7 days after the last day of instruction" (Introduction, Experiment I factors).
studies.recruitment: Experiment I: Community volunteers recruited via a call for volunteers. "Forty-seven subjects...were chosen from the local community in response to a call for volunteers in meditation study." (Experiment I, Method, Subjects). Experiment II: Recruited through local TM center. "Thirty subjects...recruited through the local TM center, participated in this experiment." (Experiment II, Method, Subjects). No recruitment dates reported.
studies.study_purpose: "The purpose of this study was to attempt to resolve the disparity among these results by using both naive subjects randomly assigned to treatment conditions and experienced meditators." (Introduction, final paragraph).
studies.study_design: Experiment I: Randomized controlled experiment with three arms (TM, BRR, NT). "subjects were randomly assigned to a treatment group" (Introduction, Experiment I factors). Experiment II: Quasi-experimental, non-randomized grouping of experienced meditators by meditation experience level. No blinding reported for participants; instructor bias toward TM was detected and reported.
studies.treatment_vs_prevention: Enhancement — rationale: Participants were community volunteers with no reported diagnosis or symptom threshold at enrollment. The study tests psychophysiological effects of meditation techniques in a general community sample. No clinical condition was being treated or prevented; the focus is on physiological arousal and relaxation in healthy adults. "Forty-seven subjects...were chosen from the local community in response to a call for volunteers in meditation study." (Experiment I, Method, Subjects).

studies.authors: Qiu, Y., & Xu, H.
studies.title: Effects of WeChat-Based Mindfulness-Based Stress Reduction on Psychological Resilience and Quality of Life Among Patients Undergoing Loose Body Removal Surgery
studies.abstract:
Background • The knee joint, a structurally intricate component, is highly susceptible to injuries, profoundly impacting the afflicted patients' life quality. Among these injuries, loose body removal stands out, historically managed through conventional open surgical interventions. However, such procedures entail complications, including infection and extended recovery periods, fostering postoperative psychological distress like anxiety and depression.
Objective • This study aims to assess the impact of WeChat-based mindfulness-based stress reduction (MBSR) on psychological resilience and quality of life in patients undergoing loose body removal.
Methods • A cohort of 87 patients undergoing surgical treatment for loose body removal in our hospital between November 2018 and August 2019 was enlisted. They were randomly allocated to either receive routine postoperative nursing (control group) or participate in WeChat-based MBSR (observation group) using a random number table method. Assessment parameters encompassed anxiety, depression, mindfulness levels, quality of life, personality traits, and psychological resilience.
Results • After treatment, patients in the observation group exhibited significantly reduced levels of depression, anxiety, and heightened mindfulness compared to the control group (P < .05). Moreover, the observation group reported superior quality of life and personality traits compared to the control group (P < .05). Additionally, patients in the observation group demonstrated enhanced psychological resilience compared to the control group (P < .05).
Conclusions • WeChat-based MBSR emerges as a promising intervention, significantly alleviating depression and anxiety while enhancing the quality of life and psychological resilience in patients undergoing loose body removal surgery, suggesting its potential for widespread clinical application. (Altern Ther Health Med. [E-pub ahead of print.])
studies.journal: Alternative Therapies in Health and Medicine
studies.total_n: 87. "A total of 87 patients with loose body removal who underwent surgical treatment in our hospital from November 2018 to August 2019 were recruited" (Materials and Methods, Study Design, paragraph 1). Control group n=42, observation group n=45.
studies.age_describe: Control group: mean age 47.42±6.77 years, range 21–62 years. Observation group: mean age 44.96±5.42 years, range 22–61 years. "In the control group...aged between 21 and 62 years (mean age: 47.42±6.77 years)...In the observation group...aged between 22 and 61 years (mean age: 44.96±5.42 years)" (Materials and Methods, Demographic Characteristics of Participants, paragraph 1).
studies.age_min: 21. "In the control group...aged between 21 and 62 years" (Materials and Methods, Demographic Characteristics of Participants, paragraph 1).
studies.age_max: 62. "In the control group...aged between 21 and 62 years" (Materials and Methods, Demographic Characteristics of Participants, paragraph 1).
studies.participants: Patients undergoing loose body removal surgery (arthroscopic knee surgery). Control group: 42 cases (18 males, 24 females); observation group: 45 cases (19 males, 26 females). "In the control group, there were 42 cases, comprising 18 males and 24 females...In the observation group, there were 45 cases, consisting of 19 males and 26 females" (Materials and Methods, Demographic Characteristics of Participants, paragraph 1).
studies.eligibility: Inclusion criteria: (1) Diagnosed with the need for loose body removal based on clinical examination and imaging; (2) Underwent unilateral knee surgery at our hospital; (3) Aged between 10 and 65 years; (4) Capable of independently using smartphones; (5) Agreed to and cooperated with the study protocol. Exclusion criteria: (1) Presence of mental illness or cognitive impairment; (2) Presence of other serious illnesses that impeded participation in the study; (3) Poor compliance with study requirements; (4) Failure to provide signed informed consent. (Materials and Methods, Inclusion and Exclusion Criteria, paragraphs 1–2).
studies.population_vulnerable: Not a vulnerable population — participants are general surgical patients undergoing knee loose body removal surgery; no specific health disparity or structural disadvantage criterion is reported. "A total of 87 patients with loose body removal who underwent surgical treatment in our hospital" (Materials and Methods, Study Design, paragraph 1).
studies.location: Cangzhou, Hebei, China. "Cangzhou Combinational Hospital of Chinese and Western Medicine; Yunhe District; Cangzhou; Hebei; China" and "Cangzhou Central Hospital; Yun He Qu; Cangzhou; Hebei; China" (Title page, author affiliations).
studies.mental_health: N/A — no psychiatric enrollment criterion. Patients with mental illness or cognitive impairment were excluded, but no psychiatric diagnosis or symptom threshold was required for enrollment.
studies.physical_health: Diagnosed with the need for loose body removal (knee joint condition) and underwent unilateral knee surgery. "Diagnosed with the need for loose body removal based on clinical examination and imaging; Underwent unilateral knee surgery at our hospital" (Materials and Methods, Inclusion and Exclusion Criteria, paragraph 1).
studies.arms: 2 arms. Arm 1: Observation group — WeChat-based MBSR plus routine postoperative care (n=45). Arm 2: Control group — routine postoperative nursing only (n=42). "randomly allocated to either receive routine postoperative nursing (control group) or participate in WeChat-based MBSR (observation group)" (Abstract, Methods).
studies.meditation_intervention: The intervention is explicitly named MBSR (Mindfulness-Based Stress Reduction) delivered via WeChat platform over 3 weeks. Content comprised three weekly modules: (1) mindful breathing — seated position, attention to inhalation/exhalation sensations; (2) mindful scanning — supine body scan, attending to sensations in each body part; (3) mindful meditation — cultivating singular awareness on the meditation state. Patients engaged approximately 2 hours of learning per day. Content delivered via video, voice, and text through WeChat groups. Physicians provided demonstrations and answered questions; nurses sent reminders, documented progress, and conducted weekly follow-up via voice call or telephone. New practice material posted weekly. "The MBSR intervention spans a duration of 3 weeks and comprises weekly exercises focusing on various topics. These exercises were divided into three distinct parts: mindful breathing, mindful scanning, and mindful meditation. Each segment was dedicated to a specific theme and was executed over the course of a week. Patients were expected to engage in approximately 2 hours of learning each day." (Materials and Methods, Implementation of MBSR).
studies.intervention_delivery: Delivered digitally via WeChat platform (group messaging, video, voice, text). Remote/home-based delivery. Group format within WeChat groups. Facilitated by one chief physician, three deputy chief physicians, head nurse, and nurses. "WeChat groups were established comprising key personnel, including one chief physician, three deputy chief physicians, the head nurse, nurses, and patients." (Materials and Methods, Establishment of WeChat Groups). No in-person sessions described for the MBSR component.
studies.digital_component_raw: Yes — WeChat platform used to deliver the entire MBSR intervention including video demonstrations, voice messages, text content, group discussions, and weekly follow-up calls. "Patients in the observation group received WeChat-based MBSR in addition to routine postoperative care." (Materials and Methods, Observation Group Protocol).
studies.intervention_tailor: No tailoring reported beyond the delivery format (WeChat). The MBSR content was adapted for delivery via WeChat to accommodate patients with mobility limitations post-surgery, but no explicit cultural or population-specific content modification is described. "WeChat, a versatile instant messaging platform, offers a solution by facilitating the integration of MBSR into patients' postoperative rehabilitation routines." (Discussion, paragraph 2).
studies.comparison: Control group: Routine postoperative nursing care (n=42). Content included: monitoring of patient condition, management of swollen joints, and encouragement to participate in tailored functional exercises. "In the control group, patients were provided with standard postoperative care aimed at ensuring optimal recovery. This encompassed vigilant monitoring of their condition to promptly address any concerns that may arise. Additionally, measures were taken to alleviate discomfort, including the management of swollen joints. Moreover, patients were encouraged to participate in tailored functional exercises to facilitate their rehabilitation process." (Materials and Methods, Intervention Protocol for Control Group).
studies.assessment_time: T0 = Baseline (0 weeks); T1 = Post-intervention (3 weeks). "The duration of the MBSR treatment was 3 weeks." (Materials and Methods, Observation Group Protocol). "the short follow-up period of three weeks" (Discussion, Study Limitations). No follow-up beyond post-intervention reported.
studies.assessment_nature: Self-report questionnaires only. Measures included: Self-Rating Anxiety Scale (SAS), Beck Depression Inventory (BDI-II), positive mindfulness scale, comprehensive quality of life rating scale, Eysenck Personality Questionnaire (EPQ), Connor-Davidson Resilience Scale (CD-RISC). "reliance on self-report measures for assessing anxiety, depression, mindfulness levels, quality of life, personality traits, and psychological resilience" (Discussion, Study Limitations).
studies.outcomes_all:
1. Anxiety — Self-Rating Anxiety Scale (SAS; scores 50–60 mild, 61–70 moderate, >70 severe)
2. Depression — Beck Depression Inventory (BDI-II; scores 0–13 no depression, 14–19 mild, 20–28 moderate, 29–63 severe)
3. Mindfulness levels — Positive Mindfulness Scale (higher scores = higher mindfulness)
4. Quality of life — Comprehensive Quality of Life Rating Scale (4 domains: physiological function, psychological function, treatment condition, social relationship; higher scores = lower QoL)
5. Personality traits — Eysenck Personality Questionnaire (EPQ; 4 dimensions: introversion/extraversion, neuroticism, psychoticism, masking)
6. Psychological resilience — Connor-Davidson Resilience Scale (CD-RISC; 3 dimensions: toughness/resilience, self-reliance, optimism; higher scores = greater resilience)
(Materials and Methods, Outcome Measures).
studies.outcomes_primary: Unclear — authors do not explicitly designate a primary outcome. The study objective states: "This study aims to assess the impact of WeChat-based mindfulness-based stress reduction (MBSR) on psychological resilience and quality of life" (Abstract, Objective), suggesting these may be primary, but no formal designation is made.
studies.outcome_timepoints: T0 = Baseline (0 weeks); T1 = Post-intervention (3 weeks). All outcomes assessed at both timepoints. "After treatment, patients in the observation group demonstrated notable improvements in depression levels, anxiety levels, and mindfulness levels" (Results, paragraph 1). No additional follow-up timepoints reported.
studies.recruitment: Patients recruited from a single hospital between November 2018 and August 2019. "A total of 87 patients with loose body removal who underwent surgical treatment in our hospital from November 2018 to August 2019 were recruited" (Materials and Methods, Study Design, paragraph 1). No further details on recruitment channels reported.
studies.study_purpose: "This study endeavors to integrate WeChat with MBSR, aiming to enhance the psychological resilience and quality of life among patients undergoing loose body removal surgery, thereby enhancing postoperative care options." (Introduction, paragraph 2).
studies.study_design: Randomized controlled trial. Random allocation via random number table method. Two arms. No blinding reported. "randomly allocated to either receive routine postoperative nursing (control group) or participate in WeChat-based MBSR (observation group) via random number table method" (Materials and Methods, Study Design, paragraph 1).
studies.treatment_vs_prevention: Treatment — participants are patients who have undergone loose body removal surgery and are experiencing or at risk of postoperative psychological distress (anxiety, depression). The intervention targets existing postoperative psychological symptoms. "arthroscopy may evoke adverse emotional responses such as postoperative anxiety and depression" (Introduction, paragraph 1). Source quote: "This study aims to assess the impact of WeChat-based mindfulness-based stress reduction (MBSR) on psychological resilience and quality of life in patients undergoing loose body removal." (Abstract, Objective).

studies.authors: Quintana-Hernández, D. J., Miró-Barrachina, M. T., Ibáñez-Fernández, I. J., Santana-del Pino, A., Quintana-Montesdeoca, M. P., Rodríguez-de Vera, B., Morales-Casanova, D., Pérez-Vieitez, M. C., Rodríguez-García, J., & Bravo-Caraduje, N.
studies.title: Mindfulness in the Maintenance of Cognitive Capacities in Alzheimer's Disease: A Randomized Clinical Trial
studies.abstract: Background: The Canary Islands longitudinal study on non-pharmacological treatments showed the overall effectiveness of mindfulness in Alzheimer's disease (AD). However, no specific data on the maintenance of cognitive capacities were presented. Objective: To determine whether the practice of mindfulness modifies the course of cognitive impairment in AD. Methods: Design: Longitudinal, non-inferiority and equivalence, randomized clinical trial, repeated-measures design, with three experimental groups and one control group. Participants: Patients with AD who voluntarily attended the Lidia García Foundation (n = 502). Only those who were treated with donepezil and MMSE≥18 were included (n = 120). Intervention: Over a two-year period, each group carried out three weekly sessions of stimulation based on mindfulness, cognitive stimulation therapy, and progressive muscle relaxation. Measures: Cognitive assessment CAMDEX-R (MMSE and CAMCOG). Statistical analysis: Repeated-measures ANOVA (p < 0.05) and the effect size Cohen's d were performed. Results: The mindfulness group showed significant scores compared with the control and muscle relaxation groups (p < 0.05), while mindfulness and cognitive stimulation therapy were equivalent (p ≥ 0.05). Group cognitive stimulation evolved better than the control (p < 0.05) group but not better than the muscle relaxation group (p ≥ 0.05). The effect size compared over two years was large for the mindfulness group (p ≥ 0.80), moderate for the relaxation group (p ≥ 0.50), and low for the cognitive stimulation group (p ≥ 0.20). Conclusion: The practice of mindfulness maintained cognitive function over a period of two years. This longitudinal study suggests that mindfulness can be used as a non-pharmacological treatment to slow cognitive impairment in AD.
studies.total_n: 120. "Only those who were treated with donepezil and MMSE≥18 were included (n = 120)." (Abstract, Methods). Note: The flow diagram mentions 502 patients attended the foundation; 120 were randomized.
studies.age_mean: Not reported
studies.age_describe: Age distribution reported categorically: [65–75] = 28 (23.3%), [76–85] = 65 (54.2%), [≥86] = 27 (22.5%). No mean or SD reported for the full sample. (Table 1, Baseline Characteristics)
studies.age_max: Not reported (upper bound of ≥86 category not specified)
studies.participants: Patients diagnosed with probable Alzheimer's disease (AD), over 65 years of age, treated with donepezil, with MMSE≥18, living at home. 55% women, 45% men. Majority aged 76–85 (54.2%). Referred by municipal social services, primary care, and specialty care in the Canary Islands Health Services. "Patients were over 65 years of age and diagnosed with probable AD, in accordance with NINCDS-ARDA criteria." (Methods, Participants paragraph)
studies.eligibility: Inclusion criteria: (1) Over 65 years of age; (2) Diagnosed with probable AD per NINCDS-ADRDA criteria; (3) Presence of regional brain atrophy (hippocampus, entorhinal cortex, or amygdala) on MRI; (4) Presence of early and significant episodic memory impairment (gradual and progressive change over >6 months); (5) GDS score 3, 4, or 5; (6) Living at home; (7) Not attending any other health service; (8) Treated with donepezil only (no other pharmacological treatment for AD); (9) MMSE ≥18. Exclusion criteria: (1) Neurological diseases other than probable AD (e.g., vascular dementia, Parkinson's disease); (2) Sudden onset; (3) Early gait disturbances, seizures, behavioral changes; (4) Focal neurological features (hemiparesis, sensory loss, visual field deficits); (5) Early extrapyramidal signs; (6) Other medical conditions severe enough to account for memory symptoms; (7) Major depression, severe psychotic traits, agitation, behavior disorders, history of schizophrenia, substance abuse; (8) Cerebrovascular disease; (9) Toxic and metabolic abnormalities; (10) MRI FLAIR or T2 signal abnormalities in medial temporal lobe consistent with infectious or vascular insults; (11) Severe geriatric syndromes reducing life expectancy to two years. (Methods, Inclusion criteria and Exclusion criteria sections)
studies.population_vulnerable: Not a vulnerable population in the sense of health disparities or structural disadvantage — participants are elderly patients with Alzheimer's disease, a clinical population defined by diagnosis rather than social disadvantage. "Patients were over 65 years of age and diagnosed with probable AD." (Methods, Inclusion criteria)
studies.location: Las Palmas de Gran Canaria, Canary Islands, Spain. "A randomized, controlled, repeated-measures, double-blind, non-inferiority and equivalence, four groups parallel design clinical trial (4 × 5) was conducted in the Canary Islands, Spain." (Methods, Design paragraph)
studies.mental_health: N/A — no psychiatric enrollment criterion. Alzheimer's disease diagnosis is the enrollment criterion (a neurological/physical health condition). Psychiatric conditions (major depression, severe psychotic traits, schizophrenia, substance abuse) appear only as exclusion criteria.
studies.physical_health: Alzheimer's disease diagnosis required for enrollment: "Patients were over 65 years of age and diagnosed with probable AD, in accordance with NINCDS-ARDA criteria." Also required: MMSE ≥18, GDS score 3, 4, or 5, treatment with donepezil. (Methods, Inclusion criteria)
studies.arms: Four arms: (1) MBAS (Mindfulness-Based Alzheimer's Stimulation) + donepezil — experimental; (2) PMR (Progressive Muscle Relaxation) + donepezil — experimental; (3) CST (Cognitive Stimulation Therapy) + donepezil — experimental; (4) Control (donepezil only) — control. "A randomized, controlled, repeated-measures, double-blind, non-inferiority and equivalence, four groups parallel design clinical trial (4 × 5) was conducted." (Methods, Design). Per-arm n not explicitly stated for the final randomized sample of 120; Table 1 shows baseline CAMCOG for mild-moderate AD with N=130 (likely includes dropouts or a different count).
studies.meditation_intervention: The MBAS (mindfulness-based Alzheimer's stimulation) program was inspired by MBSR, mindfulness-based elder care (MBEC), Kirtan Kriya technique, chair yoga exercises, and multi-sensorial stimulation exercises based on sensorial integration theory. Sessions included: (1) temporal and spatial orientation; (2) yoga in the chair; (3) attention-to-breathing exercise; (4) body scan; (5) Kirtan Kriya (finger-touching mantra: SAA, TAA, NAA, MAA); (6) guided mindful attention to one of the five senses for 10 min; (7) psychoeducation on AD clinical evolution. Formal practices during sessions with patient and caregiver; semi-informal practices at home (10 moments per day). Three weekly sessions of 90 min for two years (total 288 sessions in 96 weeks). Groups of maximum 8 participants. "The MBAS training group was inspired by the MBSR program, mindfulness-based elder care (MBEC), Kirtan Kriya technique, chair yoga exercises, and multi-sensorial stimulation exercises based on the sensorial integration theory." (Methods, Intervention section)
studies.intervention_delivery: In-person group sessions. Three weekly sessions of 90 minutes for two years. Groups of maximum 8 participants. Delivered by two clinical psychologists (MBAS and PMR) and a neuropsychologist (CST), all with at least 10 years' clinical experience in services for elderly people. The clinical psychologist delivering MBAS had five years' personal experience as a meditation practitioner. "The providers of NPT were two clinical psychologists and a neuropsychologist... All these professionals had at least 10 years' clinical experience in services for elderly people." (Methods, Participants section)
studies.digital_component_raw: No digital component. Participants completed a Review Notebook for cognitive stimulation by means of paper and pencil exercises at home. No technology-based delivery described. "Participants completed a Review Notebook for cognitive stimulation by means of paper and pencil exercises at home." (Methods, Intervention section)
studies.intervention_tailor: Yes — the MBAS program was specifically developed and adapted for patients with Alzheimer's disease, incorporating chair yoga (adapted to elderly abilities), Kirtan Kriya, multi-sensorial stimulation, and psychoeducation on AD clinical evolution. PMR was also "adapted to the abilities of the elderly." "MBAS exercises were developed in two formats: formal practices that took place during the sessions with patient and caregiver, and semi-informal practices to be carried out at home." (Methods, Intervention section)
studies.comparison: Three comparison conditions: (1) PMR (Progressive Muscle Relaxation) + donepezil: standard relaxation program involving tensing and releasing 16 muscle groups, adapted to elderly abilities, plus psychoeducation on multifactorial etiology of AD. Three weekly 90-min sessions for two years. (2) CST (Cognitive Stimulation Therapy) + donepezil: integral psychostimulation program including visual imagery, errorless learning, dyadic approaches, spaced retrieval techniques, encoding specificity with cognitive support at retrieval, external memory aids, and psychoeducation on cognitive stimulation. Three weekly 90-min sessions for two years. (3) Control (donepezil only): usual caretaking-at-home group. "The CST group followed an integral psychostimulation program... The PMR group followed a standard program of relaxation... to a usual caretaking-at-home group (control group)." (Methods, Intervention section)
studies.assessment_time: T0 = Baseline (0 weeks); T1 = 6 months (25.2 weeks); T2 = 12 months (50.4 weeks); T3 = 18 months (75.6 weeks); T4 = 24 months (100.8 weeks). "Three weekly group sessions of 90 min for two years and a total of 288 sessions in 96 weeks were carried out." Assessments every 6 months per Table 2. (Table 2, Descriptive statistics)
studies.assessment_nature: Neuropsychological/clinician-administered assessment. CAMDEX-R administered by a neuropsychologist who was blinded to group assignment. "The neuropsychologist who carried out the psychometric follow-ups of all patients did not know that a clinical trial was in place." (Methods, Blinding section). Includes MMSE and CAMCOG subscales.
studies.outcomes_all: 1. Global cognitive function — MMSE (Mini-Mental State Examination, part of CAMDEX-R); 2. Global cognitive function — CAMCOG (Cambridge Cognitive Examination, part of CAMDEX-R), including subscales: Orientation, Global Language (Understanding + Expression), Global Memory (Recent Memory + Remote Memory + Learning), Attention, Praxis (ideomotor, ideational, constructive), Calculation, Abstract Thinking, Tactile and Visual Perception.
studies.outcomes_primary: Cognitive function as measured by MMSE and CAMCOG (CAMDEX-R). "To determine whether the practice of mindfulness modifies the course of cognitive impairment in AD." The paper does not explicitly designate a single primary outcome but states: "Measures: Cognitive assessment CAMDEX-R (MMSE and CAMCOG)." (Abstract, Methods). Unclear — authors do not formally designate a single primary outcome instrument.
studies.outcome_timepoints: T0 = Baseline (0 weeks); T1 = 6 months (25.2 weeks); T2 = 12 months (50.4 weeks); T3 = 18 months (75.6 weeks); T4 = 24 months (100.8 weeks). All outcomes assessed at all timepoints. (Table 2, Descriptive statistics)
studies.recruitment: "Participants were referred by municipal social services, primary care, and specialty care in the Canary Islands Health Services. Participation in the study was voluntary; both patients and their primary caregivers were required to sign an informed consent form. Patients were assessed at the Marjorie Warren Memory Unit of the Lidia Garcia Foundation and came voluntarily to receive NPT." The patient inclusion period lasted 12 months, beginning January 2010. (Methods, Participants section)
studies.study_purpose: "To determine whether the practice of mindfulness modifies the course of cognitive impairment in AD." More specifically: "The main purpose of this longitudinal RCT is to study the efficacy of mindfulness and donepezil as a combination therapy to delay cognitive impairment, and to compare it with other combined NPT, such as CST and PMR." (Abstract, Objective; Introduction, final paragraph)
studies.study_design: Randomized, controlled, repeated-measures, double-blind (partial), non-inferiority and equivalence, four-group parallel design clinical trial (4 × 5). Simple randomization performed by administrative staff. "A randomized, controlled, repeated-measures, double-blind, non-inferiority and equivalence, four groups parallel design clinical trial (4 × 5) was conducted in the Canary Islands, Spain." Note: blinding was partial — the MBAS implementer (main researcher) was not masked. (Methods, Design and Blinding sections)
studies.treatment_vs_prevention: Treatment — participants have a confirmed diagnosis of Alzheimer's disease at enrollment (NINCDS-ADRDA criteria, MMSE ≥18, GDS 3–5). The study tests whether mindfulness-based intervention can slow cognitive decline in an existing condition. "Patients were over 65 years of age and diagnosed with probable AD, in accordance with NINCDS-ARDA criteria." (Methods, Inclusion criteria)
studies.confidence_why: • age_mean — No mean age reported; only categorical age distribution provided. Cannot calculate weighted mean without per-arm age data. • age_max — Upper bound of ≥86 category not specified. • total_n — Abstract states n=120 included; flow diagram mentions 502 attended foundation. Used 120 as randomized N per Methods. • per-arm n — Individual arm sample sizes at randomization not explicitly stated in a single location; Table 1 shows N=130 for mild-moderate AD baseline CAMCOG analysis, which differs from the stated n=120, suggesting some participants had moderate-severe AD and were analyzed separately. • dose_sessions — 288 total sessions calculated from paper (3 sessions/week × 96 weeks), but this is the total across the intervention period, not per participant.
